title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text: Part 3 · The Factorial Model

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Factorial ANOVA Models


Factorial designs can be of 3 types:

Model 1 — 2 fixed factors (the focus for today)
Model 2 — 2 random factors
Model 3 — 1 fixed, 1 random (mixed model) — often nested

Model 1 ANOVA:
\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]







Tip



🖐 Notice
The formula looks identical to Model 2 and Model 3 — what changes between them is whether α, β are treated as fixed effects (specific groups you care about) or random effects (a sample from a larger population of possible groups).

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Model Components — the Main Effects


\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]

\(y_{ijk}\): value of the k-th observation from the j-th and i-th combination of B and A (sex j of species i)
μ: overall mean (overall mass)
\(\alpha_i\): effect of the i-th level of A, pooling across all levels of B — \(\mu_i - \mu\) (difference between the average mass of all “species i” penguins and the overall mean)








Tip



🖐 Notice
Every effect in this model is defined as a deviation from a mean — the grand mean, or a group mean. This is exactly the same logic as a t-test or one-way ANOVA, just with more terms.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Model Components — the Interaction


\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]

\(\beta_j\): effect of the j-th level of B, pooling across all levels of A — \(\mu_j - \mu\) (difference between the average mass of all “sex j” penguins and the overall mean)
\((\alpha\beta)_{ij}\): effect of the interaction of level i of A and level j of B — \(\mu_{ij} - \mu_i - \mu_j + \mu\). Does the effect of B depend on the level of A? (Is the effect of sex different across the 3 species?)








Note



✅ Key idea
The interaction term is what’s left over after you subtract out both main effects and the grand mean — it’s literally “the part the additive model can’t explain.”

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Model Types and Interpretation


\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]

Model 2 ANOVA is rare in ecology
Model 3 interpretation is different:

\(\beta_j\): random variable measuring variance in y across all possible levels of B, pooling across A
\((\alpha\beta)_{ij}\) is a random variable measuring variance of the interaction between A and B across all possible levels of B (“is the effect of A consistent across all possible levels of B that could have been chosen?”)









Warning



⚠️ Watch out!
Fixed vs. random isn’t about the data — it’s about the question. Are you interested in these specific 3 species (fixed), or in “species” as a general source of variation (random)?

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text: Part 4 · Estimated Marginal Means

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
section: What a Marginal Mean Is For
text:
What a Marginal Mean Is For


A fertilizer trial run at two light levels. Biomass (g), with cell n in brackets:





low light
high light
raw mean
EMM




control
10 [2]
20 [18]
19.0
15


fertilized
30 [18]
40 [2]
31.0
35





Raw mean weights by how many plants happened to land in each cell: \(\frac{2(10)+18(20)}{20} = 19.0\)
EMM weights the two cells equally: \(\frac{10+20}{2} = 15\)

Raw says fertilizer adds 12 g. The EMM says 20 g.







Important



⚠️ Which number is the fertilizer effect?
Almost every control plant sat in high light, and almost every fertilized plant in low light. Light raises biomass on its own — so the raw comparison is handing the control group a free bonus and hiding most of the fertilizer effect.
20 g is the answer to the question you asked. The EMM gets it by refusing to let an accident of sample size decide how the two light levels are weighted.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
The Same Thing, in emmeans



set.seed(42)
toy_df <- tibble(
  fert   = rep(c("control", "fertilized"), each = 20),
  light  = c(rep("low", 2),  rep("high", 18),
             rep("low", 18), rep("high", 2)),
  target = c(rep(10, 2), rep(20, 18),
             rep(30, 18), rep(40, 2))) %>%
  group_by(fert, light) %>%
  mutate(mass = target + as.numeric(scale(rnorm(n()))) * 3) %>%
  ungroup()

# what group_by() gives you
toy_df %>% group_by(fert) %>% summarise(raw = mean(mass))
## # A tibble: 2 × 2
##   fert         raw
##   <chr>      <dbl>
## 1 control       19
## 2 fertilized    31



toy_model <- lm(mass ~ fert * light, data = toy_df)

# what emmeans() gives you
emmeans(toy_model, ~ fert)
##  fert       emmean   SE df lower.CL upper.CL
##  control        15 1.12 36     12.7     17.3
##  fertilized     35 1.12 36     32.7     37.3
## 
## Results are averaged over the levels of: light 
## Confidence level used: 0.95







Note



✅ This is the whole idea
emmeans() goes to the model, predicts each of the four cells, and then averages those four predictions unweighted.
group_by() %>% mean() goes to the data and averages the rows, so a big cell shouts louder.
Read the footer it prints: “Results are averaged over the levels of: light” — that line is emmeans telling you exactly what it just did.

text:
Estimated Marginal Means — Species


Now the real data — and a much milder version of the same thing.

Balanced cells: the EMM and the raw mean are the same number
Unbalanced cells: the EMM is the mean of the cell means; the raw mean weights by cell n

## 1    Adelie   3369 4043       73     73
## 2 Chinstrap   3527 3939       34     34

## 1    Adelie     146     3706.164
## 2 Chinstrap      68     3733.088

Warning



⚠️ Check the diff column
Two of the three species are perfectly balanced, so their two means are the same number. See the next slide.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Estimated Marginal Means — Sex



Balanced data: just the means of the groups
Unbalanced data: mean of cell means







Warning



⚠️ Different quantities, barely different numbers — here
Adelie is 73/73 and Chinstrap is 34/34, so for those two the raw mean and the EMM are identical. Only Gentoo (58 F / 61 M) moves, by ~10 g out of 5082.
Hold both facts: the raw mean is the wrong quantity whenever cells are uneven, and on a nearly-even design it is a very good approximation. A badly lopsided cell is where this stops being a technicality.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text: Part 5 · The Two-Way ANOVA Table

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
ANOVA Table Structure


On a balanced design the four pieces add up exactly:
\[SS_{total} = SS_A + SS_B + SS_{AB} + SS_{residual}\]

\(SS_{total} = \sum\sum\sum (Y_{ijk} - \bar{Y})^2\) — every observation against the grand mean
\(SS_{residual} = \sum\sum\sum (Y_{ijk} - \bar{Y}_{ij})^2\) — every observation against its own cell mean

Everything else is the same move you already know from one-way ANOVA: how far is a mean from the mean above it, squared, and counted once for every observation it stands for.




Source
df




A
p − 1


B
q − 1


AB
(p−1)(q−1)


Residual
pq(n−1)


Total
pqn − 1



where p = levels of A, q = levels of B, n = replicates per cell.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
SSA: Factor A Effects


\[SS_A = qn\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(\bar{Y}_{i\cdot} - \bar{Y}\right)^2\]

\(\bar{Y}_{i\cdot}\) is the marginal mean of level i of A — the EMM for that species
Square its distance from the grand mean, and multiply by \(qn\), the number of observations that marginal mean stands for (q levels of B × n per cell)
The multiplier is not optional. Without it you have the SS of 3 numbers, not of 204 observations, and the df would not match.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
SSB: Factor B Effects


\[SS_B = pn\sum_{j=1}^{q}\left(\bar{Y}_{\cdot j} - \bar{Y}\right)^2\]

Same move, the other way round: each column marginal mean against the grand mean
Multiplier is now \(pn\) — p levels of A × n per cell — because each sex EMM stands for that many birds

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
SSAB: Interaction Effects


\[SS_{AB} = n\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{q}\left(\bar{Y}_{ij} - \bar{Y}_{i\cdot} - \bar{Y}_{\cdot j} + \bar{Y}\right)^2\]

Take a cell mean, subtract what the two main effects alone predict for it, and you are left with the interaction
\(\bar{Y}_{i\cdot} + \bar{Y}_{\cdot j} - \bar{Y}\) is the additive prediction; the grand mean is added back because it was subtracted twice
Multiplier is just \(n\) — a cell mean stands for only the n birds in that cell







Note



✅ Key idea
\(SS_{AB}\) is the leftovers. If the additive model predicted every cell mean perfectly, every one of those brackets would be zero and \(SS_{AB} = 0\).

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
The Four SS, by Hand



nrep <- 34; plev <- 3; qlev <- 2

gm <- mean(balanced_df$body_mass_g)
cm <- tapply(balanced_df$body_mass_g,            # 3 x 2 cell means
             list(balanced_df$species, balanced_df$sex), mean)
mA <- rowMeans(cm)                               # species marginals
mB <- colMeans(cm)                               # sex marginals

ss_a   <- qlev * nrep * sum((mA - gm)^2)
ss_b   <- plev * nrep * sum((mB - gm)^2)
ss_ab  <- nrep * sum((cm - outer(mA, mB, "+") + gm)^2)
ss_res <- sum(residuals(lm(body_mass_g ~ species * sex,
                           data = balanced_df))^2)

round(c(A = ss_a, B = ss_b, AB = ss_ab, Res = ss_res))
##        A        B       AB      Res 
## 87725999 21988483  1672776 18199467



anova(lm(body_mass_g ~ species * sex,
         data = balanced_df))[, "Sum Sq"]
## [1] 87725999 21988483  1672776 18199467

all.equal(ss_a + ss_b + ss_ab + ss_res,
          sum((balanced_df$body_mass_g - gm)^2))
## [1] TRUE







Note



✅ Key idea
Four lines of arithmetic, and they match anova() to the last digit — and they add to \(SS_{total}\). That second part is true because the design is balanced. In Part 8 it stops being true.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
F-Ratio Calculations


SS converts to MS; F-ratio calculations differ depending on whether factors are fixed, random, or mixed.




Source
A, B fixed
A, B random
A fixed, B random




A
\(MS_A/MS_{Res}\)
\(MS_A/MS_{AB}\)
\(MS_A/MS_{AB}\)


B
\(MS_B/MS_{Res}\)
\(MS_B/MS_{AB}\)
\(MS_B/MS_{AB}\)


AB
\(MS_{AB}/MS_{Res}\)
\(MS_{AB}/MS_{Res}\)
\(MS_{AB}/MS_{Res}\)

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Hypotheses — Both Factors Fixed


3 hypotheses are tested in a two-way factorial ANOVA: A, B, A×B. Both factors fixed:

\(H_0(A)\): \(\mu_1 = \mu_2 = ... = \mu_p\) (no difference in marginal means of A, pooling across B)
\(H_0(B)\): \(\mu_1 = \mu_2 = ... = \mu_q\) (no difference in marginal means of B, pooling across A)
\(H_0(AB)\): \(\mu_{ij} - \mu_i - \mu_j + \mu = 0\) (no interaction effect)








Tip



🖐 Notice
These are exactly the two main-effect hypotheses from a one-way ANOVA, plus one new hypothesis just for the interaction.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Hypotheses — Mixed Model


3 hypotheses: A, B, A×B. One fixed, one random:

\(H_0(A)\): \(\mu_1 = \mu_2 = ... = \mu_p\) (no difference in marginal means of A, pooling across B)
\(H_0(B)\): \(\sigma^2_B = 0\) (no added variance due to levels of B that could have been used)
\(H_0(AB)\): \(\sigma^2_{AB} = 0\) (no added variance due to interaction between all levels of A and B that could have been used)








Warning



⚠️ Watch out!
Notice the switch from “means are equal” (fixed) to “variance is zero” (random) — that’s the fundamental difference in what a random-effect hypothesis is even asking.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
section: All Three SS Types — on Balanced Data
text:
All Three SS Types — on Balanced Data



t1 <- anova(anova_model)                 # Type I
t2 <- Anova(anova_model, type = "II")    # Type II
t3 <- Anova(anova_model, type = "III")   # Type III

data.frame(
  Effect = c("species", "sex", "species:sex"),
  Type_I   = round(t1$`Sum Sq`[1:3]),
  Type_II  = round(t2$`Sum Sq`[1:3]),
  Type_III = round(t3$`Sum Sq`[2:4])
)
##        Effect   Type_I  Type_II Type_III
## 1     species 87725999 87725999 87725999
## 2         sex 21988483 21988483 21988483
## 3 species:sex  1672776  1672776  1672776


Three different rules for allocating variance — the same three numbers.
That is not a coincidence and it is not R being lazy. With equal cell sizes the two factors are orthogonal: knowing a bird’s species tells you nothing about its chance of being male. Neither factor can “steal” SS from the other, so there is no shared variance left to argue about.






Note



✅ Key idea
The whole Type I / II / III literature exists to answer one question: who gets the variance the two factors share? A balanced design has none to share — which is why balance is worth paying for.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Understanding Type III SS


Type III sums of squares test each effect after adjusting for all other effects in the model:

Species effect: tested after adjusting for sex and interaction
Sex effect: tested after adjusting for species and interaction
Interaction: tested after adjusting for both main effects

This is especially important for unbalanced designs, but we’re using it here for consistency with the next analysis.


## Effect Sizes (partial eta-squared):
##        Effect Partial_Eta_Sq
## 1     Species         0.8282
## 2         Sex         0.5471
## 3 Interaction         0.0842







Note



📖 Partial η² — see the next slide for why
\[\eta^2_p = \frac{SS_{effect}}{SS_{effect} + SS_{residual}}\]

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Which Effect Size, and Why


\[\eta^2 = \frac{SS_{effect}}{SS_{total}} \qquad \eta^2_p = \frac{SS_{effect}}{SS_{effect} + SS_{residual}}\]

Plain η² asks “of all the variation, how much does this effect explain?” The three effects plus the residual then sum to 1.
Partial η² asks “of the variation this effect could have explained — its own plus the leftovers — how much does it?” These do not sum to 1.








Warning



⚠️ Why we use partial η² all lecture
The two agree only on a balanced design.
Type III sums of squares do not add up to \(SS_{total}\) once a design is unbalanced — so dividing a Type III SS by the sum of the Type III SS gives a number that is neither η² nor η²ₚ, and you cannot compare it to anything.
Partial η² is well defined either way, so the balanced and unbalanced models in this lecture stay comparable.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Introduction to Unbalanced Designs


The challenge of unbalanced data: real-world data is often unbalanced — unequal sample sizes across groups, missing data patterns, natural variation in sampling.
Key issues: Type I, II, and III SS stop agreeing; order of terms matters for Type I SS; marginal means ≠ simple averages.
The model is unchanged — \(Y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\) — but estimation of its parameters is not.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
How Unbalanced Is It, Really?


What matters in a factorial design is not that all six cells are the same size. It is whether the sex split is the same proportion in every species.

Adelie 73 / 73 → 50.0 % female
Chinstrap 34 / 34 → 50.0 % female
Gentoo 58 / 61 → 48.7 % female

If those three percentages were identical, the design would be proportional and the two factors would still be orthogonal — the SS types would still agree, unequal cell sizes or not.







Warning



⚠️ Honest warning about this dataset
The penguin design is nearly proportional. So the three SS types will move apart only slightly, and every p-value stays well below 0.001.
Watch that the numbers change at all — not how dramatically. A design with a half-empty cell is where this really bites, and that is the one you should be afraid of in your own data.

How Type I SS works — sequential decomposition:

First term gets all SS it can explain
Second term gets SS after removing the first
Third term gets SS after removing the first two

Problems with unbalanced data: order dependency, biased if factors are correlated, not invariant to coding.

## [1] "Type III Sums of Squares:"
## Anova Table (Type III tests)
## 
## Response: body_mass_g
##                 Sum Sq  Df   F value    Pr(>F)    
## (Intercept) 5232595969   1 54661.828 < 2.2e-16 ***
## species      143001222   2   746.924 < 2.2e-16 ***
## sex           29851220   1   311.838 < 2.2e-16 ***
## species:sex    1676557   2     8.757 0.0001973 ***
## Residuals     31302628 327                        
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



Type II — each main effect adjusted for the other main effect, but not for the interaction. Most powerful of the three when the interaction is genuinely absent.
Type III — each term adjusted for everything else, interaction included. Order invariant; tests unweighted (marginal) means.

Read the table: the interaction F is identical under all three — it is the last term in, so there is nothing left to adjust it for. Species barely moves. Sex moves the most (387 → 312), because sex is the factor whose split is uneven across species.
Type III costs: lower power with missing cells, and it is meaningless without contr.sum.

text: Part 11 · Summary and Best Practices

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Summary — Unbalanced Designs


Challenges: Type I SS depends on order; simple means ≠ EMMs; reduced power for interactions; complex interpretation.
Solutions: use Type III SS for main effects; report EMMs, not simple means; check assumptions carefully; consider the impact of imbalance.

Recommendations:

Always report: sample sizes per cell, type of SS used, EMMs with CIs
Visualization: show actual data points, include error bars, note unequal sample sizes
Interpretation: focus on effect sizes, consider practical significance, acknowledge limitations

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Final Recommendations


For experimental studies: design for balance when possible, randomize allocation, plan for attrition.
For observational studies: accept imbalance as reality, use Type III SS, report EMMs, consider covariates (ANCOVA).







Note



Statistical software defaults

R: Type I (sequential)
SAS: Type III (marginal)
SPSS: Type III (marginal)

Always specify which type you’re using!

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Wrap-up — What You Did Today



Fitted a factorial model with two categorical predictors — body_mass_g ~ species * sex
Separated main effects from the interaction: an interaction means “the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other”
Computed \(SS_A\), \(SS_B\), \(SS_{AB}\) and \(SS_{res}\) by hand and matched anova() exactly
Used estimated marginal means rather than raw group averages
Met Type I, II and III sums of squares — identical on the balanced design, slightly apart on the unbalanced one
Set contr.sum before asking for Type III
Reported partial η², the effect size that stays well defined either way








Important



⚠️ Read the interaction first
If the interaction is significant, a main effect is an average across conditions that behave differently — often not a meaningful quantity.
Interpret the interaction, then use simple effects — emmeans(model, ~ sex | species) or joint_tests(model, by = "sex") — rather than reporting the main effect as if it applied everywhere.
R even warns you: “Results may be misleading due to involvement in interactions.”

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
section: Wrap-up — The One Idea to Keep
text:
Wrap-up — The One Idea to Keep








Note



✅ Balance is a property of your design, not your analysis
A balanced design makes the two factors orthogonal, so each one’s sum of squares is unambiguous and the three SS types collapse to one number.
Imbalance makes the factors share variance — and then how you allocate that shared variance becomes a decision you have to make and defend in your methods section.









Tip



🖐 And one caveat on today’s data
The penguin imbalance is mild — five of six cells are exactly even. The SS types moved a little and no conclusion changed.
That is the common case. The uncommon case — a cell that is half empty, or empty — is where the choice decides the answer, and that is the one to watch for in your own data.








Note



Up next — Nested ANOVA

When one factor is nested inside another rather than crossed with it
Subsamples, and the right error term to test against

text: Part 3 · The Factorial Model

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Factorial ANOVA Models


Factorial designs can be of 3 types:

Model 1 — 2 fixed factors (the focus for today)
Model 2 — 2 random factors
Model 3 — 1 fixed, 1 random (mixed model) — often nested

Model 1 ANOVA:
\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]







Tip


🖐 Notice
The formula looks identical to Model 2 and Model 3 — what changes between them is whether α, β are treated as fixed effects (specific groups you care about) or random effects (a sample from a larger population of possible groups).

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Model Components — the Main Effects


\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]

\(y_{ijk}\): value of the k-th observation from the j-th and i-th combination of B and A (sex j of species i)
μ: overall mean (overall mass)
\(\alpha_i\): effect of the i-th level of A, pooling across all levels of B — \(\mu_i - \mu\) (difference between the average mass of all “species i” penguins and the overall mean)








Tip


🖐 Notice
Every effect in this model is defined as a deviation from a mean — the grand mean, or a group mean. This is exactly the same logic as a t-test or one-way ANOVA, just with more terms.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Model Components — the Interaction


\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]

\(\beta_j\): effect of the j-th level of B, pooling across all levels of A — \(\mu_j - \mu\) (difference between the average mass of all “sex j” penguins and the overall mean)
\((\alpha\beta)_{ij}\): effect of the interaction of level i of A and level j of B — \(\mu_{ij} - \mu_i - \mu_j + \mu\). Does the effect of B depend on the level of A? (Is the effect of sex different across the 3 species?)








Note


✅ Key idea
The interaction term is what’s left over after you subtract out both main effects and the grand mean — it’s literally “the part the additive model can’t explain.”

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Model Types and Interpretation


\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]

Model 2 ANOVA is rare in ecology
Model 3 interpretation is different:

\(\beta_j\): random variable measuring variance in y across all possible levels of B, pooling across A
\((\alpha\beta)_{ij}\) is a random variable measuring variance of the interaction between A and B across all possible levels of B (“is the effect of A consistent across all possible levels of B that could have been chosen?”)









Warning


⚠️ Watch out!
Fixed vs. random isn’t about the data — it’s about the question. Are you interested in these specific 3 species (fixed), or in “species” as a general source of variation (random)?

19.0
15


fertilized
30 [18]
40 [2]
31.0
35





Raw mean weights by how many plants happened to land in each cell: \(\frac{2(10)+18(20)}{20} = 19.0\)
EMM weights the two cells equally: \(\frac{10+20}{2} = 15\)

Raw says fertilizer adds 12 g. The EMM says 20 g.







Important


⚠️ Which number is the fertilizer effect?
Almost every control plant sat in high light, and almost every fertilized plant in low light. Light raises biomass on its own — so the raw comparison is handing the control group a free bonus and hiding most of the fertilizer effect.
20 g is the answer to the question you asked. The EMM gets it by refusing to let an accident of sample size decide how the two light levels are weighted.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
The Same Thing, in emmeans



set.seed(42)
toy_df <- tibble(
  fert   = rep(c("control", "fertilized"), each = 20),
  light  = c(rep("low", 2),  rep("high", 18),
             rep("low", 18), rep("high", 2)),
  target = c(rep(10, 2), rep(20, 18),
             rep(30, 18), rep(40, 2))) %>%
  group_by(fert, light) %>%
  mutate(mass = target + as.numeric(scale(rnorm(n()))) * 3) %>%
  ungroup()

# what group_by() gives you
toy_df %>% group_by(fert) %>% summarise(raw = mean(mass))
## # A tibble: 2 × 2
##   fert         raw
##   <chr>      <dbl>
## 1 control       19
## 2 fertilized    31



toy_model <- lm(mass ~ fert * light, data = toy_df)

# what emmeans() gives you
emmeans(toy_model, ~ fert)
##  fert       emmean   SE df lower.CL upper.CL
##  control        15 1.12 36     12.7     17.3
##  fertilized     35 1.12 36     32.7     37.3
## 
## Results are averaged over the levels of: light 
## Confidence level used: 0.95







Note


✅ This is the whole idea
emmeans() goes to the model, predicts each of the four cells, and then averages those four predictions unweighted.
group_by() %>% mean() goes to the data and averages the rows, so a big cell shouts louder.
Read the footer it prints: “Results are averaged over the levels of: light” — that line is emmeans telling you exactly what it just did.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text: Part 5 · The Two-Way ANOVA Table

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
ANOVA Table Structure


On a balanced design the four pieces add up exactly:
\[SS_{total} = SS_A + SS_B + SS_{AB} + SS_{residual}\]

\(SS_{total} = \sum\sum\sum (Y_{ijk} - \bar{Y})^2\) — every observation against the grand mean
\(SS_{residual} = \sum\sum\sum (Y_{ijk} - \bar{Y}_{ij})^2\) — every observation against its own cell mean

Everything else is the same move you already know from one-way ANOVA: how far is a mean from the mean above it, squared, and counted once for every observation it stands for.




Source
df




A
p − 1


B
q − 1


AB
(p−1)(q−1)


Residual
pq(n−1)


Total
pqn − 1



where p = levels of A, q = levels of B, n = replicates per cell.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
SSA: Factor A Effects


\[SS_A = qn\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(\bar{Y}_{i\cdot} - \bar{Y}\right)^2\]

\(\bar{Y}_{i\cdot}\) is the marginal mean of level i of A — the EMM for that species
Square its distance from the grand mean, and multiply by \(qn\), the number of observations that marginal mean stands for (q levels of B × n per cell)
The multiplier is not optional. Without it you have the SS of 3 numbers, not of 204 observations, and the df would not match.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
SSB: Factor B Effects


\[SS_B = pn\sum_{j=1}^{q}\left(\bar{Y}_{\cdot j} - \bar{Y}\right)^2\]

Same move, the other way round: each column marginal mean against the grand mean
Multiplier is now \(pn\) — p levels of A × n per cell — because each sex EMM stands for that many birds

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
SSAB: Interaction Effects


\[SS_{AB} = n\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{q}\left(\bar{Y}_{ij} - \bar{Y}_{i\cdot} - \bar{Y}_{\cdot j} + \bar{Y}\right)^2\]

Take a cell mean, subtract what the two main effects alone predict for it, and you are left with the interaction
\(\bar{Y}_{i\cdot} + \bar{Y}_{\cdot j} - \bar{Y}\) is the additive prediction; the grand mean is added back because it was subtracted twice
Multiplier is just \(n\) — a cell mean stands for only the n birds in that cell







Note


✅ Key idea
\(SS_{AB}\) is the leftovers. If the additive model predicted every cell mean perfectly, every one of those brackets would be zero and \(SS_{AB} = 0\).

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
The Four SS, by Hand



nrep <- 34; plev <- 3; qlev <- 2

gm <- mean(balanced_df$body_mass_g)
cm <- tapply(balanced_df$body_mass_g,            # 3 x 2 cell means
             list(balanced_df$species, balanced_df$sex), mean)
mA <- rowMeans(cm)                               # species marginals
mB <- colMeans(cm)                               # sex marginals

ss_a   <- qlev * nrep * sum((mA - gm)^2)
ss_b   <- plev * nrep * sum((mB - gm)^2)
ss_ab  <- nrep * sum((cm - outer(mA, mB, "+") + gm)^2)
ss_res <- sum(residuals(lm(body_mass_g ~ species * sex,
                           data = balanced_df))^2)

round(c(A = ss_a, B = ss_b, AB = ss_ab, Res = ss_res))
##        A        B       AB      Res 
## 87725999 21988483  1672776 18199467



anova(lm(body_mass_g ~ species * sex,
         data = balanced_df))[, "Sum Sq"]
## [1] 87725999 21988483  1672776 18199467

all.equal(ss_a + ss_b + ss_ab + ss_res,
          sum((balanced_df$body_mass_g - gm)^2))
## [1] TRUE







Note


✅ Key idea
Four lines of arithmetic, and they match anova() to the last digit — and they add to \(SS_{total}\). That second part is true because the design is balanced. In Part 8 it stops being true.

Source
A, B fixed
A, B random
A fixed, B random




A
\(MS_A/MS_{Res}\)
\(MS_A/MS_{AB}\)
\(MS_A/MS_{AB}\)


B
\(MS_B/MS_{Res}\)
\(MS_B/MS_{AB}\)
\(MS_B/MS_{AB}\)

\(MS_{AB}/MS_{Res}\)
\(MS_{AB}/MS_{Res}\)
\(MS_{AB}/MS_{Res}\)

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Hypotheses — Both Factors Fixed


3 hypotheses are tested in a two-way factorial ANOVA: A, B, A×B. Both factors fixed:

\(H_0(A)\): \(\mu_1 = \mu_2 = ... = \mu_p\) (no difference in marginal means of A, pooling across B)
\(H_0(B)\): \(\mu_1 = \mu_2 = ... = \mu_q\) (no difference in marginal means of B, pooling across A)
\(H_0(AB)\): \(\mu_{ij} - \mu_i - \mu_j + \mu = 0\) (no interaction effect)








Tip


🖐 Notice
These are exactly the two main-effect hypotheses from a one-way ANOVA, plus one new hypothesis just for the interaction.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Hypotheses — Mixed Model


3 hypotheses: A, B, A×B. One fixed, one random:

\(H_0(A)\): \(\mu_1 = \mu_2 = ... = \mu_p\) (no difference in marginal means of A, pooling across B)
\(H_0(B)\): \(\sigma^2_B = 0\) (no added variance due to levels of B that could have been used)
\(H_0(AB)\): \(\sigma^2_{AB} = 0\) (no added variance due to interaction between all levels of A and B that could have been used)








Warning


⚠️ Watch out!
Notice the switch from “means are equal” (fixed) to “variance is zero” (random) — that’s the fundamental difference in what a random-effect hypothesis is even asking.

section: All Three SS Types — on Balanced Data
text:
All Three SS Types — on Balanced Data



t1 <- anova(anova_model)                 # Type I
t2 <- Anova(anova_model, type = "II")    # Type II
t3 <- Anova(anova_model, type = "III")   # Type III

data.frame(
  Effect = c("species", "sex", "species:sex"),
  Type_I   = round(t1$`Sum Sq`[1:3]),
  Type_II  = round(t2$`Sum Sq`[1:3]),
  Type_III = round(t3$`Sum Sq`[2:4])
)
##        Effect   Type_I  Type_II Type_III
## 1     species 87725999 87725999 87725999
## 2         sex 21988483 21988483 21988483
## 3 species:sex  1672776  1672776  1672776


Three different rules for allocating variance — the same three numbers.
That is not a coincidence and it is not R being lazy. With equal cell sizes the two factors are orthogonal: knowing a bird’s species tells you nothing about its chance of being male. Neither factor can “steal” SS from the other, so there is no shared variance left to argue about.






Note


✅ Key idea
The whole Type I / II / III literature exists to answer one question: who gets the variance the two factors share? A balanced design has none to share — which is why balance is worth paying for.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Understanding Type III SS


Type III sums of squares test each effect after adjusting for all other effects in the model:

Species effect: tested after adjusting for sex and interaction
Sex effect: tested after adjusting for species and interaction
Interaction: tested after adjusting for both main effects

This is especially important for unbalanced designs, but we’re using it here for consistency with the next analysis.


## Effect Sizes (partial eta-squared):
##        Effect Partial_Eta_Sq
## 1     Species         0.8282
## 2         Sex         0.5471
## 3 Interaction         0.0842







Note


📖 Partial η² — see the next slide for why
\[\eta^2_p = \frac{SS_{effect}}{SS_{effect} + SS_{residual}}\]

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Which Effect Size, and Why


\[\eta^2 = \frac{SS_{effect}}{SS_{total}} \qquad \eta^2_p = \frac{SS_{effect}}{SS_{effect} + SS_{residual}}\]

Plain η² asks “of all the variation, how much does this effect explain?” The three effects plus the residual then sum to 1.
Partial η² asks “of the variation this effect could have explained — its own plus the leftovers — how much does it?” These do not sum to 1.








Warning


⚠️ Why we use partial η² all lecture
The two agree only on a balanced design.
Type III sums of squares do not add up to \(SS_{total}\) once a design is unbalanced — so dividing a Type III SS by the sum of the Type III SS gives a number that is neither η² nor η²ₚ, and you cannot compare it to anything.
Partial η² is well defined either way, so the balanced and unbalanced models in this lecture stay comparable.

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Introduction to Unbalanced Designs


The challenge of unbalanced data: real-world data is often unbalanced — unequal sample sizes across groups, missing data patterns, natural variation in sampling.
Key issues: Type I, II, and III SS stop agreeing; order of terms matters for Type I SS; marginal means ≠ simple averages.
The model is unchanged — \(Y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\) — but estimation of its parameters is not.

## [1] "Unbalanced sample sizes:"
## # A tibble: 6 × 3
##   species   sex        n
##   <fct>     <fct>  <int>
## 1 Adelie    female    73
## 2 Adelie    male      73
## 3 Chinstrap female    34
## 4 Chinstrap male      34
## 5 Gentoo    female    58
## 6 Gentoo    male      61
## [1] "Total N = 333"
## # A tibble: 3 × 4
##   species   female  male prop_female
##   <fct>      <int> <int>       <dbl>
## 1 Adelie        73    73       0.5  
## 2 Chinstrap     34    34       0.5  
## 3 Gentoo        58    61       0.487

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
How Unbalanced Is It, Really?


What matters in a factorial design is not that all six cells are the same size. It is whether the sex split is the same proportion in every species.

Adelie 73 / 73 → 50.0 % female
Chinstrap 34 / 34 → 50.0 % female
Gentoo 58 / 61 → 48.7 % female

If those three percentages were identical, the design would be proportional and the two factors would still be orthogonal — the SS types would still agree, unequal cell sizes or not.







Warning


⚠️ Honest warning about this dataset
The penguin design is nearly proportional. So the three SS types will move apart only slightly, and every p-value stays well below 0.001.
Watch that the numbers change at all — not how dramatically. A design with a half-empty cell is where this really bites, and that is the one you should be afraid of in your own data.

How Type I SS works — sequential decomposition:

First term gets all SS it can explain
Second term gets SS after removing the first
Third term gets SS after removing the first two

Problems with unbalanced data: order dependency, biased if factors are correlated, not invariant to coding.

Type II — each main effect adjusted for the other main effect, but not for the interaction. Most powerful of the three when the interaction is genuinely absent.
Type III — each term adjusted for everything else, interaction included. Order invariant; tests unweighted (marginal) means.

Read the table: the interaction F is identical under all three — it is the last term in, so there is nothing left to adjust it for. Species barely moves. Sex moves the most (387 → 312), because sex is the factor whose split is uneven across species.
Type III costs: lower power with missing cells, and it is meaningless without contr.sum.

text: Part 11 · Summary and Best Practices

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Summary — Unbalanced Designs


Challenges: Type I SS depends on order; simple means ≠ EMMs; reduced power for interactions; complex interpretation.
Solutions: use Type III SS for main effects; report EMMs, not simple means; check assumptions carefully; consider the impact of imbalance.

Recommendations:

Always report: sample sizes per cell, type of SS used, EMMs with CIs
Visualization: show actual data points, include error bars, note unequal sample sizes
Interpretation: focus on effect sizes, consider practical significance, acknowledge limitations

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Final Recommendations


For experimental studies: design for balance when possible, randomize allocation, plan for attrition.
For observational studies: accept imbalance as reality, use Type III SS, report EMMs, consider covariates (ANCOVA).







Note


Statistical software defaults

R: Type I (sequential)
SAS: Type III (marginal)
SPSS: Type III (marginal)

Always specify which type you’re using!

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
text:
Wrap-up — What You Did Today



Fitted a factorial model with two categorical predictors — body_mass_g ~ species * sex
Separated main effects from the interaction: an interaction means “the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other”
Computed \(SS_A\), \(SS_B\), \(SS_{AB}\) and \(SS_{res}\) by hand and matched anova() exactly
Used estimated marginal means rather than raw group averages
Met Type I, II and III sums of squares — identical on the balanced design, slightly apart on the unbalanced one
Set contr.sum before asking for Type III
Reported partial η², the effect size that stays well defined either way








Important


⚠️ Read the interaction first
If the interaction is significant, a main effect is an average across conditions that behave differently — often not a meaningful quantity.
Interpret the interaction, then use simple effects — emmeans(model, ~ sex | species) or joint_tests(model, by = "sex") — rather than reporting the main effect as if it applied everywhere.
R even warns you: “Results may be misleading due to involvement in interactions.”

title: Lecture: Two-Way ANOVA
section: Wrap-up — The One Idea to Keep
text:
Wrap-up — The One Idea to Keep








Note


✅ Balance is a property of your design, not your analysis
A balanced design makes the two factors orthogonal, so each one’s sum of squares is unambiguous and the three SS types collapse to one number.
Imbalance makes the factors share variance — and then how you allocate that shared variance becomes a decision you have to make and defend in your methods section.










Tip


🖐 And one caveat on today’s data
The penguin imbalance is mild — five of six cells are exactly even. The SS types moved a little and no conclusion changed.
That is the common case. The uncommon case — a cell that is half empty, or empty — is where the choice decides the answer, and that is the one to watch for in your own data.









Note

Averaging Out Pseudoreplication



# The 8 needles from one side of one tree are pseudoreplicates —
# average them so each tree/side is ONE data point
p_df <- pine_df %>%
  group_by(team, side) %>%
  summarise(needle_length_mm = mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

shady_df <- p_df %>% filter(side == "shady")
sunny_df <- p_df %>% filter(side == "sunny")

p_df

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text: Part 2 · Hypothesis Testing Framework

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Hypothesis Testing — the Key Components


Every test you will ever run starts with the same five lines, in this order, written down before you look at the output:

Question — the biology, in plain English. Does the sunny side of a pine tree grow longer needles than the shady side?
Prediction — what you expect to see, and why. Sunny needles will be longer, because more light means more photosynthate available for growth.
Null hypothesis (H₀) — “no effect,” the thing the test actually evaluates. H₀: μsunny = μshady
Alternative hypothesis (Hₐ) — what is true if H₀ is not. Hₐ: μsunny ≠ μshady
Significance level (α) — your threshold, chosen up front. Typically α = 0.05.

Decision rule: reject H₀ if p < α.







Important



The prediction and the alternative are not the same thing
The prediction is directional and biological — sunny is longer. The alternative hypothesis here is two-tailed — they differ, either way.
If your prediction is genuinely directional and you commit to it beforehand, you can run a one-tailed test. Deciding that after seeing the data is cheating.








Note



📖 Reference
Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics, Ch. 4 — Framing and Testing Hypotheses.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
section: The Logic of a Statistical Test
text:
The Logic of a Statistical Test


A test assesses the likelihood of the null hypothesis being true.

If H₀ is likely false, Hₐ is assumed correct
More precisely: the long-run probability of obtaining our sample value (or a more extreme one) if the null hypothesis is true
Written p(data | H₀) — the probability of the data, given H₀







Important



✅ Key idea
p(data | H₀) is not the same as p(H₀ | data). A t-test never tells you the probability that H₀ is true — only how surprising your data would be if it were.






p-value
Interpretation




p > 0.10
No evidence against H₀


0.05 – 0.10
Weak evidence against H₀


0.01 – 0.05
Moderate evidence against H₀


0.001 – 0.01
Strong evidence against H₀


p < 0.001
Very strong evidence against H₀

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text: Part 3 · The t-Distribution

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
One-Tailed Questions


One-tailed questions ask about the area of the distribution to the left (or right) of a certain value.






Note



Table-reading example — not our data
A study with n = 8 has df = n − 1 = 7. That is the row highlighted in the table beside this slide, and the only reason 8 and 7 appear together here.

95% of the observations fall to the left of t = 1.895
5% fall outside, in the one tail






Bell-shaped t-distribution curve with the area to the left of the critical value shaded, illustrating a one-tailed cutoff where the shaded region represents the proportion of the distribution below that t-value (here t = 1.895 at df = 7).






Student’s t critical-value table with the one-tail 0.05 column and df = 7 row highlighted, intersecting at the critical value 1.895, the value used for a one-tailed test at alpha = 0.05.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Two-Tailed Questions


Two-tailed questions refer to the area between certain values.
Same table-reading example — n = 8, so df = 7:

95% of the observations lie between t = −2.365 and t = 2.365 (2.5% outside on each side)
Compare to the one-tailed cutoff: t = 1.895 (5% outside)




Bell-shaped t-distribution curve with both tails shaded beyond the critical values (here t = -2.365 and t = 2.365 at df = 7), illustrating a two-tailed cutoff where the two shaded regions together represent the proportion of the distribution outside that range.






Student’s t critical-value table with the two-tail 0.05 column and df = 7 row highlighted, intersecting at the critical value 2.365, the value used for a two-tailed test/95% confidence interval at alpha = 0.05.








Tip



🖐 Notice
The two-tailed critical value is farther from zero than the one-tailed value
— splitting 5% into two tails means each tail only gets 2.5%.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
section: ✅ Key Idea · Degrees of Freedom, Once and For All
text:
✅ Key Idea · Degrees of Freedom, Once and For All


What df means: the number of values that were free to vary once you estimated a mean. Estimate one mean from n numbers and you spend one df — the last value is pinned down by the others.
So you lose one df for every mean you estimate.
Our data: 4 trees, one shady side and one sunny side each.

One-sample t-test — one group, one mean estimated df = n − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3 (4 shady tree means, compared to a fixed number like 15 mm)
Two-sample t-test — two groups, two means estimated df = n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 4 + 4 − 2 = 6 (8 tree means in total, minus one for each group mean)
Paired t-test — you first collapse each tree to one difference, then it is a one-sample test on those differences df = npairs − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3 (4 differences, not 8 values)
Welch’s t-test — the odd one out. df comes from the Welch–Satterthwaite equation, is usually not a whole number, and is always ≤ the Student’s df. Here: df ≈ 5.66.











Test
What n counts
df formula
Our df

n − 1
3

6

3

both groups, penalised
Welch–Satterthwaite

Important



The number that keeps changing is not arbitrary
n is always trees, never needles. What changes is how many means you had to estimate to run the test.
The paired test has half the df of the two-sample test on the identical 8 numbers — because it only ever looks at 4 numbers, the differences.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Calculating a Confidence Interval


Using a two-sided test:
\[\text{CI} = \bar{y} \pm t_{0.975,\,df} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
Our own shady-side trees — n = 4, so df = 3:

n_shady    <- sum(!is.na(shady_df$needle_length_mm))
mean_shady <- mean(shady_df$needle_length_mm)
se_shady   <- sd(shady_df$needle_length_mm) / sqrt(n_shady)
t_crit     <- qt(0.975, df = n_shady - 1)

mean_shady + c(-1, 1) * t_crit * se_shady

[1] 10.91210 17.32978


And the same interval, for free, from the function we sourced:

summary_stats(shady_df$needle_length_mm)

# A tibble: 1 × 6
      n  mean    sd    se ci_lower ci_upper
  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1     4  14.1  2.02  1.01     10.9     17.3









Warning



⚠️ Four trees is a wide interval
With df = 3 the critical t is 3.182, not 1.96 and not the 2.365 highlighted in the table image (that is df = 7).
Small n costs you twice: a bigger multiplier and a bigger standard error.





Student’s t critical-value table with the two-tail 0.05 column and df = 7 row highlighted, intersecting at the critical value 2.365, the value used for a two-tailed test/95% confidence interval at alpha = 0.05.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Applications of the t-Distribution



Can assess confidence that the population mean is within a certain range
Can use the t-distribution to ask:

“What is the probability of getting a sample with mean = ȳ from a population with mean = µ?” (1-sample t-test, df = n − 1)
“What is the probability that two samples came from the same population?” (2-sample t-test, df = n₁ + n₂ − 2)
“Is the average change within a subject different from zero?” (paired t-test, df = npairs − 1)









Tip



🖐 Try it yourself
Before the next slide: which of these three questions does our pine needle design actually ask?

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text: Part 4 · One-Sample T-Test

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
One-Sample T-Test — Question, Prediction, Hypotheses


Question: Is the mean needle length on the shady side different from the 15 mm reported for this species?
Prediction: Shady needles are shorter than 15 mm, because they are light-limited.

H₀: μ = 15 mm
Hₐ: μ ≠ 15 mm (two-tailed)
α = 0.05

Assumptions for a t-test:

Data are normally distributed
Observations are independent
No significant outliers








Note



✅ Degrees of freedom here
One group — the 4 shady tree means. One mean estimated.
df = n − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3








Note



📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 11, covers the one-sample t-test as the simplest hypothesis test on a normally distributed variable.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Checking Normality — QQ Plot



# The one-sample test is on the SHADY side, so that is the group
# whose normality we check -- not the two sides pooled.
qqPlot(shady_df$needle_length_mm)








[1] 4 1









Tip



🖐 Notice
Points that hug the line support normality; points that curve away — especially in the tails — are a warning sign.
qqPlot() from car adds a shaded confidence envelope automatically.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
section: Checking Normality — QQ Plot, Base R
text:
Checking Normality — QQ Plot, Base R



# The base R version -- same idea, no packages, no envelope
qqnorm(shady_df$needle_length_mm)
qqline(shady_df$needle_length_mm)















Tip



🖐 Same idea, no package
qqnorm() + qqline() gives you the same picture as qqPlot(), just without the shaded envelope. Either is fine.








Warning



⚠️ With 4 points, this is a sanity check, not proof
Four points will look “fine” on almost any QQ plot.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Checking Normality — Shapiro-Wilk Test



shapiro.test(shady_df$needle_length_mm)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  shady_df$needle_length_mm
W = 0.94326, p-value = 0.6743









Important



H₀ for Shapiro-Wilk is “the data ARE normal.” A non-significant result (p > 0.05) is what we’re hoping for — it means we fail to reject normality.








Warning



⚠️ With n = 4, this test proves almost nothing
Shapiro-Wilk on four numbers has essentially no power — it will pass almost anything. A high p-value here is not evidence that the data are normal; it is evidence that we don’t have enough data to tell.
Run it, report it, but lean on the QQ plot, the biology, and the design.








Tip



🖐 Why the shady side only?
We test the group the hypothesis is about. Pooling shady and sunny would mix two distributions with different means, which can look non-normal even when each group is perfectly normal.

text:
Checking for Outliers



box_plot

box_plot was built once in Part 1 — no reason to retype it. Points beyond the whiskers are potential outliers; always look before you test.

Running the One-Sample t-Test

one_sample_model

What does the p-value tell us?
Reject or fail to reject at α = 0.05?
What does that mean for a botanist?

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
section: One-Tailed Variation — the Same Test, One Direction
text:
One-Tailed Variation — the Same Test, One Direction


Our prediction was directional: shady needles are shorter than 15 mm. If we commit to that before collecting data, we can run a one-tailed test.

H₀: μ ≥ 15
Hₐ: μ < 15 — all 5% of α in the lower tail


one_tailed_model <- t.test(shady_df$needle_length_mm,
                           mu = 15,
                           alternative = "less")

one_tailed_model


    One Sample t-test

data:  shady_df$needle_length_mm
t = -0.87183, df = 3, p-value = 0.2237
alternative hypothesis: true mean is less than 15
95 percent confidence interval:
     -Inf 16.49382
sample estimates:
mean of x 
 14.12094 









Note



✅ Key idea
alternative = "less" or "greater" is the only thing that changed. Same data, same t, same df = 3.
Compare the two p-values:



Test
Hₐ
p




Two-tailed
μ ≠ 15
0.448


One-tailed
μ < 15
0.224



Exactly half. All of α now sits in one tail, so the observed t only has to beat one cutoff instead of two.








Warning



⚠️ Notice the confidence interval changed too
It now runs from −Inf to an upper bound. A one-tailed test makes no claim in the direction you ruled out.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
section: One-Tailed vs. Two-Tailed — What It Costs You
text:
One-Tailed vs. Two-Tailed — What It Costs You


Remember the critical values from Part 3. At df = 3:

qt(0.975, df = 3)   # two-tailed, 2.5% in each tail

[1] 3.182446

qt(0.95,  df = 3)   # one-tailed, 5% in one tail

[1] 2.353363


The one-tailed cutoff (2.353) is closer to zero than the two-tailed cutoff (3.182). That is the extra power — a smaller t will do.







Important



⚠️ The rule that makes one-tailed tests honest
You must pick the direction before you see the data, on biological grounds, and you must accept that a result in the other direction tells you nothing — no matter how big it is.
Choosing the tail after looking at your means is not a one-tailed test. It is a two-tailed test with the p-value secretly halved.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
One-Tailed, the Wrong Direction


But run the same one-tailed test the other way and watch what happens:

t.test(shady_df$needle_length_mm, mu = 15,
       alternative = "greater")


    One Sample t-test

data:  shady_df$needle_length_mm
t = -0.87183, df = 3, p-value = 0.7763
alternative hypothesis: true mean is greater than 15
95 percent confidence interval:
 11.74806      Inf
sample estimates:
mean of x 
 14.12094 


Same data, same t = −0.87, and now p = 0.776.







Tip



🖐 When is one-tailed defensible?
When the opposite result would lead to the same action as no result. A drug that makes patients worse and a drug that does nothing are both “do not approve.”
For our pine needles, “sunny is longer” and “shady is longer” are both interesting biology. Two-tailed is the honest default.

Visualizing the One-Sample Test — t Scale


















Note



✅ Key idea
This curve is drawn with df = 3, straight out of one_sample_model — not from a textbook example. The critical value is 3.182, which is why a wide, short-tailed picture like this needs a big t to reach significance.
The green line (our observed t) sits inside the dashed lines — that is what “fail to reject” looks like.

text:

Tip



🖐 Notice
Same test, same conclusion — just relabelled onto the millimetre scale instead of the t scale.
The blue line is H₀ (15 mm), the green line is our sample mean. The green line sits inside the dashed critical values, so 15 mm is a perfectly plausible population mean for these four trees.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Interpreting the One-Sample T-Test


Activity: interpret the t-test results

What does the p-value tell us?
Should we reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis?
Does the 95% CI from summary_stats() contain 15 mm — and does that agree with the p-value?








Note



How to report this result in a scientific paper
“A two-tailed, one-sample t-test at α = 0.05 showed that the mean needle length (… mm, SD = …) [was/was not] significantly different from the expected 15 mm, t(3) = …, p = …”
Two things you must always report: the degrees of freedom, in parentheses after t, and whether the test was one- or two-tailed.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text: Part 5 · Two-Sample T-Test

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Two-Sample T-Tests — the Question


Question: Do needles differ in length between the sunny and shady sides?
Prediction: Sunny needles are longer — more light, more growth.

H₀: μshady = μsunny
Hₐ: μshady ≠ μsunny (direction not specified)
α = 0.05

A two-sample t-test compares means from two independent groups.




Photo of two separate green pine branches side by side, each with needle clusters, representing the two independent samples (populations X and Y) being compared in a two-sample t-test.








Note



✅ Degrees of freedom here
Two groups, two means estimated from 8 tree means.
df = n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 4 + 4 − 2 = 6

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Two-Sample T-Test Framework


\[t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}} = \frac{\text{SIGNAL}}{\text{NOISE}}\]
Where:

x̄₁, x̄₂: sample means of the two groups
s²ₚ: pooled variance = [(n₁−1)s₁² + (n₂−1)s₂²] / (n₁+n₂−2)
Sₚ = √s²ₚ: the pooled standard deviation
Sₚ√(1/n₁ + 1/n₂): the standard error of the difference — the whole denominator








Important



The df is sitting right inside the formula
Look at the denominator of the pooled variance: n₁ + n₂ − 2. That is the degrees of freedom. It is the divisor that turns two sums of squares into one variance estimate, and the same number then indexes the t-distribution you compare your t to.
df is not a rule to memorise — it is whatever you divided by.








Note



📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 12 — Comparing Two Means.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Checking Assumptions — Normality by Group



p_df %>%
  group_by(side) %>%
  summarize(
    shapiro_p = shapiro.test(needle_length_mm)$p.value,
    .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  side  shapiro_p
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 shady     0.674
2 sunny     0.516









Tip



🖐 Each group separately
For a two-sample test the normality assumption is about the residuals within each group, so test each side on its own — never the pooled column.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Checking Assumptions — Equal Variances



leveneTest(needle_length_mm ~ factor(side), data = p_df)

Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
      Df F value Pr(>F)
group  1  0.6355 0.4557
       6               









Important



H₀ for Levene’s test is “the variances are equal.”
You want a non-significant result. If p > 0.05, the standard (Student’s) t-test is fine. If p < 0.05, use Welch’s.
leveneTest() needs the grouping variable as a factor.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Conducting the Two-Sample T-Test


Standard (Student’s) — equal variances

two_sample_model <- t.test(needle_length_mm ~ side,
                           data = p_df, var.equal = TRUE)

two_sample_model


    Two Sample t-test

data:  needle_length_mm by side
t = -0.85529, df = 6, p-value = 0.4252
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group shady and group sunny is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -4.221663  2.034788
sample estimates:
mean in group shady mean in group sunny 
           14.12094            15.21438 



Welch’s — unequal variances

welch_model <- t.test(needle_length_mm ~ side,
                      data = p_df, var.equal = FALSE)

welch_model


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  needle_length_mm by side
t = -0.85529, df = 5.6627, p-value = 0.4271
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group shady and group sunny is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -4.267394  2.080519
sample estimates:
mean in group shady mean in group sunny 
           14.12094            15.21438

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Standard vs. Welch’s t-Test


Standard t-test (Student’s)

Assumes equal variances between groups
Uses a pooled variance estimate combining both groups
Higher power when the equal-variance assumption is met
df = n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 6 — a whole number, every time


Welch’s t-test

Does not assume equal variances
Uses separate variance estimates for each group
More robust when group variances differ
df from the Welch–Satterthwaite equation — typically not a whole number, and always smaller than n₁ + n₂ − 2. Here df ≈ 5.66







Tip



🖐 The fractional df is the price of the robustness — Welch’s buys safety by spending degrees of freedom.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Interpreting the Two-Sample T-Test


What can we conclude about needle lengths on the sunny vs. shady sides?






Note



How to report this result in a scientific paper
“A two-tailed, two-sample t-test at α = 0.05 showed [a significant/no significant] difference in needle length between sunny (M = …, SD = …) and shady (M = …, SD = …) sides of pine trees, t(6) = …, p = …”
For Welch’s you report the fractional df exactly as R gives it: t(5.66) = …












df = 6 — compare the shape of this curve to the df = 3 one in Part 4.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text: Part 6 · Paired T-Test

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
section: What Does a Paired T-Test Tell Us?
text:
What Does a Paired T-Test Tell Us?


Paired t-test:

Compares two measurements from the same subject or matched pair
Tests whether the mean difference between paired observations equals zero
Uses the differences between pairs as the data
Generally more powerful, because it removes subject-to-subject variation from the noise







Note



✅ Degrees of freedom here
4 trees → 4 differences → one mean difference estimated.
df = npairs − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3
Not 6. The 8 numbers became 4 the moment you subtracted.








Warning



⚠️ Order matters for the sign
t.test(shady, sunny, paired = TRUE) computes shady − sunny. Reverse the arguments and t flips sign — the p-value is identical, but the direction you report is backwards.




p_wide_df <- p_df %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = side,
              values_from = needle_length_mm)

# shady first, then sunny -- the SAME order the
# two-sample test used
paired_model <- t.test(p_wide_df$shady,
                       p_wide_df$sunny,
                       paired = TRUE)

paired_model


    Paired t-test

data:  p_wide_df$shady and p_wide_df$sunny
t = -2.7227, df = 3, p-value = 0.07238
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -2.3714897  0.1846147
sample estimates:
mean difference 
      -1.093438

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Same Data, Two Different Answers


Both tests used exactly the same 8 numbers, and both measured shady − sunny:



Test
t
df
p




Two-sample
−0.855
6
0.425


Paired
−2.723
3
0.072



Same estimated difference (−1.09 mm, shady needles shorter). Same data. The p-value dropped by a factor of almost six.
Why?

The two-sample test throws the pairing away. Tree-to-tree variation (some teams’ trees just have longer needles) lands in the noise, swamping the signal.
The paired test looks only at the shady − sunny difference within each tree, so tree-to-tree variation cancels out entirely.



slope_plot








Each line is one tree. All four shift the same way — that consistency is exactly what the paired test measures and the two-sample test cannot see.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
section: Same Data, Two Different Answers — Why the Design Matters
text:
Same Data, Two Different Answers — Why the Design Matters








Important



And notice it did that on half the degrees of freedom
3 instead of 6 — because it is working with 4 differences, not 8 values. A smaller df makes significance harder to reach. It still won by a mile, because the noise it removed mattered far more than the df it gave up.









Note



These data are paired by design — each team measured both sides of the same tree. The two-sample test is not just less powerful, it is answering a question our design never asked.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
section: ✅ A Paired Test Is a One-Sample Test
text:
✅ A Paired Test Is a One-Sample Test


Here is the idea that makes the df finally click. Treat the shady side as each tree’s own control, and compute one difference per tree:

diff_df <- p_wide_df %>%
  mutate(difference = sunny - shady)

diff_df

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  team       shady sunny difference
  <chr>      <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>
1 botany      16.1  17.3      1.16 
2 grace_jace  15.4  15.5      0.146
3 one         13.2  14.2      0.968
4 waterbugs   11.7  13.8      2.10 









Tip



🖐 Each tree is its own control
The shady side accounts for everything about that particular tree — its genetics, its soil, its water, its team’s measuring technique. Subtracting removes all of it at once, and what is left is the effect of sun.
This is the same logic as a before/after design, and it is the seed of the blocked designs you will meet in ANOVA.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
section: ✅ A Paired Test Is a One-Sample Test — Same Numbers
text:
✅ A Paired Test Is a One-Sample Test — Same Numbers


Now throw away the pairing language entirely and run a plain one-sample t-test on those 4 differences, against μ = 0:

diff_model <- t.test(diff_df$difference, mu = 0)

diff_model


    One Sample t-test

data:  diff_df$difference
t = 2.7227, df = 3, p-value = 0.07238
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.1846147  2.3714897
sample estimates:
mean of x 
 1.093438 









Important



Identical. Same t, same df, same p.
t.test(sunny, shady, paired = TRUE) and t.test(sunny - shady, mu = 0) are the same test. paired = TRUE is nothing more than a convenience that does the subtraction for you.
That is why the paired df is npairs − 1 = 3 and not n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 6: once you subtract, you genuinely only have four numbers. A one-sample test on four numbers has 3 df. Always.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text: Part 7 · Assumptions and Wrap-Up

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Assumptions of Parametric Tests


Common assumptions for t-tests:

Normality — the data (or, for a paired test, the differences) come from a normally distributed population
Equal variances — two-sample tests only
Independence — observations are independent
No outliers — extreme values can dominate a small sample

What do we do if our data violate these?

Alternatives when assumptions are violated:

Data transformation (log, square root)
Non-parametric tests — Mann-Whitney U for two samples, Wilcoxon signed-rank for paired
Robust methods







Tip



🖐 Note the paired case
You check normality of the differences, not of the two groups. Which follows directly from the last slide — the differences are the data.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Summary and Conclusions


In this lecture we:

Went from question → prediction → H₀ / Hₐ → α, before looking at output
Tested assumptions — QQ plot, Shapiro-Wilk, Levene’s
Ran one-sample (two- and one-tailed), two-sample (Student’s and Welch’s), and paired t-tests
Saw that a paired test is a one-sample test on the differences
Learned to read and report t(df) = …, p = …








Important



Degrees of freedom — the one-line version

One-sample: n − 1 = 3
Two-sample: n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 6
Paired: npairs − 1 = 3
Welch’s: fractional, ≤ n₁ + n₂ − 2 ≈ 5.66

n is trees, never needles. You lose one df per mean you estimate.








Note



Key takeaways

Always check assumptions before you test
Plot the data before you test
Match the test to the design, not to the p-value you want
Non-parametric alternatives are coming up next

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Where We Left Off


Last time:

Histograms / frequency distributions
Probability distribution functions (PDFs)
Z-scores and t-scores
Tests of means using t-tests: one sample, two sample







Note


✅ Key idea from last lecture
A t-score is just a z-score computed with the sample standard deviation instead of the population standard deviation
— that substitution is why we need the t-distribution at all. Today we put it to work.







Diagram of a large circle labeled ‘population’ with dots representing individuals and Greek-letter parameters (mu, sigma, sigma-squared), with orange arrows showing a subset of dots being drawn down into a small circle labeled ‘sample’ with its statistics (y-bar, s, s-squared), illustrating that a sample is used to estimate unknown population parameters.








Note


Today’s roadmap

Hypothesis testing framework
The t-distribution and degrees of freedom
One-sample t-test — two-tailed and one-tailed
Two-sample t-test (Student’s and Welch’s)
Paired t-test
Checking assumptions throughout

raw_mean_se_plot















Warning


⚠️ Those error bars are a lie
They look tight — and tight error bars feel like strong evidence. They are computed as SD / √n with n = 32.
But we did not measure 32 independent things per side. We measured 4 trees, eight times each. The 32 is fake, so the precision is fake.
Hold this picture in your head. We are going to fix it on the next slide and then look again.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text: Part 2 · Hypothesis Testing Framework

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Hypothesis Testing — the Key Components


Every test you will ever run starts with the same five lines, in this order, written down before you look at the output:

Question — the biology, in plain English. Does the sunny side of a pine tree grow longer needles than the shady side?
Prediction — what you expect to see, and why. Sunny needles will be longer, because more light means more photosynthate available for growth.
Null hypothesis (H₀) — “no effect,” the thing the test actually evaluates. H₀: μsunny = μshady
Alternative hypothesis (Hₐ) — what is true if H₀ is not. Hₐ: μsunny ≠ μshady
Significance level (α) — your threshold, chosen up front. Typically α = 0.05.

Decision rule: reject H₀ if p < α.







Important


The prediction and the alternative are not the same thing
The prediction is directional and biological — sunny is longer. The alternative hypothesis here is two-tailed — they differ, either way.
If your prediction is genuinely directional and you commit to it beforehand, you can run a one-tailed test. Deciding that after seeing the data is cheating.









Note


📖 Reference
Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics, Ch. 4 — Framing and Testing Hypotheses.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
section: The Logic of a Statistical Test
text:
The Logic of a Statistical Test


A test assesses the likelihood of the null hypothesis being true.

If H₀ is likely false, Hₐ is assumed correct
More precisely: the long-run probability of obtaining our sample value (or a more extreme one) if the null hypothesis is true
Written p(data | H₀) — the probability of the data, given H₀







Important


✅ Key idea
p(data | H₀) is not the same as p(H₀ | data). A t-test never tells you the probability that H₀ is true — only how surprising your data would be if it were.







p-value
Interpretation




p > 0.10
No evidence against H₀


0.05 – 0.10
Weak evidence against H₀


0.01 – 0.05
Moderate evidence against H₀


0.001 – 0.01
Strong evidence against H₀


p < 0.001
Very strong evidence against H₀

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text: Part 3 · The t-Distribution

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
One-Tailed Questions


One-tailed questions ask about the area of the distribution to the left (or right) of a certain value.






Note


Table-reading example — not our data
A study with n = 8 has df = n − 1 = 7. That is the row highlighted in the table beside this slide, and the only reason 8 and 7 appear together here.

95% of the observations fall to the left of t = 1.895
5% fall outside, in the one tail







Bell-shaped t-distribution curve with the area to the left of the critical value shaded, illustrating a one-tailed cutoff where the shaded region represents the proportion of the distribution below that t-value (here t = 1.895 at df = 7).






Student’s t critical-value table with the one-tail 0.05 column and df = 7 row highlighted, intersecting at the critical value 1.895, the value used for a one-tailed test at alpha = 0.05.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Two-Tailed Questions


Two-tailed questions refer to the area between certain values.
Same table-reading example — n = 8, so df = 7:

95% of the observations lie between t = −2.365 and t = 2.365 (2.5% outside on each side)
Compare to the one-tailed cutoff: t = 1.895 (5% outside)




Bell-shaped t-distribution curve with both tails shaded beyond the critical values (here t = -2.365 and t = 2.365 at df = 7), illustrating a two-tailed cutoff where the two shaded regions together represent the proportion of the distribution outside that range.






Student’s t critical-value table with the two-tail 0.05 column and df = 7 row highlighted, intersecting at the critical value 2.365, the value used for a two-tailed test/95% confidence interval at alpha = 0.05.








Tip


🖐 Notice
The two-tailed critical value is farther from zero than the one-tailed value
— splitting 5% into two tails means each tail only gets 2.5%.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
section: ✅ Key Idea · Degrees of Freedom, Once and For All
text:
✅ Key Idea · Degrees of Freedom, Once and For All


What df means: the number of values that were free to vary once you estimated a mean. Estimate one mean from n numbers and you spend one df — the last value is pinned down by the others.
So you lose one df for every mean you estimate.
Our data: 4 trees, one shady side and one sunny side each.

One-sample t-test — one group, one mean estimated df = n − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3 (4 shady tree means, compared to a fixed number like 15 mm)
Two-sample t-test — two groups, two means estimated df = n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 4 + 4 − 2 = 6 (8 tree means in total, minus one for each group mean)
Paired t-test — you first collapse each tree to one difference, then it is a one-sample test on those differences df = npairs − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3 (4 differences, not 8 values)
Welch’s t-test — the odd one out. df comes from the Welch–Satterthwaite equation, is usually not a whole number, and is always ≤ the Student’s df. Here: df ≈ 5.66.











Test
What n counts
df formula
Our df




One-sample
trees in the one group
n − 1
3


Two-sample
trees in both groups
n₁ + n₂ − 2
6


Paired
differences
npairs − 1
3


Welch’s
both groups, penalised
Welch–Satterthwaite
≈ 5.66









Important


The number that keeps changing is not arbitrary
n is always trees, never needles. What changes is how many means you had to estimate to run the test.
The paired test has half the df of the two-sample test on the identical 8 numbers — because it only ever looks at 4 numbers, the differences.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Calculating a Confidence Interval


Using a two-sided test:
\[\text{CI} = \bar{y} \pm t_{0.975,\,df} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
Our own shady-side trees — n = 4, so df = 3:

n_shady    <- sum(!is.na(shady_df$needle_length_mm))
mean_shady <- mean(shady_df$needle_length_mm)
se_shady   <- sd(shady_df$needle_length_mm) / sqrt(n_shady)
t_crit     <- qt(0.975, df = n_shady - 1)

mean_shady + c(-1, 1) * t_crit * se_shady

[1] 10.91210 17.32978


And the same interval, for free, from the function we sourced:

summary_stats(shady_df$needle_length_mm)

# A tibble: 1 × 6
      n  mean    sd    se ci_lower ci_upper
  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1     4  14.1  2.02  1.01     10.9     17.3









Warning


⚠️ Four trees is a wide interval
With df = 3 the critical t is 3.182, not 1.96 and not the 2.365 highlighted in the table image (that is df = 7).
Small n costs you twice: a bigger multiplier and a bigger standard error.






Student’s t critical-value table with the two-tail 0.05 column and df = 7 row highlighted, intersecting at the critical value 2.365, the value used for a two-tailed test/95% confidence interval at alpha = 0.05.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Applications of the t-Distribution



Can assess confidence that the population mean is within a certain range
Can use the t-distribution to ask:

“What is the probability of getting a sample with mean = ȳ from a population with mean = µ?” (1-sample t-test, df = n − 1)
“What is the probability that two samples came from the same population?” (2-sample t-test, df = n₁ + n₂ − 2)
“Is the average change within a subject different from zero?” (paired t-test, df = npairs − 1)









Tip


🖐 Try it yourself
Before the next slide: which of these three questions does our pine needle design actually ask?

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text: Part 4 · One-Sample T-Test

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
One-Sample T-Test — Question, Prediction, Hypotheses


Question: Is the mean needle length on the shady side different from the 15 mm reported for this species?
Prediction: Shady needles are shorter than 15 mm, because they are light-limited.

H₀: μ = 15 mm
Hₐ: μ ≠ 15 mm (two-tailed)
α = 0.05

Assumptions for a t-test:

Data are normally distributed
Observations are independent
No significant outliers








Note


✅ Degrees of freedom here
One group — the 4 shady tree means. One mean estimated.
df = n − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3









Note


📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 11, covers the one-sample t-test as the simplest hypothesis test on a normally distributed variable.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Checking Normality — QQ Plot



# The one-sample test is on the SHADY side, so that is the group
# whose normality we check -- not the two sides pooled.
qqPlot(shady_df$needle_length_mm)








[1] 4 1









Tip


🖐 Notice
Points that hug the line support normality; points that curve away — especially in the tails — are a warning sign.
qqPlot() from car adds a shaded confidence envelope automatically.

section: Checking Normality — QQ Plot, Base R
text:
Checking Normality — QQ Plot, Base R



# The base R version -- same idea, no packages, no envelope
qqnorm(shady_df$needle_length_mm)
qqline(shady_df$needle_length_mm)















Tip


🖐 Same idea, no package
qqnorm() + qqline() gives you the same picture as qqPlot(), just without the shaded envelope. Either is fine.









Warning


⚠️ With 4 points, this is a sanity check, not proof
Four points will look “fine” on almost any QQ plot.

title: Lecture: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
Checking Normality — Shapiro-Wilk Test



shapiro.test(shady_df$needle_length_mm)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  shady_df$needle_length_mm
W = 0.94326, p-value = 0.6743









Important


H₀ for Shapiro-Wilk is “the data ARE normal.” A non-significant result (p > 0.05) is what we’re hoping for — it means we fail to reject normality.









Warning


⚠️ With n = 4, this test proves almost nothing
Shapiro-Wilk on four numbers has essentially no power — it will pass almost anything. A high p-value here is not evidence that the data are normal; it is evidence that we don’t have enough data to tell.
Run it, report it, but lean on the QQ plot, the biology, and the design.









Tip


🖐 Why the shady side only?
We test the group the hypothesis is about. Pooling shady and sunny would mix two distributions with different means, which can look non-normal even when each group is perfectly normal.
