title: Lecture: Review
text:
What is Logistic Regression?
Logistic regression is used when: - The response variable is binary (yes/no, 1/0, present/absent) - Data follows a binomial distribution (not normal) - We want to model the probability of an outcome

title: Lecture: Review
text:
Today’s Example: Lizard Sexual Maturity
We’ll explore the relationship between body length and sexual maturity in female lizards - Response variable: Sexual maturity (mature: 1 = yes, 0 = no) - Predictor variable: Body length in cm - Question: Can we predict the probability of sexual maturity from body size?

title: Lecture: Review
text:
Key Difference from Linear Regression

Linear regression: Models the actual values of Y
Logistic regression: Models the probability of Y = 1
Uses Generalized Linear Models (GLM) instead of General Linear Models

title: Lecture: Review
section: Step 1: Load and Explore the Data
text:
Step 1: Load and Explore the Data

# Load the lizard dataset
lizards_df <- read.csv("data/lizards.csv") %>% 
  clean_names()

# First few rows
head(lizards_df)
##   length mature
## 1   10.2      0
## 2   10.4      0
## 3   11.8      0
## 4   12.3      0
## 5   13.8      0
## 6   16.9      0

title: Lecture: Review
text: Step 2: Initial Data Visualization

title: Lecture: Review
text:
Creating a Boxplot
Let’s visualize how body length differs between sexually mature and immature lizards:

# Create boxplot showing length by maturity status
maturity_boxplot <- ggplot(lizards_df, aes(x = factor(mature), y = length)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = c("lightblue", "lightcoral")) +
  labs(title = "Lizard Body Length by Sexual Maturity Status",
       x = "Sexual Maturity (0 = Immature, 1 = Mature)",
       y = "Body Length (cm)") +
  theme_minimal()

maturity_boxplot

title: Lecture: Review
text:
What do we see?

There appears to be a relationship between size and sexual maturity
Mature lizards tend to be longer than immature ones
But there’s overlap - not a perfect separation
This suggests logistic regression might be appropriate

title: Lecture: Review
section: Step 3: Fit the Logistic Regression Model
text: Step 3: Fit the Logistic Regression Model

title: Lecture: Review
text:
Using glm() for Logistic Regression
The glm() function is similar to lm() but requires specifying the distribution family:

# Fit logistic regression model
# family = binomial tells R we have binary data
logistic_model <- glm(mature ~ length, 
                      data = lizards_df, 
                      family = binomial)

# Get model summary
summary(logistic_model)
## 
## Call:
## glm(formula = mature ~ length, family = binomial, data = lizards_df)
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)   
## (Intercept)  -6.6899     2.1401  -3.126  0.00177 **
## length        0.2503     0.0775   3.229  0.00124 **
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)
## 
##     Null deviance: 60.176  on 43  degrees of freedom
## Residual deviance: 34.041  on 42  degrees of freedom
## AIC: 38.041
## 
## Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 6

title: Lecture: Review
text:
Interpreting the Model Output

Coefficients:

Intercept (β₀): -5.5847 - The log-odds when length = 0
Slope (β₁): 0.2503 - Change in log-odds for each 1 cm increase in length



P-values:

Both coefficients are significant (p < 0.05)
We reject the null hypothesis that β₁ = 0
There IS a relationship between length and sexual maturity



Understanding the Slope:
The positive slope (0.2503) indicates: - Longer lizards are more likely to be sexually mature - For each 1 cm increase in length, the log-odds of maturity increase by 0.2503

title: Lecture: Review
text: Step 4: Convert Log-Odds to Odds

title: Lecture: Review
text:
Making the Results More Interpretable
Log-odds are hard to interpret. Let’s convert to odds:

# Extract the slope coefficient
slope_coefficient <- coef(logistic_model)[2]

# Convert log-odds to odds ratio
odds_ratio <- exp(slope_coefficient)
odds_ratio
##   length 
## 1.284388

# Interpretation
# For every 1 cm increase in length, the odds of being sexually mature
# increase by a factor of 1.284 (or about 28.4%)

title: Lecture: Review
section: Step 5: Create the Logistic Regression Plot
text: Step 5: Create the Logistic Regression Plot

title: Lecture: Review
text:
Visualizing the Probability Curve

# Create sequence of x-values for prediction
xvals <- seq(from = 10, to = 50, by = 0.01)

# Get predicted probabilities
yvals <- predict(logistic_model, 
                 list(length = xvals), 
                 type = "response")

# Create prediction dataframe for plotting
prediction_df <- data.frame(length = xvals, 
                           probability = yvals)


# Create the logistic regression plot
logistic_plot <- ggplot() +
  # Add data points
  geom_point(data = lizards_df, 
             aes(x = length, y = mature),
             alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  # Add logistic curve
  geom_line(data = prediction_df,
            aes(x = length, y = probability),
            color = "red", size = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Probability of Sexual Maturity vs Body Length",
       x = "Body Length (cm)",
       y = "Probability of Being Sexually Mature") +
  theme_minimal()

logistic_plot

title: Lecture: Review
text:
What the S-curve tells us:

The red line shows how probability changes with length
Small lizards (<20 cm) have very low probability of being mature
Large lizards (>40 cm) have very high probability of being mature
The steepest change occurs around 25-30 cm

title: Lecture: Review
text: Step 6: Making Predictions

title: Lecture: Review
text:
Using the Model for Prediction
Let’s predict the probability of sexual maturity for specific lizard sizes:

# Predict for a 20 cm lizard
prob_20cm <- predict(logistic_model, 
                     list(length = 20), 
                     type = "response")
prob_20cm
##         1 
## 0.1565304

# Predict for a 30 cm lizard
prob_30cm <- predict(logistic_model, 
                     list(length = 30), 
                     type = "response")
prob_30cm
##         1 
## 0.6939292

# Predict for a 40 cm lizard
prob_40cm <- predict(logistic_model, 
                     list(length = 40), 
                     type = "response")
prob_40cm
##         1 
## 0.9651551

title: Lecture: Review
text:
Interpretation:

A 20 cm lizard has about 14% probability of being sexually mature
A 30 cm lizard has about 70% probability of being sexually mature
A 40 cm lizard has about 96% probability of being sexually mature

title: Lecture: Review
text: Step 7: Model Fit Assessment

title: Lecture: Review
text:
Calculating Pseudo-R2 Values
Unlike linear regression, logistic regression doesn’t have a traditional R². We use pseudo-R² instead:

# Calculate pseudo-R2 values using pscl package
pseudo_r2 <- pR2(logistic_model)
## fitting null model for pseudo-r2
pseudo_r2
##         llh     llhNull          G2    McFadden        r2ML        r2CU 
## -17.0204762 -30.0881077  26.1352630   0.4343122   0.4478763   0.6009400

title: Lecture: Review
text:
Interpreting Pseudo-R2 Values
The last three values are the pseudo-R² statistics:

McFadden: Compares model to null model
r2ML: Maximum likelihood based R²
r2CU: Cragg-Uhler (Nagelkerke) R²

Values around 0.4-0.5 indicate moderate to good fit. Our model explains approximately 40-50% of the variation in sexual maturity status.

title: Lecture: Review
text: Step 8: Additional Diagnostics

title: Lecture: Review
section: Creating a More Detailed Summary Plot
text:
Creating a More Detailed Summary Plot

# Create a plot showing observed vs predicted probabilities
lizards_df$predicted_prob <- predict(logistic_model, type = "response")

diagnostic_plot <- ggplot(lizards_df, aes(x = length)) +
  # Add observed data as points
  geom_point(aes(y = mature), alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  # Add predicted probabilities
  geom_line(aes(y = predicted_prob), color = "blue", size = 1) +
  # Add 50% probability threshold
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  labs(title = "Observed Data and Model Predictions",
       x = "Body Length (cm)",
       y = "Probability of Sexual Maturity",
       subtitle = "Points = observed data, Blue line = model predictions") +
  theme_minimal()

diagnostic_plot

title: Lecture: Review
text: Summary: Key Takeaways

title: Lecture: Review
text:
What We Learned:

Logistic regression models probability of binary outcomes
Uses glm() with family = binomial
Coefficients represent changes in log-odds
Convert to odds ratios for interpretation: exp(coefficient)
Creates S-shaped probability curves
Use pseudo-R² to assess model fit

title: Lecture: Review
text:
Our Results:

Significant positive relationship between body length and sexual maturity
Each 1 cm increase in length increases odds of maturity by ~28%
Model explains ~40-50% of variation in maturity status
Can predict probability of maturity for any given length

title: Lecture: Review
text:
When to Use Logistic Regression:

Binary response variable (0/1, yes/no, success/failure)
Want to predict probabilities
Relationships that follow S-shaped curves
When assumptions of linear regression are violated

r2ML: Maximum likelihood based R²
r2CU: Cragg-Uhler (Nagelkerke) R²

Values around 0.4-0.5 indicate moderate to good fit. Our model explains approximately 40-50% of the variation in sexual maturity status.

section: A tool you will reuse all semester
text:
A tool you will reuse all semester
You just typed out mean, sd, n and se by hand. You will want those same four numbers in every analysis from here on — so let’s package them into a function and never type that block again.






Note



This one is a tool, not a lesson — it is already filled in for you in the script skeleton. You do not have to type it. Read it, run it, and then use it.
{ variable } (the “curly-curly” braces) is what lets you hand the function a bare column name like length_mm instead of a quoted string. It is the one piece of syntax here worth remembering.


▶ Run this — define it once:
# ── Part 1.3 · A reusable summary function ──────────────────────────────
summary_stats <- function(data, variable) {
  data %>%
    summarize(
      n        = sum(!is.na({{ variable }})),
      mean     = mean({{ variable }}, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd       = sd({{ variable }}, na.rm = TRUE),
      se       = sd / sqrt(n),
      ci_lower = mean - qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se,
      ci_upper = mean + qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se,
      .groups  = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(across(c(mean, sd, se, ci_lower, ci_upper),
                  ~ round_half_up(.x, 2)))
}
▶ Run this — now use it. Three ways, no retyping:
# ── Part 1.4 · A reusable summary function ──────────────────────────────
g_df %>% group_by(lake) %>% summary_stats(length_mm)   # per lake

g_df %>% summary_stats(length_mm)                      # both lakes pooled

g_df %>% group_by(lake) %>% summary_stats(mass_g)      # a different column
✏️ Your turn: Compare the first result to stats_df from Part 1.2. Do the mean, sd and se columns match?
________________________
✏️ Your turn: The function also returns ci_lower and ci_upper — a 95% confidence interval. We have not explained those yet. That is Part 6. For now, just notice they are there.

title: Activity: Power and Type I & II Error
text:
Worksheet: Power and Type I & II Error
📥 Pine needle data 📥 Horned lizard data
📥 Tools script (.R) 📥 Script skeleton (.R)






ImportantColumn names



pine_data.csv has the same six columns you have used all term (source_file, team, replicate, side, needle_length_mm, needle_width_mm). horned_lizards.csv has two:



Column
What it is




squamosal_horn_length_mm
horn length, millimetres (1 NA)


survival
"living" or "killed" by shrike predation








Part 1 · Setup
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 1.1 · Setup ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)
library(effectsize)  # cohens_d()
library(pwr)         # power analysis

source("themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R")

pine_df <- read_csv("data/pine_data.csv")

p_df <- pine_df %>%
  group_by(team, side) %>%
  summarise(needle_length_mm = mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

p_wide_df <- p_df %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = side, values_from = needle_length_mm)

lizard_df <- read_csv("data/horned_lizards.csv") %>%
  filter(!is.na(squamosal_horn_length_mm))

p_df
lizard_df



Part 2 · Two Ways to Be Wrong
Crossing the statistical decision against the unknown truth gives four outcomes: correct rejection, correct non-rejection, a Type I error (α) — a false positive — and a Type II error (β) — a false negative. Power = 1 − β.
✏️ Your turn: For each scenario, is it a Type I error, a Type II error, or a correct decision?
1. A study concludes sunny-side pine needles are longer, when really
   there is no difference.
   ________________________________________________________

2. A study fails to detect a real horn-length difference between
   surviving and predated lizards, and concludes there is none.
   ________________________________________________________

3. A study correctly detects that predated lizards have shorter horns.
   ________________________________________________________



Part 3 · What Is Power
Statistical power is the probability of detecting a true effect — of rejecting H₀ when it really is false. 80% power is the usual convention for an adequately powered study.
✏️ Your turn: List the four things that increase power.
1. ________________________________________________________
2. ________________________________________________________
3. ________________________________________________________
4. ________________________________________________________



Part 4 · Effect Size — Cohen’s d
Cohen proposed rough benchmarks for small, medium, and large effects:
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 4.1 · Cohen's benchmarks ────────────────────────────────────
cohen.ES(test = "t", size = "small")$effect.size
cohen.ES(test = "t", size = "medium")$effect.size
cohen.ES(test = "t", size = "large")$effect.size
▶ Run this — the real Cohen’s d for both datasets:
# ── Part 4.2 · Cohen's d, pine and lizards ───────────────────────────
d_unpaired <- cohens_d(needle_length_mm ~ side, data = p_df)
d_unpaired

d_paired <- cohens_d(p_wide_df$shady, p_wide_df$sunny, paired = TRUE)
d_paired

d_lizard <- cohens_d(squamosal_horn_length_mm ~ survival, data = lizard_df)
d_lizard
✏️ Your turn: Record all three, and which Cohen bucket (small/medium/large) each lands in.
unpaired pine d = ______  bucket: ______
paired pine d   = ______  bucket: ______
lizard d        = ______  bucket: ______



Part 5 · A Priori Power — Planning Before You Collect Data
The most useful power analysis happens before you collect data: guess or borrow an effect size, then ask what sample size gives 80% power.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 5.1 · A priori power, pine (unpaired) ───────────────────────
pwr.t.test(
  d = d_unpaired$Cohens_d,
  power = 0.80,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  type = "two.sample"
)
✏️ Your turn: How many trees per side does that call for (always round n up)? How many did we actually collect?
________________________






Tip



🖐 Practice 5 · A smaller effect
The lizards gave a large effect (d ≈ 0.87). Suppose instead you are planning a new study where you only expect a medium effect (d = 0.5). Assuming equal group sizes, how many lizards per group would you need for 80% power?
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 5.2 · Practice 5 — a priori power, medium effect ────────────
pwr.t.test(d = 0.5, power = 0.80, sig.level = 0.05, type = "two.sample")
✏️ Your turn: How does that n compare to the pine study’s per-side n from Part 5.1?
________________________





Part 6 · Unequal Group Sizes — pwr.t2n.test()
The lizard groups are far from equal (154 living vs. 30 killed). pwr.t2n.test() takes the two actual group sizes directly — no averaging, no workaround.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 6.1 · Power with unequal group sizes ────────────────────────
pwr.t2n.test(
  n1 = sum(lizard_df$survival == "living"),
  n2 = sum(lizard_df$survival == "killed"),
  d = d_lizard$Cohens_d,
  sig.level = 0.05
)
✏️ Your turn: What is the power? Compare it to the pine study’s power at n = 4 (you’ll compute that next, in Part 7).
________________________



Part 7 · Retrospective (Post-Hoc) Power
The other direction: after a study, ask what power your actual n and observed effect size gave you.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 7.1 · Retrospective power, pine (unpaired) ──────────────────
pwr.t.test(
  n = 4,
  d = d_unpaired$Cohens_d,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  type = "two.sample"
)
✏️ Your turn: What is the power? If the pine difference is completely real, how often out of 10 would a study like ours miss it?
power = ______        we would miss it ______ times out of 10






Warning



⚠️ A warning about “post-hoc power”
Computing power from the effect size you observed is a known trap — it is fine for planning the next study, but it is not a valid way to explain away a non-significant result. “Our result was non-significant, but we had low power” says the same thing twice.








Tip



🖐 Practice 6 · Retrospective power, paired
You already calculated d_paired in Part 4.2 (the same four trees, paired instead of unpaired). Compute the retrospective power of the paired design at n = 4.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 7.2 · Practice 6 — retrospective power, paired ──────────────
pwr.t.test(n = 4, d = d_paired$Cohens_d, sig.level = 0.05, type = "paired")
✏️ Your turn: How much higher is the paired power than the unpaired power from Part 7.1?
________________________





Part 8 · Pairing Buys You Power
▶ Run this — trees needed for 80% power, paired:
# ── Part 8.1 · Trees needed, paired ──────────────────────────────────
pwr.t.test(
  d = d_paired$Cohens_d,
  power = 0.80,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  type = "paired"
)
✏️ Your turn: Fill in the table using Parts 5.1, 7.1, 7.2, and 8.1.
Design       Power at n = 4      Trees for 80% power
unpaired     ______              ______ per side
paired       ______              ______ total
✏️ Your turn: Same trees. Same needles. Same measurements. Where did the extra power come from?
________________________



Part 9 · Error Bars — SD, SE, and CI
summary_stats() gives you all three from one call: SD (spread of the raw data), SE (precision of the mean, SD / sqrt(n)), and the 95% CI (plausible range for the true mean).
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 9.1 · SD, SE, and CI for the lizard data ────────────────────
lizard_df %>%
  group_by(survival) %>%
  reframe(summary_stats(squamosal_horn_length_mm))
✏️ Your turn: Which of the three (SD, SE, CI) is widest, and which is narrowest, for each group? A large sample doesn’t shrink SD — what does it shrink, and why?
________________________



Part 10 · Pseudoreplication
Pseudoreplication occurs when measurements that are not independent are analyzed as if they were — for example, treating every pine needle as an independent replicate instead of every tree.
✏️ Your turn: Our pine needle data has 64 rows (needles), but only 4 trees per side. If we (wrongly) ran the power analysis in Part 7.1 on n = 32 needles per side instead of n = 4 trees, would the power come out higher or lower than the honest answer? Would that make the study actually better, or just make us believe it was?
________________________



Summary and Conclusions
In this activity, we’ve:

Classified Type I and Type II error scenarios
Calculated Cohen’s d for pine (paired and unpaired) and horned lizards
Run a priori power analysis to find the n a study needs, including for unequal group sizes with pwr.t2n.test()
Run retrospective power analysis on our own pine needle study
Compared unpaired vs. paired designs and seen what pairing buys in power
Compared SD, SE, and CI as answers to three different questions
Connected pseudoreplication to inflated apparent power

Key takeaways:

A priori power planning is the single most useful use of this toolkit
Retrospective power is for planning the next study, not excusing a null result
Report effect size and power alongside p-values, not instead of them



Reflection Questions

Why is an a priori power analysis only as good as the effect size fed into it?
Why does pwr.t2n.test() beat the old harmonic-mean workaround for unequal groups?
Why can pairing buy more power than adding raw sample size?
How would you explain “our study wasn’t wrong, it just didn’t have enough power” to someone who has never taken a statistics course?



Review and checkpoint
At this point you can:

Classify a scenario as a Type I error, a Type II error, or a correct decision
Calculate Cohen’s d for a paired and an unpaired design
Run an a priori power analysis with pwr.t.test() to find a required sample size
Run a power analysis for unequal group sizes with pwr.t2n.test()
Run a retrospective power analysis and explain why it should not excuse a null result
Explain what SD, SE, and CI each answer, and how pseudoreplication distorts them







Note



📤 What to turn in before next class
Upload both of these to the course management system:

Your code — the scripts/ folder (or just 08_power_and_error.R)
This worksheet, with your written answers

title: Activity: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Effect size — a demonstration






Note



👀 Read this one, don’t sweat it
This section is here so you have seen effect size before we need it in the power lecture. Run the two blocks, read the output, answer the two short questions. There is nothing to get stuck on.


Your paired t-test last week gave p = 0.072 — “not significant.” But p never said how much shorter the shady needles were. Cohen’s d does: it is the difference between groups measured in standard deviations, so it carries no units and can be compared across studies.
For a paired design, d is the mean of the paired differences divided by the standard deviation of those differences.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 1.3 · Effect size (demonstration) ────────────────────────────
diffs <- p_wide_df$shady - p_wide_df$sunny

mean(diffs) / sd(diffs)     # Cohen's d, by hand

# and with a confidence interval
cohens_d(p_wide_df$shady, p_wide_df$sunny, paired = TRUE)
✏️ Your turn: Write the value of d and its confidence interval here, then say in one plain sentence what the d value means.
d  = ______        95% CI = [ ______ , ______ ]

In words: the shady side averaged ______ standard deviations
          ____________ the sunny side.
▶ Run this — why it matters:
# ── Part 1.4 · Effect size (demonstration) ────────────────────────────
2.7227 / sqrt(4)      # our paired t statistic, divided by the square root of n
Compare that number to your d. They are the same, because t = d × √n — the t-statistic is the effect size multiplied by the square root of your sample size.
✏️ Your turn: If a p-value depends on both the size of the effect and how many samples you took, why is reporting d alongside p more informative than reporting p on its own?
________________________






Important



⚠️ The sentence worth remembering
“No significant difference” sounds like we found nothing. Our four trees actually gave a large effect (d = −1.36) that we simply could not pin down (the CI runs from −2.74 to 0.10). Those are very different messages, and only the second one is honest.



Now back to the rank tests. Run them even though the assumptions held — the point of this part is to find out what that choice would have cost you.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 1.5 · The two rank-based tests ───────────────────────────────
# unpaired: Mann-Whitney U
wilcox.test(needle_length_mm ~ side, data = p_df)

# paired: Wilcoxon signed-rank
wilcox.test(p_wide_df$shady, p_wide_df$sunny, paired = TRUE)
✏️ Your turn: Fill in the comparison table.
                        parametric        non-parametric
unpaired:               p = 0.425         p = ______
paired:                 p = 0.072         p = ______
✏️ Your turn: Did the two approaches lead you to the same conclusion? Did they give the same p-value?
________________________
✏️ Your turn: Look at the signed-rank statistic, V. What value did you get, and what does it say about how consistent the four trees were?
________________________
▶ Run this — the floor:
# ── Part 1.6 · The floor ──────────────────────────────────────────────
2 / 2^4     # smallest two-sided p a signed-rank test can give with 4 pairs
✏️ Your turn: Compare that number to the p-value you got from the signed-rank test. What does that tell you about whether the test could have found our effect significant, even in principle?
________________________
✏️ Your turn: Based on all of this, which test would you report for the pine needle data, and why?
________________________






Tip



🚀 If you finish early: How many pairs would you need before a signed-rank test could possibly reach p < 0.05? Try 2 / 2^5, 2 / 2^6, and so on until you find it.

title: Activity: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Background
Male sagebrush crickets (Cyphoderris strepitans) have an unusual mating system: during copulation the female eats the tips of the male’s hind wings and drinks his haemolymph. A male who has already mated has damaged wings, and is therefore visibly “starved” relative to a virgin male.
The question is whether that costs him. Johnson et al. measured time to mating — how many hours a male waited before securing a mate — for males that had already mated (starved) and males that had not (fed).






Important



⚠️ This is Example 13.5 in Whitlock & Schluter
These are the data the textbook uses to introduce the Mann-Whitney U test in Chapter 13. That is deliberate: after you have made your own decision and written it up, you can read the chapter and see how the authors justified theirs.
Do the work first. The point of this assignment is your reasoning, not matching the book.








ImportantColumn names in sage_brush_crickets_feeding_mating.csv










Column
What it is

"fed" (virgin male) or "starved" (already mated)


time_to_mating_h

title: Activity: NMDS & PERMANOVA
text:
▶ Run this in your Script:
# ── Setup (1) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
library(vegan)
library(janitor)
library(patchwork)
library(tidyverse)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 9))
What is NMDS? NMDS (Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling) is an ordination technique that:

Visualizes dissimilarity between objects in reduced dimensions
Preserves rank order of distances, not exact distances
Works well with non-linear ecological relationships
Makes few assumptions about data structure

When to use NMDS: community data (species abundance or presence/absence matrices), non-linear relationships (when PCA assumptions are violated), or complex ecological gradients (multiple environmental factors affecting communities).
Key concepts of NMDS:

Dissimilarity matrices instead of covariance
Stress values measure goodness of fit (< 0.2 is acceptable)
Iterative algorithm to find optimal configuration
No eigenvalues - axes have no inherent meaning
Rank-based - preserves order, not exact distances







Important



Critical first step: Always check your stress value! Stress < 0.1 is excellent, 0.1-0.2 is good, > 0.2 is poor representation.

title: Activity: NMDS & PERMANOVA
text:
Step 4: Pairwise PERMANOVA
# ── Part 3.4 · PERMANOVA Analysis ───────────────────────────────────────
pairwise_permanova <- function(data_matrix, groups, distance_method = "euclidean") {
  group_levels <- unique(groups)
  comparisons <- combn(group_levels, 2)

  results_df <- data.frame(
    group1 = character(),
    group2 = character(),
    f_statistic = numeric(),
    r_squared = numeric(),
    p_value = numeric()
  )

  for(i in 1:ncol(comparisons)) {
    group1 <- comparisons[1, i]
    group2 <- comparisons[2, i]
    subset_indices <- which(groups %in% c(group1, group2))

    subset_data <- data_matrix[subset_indices, ]
    subset_groups <- groups[subset_indices]

    temp_result <- adonis2(subset_data ~ subset_groups,
                          method = distance_method,
                          permutations = 999)

    results_df <- rbind(results_df, data.frame(
      group1 = group1,
      group2 = group2,
      f_statistic = temp_result$F[1],
      r_squared = temp_result$R2[1],
      p_value = temp_result$"Pr(>F)"[1]
    ))
  }

  results_df$p_adjusted <- p.adjust(results_df$p_value, method = "bonferroni")

  return(results_df)
}

pairwise_results_df <- pairwise_permanova(iris_numeric_df, iris_df$species)

title: Activity: Multiple Regression
text:
Worksheet: Multiple Regression
📥 Bird data 📥 Tools script (.R) 📥 Script skeleton (.R)
The lecture’s dataset: 56 remnant forest patches in Victoria, Australia, from Loyn (1987). Bird abundance is the response, and six patch characteristics are the candidate predictors.
The order matters today. You will fit the predictors one at a time, then build one clean two-predictor model and read it carefully — that is the worked example. Only then do you put all six in at once and watch what happens.



Part 1 · Setup and the data
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 1.1 · Setup and the data ───────────────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)
library(car)

source("themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R")

bird_df <- read_csv("data/loyn_birds.csv") %>%
  mutate(log_area        = log10(area_ha),
         log_dist        = log10(dist_m),
         log_dist_larger = log10(dist_larger_m))

bird_df
✏️ Your turn: Why are area and the two distances logged? Look at the range of area_ha.
____________________________________________________________



Part 2 · One predictor at a time
▶ Run this — three separate simple regressions:
# ── Part 2.1 · One predictor at a time ──────────────────────────────────
summary(lm(abundance ~ log_area, data = bird_df))

summary(lm(abundance ~ grazing, data = bird_df))

summary(lm(abundance ~ year_isolated, data = bird_df))
✏️ Your turn: Record each one.
log_area:      slope = __________  p = __________

grazing:       slope = __________  p = __________

year_isolated: slope = __________  p = __________

How many are significant? __________



Part 3 · Two predictors — the worked example
Area and grazing were the two strongest predictors on their own. Put both in one model. This is the whole idea of multiple regression in its simplest form: one response, two predictors, two slopes.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 3.1 · Two predictors — the worked example ──────────────────────
reduced_model <- lm(abundance ~ log_area + grazing, data = bird_df)

summary(reduced_model)
✏️ Your turn: Write the fitted equation out, with the numbers in it.
abundance = ______ + ______ × log_area + ______ × grazing
✏️ Your turn: Read each slope as a sentence. The phrase you need is “holding the other predictor constant.”
log_area: ___________________________________________________

grazing:  ___________________________________________________
Notice that both slopes shrank compared with Part 2 — area from about 9.8 to 6.9, grazing from about −5.0 to −2.9. Part 4 is about why.



Part 4 · Now all six at once
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 4.1 · Now all six at once ──────────────────────────────────────
full_model <- lm(abundance ~ log_area + log_dist +
                   log_dist_larger + year_isolated +
                   grazing + altitude_m,
                 data = bird_df)

summary(full_model)
✏️ Your turn: Which predictors are still significant, and what happened to grazing?
Still significant: _________________________________________

grazing slope:  alone ______   two-predictor ______   here ______
✏️ Your turn: All three grazing slopes came from the same 56 patches. Is any of them wrong? Say what each one is actually measuring.
____________________________________________________________

____________________________________________________________



Part 5 · Why it happened
▶ Run this:

bird_df %>%
  select(log_area, log_dist, log_dist_larger,
         year_isolated, grazing, altitude_m) %>%
  cor() %>%
  round(2)

✏️ Your turn: Find the two most strongly correlated predictors, and say in one sentence what that correlation means on the ground.
Pair: __________ and __________   r = __________

On the ground: ______________________________________________
✏️ Your turn: All the VIFs are small. Does that mean collinearity is not a problem here?

Part 6 · Which model do you keep?
▶ Run this — test whether the four extra predictors earned anything, then compare the two models on AIC:
# ── Part 6.1 · Which model do you keep? ─────────────────────────────────
anova(reduced_model, full_model)

tibble(
  model  = c("six predictors", "log_area + grazing"),
  adj_r2 = c(summary(full_model)$adj.r.squared,
             summary(reduced_model)$adj.r.squared),
  AIC    = c(AIC(full_model), AIC(reduced_model))
)
✏️ Your turn: Do the two methods agree? Which model do you keep?

Part 7 · Check the assumptions
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 7.1 · Check the assumptions ────────────────────────────────────
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(reduced_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

shapiro.test(residuals(reduced_model))
✏️ Your turn: One line per assumption.
Linearity: __________________________________________________

Equal variance: _____________________________________________

Normality (Shapiro p = ______): _____________________________

Influential points: _________________________________________



Part 8 · Grazing as a factor
Grazing has been a number, 1 to 5, which forces every step to cost the same. Now let it be a category so each level is estimated separately.
▶ Run this — make it a factor and look at the order R chose:
# ── Part 8.1 · Grazing as a factor ──────────────────────────────────────
bird_df <- bird_df %>%
  mutate(grazing_class = factor(grazing_class))

levels(bird_df$grazing_class)

summary(lm(abundance ~ log_area + grazing_class, data = bird_df))
✏️ Your turn: Which level is R using as the reference, and why did it pick that one?
Reference level: __________   Why: _________________________
▶ Run this — put the least-grazed level first instead:
# ── Part 8.2 · Grazing as a factor ──────────────────────────────────────
bird_df <- bird_df %>%
  mutate(grazing_class = fct_relevel(grazing_class,
                                     "minimal", "light", "moderate",
                                     "heavy", "intense"))

levels(bird_df$grazing_class)

grazing_model <- lm(abundance ~ log_area + grazing_class, data = bird_df)

summary(grazing_model)
✏️ Your turn: Write down the four grazing coefficients and their p-values.
light:    __________  p = __________

moderate: __________  p = __________

heavy:    __________  p = __________

intense:  __________  p = __________
✏️ Your turn: The R² and F-statistic are identical in 8.1 and 8.2 — only the coefficients moved. Given that, what did fitting grazing as the number 1–5 (one slope of about −2.9 birds per step, back in Part 3) hide from you?
____________________________________________________________

____________________________________________________________



Part 9 · The figure you hand in
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 9.1 · The figure you hand in ───────────────────────────────────
final_plot <- ggplot(bird_df, aes(log_area, abundance,
                                  colour = grazing_class)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Bird abundance rises with patch area and falls under intense grazing",
    subtitle = "56 remnant forest patches, Victoria, Australia (Loyn 1987)",
    x = "log10 patch area (ha)",
    y = "Bird abundance",
    colour = "Grazing"
  ) +
  theme_regular(base_size = 12)

final_plot

ggsave(
  "figures/bird_regression.pdf",
  plot   = final_plot,
  width  = 7,
  height = 4.5,
  units  = "in"
)
✏️ Your turn: Open the PDF and check the legend order runs minimal → intense, not alphabetically.



Review and checkpoint
At this point you can:

Fit a two-predictor model and read each partial slope as “holding the other constant”
Explain why a slope changes when another predictor joins the model
Read a correlation matrix and vif() output
Say what a dataset cannot separate, rather than that a predictor “has no effect”

In Activity 14 you analysed the sea urchin experiment with aov(algae ~ treat + Error(patch)). It gave the right answer — F = 2.72 on 3 and 12 df, p = 0.091 — by forcing the treatment to be tested against patch-to-patch variation.
Error() is the 1960s way to get the right denominator. It works, and it is brittle: it needs a balanced design, it cannot handle more than one grouping cleanly, and it tells you nothing about how much variation lives among patches.

Part 3c · Axis limits with coord_cartesian()
Follows Lecture Part 2c — coord_cartesian().

ggplot picks the axis range from your data. That is fine while you explore, and wrong the moment a reader has to judge how big a difference is. Set the limits on purpose.
▶ Run this in your Script:

# Start the y-axis at zero so the difference is shown at its real size

  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Length by Side of Tree",
    x = "Side of tree",
    y = "Needle length (mm)"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 25)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
▶ Run this — both axes at once, on two continuous variables:
# ── Part 3c.2 · Axis limits with coord_cartesian() ──────────────────────
pine_scatter_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm, y = needle_width_mm,
                                         color = side)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Width vs. Length",
    x = "Needle length (mm)",
    y = "Needle width (mm)",
    color = "Side"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(5, 25), ylim = c(0.4, 1.8)) +
  theme_minimal()

pine_scatter_plot






Warning



⚠️ The trap we just saw on screen — use coord_cartesian(), not ylim()
ylim(14, 16) and scale_y_continuous(limits = c(14, 16)) filter your data before the geom draws it. Every row outside the range is dropped, and the median, quartiles, and whiskers are recomputed from what survives — behind a “removed rows” warning that is very easy to read past.
coord_cartesian() computes the statistics on all the data and then zooms the view. The boxes do not move.
The rule: coord_cartesian() to zoom, filter() when you actually mean to remove data — on purpose, in the data step, where you can see it.

Note



✅ Why source() instead of copy-paste

ImportantWhat you hand in




All of today’s code is right here in this activity. Type it into your script as we go and run it chunk by chunk. The skeleton has the plumbing — libraries and the two data reads — and nothing else. Every line of statistics you type yourself.
Section 6 has no code here either. By then you will have run the same three steps three times, so you do them once more on your own.
The Q boxes are things to think about, not inline homework. Read them, talk them over, answer them in your head. You do not have to type answers into the script, and they are not graded.
The write-up at the bottom — sections 8, 9, and 10 — is graded. Those answers go into the script as # comments.
Hand in scripts/15_glm_logistic_regression.R. Run it top to bottom (Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter) first — it must run with no errors.









Note🔮 Predict before you run



Today is a chain of three models where each one fails for a different reason, and the failure is the content. Before each model, say out loud whether you expect it to work — then look at the diagnostic, not the p-value.








TipThe invisible(NULL) lines in the skeleton



Every section ends with invisible(NULL). It is a bumper. Press Ctrl/Cmd + Enter on a section’s last real line and your cursor jumps to the next line that has code on it — without the bumper, that is the next section, way down past the next heading. With it, the cursor stops right there and you keep your place. It does nothing and prints nothing.


Keep the plots plain today — no labels, colors, or themes. The goal is to read them. The one exception is the final figure in section 10, which is the graded deliverable.




For the last three weeks every model has been a linear model — one-way ANOVA, factorial, nested. All of them assume the residuals are normal with constant variance. That is a fine assumption for body mass or algae cover.
It is a bad assumption for a count. A count is a whole number, it cannot go below zero, and its variance usually grows with its mean. Today is what you do instead.
A generalized linear model keeps the linear part and swaps out two things:

Why a project folder?
Everything for this project lives in one folder, so every file path is relative to it — no more hunting for where a file went.

📖 Read more: R4DS §6 — Workflow: scripts and projects, and Gotelli & Ellison Ch. 8 (Managing and Curating Data) on Canvas.



Create the folder structure
Make a new folder called pine_project. Inside it, create four sub-folders:
pine_project/
├── data/       ← your CSV and Excel files go here
├── scripts/    ← your .R code goes here
├── figures/    ← plots you save go here
└── output/    ← place to save modified dataframes
Copy pine_data.csv into pine_project/data/.

⚠️ Important: Leave this copy alone — it is raw data. We will read it but never overwrite it. (Your own field data will get cleaned up and added here starting in Wrangling Your Data.)

Part 3 · Enter your data in Excel
Before R ever sees your numbers, they have to get from your field notes into a spreadsheet. How you do that now determines how much pain you’re in later — so we do it deliberately.

Set up your header row first
Open Excel and make row 1 your column headers — nothing else goes in that row. Use the same controlled vocabulary your group already agreed on in Part 1, written the lower_snake_case way (no spaces, no units hidden in the text): what will they be?



Column
units?
What goes in it














































⚠️ Watch out! Needle Length (mm) and needle_length_mm look equally clear to a human — only one of them is a header R can use without a fight. Spaces, parentheses, and units in the header text all cause problems later.



One row = one measurement
This is the part people get wrong under time pressure: every single needle you measured gets its own row. Not one row per tree with eight length columns crammed in — one row per needle, with team, side, and replicate repeated on every row that needle belongs to. Yes, that means typing shady over and over. That repetition is doing real work — it’s what lets R filter, group, and plot by any of those columns later.






Warning



⚠️ Watch out! — Common Excel data-entry mistakes

Merged cells. They look nice, they break every import. Never merge.
Blank rows or blank columns used as visual spacers. R reads them as missing data, not as whitespace.
More than one header row, or notes typed above row 1. R will try to read your note as a column name.
Numbers stored as text. 20 mm in a cell is text; 20 is a number. Keep units in the header, not in the cell.
Inconsistent spelling of the same category — Sunny, sunny (trailing space), and sunny are three different values to R, even though they mean the same thing to you.
Color-coding instead of a column. Highlighting a row yellow to mean something is invisible to R. If it matters, it needs its own column.





Enter your group’s data

side, per tree, on _____________ trees? Show your arithmetic:

Tip



🖐 Honest preview — this probably isn’t “tidy” yet
Excel invites you to spread related numbers across columns — one column per tree, or one column per needle. That’s a completely normal way to enter data quickly, and it is not the same as tidy data: the rule (from R for Data Science) that every variable is a column, every observation is a row, and every value is a cell. If your sheet doesn’t fully follow that yet, that’s fine — turning a wide, human-friendly layout into a tidy one is exactly what we’ll do with pivot_longer() in Wrangling Your Data. Today, just get the numbers in accurately.




Save it — both formats
File → Save As, into your pine_project/data/ folder, twice:

Once as an Excel workbook (.xlsx) — keeps any formatting you added.
Once as CSV UTF-8 (.csv) — plain text, no hidden formatting, and the format every other tool (including R) can read without a special library.


⚠️ Important: Save both into data/, and — like pine_data.csv — treat them as raw data from this point on: read them, never hand-edit them again. Corrections happen in R, where every change is a line of code you can see and undo.

Part 6 · Naming things well
Good names make code readable months later: be explicit (needle_length, not x2), never start with a number, and R is case-sensitive (needle_length_mm ≠ Needle_Length_mm). Use lower_snake_case.

Part 9 · Vectors and data types
A vector is a series of values built with c() which is also called a concatenated list and we will see it more. A spreadsheet column is really just a vector.

Part 12 · Your first plot
Every ggplot is built from three pieces, joined with +: data, aes() (which columns map to x/y), and a geom (how to draw it).

📖 Read more: R4DS §1 — Data visualization. For why we plot before we test, see Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 2 (Displaying Data) on Canvas.

▶ Run this — the simplest possible plot:

  geom_point()

⚠️ Watch out! The + sits at the end of a line, never the start.

Homework
Homework 1 — Intro to R
You will build a project from scratch — directories, a Quarto file, and a script — and read in a dataset you have not seen in class: Arctic grayling from lakes I-3 and I-8, measured on the North Slope of Alaska. You read the same data twice, once from .csv and once from .xlsx, then summarise and plot it and save the figure to PDF.
Data: gray_I3_I8.csv and gray_I3_I8.xlsx — a course field dataset, not a textbook one, so there is no chapter to look up.

Worksheet: Describing Your Data
📥 Download the data (.csv) 📥 Download the data (.xlsx) 📥 Script skeleton (.R)






ImportantColumn names in pine_data.csv / pine_data.xlsx



Both files hold the same six columns, with exactly these names. Type them exactly as written — R is case-sensitive, and Needle_Length or needle_length will not work:



Column
What it is




source_file
the raw team file the row came from


team
field team — one team = one tree


replicate
needle number within a tree side (1-8)


side
sun exposure — "shady" or "sunny"


needle_length_mm
needle length, millimetres


needle_width_mm
needle width, millimetres



After you read the file in, run names(pine_df) and check the names on your screen against this table before you write any other code.





Part 1 · Load and split the data
▶ Run this in your Script:
# ── Part 1.1 · Load and split the data ──────────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)

pine_df <- read_csv("data/pine_data.csv")

shady_df <- pine_df |> filter(side == "shady")
sunny_df <- pine_df |> filter(side == "sunny")

shady_df
filter() picks rows and hands back a data frame — same six columns, fewer rows. Everything from here on stays a data frame, summarized with the pipe.

Part 3b · Quantiles, range, and IQR

📖 Read more: Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 2 (Displaying Data) — the box in a boxplot is the IQR.

▶ Run this:
# ── Part 3b.1 · Quantiles, range, and IQR ───────────────────────────────
shady_df |>
  summarize(
    min_mm   = min(needle_length_mm),
    q25_mm   = quantile(needle_length_mm, 0.25),
    med_mm   = median(needle_length_mm),
    q75_mm   = quantile(needle_length_mm, 0.75),
    max_mm   = max(needle_length_mm),
    range_mm = max_mm - min_mm,
    iqr_mm   = IQR(needle_length_mm)
  )

Part 4 · The length() trap

📖 Read more: R4DS §18 — Missing values.

▶ Run this:
# ── Part 4.1 · The `length()` trap ──────────────────────────────────────
na_demo_df <- tibble(length_mm = c(4, 3, NA, 7, NA))

na_demo_df |>
  summarize(
    rows        = n(),                     # every row, missing values included
    missing     = sum(is.na(length_mm)),
    real_values = sum(!is.na(length_mm))   # the n you actually want
  )
✏️ Your turn: Explain in your own words why n() gives the wrong answer for a sample size when there are missing values.

________________________________________________________
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 4.2 · The `length()` trap ──────────────────────────────────────
na_demo_df |>
  summarize(
    wrong_n  = n(),
    right_n  = sum(!is.na(length_mm)),
    sd_mm    = sd(length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    wrong_se = sd_mm / sqrt(wrong_n),
    right_se = sd_mm / sqrt(right_n)
  )
✏️ Your turn: Are wrong_se and right_se the same number? Why or why not?

Part 5 · Standard error, on real data

📖 Read more: Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 4 (Estimating with Uncertainty) — the chapter for the standard error.

▶ Run this:
# ── Part 5.1 · Standard error, on real data ─────────────────────────────
shady_df |>
  summarize(
    n     = sum(!is.na(needle_length_mm)),
    sd_mm = sd(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_mm = sd_mm / sqrt(n)
  )

sunny_df |>
  summarize(
    n     = sum(!is.na(needle_length_mm)),
    sd_mm = sd(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_mm = sd_mm / sqrt(n)
  )

📖 Read more: R4DS §3.5 — Groups and summarize().

shady_df |>

    n       = sum(!is.na(needle_length_mm)),
    mean_mm = round(mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    med_mm  = round(median(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    sd_mm   = round(sd(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    se_mm   = round(sd(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n), 2)

Part 7 · Tidy group stats — group_by() + summarize()

📖 Read more: R4DS §3.5 — Groups.

You just wrote the same summarize() twice — once for shady_df, once for sunny_df. group_by() removes that duplication: it splits the whole data frame by a column, and summarize() then returns one row per group. No filter(), no two objects to keep in step.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 7.1 · Tidy group stats ─────────────────────────────────────────
side_stats_df <- pine_df |>
  group_by(side) |>
  summarize(
    n       = sum(!is.na(needle_length_mm)),
    mean_mm = round(mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    med_mm  = round(median(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    sd_mm   = round(sd(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    se_mm   = round(sd(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n), 2)
  )

side_stats_df

⚠️ Watch out! Compute se_mm from the raw sd(), not from the sd_mm column above it — that one has already been rounded, and the SE would inherit the rounding error. Round only what you print.

✏️ Your turn: Do the mean_mm and se_mm values match the ones you calculated one side at a time in Parts 2 and 5?
Y / N

Tip



🚀 If you finish early: Group by both team and side at once (group_by(team, side)). How many rows does the result have, and why?





Part 7c · The n you report is a choice

📖 Read more: Gotelli & Ellison Ch. 6 (Designing Successful Field Studies) on replication and pseudoreplication; Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 4 on what the standard error is an estimate of.

Your side summary said n = 32 per side. But we sampled only 4 trees — 8 needles from each. Counting needles as independent is the pseudoreplication from Getting Started.
▶ Run this — stage 1, collapse each tree to one number:
# ── Part 7c.1 · The `n` you report is a choice ──────────────────────────
team_means_df <- pine_df |>
  group_by(team, side) |>
  summarize(team_mean_mm = mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

team_means_df
▶ Run this — stage 2, summarize those team means:
# ── Part 7c.2 · The `n` you report is a choice ──────────────────────────
side_correct_df <- team_means_df |>
  group_by(side) |>
  summarize(
    n_trees = sum(!is.na(team_mean_mm)),
    mean_mm = round(mean(team_mean_mm), 2),
    se_mm   = round(sd(team_mean_mm) / sqrt(n_trees), 2)
  )

side_correct_df
✏️ Your turn: Fill in the comparison.
                 naive (n = 32)      correct (n = 4)
mean, shady:     ______              ______
mean, sunny:     ______              ______
SE, shady:       ______              ______
SE, sunny:       ______              ______
✏️ Your turn: Which changed — the means, the standard errors, or both? What does that tell you about what pseudoreplication actually damages?
________________________



Part 7b · See it — boxplot with mean ± SE

📖 Read more: Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 2 (Displaying Data), and R4DS §10 — Exploratory data analysis.

Every number you computed today has a picture. This is the figure you will build for the rest of the term, so it is worth getting the layers straight.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 7b.1 · See it — boxplot with mean ± SE ─────────────────────────
side_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm)) +

  # layer 1 — the spread of all 64 needles
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, fill = NA, outlier.shape = NA) +

  # layer 2 — each team's mean, faded, behind the summary
  geom_point(data = team_means_df,
             aes(y = team_mean_mm, color = team),
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.5),
             size = 3, alpha = 0.5) +

  # layer 3 — the mean and its standard error, on top
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", width = 0.15) +

  labs(x = "Sun exposure",
       y = "Needle length (mm)",
       color = "Field team") +
  theme_bw()

side_plot
stat_summary() computes a statistic while plotting — you never have to build a summary table first. fun = mean draws the mean as a point; fun.data = mean_se draws the mean ± 1 standard error as an error bar.
✏️ Your turn: The box and the error bar show different things. Which one describes the spread of individual needles, and which describes how precisely we know the mean?

Error bar:    ________________________________________

       units  = "in",
       dpi    = 300)

title: Activity: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Worksheet: Correlation and Linear Regression
📥 Booby data 📥 Rope trick data 📥 Lion data 📥 Tools script (.R) 📥 Script skeleton (.R)
This worksheet runs in two halves, matching the lecture. Parts 1–4 are correlation: two measured variables, one number, no direction. Parts 5–8 are regression: a fitted line, the sums of squares it is made of, and the diagnostics that decide whether to believe it.
Three datasets, all from Whitlock & Schluter:

booby_aggression.csv — Example 16.1. Nestling visits and adult aggression in Nazca boobies
rope_trick.csv — Example 16.5. Years since seeing the Indian rope trick, and how impressive it is remembered as
lion_noses.csv — Example 17.1. Proportion of black on a male lion’s nose, and its age




Part 1 · Setup and the data
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 1.1 · Setup and the data ───────────────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

source("themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R")

booby_df <- read_csv("data/booby_aggression.csv")
rope_df  <- read_csv("data/rope_trick.csv")
lion_df  <- read_csv("data/lion_noses.csv")

booby_df



Part 2 · Correlation
▶ Run this — look at the data before you test it:
# ── Part 2.1 · Correlation ──────────────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(booby_df, aes(visits_as_nestling, future_aggression)) +
  geom_point()
✏️ Your turn: Is the trend straight, or is there a curve in it? Any point far off on its own?


____________________________________________________________
▶ Run this — the coefficient, then the test:
# ── Part 2.2 · Correlation ──────────────────────────────────────────────
cor(booby_df$visits_as_nestling, booby_df$future_aggression)

cor.test(booby_df$visits_as_nestling, booby_df$future_aggression)
▶ Run this — square it for the variance explained:
# ── Part 2.3 · Correlation ──────────────────────────────────────────────
r_booby <- cor(booby_df$visits_as_nestling, booby_df$future_aggression)

r_booby^2
✏️ Your turn: Fill these in from the output above.


r = ____________   p = ____________   r squared = ____________

What share of the variation do the two variables share? ____________ %

✏️ Your turn: Write one sentence stating what the correlation means biologically — without using the word “cause.”

____________________________________________________________


____________________________________________________________



Part 3 · Correlation assumptions
Pearson’s r assumes both variables are normal, the relationship is linear, and no outlier is driving it.
▶ Run this — the formal test on each variable:
# ── Part 3.1 · Correlation assumptions ──────────────────────────────────
shapiro.test(booby_df$visits_as_nestling)

shapiro.test(booby_df$future_aggression)
▶ Run this — and the picture:
# ── Part 3.2 · Correlation assumptions ──────────────────────────────────
h1 <- ggplot(booby_df, aes(visits_as_nestling)) + geom_histogram(bins = 10)
h2 <- ggplot(booby_df, aes(future_aggression)) + geom_histogram(bins = 10)
q1 <- ggplot(booby_df, aes(sample = visits_as_nestling)) + geom_qq() + geom_qq_line()
q2 <- ggplot(booby_df, aes(sample = future_aggression)) + geom_qq() + geom_qq_line()

(h1 / h2) | (q1 / q2)
✏️ Your turn: Remember H₀ here is “these data ARE normal.” Do both variables pass?


visits: p = __________ pass? ______    aggression: p = __________ pass? ______
✏️ Your turn: One of them lands very close to 0.05 while its QQ plot looks fine. At n = 24, which do you believe, and does it change the coefficient you report?


____________________________________________________________



Part 4 · When normality fails
Same workflow, a dataset that does not cooperate: an impressiveness score, which is bounded and lumpy.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 4.1 · When normality fails ─────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(rope_df, aes(years_since_seen, impressiveness)) +
  geom_point()

shapiro.test(rope_df$impressiveness)
▶ Run this — both coefficients on the same data:
# ── Part 4.2 · When normality fails ─────────────────────────────────────
cor.test(rope_df$years_since_seen, rope_df$impressiveness)

cor.test(rope_df$years_since_seen, rope_df$impressiveness,
         method = "spearman")
✏️ Your turn: Which coefficient do you report for these data, and why?

Pearson r = __________   Spearman rho = __________

I report ______________ because ______________________________
✏️ Your turn: Spearman works on ranks. What did you give up by switching to it?
____________________________________________________________
That is the correlation half. The rest of the worksheet fits a line.



Part 5 · Fitting a regression
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 5.1 · Fitting a regression ─────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(lion_df, aes(proportion_black, age_years)) +
  geom_point()

lion_model <- lm(age_years ~ proportion_black, data = lion_df)

summary(lion_model)
✏️ Your turn: Write the fitted equation, then the slope as a sentence in the units of the data.

age = ____________ + ____________ x proportion_black


For every 0.1 more black on the nose, predicted age goes up by ______ years.
✏️ Your turn: The intercept is the predicted age at proportion_black = 0. The youngest lion measured was 1.1 years old. Is the intercept a statement about newborn lions? Why not?

____________________________________________________________
▶ Run this — the line with its confidence band:
# ── Part 5.2 · Fitting a regression ─────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(lion_df, aes(proportion_black, age_years)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
▶ Run this — predict a lion with a half-black nose, two ways:
# ── Part 5.3 · Fitting a regression ─────────────────────────────────────
new_lion <- tibble(proportion_black = 0.50)

predict(lion_model, new_lion, interval = "confidence")

predict(lion_model, new_lion, interval = "prediction")
✏️ Your turn: Which interval is wider, and what question does each one answer?
____________________________________________________________



Part 6 · Sums of squares
The lecture’s centrepiece: build the partition yourself, then let R hand you the same numbers.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 6.1 · Sums of squares ──────────────────────────────────────────
fitted_age <- predict(lion_model)
mean_age   <- mean(lion_df$age_years)

ss_total <- sum((lion_df$age_years - mean_age)^2)
ss_reg   <- sum((fitted_age - mean_age)^2)
ss_resid <- sum((lion_df$age_years - fitted_age)^2)

c(total = ss_total, regression = ss_reg, residual = ss_resid)

ss_reg + ss_resid
✏️ Your turn: Does the partition add up, and what fraction of the total does the line account for?
ss_reg + ss_resid = __________   ss_total = __________

ss_reg / ss_total = __________   Where have you seen that number before? ______
▶ Run this — the same three numbers from R:
# ── Part 6.2 · Sums of squares ──────────────────────────────────────────
anova(lion_model)
✏️ Your turn: Match the table to what you computed.
Sum Sq, proportion_black row = __________   Sum Sq, Residuals row = __________

Df = ______ and ______      Mean Sq = Sum Sq / ______
▶ Run this — the t on the slope, squared:
# ── Part 6.3 · Sums of squares ──────────────────────────────────────────
summary(lion_model)$coefficients

summary(lion_model)$coefficients[2, 3]^2
✏️ Your turn: Compare that to the F value in the ANOVA table. What does the match tell you about the two tests?
t squared = __________   F = __________

____________________________________________________________



Part 7 · Regression assumptions
Every check from here is on the residuals, not the raw data.
▶ Run this — the four standard diagnostic plots:
# ── Part 7.1 · Regression assumptions ───────────────────────────────────
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(lion_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
▶ Run this — the formal test on the residuals:
# ── Part 7.2 · Regression assumptions ───────────────────────────────────
shapiro.test(residuals(lion_model))
✏️ Your turn: One line per assumption. Say what you looked at, not just pass or fail.
Linearity (residuals vs fitted): ____________________________

Equal variance (scale-location): ____________________________

Normality (QQ + Shapiro p = ______): ________________________

Influential points (Cook's distance): _______________________
✏️ Your turn: Would you report this model as it stands? One sentence.
____________________________________________________________



Part 8 · The figure you hand in
Everything above was for looking. This one is for showing, so it gets the full treatment.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 8.1 · The figure you hand in ───────────────────────────────────
final_plot <- ggplot(lion_df, aes(proportion_black, age_years)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "blue") +
  AND MAKE IT YOUR OWN

final_plot

ggsave(
  "figures/yourname_lion_regression.pdf",
  plot   = final_plot,
  width  = 6,
  height = 4,
  units  = "in"
)
✏️ Your turn: Open the PDF and check the axis labels are readable before you submit it.



Review and checkpoint
At this point you can:

Run and interpret cor.test(), and square r for the variance explained
Check correlation assumptions on the raw variables and switch to Spearman when they fail
Fit a line with lm() and state the slope in the units of the data
Build \(SS_{regression}\), \(SS_{residual}\) and \(SS_{total}\) by hand and match them to anova()
Show that t² = F for a one-predictor model
Read the four regression diagnostics off the residuals
Export a labelled figure to PDF







Note



📤 What to turn in

10_correlation_linear_models.R
figures/lion_regression.pdf
This worksheet, with your written answers






Homework
Homework 5 — Correlation & Regression: The Transformation You Have to Find
One hundred stream invertebrate species, body mass against population density. You run Parts 5–8 of this worksheet again — fit, interpret, partition into sums of squares, check the residuals — in the same order and with the same functions.
The difference is that here the diagnostics do not confirm the model. On the raw data the regression says there is nothing there: a slope near zero, R² of 0.001, p = 0.73. The residuals say otherwise, and finding the transformation that fixes it is the assignment. Once you have it, there is a second question waiting: the slope has a predicted value from theory, so “is the slope different from zero” is not the interesting test.
Data: stream_invertebrates.csv — Whitlock & Schluter, The Analysis of Biological Data, Chapter 16, Figure 16.4-1. Note that the book ships these data already log-transformed; ours are the back-transformed raw values, so look the figure up after you have run your own diagnostics, not before.
Hand in: your 10_correlation_regression_homework.R script, your final figure as a PDF, and the worksheet with your written answers.

title: Activity: ANCOVA
text:
Say what a covariate is, and the two different jobs it does
Test homogeneity of slopes, and know why it comes first
Fit an additive ANCOVA and read its ANOVA table
Measure what the covariate bought you — in residual SS and in F
Read adjusted means, and say how they differ from raw means
Recognise heterogeneous slopes and stop before fitting the wrong model
Use emtrends() to compare slopes, and contrast groups at covariate values
Say where an ANCOVA adjustment becomes extrapolation







Tip📂 Files for today



📥 Script skeleton (.R) 📥 Fruitfly data 📥 Grayling data

Save the skeleton as scripts/17_ancova.R, and both .csv files in your data/ folder.
You already have gray_I3_I8.csv from week 5 — same fish, new question.









ImportantWhat you hand in




All of today’s code is right here in this activity. Type it into your script as we go and run it chunk by chunk. The skeleton has the plumbing — libraries and the two data reads — and nothing else. Every line of statistics you type yourself.
Section 6 has no code here either. By then you will have run the whole workflow once, so you start it again on your own.
The Q boxes are things to think about, not inline homework. Read them, talk them over, answer them in your head. You do not have to type answers into the script, and they are not graded.
The write-up at the bottom — sections 8, 9, and 10 — is graded. Those answers go into the script as # comments.
Hand in scripts/17_ancova.R. Run it top to bottom (Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter) first — it must run with no errors.









Note🔮 Predict before you run



Today has one decision in it, and everything downstream depends on getting it right: are the slopes parallel? You will meet one dataset where they are and one where they are not. Before each test, look at the plot and commit to an answer out loud.








TipThe invisible(NULL) lines in the skeleton



Every section ends with invisible(NULL). It is a bumper. Press Ctrl/Cmd + Enter on a section’s last real line and your cursor jumps to the next line that has code on it — without the bumper, that is the next section, way down past the next heading. With it, the cursor stops right there and you keep your place. It does nothing and prints nothing.


Keep the plots plain today — no labels, colors, or themes. The goal is to read them. The one exception is the final figure in section 10, which is the graded deliverable.




Week 10 changed the distribution. Week 11 changed the error structure. Today changes neither — it goes back to the ordinary linear model and asks what happens when you have one categorical predictor and one continuous predictor at the same time.
That is an ANCOVA, and it is the model that joins the ANOVA half of this course to the regression half.









What it is
Example today




Response
continuous
fruitfly longevity, days


Factor
categorical, the thing you care about
mating treatment


Covariate
continuous, the thing you adjust for
thorax length, mm



A covariate does two different jobs, and they are worth keeping separate in your head:








Job
What goes wrong without it
Fixed by




Confounding
groups sit at different covariate values, so a raw comparison of means confuses the two
comparing at a common covariate value


Noise
the covariate’s variation sits in the error term, shrinking your F
removing it from the residual









Important



The one rule. The covariate must be measured independently of the treatment and must not be affected by it. Adjusting for something your treatment caused deletes the effect you are trying to measure. No diagnostic will catch this — only knowing how the data were collected.





Sections 1–2: meet the fruitflies, then run the one test that decides everything else.

title: Activity: Analysis of Variance
text:
Worksheet: One-Way ANOVA
📥 Crab data 📥 Tools script (.R) 📥 Script skeleton (.R)
The lecture’s dataset: 84 fiddler crabs, 21 in each of four groups, with body temperature above ambient measured in the field. Does the male’s oversized major claw act as a heat radiator?

intact male — the control
male major removed — the big claw taken off
male minor removed — a small claw taken off, the procedural control
female — never had a major claw

If the claw sheds heat, removing it should make males hotter.



Part 1 · Setup and the data
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 1.1 · Setup and the data ───────────────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)
library(car)
library(emmeans)

source("themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R")

crab_df <- read_csv("data/fiddler_crabs.csv") %>%
  mutate(crab_type = factor(crab_type))

count(crab_df, crab_type)
▶ Run this — look at the data before you test it:
# ── Part 1.2 · Setup and the data ───────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(crab_df, aes(crab_type, body_temp_c)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5)
✏️ Your turn: Which group looks warmest, and does the picture match the radiator prediction?
____________________________________________________________



Part 2 · Build the sums of squares
▶ Run this — it is already in the skeleton, so read it rather than retyping it:
# ── Part 2.1 · Build the sums of squares ────────────────────────────────
grand_mean <- mean(crab_df$body_temp_c)

crab_parts <- crab_df %>%
  group_by(crab_type) %>%
  mutate(group_mean = mean(body_temp_c)) %>%
  ungroup()

ss_total  <- sum((crab_parts$body_temp_c - grand_mean)^2)
ss_among  <- sum((crab_parts$group_mean  - grand_mean)^2)
ss_within <- sum((crab_parts$body_temp_c - crab_parts$group_mean)^2)

c(total = ss_total, among = ss_among, within = ss_within)

ss_among + ss_within
✏️ Your turn: Does the partition add up, and what fraction does the grouping explain?
ss_among + ss_within = __________   ss_total = __________

ss_among / ss_total = __________



Part 3 · The ANOVA
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 3.1 · The ANOVA ────────────────────────────────────────────────
crab_model <- lm(body_temp_c ~ crab_type, data = crab_df)

summary(crab_model)

anova(crab_model)
✏️ Your turn: Match the table to what you computed in Part 2.
Sum Sq, crab_type = __________   Sum Sq, Residuals = __________

Df = ______ and ______      F = __________   p = __________

R squared = __________  (compare it with ss_among / ss_total)

(Intercept) = __________  -- which group's mean is that, and why?

____________________________________________________________
✏️ Your turn: Write down exactly what this p-value licenses you to say — and one thing it does not.
It says: ____________________________________________________

It does not say: ____________________________________________



Part 4 · Check the assumptions
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 4.1 · Check the assumptions ────────────────────────────────────
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(crab_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
▶ Run this — the two formal tests:
# ── Part 4.2 · Check the assumptions ────────────────────────────────────
shapiro.test(residuals(crab_model))

leveneTest(body_temp_c ~ crab_type, data = crab_df)
✏️ Your turn: Both tests have a null hypothesis you want to keep. Fill in.
Shapiro H0 = ________________  p = __________  pass? ______

Levene  H0 = ________________  p = __________  pass? ______
✏️ Your turn: The third assumption is independence. Why can no plot or test on this slide check it?
____________________________________________________________



Part 5 · Set the reference level
▶ Run this — see the order R chose for you:
# ── Part 5.1 · Set the reference level ──────────────────────────────────
levels(crab_df$crab_type)

summary(crab_model)$coefficients
✏️ Your turn: Which level is the reference, why did R pick it, and what is each coefficient comparing?

What did not change: ________________________________________

male major removed - intact male = __________

crab_emm

text:
The goal of this assignment is to test whether crayfish chelae (claw) length differs between upstream and downstream locations in six different rivers where waterfalls separate them. We hypothesize that downstream crayfish will have larger chelae due to increased food availability and different selective pressures.
Yo goal is to use an ANOVA of some sort to analyze this data.
