crab_typemale minor removed -0.46667    0.06425  -7.263 2.20e-10 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.2082 on 80 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4324,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.4111 
F-statistic: 20.31 on 3 and 80 DF,  p-value: 6.997e-10



Same model, two different tables. summary() gives you the coefficients; anova() gives you the partition.

(Intercept) = 1.676 — the mean of the reference level, which R picked alphabetically: female
Each slope — that level’s mean minus the reference, not its own mean
Bottom line — the same overall F = 20.31 on the same two df that anova() is about to print







Note



🖐 Where to look for what
The intercept only ever appears in summary() and in a Type III table. anova() and Anova(type = "II") do not print an (Intercept) row at all.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
The ANOVA Table from R



anova(crab_model)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: body_temp_c
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
crab_type  3 2.6413 0.88044  20.312 6.997e-10 ***
Residuals 80 3.4676 0.04335                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



Every number is one you just built:

Sum Sq — 2.64 and 3.47
Df — a − 1 = 3, N − a = 80
Mean Sq — Sum Sq ÷ Df
F value — the ratio of those two mean squares

F = 20.31, p = 7.00e-10.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · What Does That F Tell You?
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · What Does That F Tell You?


The ANOVA returns F = 20.31, p = 7.00e-10.
What have you just learned?

All four crab types have different mean temperatures
At least one crab type differs from at least one other
Removing the major claw raises body temperature
The major claw explains 43.2% of the variation in temperature, so the radiator hypothesis is supported







Warning



✍️ One letter. Write it down.









Note



The question to ask

What was the null hypothesis, exactly?
A test can only tell you about the hypothesis it tested.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: What F Does and Does Not Say
text:
What F Does and Does Not Say








Important



✅ The answer is (b).
H₀ was “all four means are equal.” Rejecting it says at least one differs — not which, not how many, and not in which direction.
(a) claims far more than the test supports. (c) is a directional claim about one specific pair; that needs a post-hoc comparison, and Part 8 shows it is not even true. (d) misreads R²: 0.432 is the variance explained by crab type, which bundles sex and two surgeries together, not by the claw alone.









Warning



⚠️ The most common ANOVA mistake
Reporting a significant F and then describing whichever group means look farthest apart, as though the F test had said so.
It did not. The F test is an entry ticket, not an answer.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: Which Sums of Squares Did You Just Use?
text:
Which Sums of Squares Did You Just Use?


anova() gives Type I — sequential sums of squares. It adds terms to the model in the order you wrote them and credits each one with whatever variation is left over at that point.
With three types in circulation:

Type I (sequential) — each term adjusted for the terms before it. Order matters
Type II (hierarchical) — each term adjusted for all other terms at the same level, ignoring interactions
Type III (marginal) — each term adjusted for every other term, interactions included

anova() is Type I only. Types II and III come from car::Anova() — capital A.


Anova(crab_model, type = "II")

Anova Table (Type II tests)

Response: body_temp_c
          Sum Sq Df F value    Pr(>F)    
crab_type 2.6413  3  20.312 6.997e-10 ***
Residuals 3.4676 80                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Sum Sq 2.6413, F = 20.31 — identical to the anova() table a few slides back.






Important



✅ In a one-way ANOVA all three types agree
One predictor, so there is nothing to adjust it for. Balanced or unbalanced, Type I = Type II = Type III here — imbalance alone is never enough; it takes two predictors sharing variation.
So this is the safe place to learn the machinery, before the choice changes your answer.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: Type III Needs a Different Contrast Setting
text:
Type III Needs a Different Contrast Setting


Type III tests each term at the average of the others, and that is only well defined if the factor’s coding is centred on the grand mean. R’s default contr.treatment is not — it is centred on the reference level.
So a true Type III needs the option switched, and the model refit:

options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))

crab_sum <- lm(body_temp_c ~ crab_type, data = crab_df)
Anova(crab_sum, type = "III")

Anova Table (Type III tests)

Response: body_temp_c
             Sum Sq Df  F value    Pr(>F)    
(Intercept) 163.801  1 3778.986 < 2.2e-16 ***
crab_type     2.641  3   20.312 6.997e-10 ***
Residuals     3.468 80                       
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))

The crab_type row is still 2.6413 and F = 20.31. Only the (Intercept) row moved — it now tests the grand mean instead of the reference group’s mean. The next slide shows that row in summary().







Warning



⚠️ Contrasts are baked in at fit time
options() changes nothing about a model you already fitted. Change the option then refit — otherwise Anova(..., type = "III") silently reports Type III sums of squares computed from treatment coding, which are not the Type III anyone means.








Note



📖 What contr.sum actually changes

Nothing about the data or the fit — only how the factor’s dummy columns are built. contr.treatment codes each level against the reference level; contr.sum codes it against the grand mean.
Same model, same residuals, same F. Different bookkeeping.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: It Is the Coding That Moves the Intercept
text:
It Is the Coding That Moves the Intercept


anova() never showed you the intercept, so run summary() on both fits and watch the one row that changed:

# contr.treatment — R's default
round(summary(crab_model)$coefficients[, 1:2], 3)

                            Estimate Std. Error
(Intercept)                    1.676      0.045
crab_typeintact male          -0.390      0.064
crab_typemale major removed   -0.262      0.064
crab_typemale minor removed   -0.467      0.064

# contr.sum — the model refit for Type III
round(summary(crab_sum)$coefficients[, 1:2], 3)

            Estimate Std. Error
(Intercept)    1.396      0.023
crab_type1     0.280      0.039
crab_type2    -0.111      0.039
crab_type3     0.018      0.039



1.676 is the reference group’s mean (female). 1.396 is the grand mean — and the slopes are now deviations from it, crab_type1…crab_type3.






Important



✅ Type III does not move the intercept — contr.sum does
They just travel together, because Type III is only well defined under grand-mean coding. Ask a treatment-coded model for Type III and its (Intercept) row still tests the reference mean: SS = 59 against 163.8 under contr.sum.
The crab_type row is 2.641 either way.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: options() Is Global · Always Set It Back
text:
options() Is Global · Always Set It Back



options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))

# ... your Type III model and Anova() call ...

options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))

options() is global and sticky for the whole session. It is not attached to a model, a data frame or a script — it stays changed until you change it back or restart R.
Put the two calls in the same block, with the Type III work sandwiched between them. Not at the top of the script and “later.” Not in a different chunk.







Warning



⚠️ What going home with contr.sum left on looks like
Every summary() you run afterwards prints
crab_type1   crab_type2   crab_type3
— deviations from the grand mean — instead of named contrasts against your control. emmeans and TukeyHSD still work, but your coefficient table is answering a different question.
Nothing errors. The output just quietly stops meaning what you think it means, and that is far worse than a crash.


Two-way ANOVA is where this starts to bite — that is where Type I and Type III give genuinely different answers, and where you will set this option on purpose.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: Type I in Detail · Order Is the Whole Story
text:
Type I in Detail · Order Is the Whole Story


The slide before said all three types agree in a one-way ANOVA. That still holds — it had one predictor. Add a second one and imbalance finally has something to act on, so here is next week’s penguin data: body mass ~ species + sex, 333 birds, and the species–sex counts are not quite equal.
Type I walks the formula left to right. The first term is tested against nothing; the second is tested against whatever variation the first one left behind.

anova(lm(body_mass_g ~ species + sex, peng_df))["species", "Sum Sq"]

[1] 145190219

anova(lm(body_mass_g ~ sex + species, peng_df))["species", "Sum Sq"]

[1] 143401584


Same data. Same two predictors. Same model. Species is worth 145.2 million when it goes first and 143.4 million when it goes second.
Type I sums of squares do add exactly to \(SS_{total}\) — the one thing they have going for them, and why anova() still defaults to them.







Note



📖 Where the difference comes from
Species and sex are slightly correlated here — the species are not sampled in identical sex ratios. That overlap is 1.8 million of variation that either predictor could claim.
Type I gives all of it to whichever one you typed first. The second term gets the leftovers.








Warning



⚠️ This is a real decision, made by accident
Nobody chooses “species should get credit for the overlap.” They just type species + sex because species felt like the main thing.
Type I turns the order of your typing into a statistical claim.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: Why Type II or III · What Type II Does
text:
Why Type II or III · What Type II Does


Type II asks a cleaner question: what is each term worth after adjusting for all the others? No order, because every term is adjusted for every other one.

Anova(lm(body_mass_g ~ species + sex, peng_df), type = "II")

Anova Table (Type II tests)

Response: body_mass_g
             Sum Sq  Df F value    Pr(>F)    
species   143401584   2  715.29 < 2.2e-16 ***
sex        37090262   1  370.01 < 2.2e-16 ***
Residuals  32979185 329                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Species gets 143.4 million — exactly its “went last” Type I value. That is the trick to remembering it:

Type II gives every term the sequential SS it would get if it went last.

Nobody pockets the overlap, so Type II sums of squares do not add to \(SS_{total}\). The 1.8 million of shared variation is simply not credited to anyone, which is the honest answer.







Tip



🖐 Which one to use

Type II — your default when there is no interaction, or the interaction is not significant. It is the most powerful of the three, because it does not hold back the variation an absent interaction would have claimed
Type III — when you are keeping an interaction. It goes one step further than Type II and adjusts each main effect for the interaction too, which is why it needs contr.sum to mean anything
Type I — only when the order is your hypothesis: fitting a covariate first to strip it out before testing your treatment

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: Balance Makes the Whole Problem Vanish
text:
Balance Makes the Whole Problem Vanish


Take the same penguins, force 34 per species-by-sex cell, and run both orders again:

set.seed(12)
peng_bal <- peng_df %>%
  group_by(species, sex) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 34) %>%
  ungroup()

anova(lm(body_mass_g ~ species + sex, peng_bal))["species", "Sum Sq"]

[1] 95895631

anova(lm(body_mass_g ~ sex + species, peng_bal))["species", "Sum Sq"]

[1] 95895631


Identical, to the last digit. With equal n the two predictors are perfectly uncorrelated, there is no shared variation to fight over, and Type I = Type II = Type III.







Important



✅ Why this matters to us specifically
The Type I / II / III problem needs both ingredients: two or more predictors and imbalance. Take either one away — one predictor, or equal n — and it disappears.
And ecological data is almost never balanced: animals die, plots flood, a site gets sampled twice, a treatment fails, a field season ends early. The penguins above are only barely unbalanced — counts of 73/73, 34/34, 58/61 — and the sums of squares still move by 1.8 million.
Plan for equal n. Report Type II or III when you do not get it.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text: Part 5 · The F-Ratio

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
What F Actually Is


\[F = \frac{MS_{among}}{MS_{within}}\]

\(MS_{within}\) estimates the background variance σ² — pooled from inside the groups, where the treatment cannot reach
\(MS_{among}\) estimates that same σ², plus anything real that separates the group means
If H₀ is true, both estimate σ² and F ≈ 1

Here F = 20.31 — the group means are 20 times further apart than within-group noise alone can explain.







Tip



🖐 Why F is never negative
It is a ratio of two variances, and a variance is a sum of squares. The direction of a difference disappears the moment you square it — which is why a significant F cannot tell you which way anything went.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: F and t Are the Same Test
text:
F and t Are the Same Test


Take just two of the four groups — intact males and females — and test them both ways:

crab_two <- crab_df %>%
  filter(crab_type %in% c("intact male", "female")) %>%
  droplevels()

t.test(body_temp_c ~ crab_type, data = crab_two, var.equal = TRUE)$statistic

       t 
5.958321 

anova(lm(body_temp_c ~ crab_type, data = crab_two))[1, "F value"]

[1] 35.50158



t = 5.958, so t² = 35.5 — and F = 35.5.
Identical, with identical p-values.






Important



✅ ANOVA generalises the t-test
With two groups they are the same test. With three or more, the t-test has nowhere to go and ANOVA does.
This is the same t² = F identity you proved on a regression slope in Week 6.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
Variance Explained


\[R^2 = \frac{SS_{among}}{SS_{total}} = \frac{2.64}{6.11} = 0.432\]
Crab type accounts for about 43.2% of the variation in body temperature. The rest is individual crabs being individual crabs.

summary(crab_model)$r.squared

[1] 0.4323687









Note



Significant and partial, at the same time
p = 7.00e-10 says the group differences are not noise. R² = 0.43 says they explain under half of what is going on.
Both are true, and a results section should carry both.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text: Part 6 · Assumptions and Diagnostics

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
The Three Assumptions


One-way ANOVA assumes:

Independence — observations do not depend on each other. This one comes from the design, and no plot can rescue it
Normality — of the residuals, not of the raw response
Equal variance (homoscedasticity) across groups

ANOVA is fairly robust to mild departures from 2 and 3 when the design is balanced, which is one more reason to plan for equal n.







Warning



⚠️ Normality of what?
Not body_temp_c. Not each group separately. The residuals of the fitted model — exactly as in regression.
A response that looks bimodal because the groups differ is perfectly fine; that is the effect you are testing.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
The Four Diagnostic Plots


The same four panels you read for a regression:

Residuals vs fitted — with a factor, the points stack in vertical columns, one per group. You are looking for equal spread in each column
QQ plot — residuals against normal
Scale-location — same check, easier to see
Residuals vs leverage — influential points

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
Levene’s Test — Equal Variances



leveneTest(body_temp_c ~ crab_type, data = crab_df)

Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
      Df F value Pr(>F)
group  3  0.1587 0.9238
      80               


H₀ is “the variances are equal”, so a large p-value is the good outcome — the same backwards logic as Shapiro-Wilk.

p = 0.924 — nothing to worry about.






Tip



🖐 Levene vs Bartlett
Bartlett’s test is more powerful but assumes normality itself. Levene’s works on absolute deviations from the group median, so it is far more robust. Use Levene.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
Shapiro-Wilk — Normality of the Residuals



shapiro.test(residuals(crab_model))


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  residuals(crab_model)
W = 0.97566, p-value = 0.112


Note what goes inside: residuals(crab_model).

p = 0.112 — the residuals are consistent with normal.






Warning



⚠️ Do not let the test overrule the plot
At small n it cannot detect real problems; at large n it flags departures too small to matter. The QQ plot is the primary evidence.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: One Call for All of It
text:
One Call for All of It


performance::check_model() draws every assumption check in one labelled panel, with a plain-English caption on each.
check_model(crab_model)
Useful for a quick look. Still worth knowing what each panel is, which is why we did them one at a time first.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text: Part 7 · The Reference Level, Again

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
R Sorts Alphabetically — Still


Read the file without thinking about it and the four crab types become a factor in alphabetical order:

levels(crab_df$crab_type)

[1] "female"             "intact male"        "male major removed"
[4] "male minor removed"


So the reference is female — and every coefficient in the model becomes “compared with a female crab.”







Warning



⚠️ That is the wrong baseline for this experiment
The question is what happens when you remove a claw from a male. The comparison that answers it is against an intact male, not against a female.
The model fits identically either way. The output only answers your question if you tell it what your question was.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · Which Crab Is the Control?
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · Which Crab Is the Control?


You are about to set the reference level deliberately.
Which level should it be, and why?

female — keep R’s default; the model fit is identical anyway
intact male — the untouched version of the animals that were manipulated
male minor removed — it is the procedural control, so it accounts for the surgery
It makes no difference, because the F-test and R² do not change







Warning



✍️ Careful — two of these are true statements. Only one is the right decision.









Note



The question to ask
Which single comparison do I most want to read straight off the coefficient table?

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
fct_relevel() · Saying What You Meant








Important



✅ The answer is (b).

is true — F, R², and the ANOVA table are identical whichever level is the reference. That is not a reason to accept a default chosen by spelling.
is tempting and it is the right comparison to make eventually — but as the baseline it hides the very contrast the experiment was built around.




crab_df <- crab_df %>%
  mutate(crab_type = fct_relevel(crab_type, "intact male"))

crab_model <- lm(body_temp_c ~ crab_type, data = crab_df)

summary(crab_model)$coefficients %>% round(3)

                            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)                    1.286      0.045  28.300    0.000
crab_typefemale                0.390      0.064   6.077    0.000
crab_typemale major removed    0.129      0.064   2.001    0.049
crab_typemale minor removed   -0.076      0.064  -1.186    0.239



Now every row reads as “degrees hotter than an intact male”:

female +0.39 — clearly hotter
male major removed +0.13
male minor removed -0.08







Tip



🖐 The habit
Set the reference in the same line that creates the factor. fct_relevel(x, "control") moves one level to the front and leaves the rest alone.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text: Part 8 · Post-Hoc Testing

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
What Post-Hoc Tests Are For


The F-test said something differs. Post-hoc tests say what, while keeping the family-wide error rate at α.

Planned (a priori) comparisons — a small number of contrasts you committed to before seeing the data. More powerful, because there are fewer of them
Unplanned (post-hoc) comparisons — all pairs, after the fact. Safer, less powerful

Tukey’s HSD is the standard for all pairwise comparisons with equal n. We run it twice: once with TukeyHSD(), then with emmeans — the same answer, from the tool we use for every model after this one.







Warning



⚠️ Deciding after you look is not a plan
Choosing which comparisons to make because they looked big re-introduces exactly the multiple-comparisons problem the correction exists to solve.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
Tukey’s HSD



TukeyHSD(aov(crab_model))

  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = crab_model)

$crab_type
                                             diff         lwr         upr
female-intact male                     0.39047619  0.22189182  0.55906056
male major removed-intact male         0.12857143 -0.04001294  0.29715579
male minor removed-intact male        -0.07619048 -0.24477484  0.09239389
male major removed-female             -0.26190476 -0.43048913 -0.09332040
male minor removed-female             -0.46666667 -0.63525103 -0.29808230
male minor removed-male major removed -0.20476190 -0.37334627 -0.03617754
                                          p adj
female-intact male                    0.0000002
male major removed-intact male        0.1962212
male minor removed-intact male        0.6375171
male major removed-female             0.0006106
male minor removed-female             0.0000000
male minor removed-male major removed 0.0108312



Each row is one pair: the difference in means, a confidence interval, and a p-value already adjusted for the whole family of six comparisons.
A pair differs when its interval excludes zero.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · Reading the Tukey Output


The radiator hypothesis predicts that a male whose major claw was removed should run hotter than an intact male.
Tukey gives male major removed − intact male a difference of +0.129 with an adjusted p = 0.196.
What should you conclude?
(a) The hypothesis is supported — the difference is in the predicted direction
(b) The hypothesis fails — removing the major claw did not significantly change temperature
(c) The hypothesis is supported, because females are significantly hotter than every male group
(d) Nothing can be concluded, because the overall ANOVA was significant






Warning



✍️ One letter, then argue it with your neighbour.









Note



The question to ask
Which comparison does the hypothesis actually make a prediction about?

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
What Tukey Actually Found








Important



✅ The answer is (b).
Removing the major claw moved temperature by 0.13 °C, adjusted p = 0.2 — not distinguishable from zero. The direction is right and the evidence is not there.
(c) is the trap: females are hotter than every male group, but females differ from males in many ways besides the claw. That comparison cannot test a claw-removal hypothesis.



What did differ (adjusted p):








Comparison
p




female − intact male
0


major removed − intact
0.196


minor removed − intact
0.638


major − minor removed
0.011




The big effect in this dataset is sex, not surgery.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
Estimated Marginal Means · emmeans


TukeyHSD() is the end of the road. emmeans is the tool you will use for every model from here on. Step one is the estimated marginal means — the model’s estimate of each group’s mean:

crab_emm <- emmeans(crab_model, ~crab_type)
crab_emm

 crab_type          emmean     SE df lower.CL upper.CL
 intact male          1.29 0.0454 80     1.20     1.38
 female               1.68 0.0454 80     1.59     1.77
 male major removed   1.41 0.0454 80     1.32     1.50
 male minor removed   1.21 0.0454 80     1.12     1.30

Confidence level used: 0.95 









Note



🖐 Not the same as group_by() means
The SEs come from the pooled \(MS_{within}\), not each group’s own SD. These are the means you plot.








Tip



🖐 A lot of machinery for nothing?
With one factor each EMM equals its group mean exactly — only the SEs differ. That is what “averaging over the other factors” does when there are none.
Next week there will be, and that is where emmeans stops agreeing with group_by() %>% mean().

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
Pairwise Contrasts with emmeans


Step two: feed those means to pairs().

pairs(crab_emm, adjust = "tukey")

 contrast                                estimate     SE df t.ratio p.value
 intact male - female                     -0.3905 0.0643 80  -6.077 <0.0001
 intact male - male major removed         -0.1286 0.0643 80  -2.001  0.1962
 intact male - male minor removed          0.0762 0.0643 80   1.186  0.6375
 female - male major removed               0.2619 0.0643 80   4.076  0.0006
 female - male minor removed               0.4667 0.0643 80   7.263 <0.0001
 male major removed - male minor removed   0.2048 0.0643 80   3.187  0.0108

P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates 


Same six comparisons, same adjusted p-values as TukeyHSD() — but watch the subtraction order, which runs the other way, so the signs flip. Wrap it in confint() if you want the intervals back.







Tip



🖐 Why emmeans and not TukeyHSD()
TukeyHSD() only does all-pairs on a balanced aov. emmeans handles unbalanced designs, covariates, several factors and planned contrasts — and it is what you will use from Week 9 onward.
adjust = also takes "bonferroni", "sidak", "BH" or "none".

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
Compact Letter Display


Six pairwise p-values is more than a reader can hold at once. cld() collapses them into letters:

multcomp::cld(crab_emm, Letters = letters,
              adjust = "tukey")

 crab_type          emmean     SE df lower.CL upper.CL .group
 male minor removed   1.21 0.0454 80     1.09     1.33  a    
 intact male          1.29 0.0454 80     1.17     1.40  ab   
 male major removed   1.41 0.0454 80     1.30     1.53   b   
 female               1.68 0.0454 80     1.56     1.79    c  

Confidence level used: 0.95 
Conf-level adjustment: sidak method for 4 estimates 
P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates 
significance level used: alpha = 0.05 
NOTE: If two or more means share the same grouping symbol,
      then we cannot show them to be different.
      But we also did not show them to be the same. 


Groups that share a letter were not shown to differ. These are the letters that go above the bars in your final figure.







Warning



⚠️ Do not library(multcomp)
It pulls in MASS, which masks dplyr::select() and will break your pipes with a baffling error three chunks later. Use the multcomp:: prefix and nothing gets attached.








Important



✅ A shared letter is not “the same”
intact male and male major removed share b: we failed to show a difference. That is not evidence they are equal.
cld() prints that warning itself, at the bottom of its own output. It is the most misread table in biology.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text: Part 9 · Reporting

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
Reporting an ANOVA


A results sentence needs the test, the statistic with both df, the p-value, and the direction — then the post-hoc detail.

Body temperature differed among crab types (one-way ANOVA, F~3,80~ = 20.31, p < 0.001, R² = 0.43). Females were warmer than intact males by 0.39 °C (Tukey HSD, adjusted p < 0.001), but removing the major claw did not detectably change male temperature (0.13 °C, adjusted p = 0.2).








Note



✅ What that sentence does

Names the test
Gives both degrees of freedom
Reports effect size, not just p
States the post-hoc method and that its p-values are adjusted
Reports the non-significant comparison the hypothesis was about, rather than quietly dropping it

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text: Part 10 · When the Assumptions Fail

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
A Second Dataset · Nematode Lifespan


The crab data behaved. Most data do not.
Here are 200 nematodes, 50 in each of four treatments, exposed to a parasite as larvae, as adults, as both, or to water as a control. The response is lifespan in days.

worm_df <- read_csv("data/nematode_lifespan.csv") %>%
  mutate(treatment = fct_relevel(treatment, "water"))

count(worm_df, treatment)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  treatment       n
  <fct>       <int>
1 water          50
2 adult          50
3 larva          50
4 larva+adult    50












Note that the water control sorts last alphabetically — another reason to relevel on purpose.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
These Assumptions Genuinely Fail



worm_model <- lm(lifespan_days ~ treatment, data = worm_df)

shapiro.test(residuals(worm_model))


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  residuals(worm_model)
W = 0.97626, p-value = 0.001808

leveneTest(lifespan_days ~ treatment, data = worm_df)

Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
       Df F value    Pr(>F)    
group   3  22.481 1.493e-12 ***
      196                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




Shapiro-Wilk p = 0.00181 — residuals are not normal
Levene p = 1.49e-12 — variances are nowhere near equal

Look back at the boxplots: group SDs run from 3.3 to 8.7 days.






Warning



⚠️ Nothing here is simulated
This is the published dataset, unmodified. Real data fails these tests routinely.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · What Do You Do Now?
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · What Do You Do Now?


An ANOVA on these data returns F = 15.25, p = 5.87e-09 — but the residuals are non-normal and the variances are unequal.
What is the right next step?
(a) Report the ANOVA — it is significant, and ANOVA is robust
(b) Drop the group with the biggest variance and re-run
(c) Try a transformation, and if that fails use a rank-based test such as Kruskal-Wallis
(d) Report nothing — the data cannot be analysed






Warning



✍️ Write your letter down, then vote.









Note



The question to ask
Is the problem with the data, or with the test I chose for it?

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
The Kruskal-Wallis Test








Important



✅ The answer is (c).
Transform first — a log or square root often fixes both problems at once, and keeps you in a framework that extends to more factors. If it does not, move to a rank-based test.
(b) is data deletion to make a test pass, which is not a repair.



kruskal.test(lifespan_days ~ treatment, data = worm_df)


    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  lifespan_days by treatment
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 29.463, df = 3, p-value = 1.79e-06



Kruskal-Wallis replaces every value by its rank and asks whether the rank totals differ more than chance — so it needs no normality and is not thrown by unequal spread.
χ² = 29.46, df = 3, p = 1.79e-06.
The conclusion survives. What changes is that you can now defend it.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: Dunn’s Test — the Post-Hoc for Ranks
text:
Dunn’s Test — the Post-Hoc for Ranks


Kruskal-Wallis has the same limit as F: it says something differs, not what. Dunn’s test is its post-hoc.

dunnTest(lifespan_days ~ treatment, data = worm_df, method = "bh")$res %>%
       mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 3)))

           Comparison      Z  P.unadj    P.adj
1       water - adult -3.120 1.78e-03 2.67e-03
2       water - larva  0.917 3.59e-01 4.31e-01
3       adult - larva  4.040 5.32e-05 1.60e-04
4 water - larva+adult -3.510 4.56e-04 9.11e-04
5 adult - larva+adult -0.381 7.03e-01 7.03e-01
6 larva - larva+adult -4.420 9.76e-06 5.85e-05









Note



Which adjustment?
"bonferroni" is the strictest and costs the most power. "bh" (Benjamini-Hochberg) controls the false discovery rate instead, and is the usual choice when you have more than a handful of comparisons.


pairwise.wilcox.test() does a similar job; Dunn’s is preferred because it uses the same ranking as the Kruskal-Wallis it follows.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
Which Test Should You Use?









Situation
Parametric route
Non-parametric route




Compare 2 groups
t-test
Mann-Whitney U / Wilcoxon rank-sum


Compare 3+ groups
one-way ANOVA
Kruskal-Wallis


Post-hoc, all pairs
emmeans (Tukey-adjusted)
Dunn’s test, pairwise Wilcoxon


What it compares
means
mean ranks (≈ medians)


Needs
normal residuals, equal variance
neither


Costs you
nothing, when assumptions hold
power, and the original units




Try a transformation before you give up the parametric route — it keeps your effect sizes interpretable and extends to the multi-factor designs coming in Week 9.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
Reporting a Non-Parametric Result



Nematode lifespan differed among parasite-exposure treatments (Kruskal-Wallis χ²~3~ = 29.46, p < 0.001). A Kruskal-Wallis test was used because the residuals of the equivalent ANOVA were non-normal (Shapiro-Wilk p = 0.00181) and variances were unequal (Levene p = 1.49e-12). Dunn’s tests with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment showed that larva-exposed worms outlived worms exposed as adults or as both.








Important



✅ Say why you went non-parametric
A reader cannot tell whether you chose a rank test because your data required it or because it gave you the answer you wanted — unless you show the assumption checks that made the decision.
Report the numbers that drove the choice, not just the choice.

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
Wrap-up
Today you:

Saw that ANOVA is regression with a categorical predictor — the same lm(), the same partition, the same F
Worked out why six t-tests carry a 26% chance of a false positive, and what ANOVA does about it
Built \(SS_{among}\) and \(SS_{within}\) by hand and matched them to anova()
Confirmed t² = F on a two-group subset, for the second time this term
Checked independence, normality and equal variance — the last two on the residuals
Set the reference level with fct_relevel() so the coefficients answered the experiment’s question
Used Tukey HSD and then emmeans to find which pairs differ, and learned that the claw-removal comparison was not one of them
Moved to Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn’s test on a dataset whose assumptions genuinely failed

title: Lecture: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
section: The Three Things to Carry Out of Here
text:
The Three Things to Carry Out of Here








Important



⚠️ A significant F is an entry ticket
It says at least one group differs. It never says which, how many, or in which direction. Everything past that comes from post-hoc comparisons you planned or corrected for.








Note



✅ Assumptions live in the residuals
Except independence, which lives in the design — and no plot will ever show it to you.









Important



✅ Set the reference level
fct_relevel(x, "control"), in the line that makes the factor. The fit never changes; the readability always does.








Note



Up next — Two-Way ANOVA
Two factors at once, and the thing that only exists when you have two: the interaction.

Overview

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Introduction to ANCOVA


ANCOVA = Analysis of COVAriance — regression and ANOVA in one model. You use it when you have:

a continuous response (Y)
a categorical predictor (factor A)
a continuous predictor, the covariate (X)

Two things it is for:

Compare group means after adjusting for the covariate
Ask whether two or more regression lines differ — in slope, in intercept, or both

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
When to Use ANCOVA

Common Applications of ANCOVA

Increasing statistical power

The covariate (e.g., body size, initial temperature) explains some of the “noise” (residual error) in the response variable.
By “removing” this variation, we reduce the residual error, making it easier to detect the true effect of our categorical factor.
This results in a more powerful test of treatment effects.

Adjusting for confounding variables

Imagine your treatment groups happen to differ in their average covariate value (e.g., Group A was tested in a warmer room than Group B).
ANCOVA allows you to separate the treatment effect from the covariate effect.

Testing equality of regression lines

Do treatments have the same relationship (slope) with a continuous variable?

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: The Motivating Problem — Grayling in Two Lakes
text:
The Motivating Problem — Grayling in Two Lakes


Back to the Arctic grayling from week 5 — the same fish, a new question.
Lake I8 fish weigh more than lake I3 fish. But I8 fish are also longer (mean 364 mm vs 266 mm).

Is there a lake effect on mass at all, or are I8 fish simply bigger?

You cannot answer that by comparing mean masses. The groups differ in the very thing that drives the response.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Two Problems, One Tool


Problem 1 — confounding. The groups differ in the covariate, so a raw comparison of means confuses the treatment with the covariate. This is the grayling problem, and the classic cricket problem (two species measured at different temperatures).
Problem 2 — noise. Even when the groups are balanced on the covariate, the covariate still soaks up residual variation. Removing it shrinks the error term and makes the test of the factor more powerful. This is the fruitfly problem in Part 4.







Important


ANCOVA does both with one model
\[y \sim \underbrace{x}_{\text{covariate}} + \underbrace{A}_{\text{factor}}\]
It compares groups at a common value of the covariate — the “level playing field” comparison — instead of wherever each group happened to sit.









Warning


⚠️ One rule before you start
The covariate must be measured independently of the treatment, and must not be affected by it. Adjusting for something the treatment caused removes the very effect you are trying to measure.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text: Part 2 · The ANCOVA Model

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
ANCOVA Linear Model: Conceptual Framework

The ANCOVA Model

Key concept: Dfference between “unadjusted” group means and “adjusted” means

In this visualization:

Group Means (asterisks): The raw average X and Y for each group.
Group A and Group B have different mean X values. Comparing directly misleading
Adjusted Means (triangles): ANCOVA statistically “moves” each group mean along regression line to single, common X value (the overall mean X).
ANCOVA compares heights (the Y values) of adjusted means.
Adjustment “levels the playing field,” estimating each group’s mean if all groups had same average covariate value

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text: ANCOVA Model Visualization

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Mathematical Model for ANCOVA

Single-factor ANCOVA with

factor A (p levels, i = 1 to p), a continuous covariate (x), and response variable (y): \(Y_{ij} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta(X_{ij} - \bar{X}) + \varepsilon_{ij}\)

Where:

\(Y_{ij}\) = response value for observation j in level i of factor A
\(\mu\) = overall mean
\(\alpha_i\) = effect of level i of factor A (what we test in ANOVA)
\(\beta\) = common regression slope relating Y to X (what we test in Regression)
\(X_{ij}\) = covariate value for observation j in level i of factor A
\(\bar{X}\) = mean value of covariate
\(\varepsilon_{ij}\) = error term

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
ANCOVA Parameters Interpretation



Interpretation of Parameters

\(\mu\) = overall mean response
\(\alpha_i\) = effect of level i (difference between group’s adjusted mean and overall mean)
\(\beta\) = pooled within-group regression coefficient (the slope)
\(X_{ij}\) = covariate value for observation j in group i
\(\bar{X}\) = overall mean of covariate
\(\varepsilon_{ij}\) = unexplained error

Model assumes homogeneous slopes (i.e., \(\beta\) same for all groups) .

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: Building the ANCOVA Model in R
text:
Building the ANCOVA Model in R

Remember lm(y ~ predictor).

ANCOVA combines the predictors from ANOVA and regression.

Simple Linear Regression:

Predict y using a continuous variable x.

model_reg <- lm(y ~ x, data = mydata)


One-Way ANOVA:

We want to compare y among groups in a categorical factor A.

model_aov <- lm(y ~ A, data = mydata)


ANCOVA (Additive Model):

Compare y among groups in A, after accounting for effect of x.
Add terms together

model_ancova <- lm(y ~ A + x, data = mydata)

Model assumes slope of y ~ x relationship is same for all groups in A.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: Building the ANCOVA Model in R — The Two Formulas
text:
Building the ANCOVA Model in R — The Two Formulas

ANCOVA (Interaction Model):

What if the slopes are different for each group?
Test for interaction between factor and covariate.

model_int <- lm(y ~ A * x, data = mydata)

Shorthand for: lm(y ~ A + x + A:x, data = mydata)
The A:x term tests if the slopes are different.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: ANCOVA in R: Workflow Steps 1 and 2
text:
ANCOVA in R: Workflow Steps 1 and 2

Step 1: Test for Homogeneity of Slopes - Always Start Here

Fit interaction model first - tests key assumption that all groups share same slope.

# The asterisk * tests for both main effects AND the interaction
model_int <- lm(y ~ A * x, data = mydata)
Step 2: Examine the Interaction Term

ANOVA table for model_int and find the p-value for interaction term (A:x).

    Anova(model_int, type = "III")

If p > 0.05 (e.g., p = 0.4) - interaction IS NOT significant - slopes are homogeneous (parallel).
If p < 0.05 (e.g., p = 0.02): - interaction IS significant - slopes heterogeneous (NOT parallel).
** standard ANCOVA model (y ~ A + x) inappropriate**
Analysis stops here and interpret interaction (often most interesting result!)

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
ANCOVA in R: Workflow Step 3

Step 3: Run the ANCOVA (Additive Model)

If interaction not significant, run the simpler additive model the final ANCOVA model.

# We use the + sign, which means "additive"
model_ancova <- lm(y ~ A + x, data = mydata)
# Get the final ANCOVA table
Anova(model_ancova, type = "III")
# Get the adjusted means
library(emmeans)
emmeans(model_ancova, "A")

text:
ANOVA Table for ANCOVA
The ANOVA table for a single-factor ANCOVA has these components:


# Create a tibble with ANOVA table information
anova_table <- tibble(
  Source = c("Factor A (adjusted)", "Covariate", "Residual", "Total"),
  df = c("(p-1)", "1", "n-p-1", "n-1"),
  `Sum of Squares` = c("SS_A(adj)", "SS_Covariate", "SS_Residual", "SS_Total"),
  `Mean Square` = c(
    "MS_A(adj) = SS_A(adj)/(p-1)",
    "MS_Covariate = SS_Covariate/1",
    "MS_Residual = SS_Residual/(n-p-1)",
    ""
  ),
  `F-ratio` = c("MS_A(adj)/MS_Residual", "MS_Covariate/MS_Residual", "", ""),
  `Expected MS` = c("σ² + n∑α²/(p-1)", "σ² + β²∑(X-X̄)²", "σ²", "")
)

# Create
anova_table

## 1 Factor A (adjust… (p-1) SS_A(adj)        "MS_A(adj) =… "MS_A(ad… "σ² + n∑α²/(…
## 2 Covariate         1     SS_Covariate     "MS_Covariat… "MS_Cova… "σ² + β²∑(X-…
## 3 Residual          n-p-1 SS_Residual      "MS_Residual… ""        "σ²"         
## 4 Total             n-1   SS_Total         ""            ""        ""

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Null Hypotheses in ANCOVA
Homogeneity of Slopes (Test this first!)
\[H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = ... = \beta_p\]
Are the regression slopes the same for all groups?
Test with the A:x interaction term in lm(y ~ A * x).






Important


This one is an assumption check, not a result. You want to fail to reject it before going any further.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: Null Hypotheses in ANCOVA — the Two Results
text:
Null Hypotheses in ANCOVA — the Two Results


Treatment effect, adjusted
\[H_0: \alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = \dots = \alpha_p = 0\]
Are the adjusted group means equal?
\[F = \frac{MS_{A(adj)}}{MS_{residual}}\]
the A term in lm(y ~ x + A).

Covariate effect
\[H_0: \beta = 0\]
Does the covariate relate to the response at all?
\[F = \frac{MS_{covariate}}{MS_{residual}}\]
the x term in lm(y ~ x + A).

Partridge Example: Steps 1–2 — Test Homogeneity of Slopes



homo_slopes_model <- lm(LONGEV ~ THORAX * treatment,
                        data = partridge)

Anova(homo_slopes_model, type = "III")
## Anova Table (Type III tests)
## 
## Response: LONGEV
##                   Sum Sq  Df  F value                Pr(>F)

THORAX: covariate highly significant
thorax length explains significant amount of variance in longevity
treatment: treatment effect, after adjusting for thorax length, is highly significant

text:
What the Covariate Bought You


Run the same question without the covariate, and compare:

# one-way ANOVA, covariate ignored
Anova(lm(LONGEV ~ treatment, data = partridge),
      type = 2)
## Anova Table (Type II tests)
## 
## Response: LONGEV
##           Sum Sq  Df F value         Pr(>F)    
## treatment  11939   4  13.612 0.000000003516 ***
## Residuals  26314 120                           
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


# ANCOVA, thorax length included
Anova(lm(LONGEV ~ THORAX + treatment, data = partridge),
      type = 2)
## Anova Table (Type II tests)
## 
## Response: LONGEV
##            Sum Sq  Df F value                Pr(>F)    
## THORAX    13168.9   1 119.219 < 0.00000000000000022 ***
## treatment  9611.5   4  21.753    0.0000000000001719 ***
## Residuals 13144.7 119                                  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1







one-way ANOVA
ANCOVA




residual SS
26,314
13,145


residual df
120
119


treatment F
13.61
21.75










Important


Thorax length absorbed half the residual variation.
One degree of freedom spent on the covariate cut the error term from 26,314 to 13,145, and the test of treatment got 60% bigger (F 13.6 → 21.8) — on identical data and an identical question.
That is the power argument, and it is why you measure a covariate even when your groups are perfectly balanced on it.



Here the treatment effect was significant either way. On a smaller or noisier dataset, that difference is the difference between finding the effect and missing it.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Partridge Example: Getting Adjusted Means

The ANOVA table tells us the treatments are different, but not which ones.

Use emmeans package to get the adjusted means / perform pairwise comparisons
The “estimated marginal mean” (or adjusted mean)
predicted longevity for each group, assuming an average thorax length
This is the “level playing field” comparison.




# Get adjusted means using emmeans
library(emmeans)
adjusted_means <- emmeans(ancova_model, "treatment")
adjusted_means

Six of the ten are significant. The four that are not:

No females vs. one inseminated — p = 0.90
No females vs. eight inseminated — p = 0.68
One vs. eight inseminated — p = 0.99
No females vs. one virgin — p = 0.13

Every group that actually mated differs from the groups that did not, except the single-virgin group — the mildest treatment.

section: Partridge Example: Pairwise Comparisons — Compact Letters
text:
Partridge Example: Pairwise Comparisons — Compact Letters



##  treatment                       emmean   SE  df lower.CL upper.CL .group
##  Eight virgin females daily        41.6 2.12 119     37.4     45.8  a    
##  One virgin female daily           54.5 2.11 119     50.3     58.7   b   
##  No females                        61.5 2.11 119     57.3     65.7   bc  
##  One inseminated female daily      64.2 2.10 119     60.0     68.3    c  
##  Eight inseminated females daily   65.4 2.11 119     61.3     69.6    c  
## 
## Confidence level used: 0.95 
## P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 5 estimates 
## significance level used: alpha = 0.05 
## NOTE: If two or more means share the same grouping symbol,
##       then we cannot show them to be different.
##       But we also did not show them to be the same.











Groups sharing a letter are not distinguishable. The red arrows say the same thing — overlapping arrows mean no significant difference.






Important


Read the pattern, not the ranking
The three non-mating groups are one block. One virgin female pulls longevity down a little; eight pulls it down a lot.
The dose that matters is matings, not company.

text: Part 5 · Heterogeneous Slopes & Assumptions

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: What if the Slopes Are HETEROGENEOUS?
text:
What if the Slopes Are HETEROGENEOUS?


Back to the grayling. Fit the interaction model first, as always:

g_int <- lm(log_mass ~ log_len * lake, data = g_df)

Anova(g_int, type = 3)
## Anova Table (Type III tests)
## 
## Response: log_mass
##              Sum Sq  Df   F value                Pr(>F)    
## (Intercept)  1.8929   1 1337.5062 < 0.00000000000000022 ***
## log_len      4.0602   1 2868.9446 < 0.00000000000000022 ***
## lake         0.0094   1    6.6452              0.010833 *  
## log_len:lake 0.0117   1    8.2518              0.004617 ** 
## Residuals    0.2293 162                                    
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The interaction is significant (p = 0.0046). The two lakes do not share a slope.







Important


Stop. Do not fit the additive model.
log_mass ~ log_len + lake would force one common slope through two populations that do not have one, and then report a single “lake effect” that is true at no particular length.
There is no such thing as the difference between the lakes here. The difference depends on how big the fish is.









Note


📖 This is not a failure
A significant interaction is usually the more interesting result. It says the groups differ in how the response scales, not merely in where it sits.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Reading Heterogeneous Slopes — emtrends()



emtrends(g_int, "lake", var = "log_len")
##  lake log_len.trend     SE  df lower.CL upper.CL
##  I3            2.79 0.0943 162     2.61     2.98
##  I8            3.11 0.0569 162     3.00     3.22
## 
## Confidence level used: 0.95

pairs(emtrends(g_int, "lake", var = "log_len"))
##  contrast estimate   SE  df t.ratio p.value
##  I3 - I8    -0.316 0.11 162  -2.873  0.0046


emtrends() is emmeans() for slopes. It gives one slope per group, with a standard error, and pairs() tests whether they differ.
On log-log axes the slope is the allometric exponent: mass ∝ lengthb.






Important


The biology is in the exponent

I8: b = 3.11 — not distinguishable from 3 (p = 0.058). Isometric: these fish keep their shape as they grow.
I3: b = 2.79 — significantly below 3 (p = 0.029). I3 grayling get relatively lighter as they lengthen.

That is a condition difference between the lakes, and an additive ANCOVA would have hidden it entirely.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: Where Do the Groups Actually Differ?
text:
Where Do the Groups Actually Differ?


With non-parallel lines, the gap between groups changes along the covariate. So ask for the contrast at specific covariate values:

lens <- log10(c(200, 250, 300))

pairs(emmeans(g_int, ~ lake | log_len,
              at = list(log_len = lens)))
## log_len = 2.30:
##  contrast estimate      SE  df t.ratio p.value
##  I3 - I8   -0.0299 0.01940 162  -1.540  0.1256
## 
## log_len = 2.40:
##  contrast estimate      SE  df t.ratio p.value
##  I3 - I8   -0.0605 0.01110 162  -5.479 <0.0001
## 
## log_len = 2.48:
##  contrast estimate      SE  df t.ratio p.value
##  I3 - I8   -0.0856 0.00914 162  -9.370 <0.0001






Length
I3 − I8 (log mass)
p




200 mm
−0.030
0.13


250 mm
−0.061
<0.0001


300 mm
−0.107
<0.0001




At 200 mm the two lakes are indistinguishable. The gap opens as the fish get longer, and by 300 mm an I3 grayling is about 20% lighter than an I8 grayling of the same length.






Warning


⚠️ johnson_neyman = TRUE does not work here
The Johnson–Neyman procedure needs a continuous moderator. interactions::sim_slopes() will warn “Johnson-Neyman intervals are not available for factor predictors or moderators” and give you nothing. With a categorical factor, the contrast-at-covariate-values above is the right tool.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Handling Heterogeneous Slopes — the Options


When the interaction is significant:

Report the interaction. It is the result. Give the slopes, not an adjusted mean.
emtrends() for a slope per group, with pairs() to test them.
Contrast at chosen covariate values — emmeans(~ A | x, at = ...) — to say where along the covariate the groups separate.
Johnson–Neyman, but only when the moderator is continuous.
Separate regressions per group. Simple, honest, least powerful, and it gives up the shared error term.








Warning


⚠️ Mind the covariate ranges
I3 fish run 191–320 mm; I8 fish run 207–440 mm. The lines can only be compared where both groups have data.
Reporting a lake difference at 400 mm would mean extrapolating the I3 line past every I3 fish ever measured. ANCOVA will do that arithmetic without complaint. You have to be the one who refuses.









Note


This caution applies to the additive model too — an “adjusted mean” at \(\bar{x}\) is an extrapolation for any group whose data does not reach \(\bar{x}\).

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Assumptions of ANCOVA






#
Assumption
How you check it




1
Independence
design, not a test


2
Normal residuals
Q-Q plot


3
Equal variances
residuals vs. fitted


4
Linearity of Y on X within each group
scatterplot


5
Homogeneity of slopes
the A:x interaction











Important


#5 is the one that is special to ANCOVA, and the only one you test before fitting the model you will report. The other four are the ordinary linear-model assumptions you have been checking since week 7.









Warning


⚠️ And one that is not on the list
The covariate must be independent of the treatment. No test will catch a violation — only knowing how the data were collected will.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Checking Assumptions in R












Check assumptions 2 and 3 on the final model — the additive one, if the slopes let you fit it.

Residuals vs. fitted — red line roughly flat at 0 ✅
Normal Q-Q — points on the dashed line ✅
Scale-location — red line flat ✅
Residuals vs. leverage — nothing stranded in the right-hand corners ✅







Note


Conclusion: the assumptions are met, so the ANCOVA table on the previous slides can be reported as it stands.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Robust ANCOVA Approaches


When the assumptions are badly violated — not marginally:

Rank transformation — rank both Y and X, then run the ordinary ANCOVA on the ranks: lm(rank(y) ~ rank(x) + A)
Bootstrapping — resample to get intervals without assuming normality
Quantile regression — model the median, or any quantile, instead of the mean
Permutation tests — randomise the treatment labels to build the null distribution







Tip


🖐 Run it as a sensitivity check. If the robust version agrees with the parametric one, report the parametric one and say you checked.





rank_ancova <- lm(rank(LONGEV) ~ rank(THORAX) + treatment,
                  data = partridge)

signif(c(
  parametric = Anova(ancova_model, type = "III")["treatment", "Pr(>F)"],
  rank_based = Anova(rank_ancova,  type = "III")["treatment", "Pr(>F)"]), 3)
##        parametric        rank_based 
## 0.000000000000172 0.000000000000654

Both vanishingly small — the parametric result stands.

text: Part 6 · Reporting Results

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Writing Up ANCOVA Results
Scientific Writing Example
Here’s how you might write up ANCOVA results for publication:

“We analyzed the effects of mating opportunity on male fruitfly longevity using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), with thorax length as a covariate. Before conducting the main analysis, we tested the homogeneity-of-slopes assumption and found no significant treatment × thorax length interaction (F₄,₁₁₅ = 0.09, P = 0.98), indicating that the effect of body size on longevity was consistent across treatments.
The ANCOVA revealed significant effects of both treatment (F₄,₁₁₉ = 21.75, P < 0.001) and thorax length (F₁,₁₁₉ = 119.22, P < 0.001) on longevity. Thorax length was positively associated with longevity.
After adjusting for body size, longevity declined with the number of virgin females a male was housed with (adjusted mean ± SE: 54.5 ± 2.11 days for one virgin female and 41.6 ± 2.12 days for eight, versus 61.5 ± 2.11 days for males housed alone). Males housed with inseminated females — which do not mate — did not differ from males housed alone (64.2 ± 2.10 and 65.4 ± 2.11 days; Tukey P = 0.90 and P = 0.68). Six of the ten pairwise comparisons were significant at P < 0.05; the four that were not were the three comparisons among the non-mating groups and the no-females vs. one-virgin-female comparison (P = 0.13).”

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: Why the Inseminated-Female Groups Are the Design
text:
Why the Inseminated-Female Groups Are the Design








Important


The control that makes the experiment work
Newly inseminated females will not mate. Males housed with them get the presence of females without the mating.
Those groups isolate the cost of mating itself from the cost of simply having company — and they show no reduction in longevity at all (65.4 and 64.2 days, against 61.5 for males housed alone).










Note


📖 What this buys the write-up
Without those two groups you could only say “males near females die younger,” which has at least three explanations. With them, the conclusion narrows to one.
Design, not statistics, is what rules out the alternatives. ANCOVA just made the comparison fair on body size.

text: Publication Quality Figure

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Summary


What it is for

Combines regression and ANOVA
Increases power by soaking up residual variation with a covariate
Adjusts for confounds by comparing groups at a common covariate value


The workflow

Always test homogeneity of slopes first — lm(y ~ A * x)
Slopes homogeneous (p > 0.05) → fit the additive model, lm(y ~ x + A), and report adjusted means
Slopes heterogeneous (p < 0.05) → stop. Interpret the interaction and report slopes

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Summary — Interpreting and Reporting


Interpretation

car::Anova(model, type = "III") for the table
emmeans() for adjusted means and pairwise comparisons
emtrends() for slopes, when the interaction is the result
Report adjusted means, and say what covariate value they are adjusted to


The five assumptions

Independence
Normal residuals
Equal variances
Linearity within groups
Homogeneity of slopes — the one you test first







Important


And the one no test will find: the covariate must not be affected by the treatment.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Introduction to ANCOVA


ANCOVA = Analysis of COVAriance — regression and ANOVA in one model. You use it when you have:

a continuous response (Y)
a categorical predictor (factor A)
a continuous predictor, the covariate (X)

Two things it is for:

Compare group means after adjusting for the covariate
Ask whether two or more regression lines differ — in slope, in intercept, or both

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
When to Use ANCOVA

Common Applications of ANCOVA

Increasing statistical power

The covariate (e.g., body size, initial temperature) explains some of the “noise” (residual error) in the response variable.
By “removing” this variation, we reduce the residual error, making it easier to detect the true effect of our categorical factor.
This results in a more powerful test of treatment effects.

Adjusting for confounding variables

Imagine your treatment groups happen to differ in their average covariate value (e.g., Group A was tested in a warmer room than Group B).
ANCOVA allows you to separate the treatment effect from the covariate effect.

Testing equality of regression lines

Do treatments have the same relationship (slope) with a continuous variable?

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: The Motivating Problem — Grayling in Two Lakes
text:
The Motivating Problem — Grayling in Two Lakes


Back to the Arctic grayling from week 5 — the same fish, a new question.
Lake I8 fish weigh more than lake I3 fish. But I8 fish are also longer (mean 364 mm vs 266 mm).

Is there a lake effect on mass at all, or are I8 fish simply bigger?

You cannot answer that by comparing mean masses. The groups differ in the very thing that drives the response.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Two Problems, One Tool


Problem 1 — confounding. The groups differ in the covariate, so a raw comparison of means confuses the treatment with the covariate. This is the grayling problem, and the classic cricket problem (two species measured at different temperatures).
Problem 2 — noise. Even when the groups are balanced on the covariate, the covariate still soaks up residual variation. Removing it shrinks the error term and makes the test of the factor more powerful. This is the fruitfly problem in Part 4.







Important



ANCOVA does both with one model
\[y \sim \underbrace{x}_{\text{covariate}} + \underbrace{A}_{\text{factor}}\]
It compares groups at a common value of the covariate — the “level playing field” comparison — instead of wherever each group happened to sit.








Warning



⚠️ One rule before you start
The covariate must be measured independently of the treatment, and must not be affected by it. Adjusting for something the treatment caused removes the very effect you are trying to measure.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text: Part 2 · The ANCOVA Model

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
ANCOVA Linear Model: Conceptual Framework

The ANCOVA Model

Key concept: Dfference between “unadjusted” group means and “adjusted” means

In this visualization:

Group Means (asterisks): The raw average X and Y for each group.
Group A and Group B have different mean X values. Comparing directly misleading
Adjusted Means (triangles): ANCOVA statistically “moves” each group mean along regression line to single, common X value (the overall mean X).
ANCOVA compares heights (the Y values) of adjusted means.
Adjustment “levels the playing field,” estimating each group’s mean if all groups had same average covariate value

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text: ANCOVA Model Visualization

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Mathematical Model for ANCOVA

Single-factor ANCOVA with

factor A (p levels, i = 1 to p), a continuous covariate (x), and response variable (y): \(Y_{ij} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta(X_{ij} - \bar{X}) + \varepsilon_{ij}\)

Where:

\(Y_{ij}\) = response value for observation j in level i of factor A
\(\mu\) = overall mean
\(\alpha_i\) = effect of level i of factor A (what we test in ANOVA)
\(\beta\) = common regression slope relating Y to X (what we test in Regression)
\(X_{ij}\) = covariate value for observation j in level i of factor A
\(\bar{X}\) = mean value of covariate
\(\varepsilon_{ij}\) = error term

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
ANCOVA Parameters Interpretation



Interpretation of Parameters

\(\mu\) = overall mean response
\(\alpha_i\) = effect of level i (difference between group’s adjusted mean and overall mean)
\(\beta\) = pooled within-group regression coefficient (the slope)
\(X_{ij}\) = covariate value for observation j in group i
\(\bar{X}\) = overall mean of covariate
\(\varepsilon_{ij}\) = unexplained error

Model assumes homogeneous slopes (i.e., \(\beta\) same for all groups) .

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: Building the ANCOVA Model in R
text:
Building the ANCOVA Model in R

Remember lm(y ~ predictor).

ANCOVA combines the predictors from ANOVA and regression.

Simple Linear Regression:

Predict y using a continuous variable x.

model_reg <- lm(y ~ x, data = mydata)


One-Way ANOVA:

We want to compare y among groups in a categorical factor A.

model_aov <- lm(y ~ A, data = mydata)


ANCOVA (Additive Model):

Compare y among groups in A, after accounting for effect of x.
Add terms together

model_ancova <- lm(y ~ A + x, data = mydata)

Model assumes slope of y ~ x relationship is same for all groups in A.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: Building the ANCOVA Model in R — The Two Formulas
text:
Building the ANCOVA Model in R — The Two Formulas

ANCOVA (Interaction Model):

What if the slopes are different for each group?
Test for interaction between factor and covariate.

model_int <- lm(y ~ A * x, data = mydata)

Shorthand for: lm(y ~ A + x + A:x, data = mydata)
The A:x term tests if the slopes are different.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: ANCOVA in R: Workflow Steps 1 and 2
text:
ANCOVA in R: Workflow Steps 1 and 2

Step 1: Test for Homogeneity of Slopes - Always Start Here

Fit interaction model first - tests key assumption that all groups share same slope.

# The asterisk * tests for both main effects AND the interaction
model_int <- lm(y ~ A * x, data = mydata)
Step 2: Examine the Interaction Term

ANOVA table for model_int and find the p-value for interaction term (A:x).

    Anova(model_int, type = "III")

If p > 0.05 (e.g., p = 0.4) - interaction IS NOT significant - slopes are homogeneous (parallel).
If p < 0.05 (e.g., p = 0.02): - interaction IS significant - slopes heterogeneous (NOT parallel).
** standard ANCOVA model (y ~ A + x) inappropriate**
Analysis stops here and interpret interaction (often most interesting result!)

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
ANCOVA in R: Workflow Step 3

Step 3: Run the ANCOVA (Additive Model)

If interaction not significant, run the simpler additive model the final ANCOVA model.

# We use the + sign, which means "additive"
model_ancova <- lm(y ~ A + x, data = mydata)
# Get the final ANCOVA table
Anova(model_ancova, type = "III")
# Get the adjusted means
library(emmeans)
emmeans(model_ancova, "A")

ANOVA Table for ANCOVA
The ANOVA table for a single-factor ANCOVA has these components:


# Create a tibble with ANOVA table information
anova_table <- tibble(
  Source = c("Factor A (adjusted)", "Covariate", "Residual", "Total"),
  df = c("(p-1)", "1", "n-p-1", "n-1"),
  `Sum of Squares` = c("SS_A(adj)", "SS_Covariate", "SS_Residual", "SS_Total"),
  `Mean Square` = c(
    "MS_A(adj) = SS_A(adj)/(p-1)",
    "MS_Covariate = SS_Covariate/1",
    "MS_Residual = SS_Residual/(n-p-1)",
    ""
  ),
  `F-ratio` = c("MS_A(adj)/MS_Residual", "MS_Covariate/MS_Residual", "", ""),
  `Expected MS` = c("σ² + n∑α²/(p-1)", "σ² + β²∑(X-X̄)²", "σ²", "")
)

anova_table

## 1 Factor A (adjust… (p-1) SS_A(adj)        "MS_A(adj) =… "MS_A(ad… "σ² + n∑α²/(…
## 2 Covariate         1     SS_Covariate     "MS_Covariat… "MS_Cova… "σ² + β²∑(X-…
## 3 Residual          n-p-1 SS_Residual      "MS_Residual… ""        "σ²"         
## 4 Total             n-1   SS_Total         ""            ""        ""

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Null Hypotheses in ANCOVA

Homogeneity of Slopes (Test this first!)
\[H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = ... = \beta_p\]
Are the regression slopes the same for all groups?
Test with the A:x interaction term in lm(y ~ A * x).






Important



This one is an assumption check, not a result. You want to fail to reject it before going any further.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: Null Hypotheses in ANCOVA — the Two Results
text:
Null Hypotheses in ANCOVA — the Two Results



Treatment effect, adjusted
\[H_0: \alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = \dots = \alpha_p = 0\]
Are the adjusted group means equal?
\[F = \frac{MS_{A(adj)}}{MS_{residual}}\]
the A term in lm(y ~ x + A).



Covariate effect
\[H_0: \beta = 0\]
Does the covariate relate to the response at all?
\[F = \frac{MS_{covariate}}{MS_{residual}}\]
the x term in lm(y ~ x + A).

text:
Partridge Example: Steps 1–2 — Test Homogeneity of Slopes



homo_slopes_model <- lm(LONGEV ~ THORAX * treatment,
                        data = partridge)

Anova(homo_slopes_model, type = "III")
## Anova Table (Type III tests)
## 
## Response: LONGEV
##                   Sum Sq  Df  F value                Pr(>F)    
## (Intercept)       2963.8   1  26.0142           0.000001349 ***
## THORAX           12805.8   1 112.3988 < 0.00000000000000022 ***
## treatment           36.9   4   0.0810                0.9881    
## THORAX:treatment    42.5   4   0.0933                0.9844    
## Residuals        13102.1 115                                   
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The interaction THORAX:treatment has p = 0.984 — about as far from significant as it gets.
The five treatment groups share a common slope: body size buys the same amount of extra life in every group.






Note

text:
Partridge Example: Step 3 — Fit the Additive ANCOVA

Since the interaction was not significant, we re-run the model without it.

Interpretation:

THORAX: covariate highly significant
thorax length explains significant amount of variance in longevity
treatment: treatment effect, after adjusting for thorax length, is highly significant





# Step 3: Fit the ANCOVA model (additive model)
ancova_model <- lm(LONGEV ~ THORAX + treatment, data = partridge)
# View the final ANCOVA table
Anova(ancova_model, type = "III")

## Response: LONGEV
##              Sum Sq  Df F value                Pr(>F)

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
What the Covariate Bought You


Run the same question without the covariate, and compare:

# one-way ANOVA, covariate ignored
Anova(lm(LONGEV ~ treatment, data = partridge),
      type = 2)
## Anova Table (Type II tests)
## 
## Response: LONGEV
##           Sum Sq  Df F value         Pr(>F)    
## treatment  11939   4  13.612 0.000000003516 ***
## Residuals  26314 120                           
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


# ANCOVA, thorax length included
Anova(lm(LONGEV ~ THORAX + treatment, data = partridge),
      type = 2)
## Anova Table (Type II tests)
## 
## Response: LONGEV
##            Sum Sq  Df F value                Pr(>F)    
## THORAX    13168.9   1 119.219 < 0.00000000000000022 ***
## treatment  9611.5   4  21.753    0.0000000000001719 ***
## Residuals 13144.7 119                                  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1







one-way ANOVA
ANCOVA




residual SS
26,314
13,145


residual df
120
119


treatment F
13.61
21.75










Important



Thorax length absorbed half the residual variation.
One degree of freedom spent on the covariate cut the error term from 26,314 to 13,145, and the test of treatment got 60% bigger (F 13.6 → 21.8) — on identical data and an identical question.
That is the power argument, and it is why you measure a covariate even when your groups are perfectly balanced on it.


Here the treatment effect was significant either way. On a smaller or noisier dataset, that difference is the difference between finding the effect and missing it.

text:
Partridge Example: Getting Adjusted Means

The ANOVA table tells us the treatments are different, but not which ones.

Use emmeans package to get the adjusted means / perform pairwise comparisons
The “estimated marginal mean” (or adjusted mean)
predicted longevity for each group, assuming an average thorax length
This is the “level playing field” comparison.




# Get adjusted means using emmeans
library(emmeans)
adjusted_means <- emmeans(ancova_model, "treatment")
adjusted_means

Groups sharing a letter are not distinguishable. The red arrows say the same thing — overlapping arrows mean no significant difference.






Important



Read the pattern, not the ranking
The three non-mating groups are one block. One virgin female pulls longevity down a little; eight pulls it down a lot.
The dose that matters is matings, not company.
