title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text: Part 5 · Heterogeneous Slopes & Assumptions

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: What if the Slopes Are HETEROGENEOUS?
text:
What if the Slopes Are HETEROGENEOUS?


Back to the grayling. Fit the interaction model first, as always:

g_int <- lm(log_mass ~ log_len * lake, data = g_df)

Anova(g_int, type = 3)
## Anova Table (Type III tests)
## 
## Response: log_mass
##              Sum Sq  Df   F value                Pr(>F)    
## (Intercept)  1.8929   1 1337.5062 < 0.00000000000000022 ***
## log_len      4.0602   1 2868.9446 < 0.00000000000000022 ***
## lake         0.0094   1    6.6452              0.010833 *  
## log_len:lake 0.0117   1    8.2518              0.004617 ** 
## Residuals    0.2293 162                                    
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The interaction is significant (p = 0.0046). The two lakes do not share a slope.







Important



Stop. Do not fit the additive model.
log_mass ~ log_len + lake would force one common slope through two populations that do not have one, and then report a single “lake effect” that is true at no particular length.
There is no such thing as the difference between the lakes here. The difference depends on how big the fish is.








Note



📖 This is not a failure
A significant interaction is usually the more interesting result. It says the groups differ in how the response scales, not merely in where it sits.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Reading Heterogeneous Slopes — emtrends()



emtrends(g_int, "lake", var = "log_len")
##  lake log_len.trend     SE  df lower.CL upper.CL
##  I3            2.79 0.0943 162     2.61     2.98
##  I8            3.11 0.0569 162     3.00     3.22
## 
## Confidence level used: 0.95

pairs(emtrends(g_int, "lake", var = "log_len"))
##  contrast estimate   SE  df t.ratio p.value
##  I3 - I8    -0.316 0.11 162  -2.873  0.0046


emtrends() is emmeans() for slopes. It gives one slope per group, with a standard error, and pairs() tests whether they differ.
On log-log axes the slope is the allometric exponent: mass ∝ lengthb.






Important



The biology is in the exponent

I8: b = 3.11 — not distinguishable from 3 (p = 0.058). Isometric: these fish keep their shape as they grow.
I3: b = 2.79 — significantly below 3 (p = 0.029). I3 grayling get relatively lighter as they lengthen.

That is a condition difference between the lakes, and an additive ANCOVA would have hidden it entirely.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: Where Do the Groups Actually Differ?
text:
Where Do the Groups Actually Differ?


With non-parallel lines, the gap between groups changes along the covariate. So ask for the contrast at specific covariate values:

lens <- log10(c(200, 250, 300))

pairs(emmeans(g_int, ~ lake | log_len,
              at = list(log_len = lens)))
## log_len = 2.30:
##  contrast estimate      SE  df t.ratio p.value
##  I3 - I8   -0.0299 0.01940 162  -1.540  0.1256
## 
## log_len = 2.40:
##  contrast estimate      SE  df t.ratio p.value
##  I3 - I8   -0.0605 0.01110 162  -5.479 <0.0001
## 
## log_len = 2.48:
##  contrast estimate      SE  df t.ratio p.value
##  I3 - I8   -0.0856 0.00914 162  -9.370 <0.0001






Length
I3 − I8 (log mass)
p




200 mm
−0.030
0.13


250 mm
−0.061
<0.0001


300 mm
−0.107
<0.0001




At 200 mm the two lakes are indistinguishable. The gap opens as the fish get longer, and by 300 mm an I3 grayling is about 20% lighter than an I8 grayling of the same length.






Warning



⚠️ johnson_neyman = TRUE does not work here
The Johnson–Neyman procedure needs a continuous moderator. interactions::sim_slopes() will warn “Johnson-Neyman intervals are not available for factor predictors or moderators” and give you nothing. With a categorical factor, the contrast-at-covariate-values above is the right tool.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Handling Heterogeneous Slopes — the Options


When the interaction is significant:

Report the interaction. It is the result. Give the slopes, not an adjusted mean.
emtrends() for a slope per group, with pairs() to test them.
Contrast at chosen covariate values — emmeans(~ A | x, at = ...) — to say where along the covariate the groups separate.
Johnson–Neyman, but only when the moderator is continuous.
Separate regressions per group. Simple, honest, least powerful, and it gives up the shared error term.








Warning



⚠️ Mind the covariate ranges
I3 fish run 191–320 mm; I8 fish run 207–440 mm. The lines can only be compared where both groups have data.
Reporting a lake difference at 400 mm would mean extrapolating the I3 line past every I3 fish ever measured. ANCOVA will do that arithmetic without complaint. You have to be the one who refuses.








Note



This caution applies to the additive model too — an “adjusted mean” at \(\bar{x}\) is an extrapolation for any group whose data does not reach \(\bar{x}\).

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Assumptions of ANCOVA






#
Assumption
How you check it




1
Independence
design, not a test


2
Normal residuals
Q-Q plot


3
Equal variances
residuals vs. fitted


4
Linearity of Y on X within each group
scatterplot


5
Homogeneity of slopes
the A:x interaction











Important



#5 is the one that is special to ANCOVA, and the only one you test before fitting the model you will report. The other four are the ordinary linear-model assumptions you have been checking since week 7.








Warning



⚠️ And one that is not on the list
The covariate must be independent of the treatment. No test will catch a violation — only knowing how the data were collected will.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Checking Assumptions in R












Check assumptions 2 and 3 on the final model — the additive one, if the slopes let you fit it.

Residuals vs. fitted — red line roughly flat at 0 ✅
Normal Q-Q — points on the dashed line ✅
Scale-location — red line flat ✅
Residuals vs. leverage — nothing stranded in the right-hand corners ✅







Note



Conclusion: the assumptions are met, so the ANCOVA table on the previous slides can be reported as it stands.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Robust ANCOVA Approaches


When the assumptions are badly violated — not marginally:

Rank transformation — rank both Y and X, then run the ordinary ANCOVA on the ranks: lm(rank(y) ~ rank(x) + A)
Bootstrapping — resample to get intervals without assuming normality
Quantile regression — model the median, or any quantile, instead of the mean
Permutation tests — randomise the treatment labels to build the null distribution







Tip



🖐 Run it as a sensitivity check. If the robust version agrees with the parametric one, report the parametric one and say you checked.




rank_ancova <- lm(rank(LONGEV) ~ rank(THORAX) + treatment,
                  data = partridge)

signif(c(
  parametric = Anova(ancova_model, type = "III")["treatment", "Pr(>F)"],
  rank_based = Anova(rank_ancova,  type = "III")["treatment", "Pr(>F)"]), 3)
##        parametric        rank_based 
## 0.000000000000172 0.000000000000654

Both vanishingly small — the parametric result stands.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text: Part 6 · Reporting Results

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Writing Up ANCOVA Results
Scientific Writing Example
Here’s how you might write up ANCOVA results for publication:

“We analyzed the effects of mating opportunity on male fruitfly longevity using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), with thorax length as a covariate. Before conducting the main analysis, we tested the homogeneity-of-slopes assumption and found no significant treatment × thorax length interaction (F₄,₁₁₅ = 0.09, P = 0.98), indicating that the effect of body size on longevity was consistent across treatments.
The ANCOVA revealed significant effects of both treatment (F₄,₁₁₉ = 21.75, P < 0.001) and thorax length (F₁,₁₁₉ = 119.22, P < 0.001) on longevity. Thorax length was positively associated with longevity.
After adjusting for body size, longevity declined with the number of virgin females a male was housed with (adjusted mean ± SE: 54.5 ± 2.11 days for one virgin female and 41.6 ± 2.12 days for eight, versus 61.5 ± 2.11 days for males housed alone). Males housed with inseminated females — which do not mate — did not differ from males housed alone (64.2 ± 2.10 and 65.4 ± 2.11 days; Tukey P = 0.90 and P = 0.68). Six of the ten pairwise comparisons were significant at P < 0.05; the four that were not were the three comparisons among the non-mating groups and the no-females vs. one-virgin-female comparison (P = 0.13).”

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
section: Why the Inseminated-Female Groups Are the Design
text:
Why the Inseminated-Female Groups Are the Design








Important



The control that makes the experiment work
Newly inseminated females will not mate. Males housed with them get the presence of females without the mating.
Those groups isolate the cost of mating itself from the cost of simply having company — and they show no reduction in longevity at all (65.4 and 64.2 days, against 61.5 for males housed alone).









Note



📖 What this buys the write-up
Without those two groups you could only say “males near females die younger,” which has at least three explanations. With them, the conclusion narrows to one.
Design, not statistics, is what rules out the alternatives. ANCOVA just made the comparison fair on body size.

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text: Publication Quality Figure

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Summary


What it is for

Combines regression and ANOVA
Increases power by soaking up residual variation with a covariate
Adjusts for confounds by comparing groups at a common covariate value


The workflow

Always test homogeneity of slopes first — lm(y ~ A * x)
Slopes homogeneous (p > 0.05) → fit the additive model, lm(y ~ x + A), and report adjusted means
Slopes heterogeneous (p < 0.05) → stop. Interpret the interaction and report slopes

title: Lecture: ANCOVA — Analysis of Covariance
text:
Summary — Interpreting and Reporting


Interpretation

car::Anova(model, type = "III") for the table
emmeans() for adjusted means and pairwise comparisons
emtrends() for slopes, when the interaction is the result
Report adjusted means, and say what covariate value they are adjusted to


The five assumptions

Independence
Normal residuals
Equal variances
Linearity within groups
Homogeneity of slopes — the one you test first







Important



And the one no test will find: the covariate must not be affected by the treatment.

The fruitfly data are Partridge & Farquhar’s, reproduced in Quinn & Keough Box 12-1. The Arctic grayling are from the Arctic LTER — the same lakes you met in week 5.
The textbook PDFs are on Canvas.

text: Part 1 · Overview

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Today’s Objectives


Two techniques, one idea — a straight line through a cloud of points:

Correlation — how tightly do two variables move together?
Regression — what equation predicts Y from X?
Assumptions for each, and what to do when they fail
Sums of squares — how a fitted line becomes an ANOVA table

This lecture runs over two class days: correlation first, regression second.
📥 Booby data 📥 Rope trick data 📥 Lion data 📥 Script skeleton (.R)







Note


📖 Reading

Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 16 (Correlation) and Ch. 17 (Regression).
Gotelli & Ellison, Ch. 9 (Regression).

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
🗳️ How Today Works






Warning


🗳️ Six times over the two days, you make the call
Six slides are marked 🗳️ DECIDE. Each asks a multiple-choice question, and I will not tell you the answer on that slide.
How it works: write your letter down — actually write it — then hold up fingers 1–4. If the room splits, turn to the person next to you, argue for ninety seconds, and we vote again. Nothing here is graded. The point is that you commit before you find out.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text: Part 2 · Correlation vs. Regression

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Correlation vs. Regression — What’s the Difference?
text:
Correlation vs. Regression — What’s the Difference?


Correlation

Measures the strength and direction of a relationship
Both X and Y are measured; neither is manipulated
The variables are on equal footing — swap them and r is unchanged
r2 = percent variation explained
One number, from −1 to +1

Regression

Produces an equation predicting Y from X
You assume a direction, X → Y, when you choose which is which - Y is dependent on X
Swap X and Y and you get a different line - and it becomes a different type of regression
Gives you a slope, an intercept, and predictions

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Choosing X Does Not Make It a Cause
text:
Choosing X Does Not Make It a Cause








Warning


⚠️ Regression does not earn you causation
lm(y ~ x) will fit a slope to any two numeric columns you hand it, including ones with no causal link at all. Putting a variable on the right-hand side is a decision you made, not a finding.
What licenses a causal claim is the study design — manipulation, randomization, controls — not the model you fit afterwards.



Last week’s inference gradient, in one line: the same lm() output supports a weak claim from an observational survey and a strong claim from a randomized experiment. The design decides which one you are allowed to write.







Note


Which do I report?

Both variables measured, no direction implied → correlation
One variable predicts or sets the other, or you want predictions → regression
Reporting both is fine; claiming cause from either is not

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text: Part 3 · Correlation Analysis

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
What Is Correlation?


Correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two numerical variables. It runs from −1 to +1:

+1 — perfect positive
0 — no linear relationship
−1 — perfect negative

The Pearson correlation coefficient:
\[r = \frac{\sum_{i}(X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i}(X_i - \bar{X})^2 \sum_{i}(Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}}\]
which is
\[r = \frac{\text{Covariance}(X, Y)}{s_X \cdot s_Y}\]

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · Which One Has r Closest to Zero?
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · Which One Has r Closest to Zero?


Four datasets, plotted on the right. No correlation coefficients shown — on purpose.
Which panel has the Pearson correlation closest to zero?

Panel A
Panel B
Panel C
Panel D







Warning


✍️ Write your letter down, then vote.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: What r Can and Cannot See
text:
What r Can and Cannot See








Important


✅ The answer is (b) — Panel B.

Panel B is the most tightly related pair on the slide: give me x and I can tell you y almost exactly.
Its correlation is near zero anyway, because the relationship is an arch, not a line.
Panel C looks like the messiest, so most rooms vote (c). It has a weak but genuine linear trend, so its r sits farther from zero than B’s.





r measures one thing only: how close the points lie to a straight line.
A perfect relationship with a curve in it reads as “no correlation.”
Panel D is the other warning — a single far-out point can manufacture a large r out of a cloud with no trend in it.











Always plot the data before you trust a correlation coefficient.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Example 16.1 · Flipping the Bird


Nazca boobies (Sula granti): do the visits a chick receives from non-parent adults predict how aggressive it is as an adult?

booby_df <- read_csv("data/booby_aggression.csv")

cor.test(booby_df$visits_as_nestling,
         booby_df$future_aggression)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  booby_df$visits_as_nestling and booby_df$future_aggression
t = 2.9603, df = 22, p-value = 0.007229
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1660840 0.7710999
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.5337225

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Example 16.1 · Interpretation


r = 0.534 — a moderate positive relationship, p = 0.00723.

Square it for the variance explained: r² = 0.285, so about 28.5% of the variation in one variable is accounted for by the other
Standard error: \(\text{SE}_r = \sqrt{\dfrac{1-r^2}{n-2}}\) = 0.18
Tested with a t-test: \(t = r / SE_r\), df = n − 2

In words: boobies visited more often as nestlings tend to be more aggressive adults. Nothing here says the visits caused it.







Note


🔮 Predict first
Next we run Shapiro-Wilk on both booby variables, then look at their histograms and QQ plots.
If the formal test and the picture disagree at n = 24, which would you trust?

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Testing Assumptions for Correlation


Pearson correlation assumes:

Random sampling from the population
Bivariate normality — each variable normal, and normal jointly
A linear relationship — not a curve
No extreme outliers driving the result


shapiro.test(booby_df$visits_as_nestling)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  booby_df$visits_as_nestling
W = 0.95783, p-value = 0.3965




shapiro.test(booby_df$future_aggression)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  booby_df$future_aggression
W = 0.91575, p-value = 0.04709








Note


H₀ is “these data ARE normal”
A large p-value is the good outcome — the same backwards logic as Levene’s test.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Checking the Same Assumptions by Eye
text:
Checking the Same Assumptions by Eye


The two tests do not agree with each other:

visits, p = 0.396 — clean
aggression, p = 0.047 — just under 0.05

Now look at the pictures. No strong skew, points close to both QQ lines, and the scatterplot was straight rather than curved.






Important


✅ This is the case the last slide asked you to predict
At n = 24, a normality p of 0.047 is a coin-flip verdict, not evidence of a real problem. W&S report Pearson’s r for these data, and so do we.
Compare that with the next dataset, where the test and the picture agree that something is wrong.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
When the Assumption Fails — Example 16.5


W&S Example 16.5: people who had seen the Indian rope trick were asked, years later, how impressive it was — on a subjective score.
That score is bounded and lumpy, and it fails Shapiro badly. Three options when normality fails:

Transform one or both variables (log, square root)
Switch to a rank-based correlation — Spearman’s ρ or Kendall’s τ
Hunt down the outlier that is doing the work


rope_df <- read_csv("data/rope_trick.csv")

shapiro.test(rope_df$impressiveness)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  rope_df$impressiveness
W = 0.82319, p-value = 0.001517












The longer ago someone saw the trick, the more impressive they remember it being.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Spearman’s Rho nonparametric correlation



cor.test(rope_df$years_since_seen,
         rope_df$impressiveness,
         method = "spearman")


    Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  rope_df$years_since_seen and rope_df$impressiveness
S = 332.12, p-value = 2.571e-05
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
      rho 
0.7843363 



Spearman replaces each value with its rank and correlates the ranks — so it needs no normality and is not thrown by one extreme value.

Pearson r = 0.848
Spearman ρ = 0.784

Square ρ the same way: ρ² = 0.615 — about 61.5% of the variation in the ranks.






Note


The cost of switching
You keep an honest p-value and lose the original units. ρ is about ranks, so it can no longer be read as “score per year.”

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · The Correlation That Shrank


A colleague reports r = 0.82 between body size and fecundity across a set of populations.
You repeat the study, carefully, at one site — where the animals are all close to the same size — and get r = 0.31 from data that are every bit as clean.
What is the most likely explanation?
(a) The original result was a false positive
(b) Your sample size was too small
(c) Restricting the range of X shrank r, with the underlying relationship unchanged
(d) Measurement error in your study inflated r






Warning


✍️ One letter. Write it down.










Note


The question to ask
Did the relationship change — or did the slice of the world I looked at change?

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Two Things That Move r Without Touching the Biology
text:
Two Things That Move r Without Touching the Biology








Important


✅ The answer is (c).
Range restriction. r depends on the spread of X you sampled. Look at a narrow slice of a real relationship and r falls, even though the slope is unchanged. This is why correlations from studies with different ranges cannot be compared head to head.









Warning


⚠️ Attenuation
Measurement error in X or Y pushes r toward zero, never away from it. The true correlation is usually stronger than the one you observed — so (d) has the direction backwards.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Correlation — What to Carry Forward



r measures straight-line association only — always plot first
r² is the variance the two variables share
The range you sampled sets the ceiling on r; measurement error lowers it further
Correlation does not imply causation. Three explanations always survive: X causes Y, Y causes X, or Z causes both
The test: H₀ is ρ = 0, statistic t = r / SE(r), df = n − 2
When normality fails, switch to rank-based Spearman’s ρ








Note


✅ End of the correlation half
You can now run cor.test(), check its assumptions on the raw variables, switch to Spearman when they fail, and say what r and r² mean.
Next: the same cloud of points — but now we fit a line to it and ask what that line is made of.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text: Part 4 · Linear Regression — the Model

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
The Simple Linear Regression Model


Regression models the response Y as a straight-line function of the predictor X.
The population model: \(Y = \alpha + \beta X + \varepsilon\)

α is the intercept — the value of Y when X = 0
β is the slope — the change in Y per one-unit change in X
ε is the error — the random deviation of a point from the line

The sample equation: \(\hat{Y} = a + bX\), where a estimates α and b estimates β.
Method of least squares: of all possible lines, take the one that makes
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\]
as small as possible — the sum of the squared vertical distances.


Least squares picks the third one.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Fitting the Lion Model


Male lions accumulate black pigment on the nose as they age — so nose colour can age a lion in the field without anyone killing it.

lion_df <- read_csv("data/lion_noses.csv")

lion_model <- lm(age_years ~ proportion_black,
                 data = lion_df)
coef(lion_model)

     (Intercept) proportion_black 
       0.8790062       10.6471194 


Read the formula as response ~ predictor.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Reading the Model Output



summary(lion_model)


Call:
lm(formula = age_years ~ proportion_black, data = lion_df)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-2.5449 -1.1117 -0.5285  0.9635  4.3421 

Coefficients:
                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        0.8790     0.5688   1.545    0.133    
proportion_black  10.6471     1.5095   7.053 7.68e-08 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1.669 on 30 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6238,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6113 
F-statistic: 49.75 on 1 and 30 DF,  p-value: 7.677e-08



\[\widehat{\text{age}} = 0.88 + 10.65 \times \text{prop. black}\]

Estimate — the intercept and the slope
Std. Error — how precisely each is pinned down
t value — estimate ÷ SE, testing H₀: β = 0
Multiple R-squared = 0.624 — the share of variation in age explained by nose colour







Note


Notice
Correlating these same two variables and squaring r gives the same 0.624. Hold that thought — Part 5 explains why.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · What the Slope and Intercept Say
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · What the Slope and Intercept Say


The fitted line is \(\widehat{\text{age}} = 0.88 + 10.65 \times \text{prop. black}\).
Which statement is correct?
(a) A lion’s nose darkens by 10.65 units for every year it ages
(b) Going from a nose 10% black to one 20% black predicts about 1.06 more years of age
(c) A newborn lion is predicted to be 0.88 years old, so the model is wrong
(d) 62.4% of lions are aged correctly by this equation






Warning


✍️ Write your letter down, then vote.










Note


Ask yourself
What are the units on this slope?
A slope is always units of Y per one unit of X — and here one unit of X is the whole range, from a clean nose to a fully black one.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Slope and Intercept, in Words








Important


✅ The answer is (b).
The slope is 10.65 years per unit of proportion black, and one unit is the entire 0-to-1 range. A 0.1 change in blackness therefore predicts about 1.06 years.
(a) reverses the variables — that is the regression of blackness on age, a different line.
(c) misreads the intercept: it is 0.88 years at proportion black = 0, and the youngest lion measured was 1.1 years old, so X = 0 sits outside the data. The intercept anchors the line; it is not a claim about newborns.
(d) confuses R² with an accuracy rate. R² is variance explained, not the percentage of lions got right.










Warning


⚠️ Extrapolation
A fitted line says nothing about X values you never sampled, and the confidence band is widest exactly where you have no data.









Tip


🖐 The habit to build
Write every slope out as a sentence in the units of the data — “for every extra , Y changes by” — before you write a word about significance.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Calculating the Slope and Intercept by Hand
text:
Calculating the Slope and Intercept by Hand


\[b = \frac{\sum_i(X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\sum_i(X_i - \bar{X})^2}
\qquad a = \bar{Y} - b\bar{X}\]
The numerator is a sum of cross-products; the denominator is a sum of squares. Both are the same kind of quantity the ANOVA table is built from in a moment.

x <- lion_df$proportion_black
y <- lion_df$age_years

b <- sum((x - mean(x)) * (y - mean(y))) / sum((x - mean(x))^2)
a <- mean(y) - b * mean(x)
c(intercept = a, slope = b)

 intercept      slope 
 0.8790062 10.6471194 



Compare that with what lm() reported:

coef(lion_model)

     (Intercept) proportion_black 
       0.8790062       10.6471194 








Note


Same answer, no magic
lm() is doing this arithmetic. Everything harder than this — multiple predictors, ANOVA, mixed models — is the same idea written in matrix form.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Making Predictions



new_lion <- tibble(proportion_black = 0.50)

predict(lion_model, new_lion, interval = "confidence")

       fit      lwr     upr
1 6.202566 5.388042 7.01709

predict(lion_model, new_lion, interval = "prediction")

       fit      lwr     upr
1 6.202566 2.698512 9.70662



Both intervals sit on the same predicted age, and answer different questions:

Confidence interval — where the mean age of all lions with 50% black noses lies
Prediction interval — where a single new lion’s age lies

The prediction interval is always wider: it carries the scatter of individual lions plus the uncertainty in the line itself.
Both are narrowest at \(\bar{X}\) and flare out toward the edges of the data.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Example 17.3 · Prairie Biodiversity and Stability


Tilman et al. (2006): does a more diverse plant community produce more stable biomass? 161 plots, seeded with 1 to 16 species.

prairie_df <- read_csv("data/prairie_stability.csv")

prairie_model <- lm(log(biomass_stability) ~ species_number,
                    data = prairie_df)
summary(prairie_model)$coefficients

                Estimate  Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)    1.1982943 0.041298043 29.015766 2.075490e-65
species_number 0.0329259 0.004883691  6.742012 2.733315e-10

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
The Prairie Model — Interpretation


The hypothesis test is about the slope:

H₀: β = 0 — species number has no effect on stability
H₁: β ≠ 0

Slope = 0.0329 — log stability rises by about 0.033 per extra species, so a 16-species plot sits roughly 0.49 log units above a monoculture.
p = 2.73e-10 — strong evidence against a zero slope.
R² = 0.222 — diversity explains about 22.2% of the variation in stability. Real, and nowhere near the whole story.







Note


Significant ≠ large
A tiny p-value alongside R² = 0.22 is completely ordinary in ecology.
The p-value says the slope is not zero. R² says how much of the world it accounts for. Report both.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Part 5 · Sums of Squares — the Engine of Everything After This
text: Part 5 · Sums of Squares — the Engine of Everything After This

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Where the Variation Goes


Take one data point. Its distance from the overall mean \(\bar{y}\) splits, exactly, into two pieces:
\[\underbrace{(y_i - \bar{y})}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})}_{\text{explained}} + \underbrace{(y_i - \hat{y}_i)}_{\text{left over}}\]
Square those deviations and add them up over every point, and the same split holds for the whole dataset:
\[SS_{total} = SS_{regression} + SS_{residual}\]

\(SS_{regression}\) — variation the line accounts for; df = 1
\(SS_{residual}\) — variation it does not; df = n − 2
\(SS_{total}\) — all of it; df = n − 1

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · Which Fit Has the Bigger Sums of Squares?
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · Which Fit Has the Bigger Sums of Squares?


Four fitted regressions, on the right.
Which statement is true?
(a) \(SS_{regression}\) is larger in (d) than in (c)
(b) \(SS_{residual}\) is larger in (b) than in (a)
(c) \(SS_{total}\) is larger in (a) than in (b)
(d) \(SS_{residual}\) is zero in (c)






Warning


✍️ One letter. Write it down, then argue it with your neighbour.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Reading the Partition Off a Picture
text:
Reading the Partition Off a Picture








Important


✅ The answer is (b).
\(SS_{residual}\) is the scatter around the line, and the points in (b) sit farther off their line than those in (a).
(a) is backwards: \(SS_{regression}\) grows with how steeply the fitted line climbs, and (c) is steeper than (d).
(c) is the trap — \(SS_{total}\) does not depend on the fit at all. It is the spread of Y around its own mean, and the line has nothing to do with it.
(d) would require every point to sit exactly on the line.










Note


The three pictures to keep

\(SS_{total}\) → distance from the flat mean line
\(SS_{regression}\) → how far the fitted line climbs away from that flat line
\(SS_{residual}\) → how far the points sit off the fitted line




A fit is good when the line does a lot of climbing and the points stay close to it.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Computing the Three Sums of Squares
text:
Computing the Three Sums of Squares



fitted_age <- predict(lion_model)
mean_age   <- mean(lion_df$age_years)

ss_total <- sum((lion_df$age_years - mean_age)^2)
ss_reg   <- sum((fitted_age - mean_age)^2)
ss_resid <- sum((lion_df$age_years - fitted_age)^2)

c(total = ss_total, regression = ss_reg, residual = ss_resid)

     total regression   residual 
 222.08719  138.54398   83.54321 

ss_reg + ss_resid          # does it add back up?

[1] 222.0872



138.5 + 83.5 = 222.1 — exactly.
And the share the line accounts for:
\[R^2 = \frac{SS_{regression}}{SS_{total}} = \frac{138.5}{222.1} = 0.624\]






Important


✅ This is where R² comes from
R² is not a separate statistic. It is the regression sum of squares as a fraction of the total — and with one predictor it is exactly the correlation coefficient squared.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: The Same Numbers, Straight from R
text:
The Same Numbers, Straight from R



anova(lion_model)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: age_years
                 Df  Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
proportion_black  1 138.544 138.544   49.75 7.677e-08 ***
Residuals        30  83.543   2.785                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



Every number in that table you have now built by hand:

Sum Sq — the two sums of squares, 138.5 and 83.5
Df — 1 for the predictor, n − 2 = 30 for the residual
Mean Sq — Sum Sq ÷ Df
F value — the ratio of those two mean squares







Note


This table has a shape, not a topic
The identical five columns show up for one-way ANOVA, two-way ANOVA, nested ANOVA and ANCOVA. Only the rows change.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: From Sums of Squares to Mean Squares
text:
From Sums of Squares to Mean Squares


A sum of squares keeps growing as you add data, so it cannot be compared across studies. Divide by degrees of freedom and you get a mean square — a variance, which does not grow with n:
\[MS = \frac{SS}{df} \qquad F = \frac{MS_{regression}}{MS_{residual}}\]

\(MS_{residual}\) = 2.785 — estimates the background variance σ²
\(MS_{regression}\) = 138.54 — estimates that same σ², plus whatever the X–Y relationship adds
If the slope is truly zero, both estimate the same thing and F ≈ 1. Here F = 49.75

Sums of squares add up. Mean squares do not.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · You Double the Sample Size
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · You Double the Sample Size


You repeat the lion study and come back with 64 lions instead of 32. The relationship is identical — same slope, same scatter around the line.
Compared with the original analysis, what happens?
(a) \(SS_{total}\) roughly doubles, and \(MS_{residual}\) roughly doubles with it
(b) \(SS_{total}\) roughly doubles, but \(MS_{residual}\) stays about the same
(c) Both stay about the same — doubling n changes neither
(d) \(SS_{total}\) stays about the same and \(MS_{residual}\) halves






Warning


✍️ Write your letter down. This one decides whether you can read the table.










Note


The question to ask
Which of these is a total, and which is an average?

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Why Mean Squares Exist At All
text:
Why Mean Squares Exist At All








Important


✅ The answer is (b).
\(SS_{total}\) is a sum over every observation, so twice the data is roughly twice the sum. \(MS_{residual}\) is that sum divided by its degrees of freedom — an average squared deviation — so it estimates the same σ² no matter how many lions you measure.
That is exactly why the table converts sums of squares into mean squares before testing anything. You cannot compare two sums built from different amounts of data; you can compare two variances.










Tip


🖐 What doubling n actually buys
σ² does not change, but the standard error of the slope shrinks with √n — so F rises and the confidence band tightens.
More data does not reduce the scatter in nature. It reduces your uncertainty about the line running through it.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: The Bridge · One Table, Every Model From Here
text:
The Bridge · One Table, Every Model From Here


For the lion model, all of these are the same test:




Route
Value




t on the slope
7.053


t²
49.75


F from anova()
49.75


p, either way
7.68e-08




t² = F. The t-test on a slope and the F-test in the ANOVA table are one test asked two ways — and \(r^2 = SS_{reg}/SS_{total}\) ties both back to the correlation half of this lecture.







Important


✅ Why this is the most important slide today
Every analysis for the rest of the course is this same partition with more rows:

One-way ANOVA — groups instead of a slope
Two-way ANOVA — a row per factor, plus interaction
Nested ANOVA — a row per level of nesting
ANCOVA — a slope row and a group row

Learn to read this table once and you can read all of them.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text: Part 6 · Testing Regression Assumptions

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Testing Regression Assumptions — Overview


Simple linear regression assumes:

Linearity — the true relationship is a straight line
Independence — observations do not depend on each other
Homoscedasticity — equal scatter at every value of X
Normality — the residuals are normally distributed

Stated formally: the error \(\varepsilon_i\) is normal, with a mean of 0 and the same variance, at every value of x.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Every Check Is About the Residuals
text:
Every Check Is About the Residuals


Every assumption check from here on uses the residuals, not the raw data. That is the single most common mix-up in regression.
The error \(\varepsilon_i\) is estimated by the residual \(e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\) — the same red segment you have seen on every lion plot today, and the same quantity that got squared and summed to build \(SS_{residual}\).
Least squares already made these as small as possible. The diagnostics ask whether what is left over looks like random noise.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Checking Linearity — Residuals vs. Fitted


What you want: a shapeless cloud, scattered evenly above and below the horizontal line at zero.
What is a problem: any curve in the trend line. A U-shape or an arch means a straight line is the wrong shape for these data — the exact failure Panel B showed back in the correlation half.
The plot doubles as a homoscedasticity check: if the cloud fans out or funnels in from left to right, the variance is not constant.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Checking Normality — QQ Plot of Residuals
text:
Checking Normality — QQ Plot of Residuals


The QQ plot compares your residuals with what perfectly normal residuals would look like.
What you want: points hugging the diagonal.
What is a problem: systematic curvature, or points peeling away at the ends. Tails are where non-normality shows up first, and tails are what p-values depend on.
Note we check the residuals, not age_years itself. The raw ages are right-skewed, and that is allowed. It is the residuals that have to behave.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Checking Normality — Shapiro-Wilk on Residuals



shapiro.test(residuals(lion_model))


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  residuals(lion_model)
W = 0.93879, p-value = 0.0692


residuals(model) — not lion_df$age_years. Testing the raw response is a different, and usually wrong, question.







Note


H₀ is “the residuals ARE normal”
So a large p-value is the good outcome.









Warning


⚠️ Do not let this test overrule your eyes
At small n it has almost no power to detect a real problem; at large n it flags departures far too small to matter. Read the QQ plot first and use the test to support it — not to replace it.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
What Violations Actually Look Like


When an assumption fails:

Transform one or both variables (W&S §17.6) — a log on a curved or fanning relationship fixes both problems more often than not
Weighted least squares for heteroscedasticity
A non-linear model (§17.8), or a GLM in Week 11

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · One Island


Gotelli & Ellison’s Galápagos data: 17 islands, plant species richness against island area, both log-transformed. The fit is solid — R² = 0.585, p = 3.50e-04.
Now one more point arrives: a large island reported with very few species (red).
What does that single point do?
(a) Very little — one point in 18 cannot matter much
(b) It raises R², because the range of X just got wider
(c) It roughly halves R² and pushes p to the edge of significance
(d) It can change R² but not the slope






Warning


✍️ One letter, before the next slide.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
What One Point Did



galap_plot <- galap_df %>%
  mutate(log_area = log10(area_km2),
         log_species = log10(n_species))

# a big island reported with very few species
galap_bad <- galap_plot %>%
  add_row(log_area = 3, log_species = 0.65)

clean_model <- lm(log_species ~ log_area, galap_plot)
bad_model   <- lm(log_species ~ log_area, galap_bad)

tibble(data  = c("17 islands", "plus the suspect point"),
       slope = c(coef(clean_model)[2], coef(bad_model)[2]),
       r2    = c(summary(clean_model)$r.squared,
                 summary(bad_model)$r.squared))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  data                   slope    r2
  <chr>                  <dbl> <dbl>
1 17 islands             0.331 0.585
2 plus the suspect point 0.233 0.228









Important


✅ The answer is (c).
One point out of 18 cuts R² from 0.58 to 0.23 and moves p from 3.50e-04 to 0.0449 — from convincing to barely publishable. The slope drops too, so (d) is out.
It is influential because it lies far out in X and far off the trend. Cook’s distance flags it at once — that is what panel 4 of plot(model) is for.



No diagnostic can tell you whether it is a typo or a real island. That takes going back to the data sheet.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text: Part 7 · Wrap-up

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Wrap-up


Over the two days you:

Separated correlation from regression, and saw that neither earns causation
Computed Pearson’s r, squared it for variance explained, and tested it with cor.test()
Switched to Spearman’s ρ when normality failed
Fitted a line with lm() and read the slope in the units of the data
Built \(SS_{regression}\) and \(SS_{residual}\) by hand, watched them add to \(SS_{total}\), and turned them into mean squares and an F
Confirmed t² = F and r² = SS_reg / SS_total
Checked all four assumptions on the residuals, and watched one influential island halve an R²








Important


✅ The one idea to keep
A line can be fitted to any two numeric columns. What makes it trustworthy lives in the residuals; what makes it interpretable lives in the sums of squares. Neither lives in the p-value.









Note


Up next — Multiple Regression
More than one predictor, predictors correlated with each other, and choosing between competing models. Same table, more rows.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Today’s Objectives


Two techniques, one idea — a straight line through a cloud of points:

Correlation — how tightly do two variables move together?
Regression — what equation predicts Y from X?
Assumptions for each, and what to do when they fail
Sums of squares — how a fitted line becomes an ANOVA table

This lecture runs over two class days: correlation first, regression second.
📥 Booby data 📥 Rope trick data 📥 Lion data 📥 Script skeleton (.R)







Note

Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 16 (Correlation) and Ch. 17 (Regression).
Gotelli & Ellison, Ch. 9 (Regression).

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
🗳️ How Today Works






Warning

Six slides are marked 🗳️ DECIDE. Each asks a multiple-choice question, and I will not tell you the answer on that slide.
How it works: write your letter down — actually write it — then hold up fingers 1–4. If the room splits, turn to the person next to you, argue for ninety seconds, and we vote again. Nothing here is graded. The point is that you commit before you find out.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text: Part 2 · Correlation vs. Regression

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Correlation vs. Regression — What’s the Difference?
text:
Correlation vs. Regression — What’s the Difference?


Correlation

Measures the strength and direction of a relationship
Both X and Y are measured; neither is manipulated
The variables are on equal footing — swap them and r is unchanged
r2 = percent variation explained
One number, from −1 to +1

Regression

Produces an equation predicting Y from X
You assume a direction, X → Y, when you choose which is which - Y is dependent on X
Swap X and Y and you get a different line - and it becomes a different type of regression
Gives you a slope, an intercept, and predictions

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Choosing X Does Not Make It a Cause
text:
Choosing X Does Not Make It a Cause








Warning



⚠️ Regression does not earn you causation
lm(y ~ x) will fit a slope to any two numeric columns you hand it, including ones with no causal link at all. Putting a variable on the right-hand side is a decision you made, not a finding.
What licenses a causal claim is the study design — manipulation, randomization, controls — not the model you fit afterwards.


Last week’s inference gradient, in one line: the same lm() output supports a weak claim from an observational survey and a strong claim from a randomized experiment. The design decides which one you are allowed to write.







Note



Which do I report?

Both variables measured, no direction implied → correlation
One variable predicts or sets the other, or you want predictions → regression
Reporting both is fine; claiming cause from either is not

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text: Part 3 · Correlation Analysis

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
What Is Correlation?


Correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two numerical variables. It runs from −1 to +1:

+1 — perfect positive
0 — no linear relationship
−1 — perfect negative

The Pearson correlation coefficient:
\[r = \frac{\sum_{i}(X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i}(X_i - \bar{X})^2 \sum_{i}(Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}}\]
which is
\[r = \frac{\text{Covariance}(X, Y)}{s_X \cdot s_Y}\]

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · Which One Has r Closest to Zero?
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · Which One Has r Closest to Zero?


Four datasets, plotted on the right. No correlation coefficients shown — on purpose.
Which panel has the Pearson correlation closest to zero?

Panel A
Panel B
Panel C
Panel D







Warning



✍️ Write your letter down, then vote.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: What r Can and Cannot See
text:
What r Can and Cannot See








Important



✅ The answer is (b) — Panel B.

Panel B is the most tightly related pair on the slide: give me x and I can tell you y almost exactly.
Its correlation is near zero anyway, because the relationship is an arch, not a line.
Panel C looks like the messiest, so most rooms vote (c). It has a weak but genuine linear trend, so its r sits farther from zero than B’s.




r measures one thing only: how close the points lie to a straight line.
A perfect relationship with a curve in it reads as “no correlation.”
Panel D is the other warning — a single far-out point can manufacture a large r out of a cloud with no trend in it.











Always plot the data before you trust a correlation coefficient.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Example 16.1 · Flipping the Bird


Nazca boobies (Sula granti): do the visits a chick receives from non-parent adults predict how aggressive it is as an adult?

booby_df <- read_csv("data/booby_aggression.csv")

cor.test(booby_df$visits_as_nestling,
         booby_df$future_aggression)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  booby_df$visits_as_nestling and booby_df$future_aggression
t = 2.9603, df = 22, p-value = 0.007229
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1660840 0.7710999
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.5337225

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Example 16.1 · Interpretation


r = 0.534 — a moderate positive relationship, p = 0.00723.

Square it for the variance explained: r² = 0.285, so about 28.5% of the variation in one variable is accounted for by the other
Standard error: \(\text{SE}_r = \sqrt{\dfrac{1-r^2}{n-2}}\) = 0.18
Tested with a t-test: \(t = r / SE_r\), df = n − 2

In words: boobies visited more often as nestlings tend to be more aggressive adults. Nothing here says the visits caused it.







Note



🔮 Predict first
Next we run Shapiro-Wilk on both booby variables, then look at their histograms and QQ plots.
If the formal test and the picture disagree at n = 24, which would you trust?

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Testing Assumptions for Correlation


Pearson correlation assumes:

Random sampling from the population
Bivariate normality — each variable normal, and normal jointly
A linear relationship — not a curve
No extreme outliers driving the result


shapiro.test(booby_df$visits_as_nestling)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  booby_df$visits_as_nestling
W = 0.95783, p-value = 0.3965




shapiro.test(booby_df$future_aggression)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  booby_df$future_aggression
W = 0.91575, p-value = 0.04709








Note



H₀ is “these data ARE normal”
A large p-value is the good outcome — the same backwards logic as Levene’s test.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Checking the Same Assumptions by Eye
text:
Checking the Same Assumptions by Eye


The two tests do not agree with each other:

visits, p = 0.396 — clean
aggression, p = 0.047 — just under 0.05

Now look at the pictures. No strong skew, points close to both QQ lines, and the scatterplot was straight rather than curved.






Important



✅ This is the case the last slide asked you to predict
At n = 24, a normality p of 0.047 is a coin-flip verdict, not evidence of a real problem. W&S report Pearson’s r for these data, and so do we.
Compare that with the next dataset, where the test and the picture agree that something is wrong.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
When the Assumption Fails — Example 16.5


W&S Example 16.5: people who had seen the Indian rope trick were asked, years later, how impressive it was — on a subjective score.
That score is bounded and lumpy, and it fails Shapiro badly. Three options when normality fails:

Transform one or both variables (log, square root)
Switch to a rank-based correlation — Spearman’s ρ or Kendall’s τ
Hunt down the outlier that is doing the work


rope_df <- read_csv("data/rope_trick.csv")

shapiro.test(rope_df$impressiveness)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  rope_df$impressiveness
W = 0.82319, p-value = 0.001517












The longer ago someone saw the trick, the more impressive they remember it being.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Spearman’s Rho nonparametric correlation



cor.test(rope_df$years_since_seen,
         rope_df$impressiveness,
         method = "spearman")


    Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  rope_df$years_since_seen and rope_df$impressiveness
S = 332.12, p-value = 2.571e-05
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
      rho 
0.7843363 



Spearman replaces each value with its rank and correlates the ranks — so it needs no normality and is not thrown by one extreme value.

Pearson r = 0.848
Spearman ρ = 0.784

Square ρ the same way: ρ² = 0.615 — about 61.5% of the variation in the ranks.






Note



The cost of switching
You keep an honest p-value and lose the original units. ρ is about ranks, so it can no longer be read as “score per year.”

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · The Correlation That Shrank


A colleague reports r = 0.82 between body size and fecundity across a set of populations.
You repeat the study, carefully, at one site — where the animals are all close to the same size — and get r = 0.31 from data that are every bit as clean.
What is the most likely explanation?
(a) The original result was a false positive
(b) Your sample size was too small
(c) Restricting the range of X shrank r, with the underlying relationship unchanged
(d) Measurement error in your study inflated r






Warning



✍️ One letter. Write it down.









Note



The question to ask
Did the relationship change — or did the slice of the world I looked at change?

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Two Things That Move r Without Touching the Biology
text:
Two Things That Move r Without Touching the Biology








Important



✅ The answer is (c).
Range restriction. r depends on the spread of X you sampled. Look at a narrow slice of a real relationship and r falls, even though the slope is unchanged. This is why correlations from studies with different ranges cannot be compared head to head.








Warning



⚠️ Attenuation
Measurement error in X or Y pushes r toward zero, never away from it. The true correlation is usually stronger than the one you observed — so (d) has the direction backwards.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Correlation — What to Carry Forward



r measures straight-line association only — always plot first
r² is the variance the two variables share
The range you sampled sets the ceiling on r; measurement error lowers it further
Correlation does not imply causation. Three explanations always survive: X causes Y, Y causes X, or Z causes both
The test: H₀ is ρ = 0, statistic t = r / SE(r), df = n − 2
When normality fails, switch to rank-based Spearman’s ρ








Note



✅ End of the correlation half
You can now run cor.test(), check its assumptions on the raw variables, switch to Spearman when they fail, and say what r and r² mean.
Next: the same cloud of points — but now we fit a line to it and ask what that line is made of.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text: Part 4 · Linear Regression — the Model

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
The Simple Linear Regression Model


Regression models the response Y as a straight-line function of the predictor X.
The population model: \(Y = \alpha + \beta X + \varepsilon\)

α is the intercept — the value of Y when X = 0
β is the slope — the change in Y per one-unit change in X
ε is the error — the random deviation of a point from the line

The sample equation: \(\hat{Y} = a + bX\), where a estimates α and b estimates β.
Method of least squares: of all possible lines, take the one that makes
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\]
as small as possible — the sum of the squared vertical distances.


Least squares picks the third one.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Fitting the Lion Model


Male lions accumulate black pigment on the nose as they age — so nose colour can age a lion in the field without anyone killing it.

lion_df <- read_csv("data/lion_noses.csv")

lion_model <- lm(age_years ~ proportion_black,
                 data = lion_df)
coef(lion_model)

     (Intercept) proportion_black 
       0.8790062       10.6471194 


Read the formula as response ~ predictor.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Reading the Model Output



summary(lion_model)


Call:
lm(formula = age_years ~ proportion_black, data = lion_df)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-2.5449 -1.1117 -0.5285  0.9635  4.3421 

Coefficients:
                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        0.8790     0.5688   1.545    0.133    
proportion_black  10.6471     1.5095   7.053 7.68e-08 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1.669 on 30 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6238,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6113 
F-statistic: 49.75 on 1 and 30 DF,  p-value: 7.677e-08



\[\widehat{\text{age}} = 0.88 + 10.65 \times \text{prop. black}\]

Estimate — the intercept and the slope
Std. Error — how precisely each is pinned down
t value — estimate ÷ SE, testing H₀: β = 0
Multiple R-squared = 0.624 — the share of variation in age explained by nose colour







Note



Notice
Correlating these same two variables and squaring r gives the same 0.624. Hold that thought — Part 5 explains why.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · What the Slope and Intercept Say
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · What the Slope and Intercept Say


The fitted line is \(\widehat{\text{age}} = 0.88 + 10.65 \times \text{prop. black}\).
Which statement is correct?
(a) A lion’s nose darkens by 10.65 units for every year it ages
(b) Going from a nose 10% black to one 20% black predicts about 1.06 more years of age
(c) A newborn lion is predicted to be 0.88 years old, so the model is wrong
(d) 62.4% of lions are aged correctly by this equation






Warning



✍️ Write your letter down, then vote.









Note



Ask yourself
What are the units on this slope?
A slope is always units of Y per one unit of X — and here one unit of X is the whole range, from a clean nose to a fully black one.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Slope and Intercept, in Words








Important



✅ The answer is (b).
The slope is 10.65 years per unit of proportion black, and one unit is the entire 0-to-1 range. A 0.1 change in blackness therefore predicts about 1.06 years.
(a) reverses the variables — that is the regression of blackness on age, a different line.
(c) misreads the intercept: it is 0.88 years at proportion black = 0, and the youngest lion measured was 1.1 years old, so X = 0 sits outside the data. The intercept anchors the line; it is not a claim about newborns.
(d) confuses R² with an accuracy rate. R² is variance explained, not the percentage of lions got right.









Warning



⚠️ Extrapolation
A fitted line says nothing about X values you never sampled, and the confidence band is widest exactly where you have no data.








Tip



🖐 The habit to build
Write every slope out as a sentence in the units of the data — “for every extra , Y changes by” — before you write a word about significance.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Calculating the Slope and Intercept by Hand
text:
Calculating the Slope and Intercept by Hand


\[b = \frac{\sum_i(X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\sum_i(X_i - \bar{X})^2}
\qquad a = \bar{Y} - b\bar{X}\]
The numerator is a sum of cross-products; the denominator is a sum of squares. Both are the same kind of quantity the ANOVA table is built from in a moment.

x <- lion_df$proportion_black
y <- lion_df$age_years

b <- sum((x - mean(x)) * (y - mean(y))) / sum((x - mean(x))^2)
a <- mean(y) - b * mean(x)
c(intercept = a, slope = b)

 intercept      slope 
 0.8790062 10.6471194 



Compare that with what lm() reported:

coef(lion_model)

     (Intercept) proportion_black 
       0.8790062       10.6471194 








Note



Same answer, no magic
lm() is doing this arithmetic. Everything harder than this — multiple predictors, ANOVA, mixed models — is the same idea written in matrix form.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Making Predictions



new_lion <- tibble(proportion_black = 0.50)

predict(lion_model, new_lion, interval = "confidence")

       fit      lwr     upr
1 6.202566 5.388042 7.01709

predict(lion_model, new_lion, interval = "prediction")

       fit      lwr     upr
1 6.202566 2.698512 9.70662



Both intervals sit on the same predicted age, and answer different questions:

Confidence interval — where the mean age of all lions with 50% black noses lies
Prediction interval — where a single new lion’s age lies

The prediction interval is always wider: it carries the scatter of individual lions plus the uncertainty in the line itself.
Both are narrowest at \(\bar{X}\) and flare out toward the edges of the data.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Example 17.3 · Prairie Biodiversity and Stability


Tilman et al. (2006): does a more diverse plant community produce more stable biomass? 161 plots, seeded with 1 to 16 species.

prairie_df <- read_csv("data/prairie_stability.csv")

prairie_model <- lm(log(biomass_stability) ~ species_number,
                    data = prairie_df)
summary(prairie_model)$coefficients

                Estimate  Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)    1.1982943 0.041298043 29.015766 2.075490e-65
species_number 0.0329259 0.004883691  6.742012 2.733315e-10

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
The Prairie Model — Interpretation


The hypothesis test is about the slope:

H₀: β = 0 — species number has no effect on stability
H₁: β ≠ 0

Slope = 0.0329 — log stability rises by about 0.033 per extra species, so a 16-species plot sits roughly 0.49 log units above a monoculture.
p = 2.73e-10 — strong evidence against a zero slope.
R² = 0.222 — diversity explains about 22.2% of the variation in stability. Real, and nowhere near the whole story.







Note



Significant ≠ large
A tiny p-value alongside R² = 0.22 is completely ordinary in ecology.
The p-value says the slope is not zero. R² says how much of the world it accounts for. Report both.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Part 5 · Sums of Squares — the Engine of Everything After This
text: Part 5 · Sums of Squares — the Engine of Everything After This

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Where the Variation Goes


Take one data point. Its distance from the overall mean \(\bar{y}\) splits, exactly, into two pieces:
\[\underbrace{(y_i - \bar{y})}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})}_{\text{explained}} + \underbrace{(y_i - \hat{y}_i)}_{\text{left over}}\]
Square those deviations and add them up over every point, and the same split holds for the whole dataset:
\[SS_{total} = SS_{regression} + SS_{residual}\]

\(SS_{regression}\) — variation the line accounts for; df = 1
\(SS_{residual}\) — variation it does not; df = n − 2
\(SS_{total}\) — all of it; df = n − 1

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · Which Fit Has the Bigger Sums of Squares?
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · Which Fit Has the Bigger Sums of Squares?


Four fitted regressions, on the right.
Which statement is true?
(a) \(SS_{regression}\) is larger in (d) than in (c)
(b) \(SS_{residual}\) is larger in (b) than in (a)
(c) \(SS_{total}\) is larger in (a) than in (b)
(d) \(SS_{residual}\) is zero in (c)






Warning



✍️ One letter. Write it down, then argue it with your neighbour.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Reading the Partition Off a Picture
text:
Reading the Partition Off a Picture








Important



✅ The answer is (b).
\(SS_{residual}\) is the scatter around the line, and the points in (b) sit farther off their line than those in (a).
(a) is backwards: \(SS_{regression}\) grows with how steeply the fitted line climbs, and (c) is steeper than (d).
(c) is the trap — \(SS_{total}\) does not depend on the fit at all. It is the spread of Y around its own mean, and the line has nothing to do with it.
(d) would require every point to sit exactly on the line.









Note



The three pictures to keep

\(SS_{total}\) → distance from the flat mean line
\(SS_{regression}\) → how far the fitted line climbs away from that flat line
\(SS_{residual}\) → how far the points sit off the fitted line



A fit is good when the line does a lot of climbing and the points stay close to it.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Computing the Three Sums of Squares
text:
Computing the Three Sums of Squares



fitted_age <- predict(lion_model)
mean_age   <- mean(lion_df$age_years)

ss_total <- sum((lion_df$age_years - mean_age)^2)
ss_reg   <- sum((fitted_age - mean_age)^2)
ss_resid <- sum((lion_df$age_years - fitted_age)^2)

c(total = ss_total, regression = ss_reg, residual = ss_resid)

     total regression   residual 
 222.08719  138.54398   83.54321 

ss_reg + ss_resid          # does it add back up?

[1] 222.0872



138.5 + 83.5 = 222.1 — exactly.
And the share the line accounts for:
\[R^2 = \frac{SS_{regression}}{SS_{total}} = \frac{138.5}{222.1} = 0.624\]






Important



✅ This is where R² comes from
R² is not a separate statistic. It is the regression sum of squares as a fraction of the total — and with one predictor it is exactly the correlation coefficient squared.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: The Same Numbers, Straight from R
text:
The Same Numbers, Straight from R



anova(lion_model)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: age_years
                 Df  Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
proportion_black  1 138.544 138.544   49.75 7.677e-08 ***
Residuals        30  83.543   2.785                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



Every number in that table you have now built by hand:

Sum Sq — the two sums of squares, 138.5 and 83.5
Df — 1 for the predictor, n − 2 = 30 for the residual
Mean Sq — Sum Sq ÷ Df
F value — the ratio of those two mean squares







Note



This table has a shape, not a topic
The identical five columns show up for one-way ANOVA, two-way ANOVA, nested ANOVA and ANCOVA. Only the rows change.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: From Sums of Squares to Mean Squares
text:
From Sums of Squares to Mean Squares


A sum of squares keeps growing as you add data, so it cannot be compared across studies. Divide by degrees of freedom and you get a mean square — a variance, which does not grow with n:
\[MS = \frac{SS}{df} \qquad F = \frac{MS_{regression}}{MS_{residual}}\]

\(MS_{residual}\) = 2.785 — estimates the background variance σ²
\(MS_{regression}\) = 138.54 — estimates that same σ², plus whatever the X–Y relationship adds
If the slope is truly zero, both estimate the same thing and F ≈ 1. Here F = 49.75

Sums of squares add up. Mean squares do not.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · You Double the Sample Size
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · You Double the Sample Size


You repeat the lion study and come back with 64 lions instead of 32. The relationship is identical — same slope, same scatter around the line.
Compared with the original analysis, what happens?
(a) \(SS_{total}\) roughly doubles, and \(MS_{residual}\) roughly doubles with it
(b) \(SS_{total}\) roughly doubles, but \(MS_{residual}\) stays about the same
(c) Both stay about the same — doubling n changes neither
(d) \(SS_{total}\) stays about the same and \(MS_{residual}\) halves






Warning



✍️ Write your letter down. This one decides whether you can read the table.









Note



The question to ask
Which of these is a total, and which is an average?

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Why Mean Squares Exist At All
text:
Why Mean Squares Exist At All








Important



✅ The answer is (b).
\(SS_{total}\) is a sum over every observation, so twice the data is roughly twice the sum. \(MS_{residual}\) is that sum divided by its degrees of freedom — an average squared deviation — so it estimates the same σ² no matter how many lions you measure.
That is exactly why the table converts sums of squares into mean squares before testing anything. You cannot compare two sums built from different amounts of data; you can compare two variances.









Tip



🖐 What doubling n actually buys
σ² does not change, but the standard error of the slope shrinks with √n — so F rises and the confidence band tightens.
More data does not reduce the scatter in nature. It reduces your uncertainty about the line running through it.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: The Bridge · One Table, Every Model From Here
text:
The Bridge · One Table, Every Model From Here


For the lion model, all of these are the same test:




Route
Value




t on the slope
7.053


t²
49.75


F from anova()
49.75


p, either way
7.68e-08




t² = F. The t-test on a slope and the F-test in the ANOVA table are one test asked two ways — and \(r^2 = SS_{reg}/SS_{total}\) ties both back to the correlation half of this lecture.







Important



✅ Why this is the most important slide today
Every analysis for the rest of the course is this same partition with more rows:

One-way ANOVA — groups instead of a slope
Two-way ANOVA — a row per factor, plus interaction
Nested ANOVA — a row per level of nesting
ANCOVA — a slope row and a group row

Learn to read this table once and you can read all of them.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text: Part 6 · Testing Regression Assumptions

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Testing Regression Assumptions — Overview


Simple linear regression assumes:

Linearity — the true relationship is a straight line
Independence — observations do not depend on each other
Homoscedasticity — equal scatter at every value of X
Normality — the residuals are normally distributed

Stated formally: the error \(\varepsilon_i\) is normal, with a mean of 0 and the same variance, at every value of x.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Every Check Is About the Residuals
text:
Every Check Is About the Residuals


Every assumption check from here on uses the residuals, not the raw data. That is the single most common mix-up in regression.
The error \(\varepsilon_i\) is estimated by the residual \(e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\) — the same red segment you have seen on every lion plot today, and the same quantity that got squared and summed to build \(SS_{residual}\).
Least squares already made these as small as possible. The diagnostics ask whether what is left over looks like random noise.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Checking Linearity — Residuals vs. Fitted


What you want: a shapeless cloud, scattered evenly above and below the horizontal line at zero.
What is a problem: any curve in the trend line. A U-shape or an arch means a straight line is the wrong shape for these data — the exact failure Panel B showed back in the correlation half.
The plot doubles as a homoscedasticity check: if the cloud fans out or funnels in from left to right, the variance is not constant.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
section: Checking Normality — QQ Plot of Residuals
text:
Checking Normality — QQ Plot of Residuals


The QQ plot compares your residuals with what perfectly normal residuals would look like.
What you want: points hugging the diagonal.
What is a problem: systematic curvature, or points peeling away at the ends. Tails are where non-normality shows up first, and tails are what p-values depend on.
Note we check the residuals, not age_years itself. The raw ages are right-skewed, and that is allowed. It is the residuals that have to behave.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Checking Normality — Shapiro-Wilk on Residuals



shapiro.test(residuals(lion_model))


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  residuals(lion_model)
W = 0.93879, p-value = 0.0692


residuals(model) — not lion_df$age_years. Testing the raw response is a different, and usually wrong, question.







Note



H₀ is “the residuals ARE normal”
So a large p-value is the good outcome.








Warning



⚠️ Do not let this test overrule your eyes
At small n it has almost no power to detect a real problem; at large n it flags departures far too small to matter. Read the QQ plot first and use the test to support it — not to replace it.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
What Violations Actually Look Like


When an assumption fails:

Transform one or both variables (W&S §17.6) — a log on a curved or fanning relationship fixes both problems more often than not
Weighted least squares for heteroscedasticity
A non-linear model (§17.8), or a GLM in Week 11

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · One Island


Gotelli & Ellison’s Galápagos data: 17 islands, plant species richness against island area, both log-transformed. The fit is solid — R² = 0.585, p = 3.50e-04.
Now one more point arrives: a large island reported with very few species (red).
What does that single point do?
(a) Very little — one point in 18 cannot matter much
(b) It raises R², because the range of X just got wider
(c) It roughly halves R² and pushes p to the edge of significance
(d) It can change R² but not the slope






Warning



✍️ One letter, before the next slide.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
What One Point Did



galap_plot <- galap_df %>%
  mutate(log_area = log10(area_km2),
         log_species = log10(n_species))

# a big island reported with very few species
galap_bad <- galap_plot %>%
  add_row(log_area = 3, log_species = 0.65)

clean_model <- lm(log_species ~ log_area, galap_plot)
bad_model   <- lm(log_species ~ log_area, galap_bad)

tibble(data  = c("17 islands", "plus the suspect point"),
       slope = c(coef(clean_model)[2], coef(bad_model)[2]),
       r2    = c(summary(clean_model)$r.squared,
                 summary(bad_model)$r.squared))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  data                   slope    r2
  <chr>                  <dbl> <dbl>
1 17 islands             0.331 0.585
2 plus the suspect point 0.233 0.228









Important



✅ The answer is (c).
One point out of 18 cuts R² from 0.58 to 0.23 and moves p from 3.50e-04 to 0.0449 — from convincing to barely publishable. The slope drops too, so (d) is out.
It is influential because it lies far out in X and far off the trend. Cook’s distance flags it at once — that is what panel 4 of plot(model) is for.


No diagnostic can tell you whether it is a typo or a real island. That takes going back to the data sheet.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text: Part 7 · Wrap-up

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Wrap-up


Over the two days you:

Separated correlation from regression, and saw that neither earns causation
Computed Pearson’s r, squared it for variance explained, and tested it with cor.test()
Switched to Spearman’s ρ when normality failed
Fitted a line with lm() and read the slope in the units of the data
Built \(SS_{regression}\) and \(SS_{residual}\) by hand, watched them add to \(SS_{total}\), and turned them into mean squares and an F
Confirmed t² = F and r² = SS_reg / SS_total
Checked all four assumptions on the residuals, and watched one influential island halve an R²








Important



✅ The one idea to keep
A line can be fitted to any two numeric columns. What makes it trustworthy lives in the residuals; what makes it interpretable lives in the sums of squares. Neither lives in the p-value.








Note



Up next — Multiple Regression
More than one predictor, predictors correlated with each other, and choosing between competing models. Same table, more rows.

title: Lecture: Correlation vs Linear Models
text:
Readings

Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 16 — Correlation (§16.3 assumptions; §16.5 Spearman’s rank correlation), and Ch. 17 — Regression (§17.6 transformations; §17.8 non-linear relationships).
Gotelli & Ellison, Ch. 9 — Regression, for the variance-partitioning treatment and the Galápagos species–area example.
Tilman, D., Reich, P. B., & Knops, J. M. H. (2006). Biodiversity and ecosystem stability in a decade-long grassland experiment. Nature, 441, 629–632.

Note

Mean and median
