title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
section: Histograms — the Shape Behind the Summary
text:
Histograms — the Shape Behind the Summary






Note


🔮 Predict first: In Describing Your Data we found the overall mean(needle_length_mm) ≈ 14.67 and the median ≈ 14.55 — nearly identical. What shape do you expect the full distribution to have — symmetric, or skewed?






ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "darkblue", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Needle Length",
    x = "Needle length (mm)",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)










binwidth sets the width of each bar in data units (here, 2mm)
Too wide hides structure; too narrow shows noise — try a few values







Tip


🖐 Try it yourself
Change binwidth = 2 to binwidth = 0.5 and to binwidth = 5. Which tells the real story?









Note


📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 2 — Displaying Data, on frequency distributions and choosing bin width.
📖 R4DS §10.3 — Variation

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
section: Histograms by Group — fill and facet_wrap() Together
text:
Histograms by Group — fill and facet_wrap() Together



ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, color = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~side, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Needle length (mm)", y = "Count", fill = "Side") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")















Note


✅ Key idea
Overlapping histograms on one panel are hard to read. Faceting stacks them into separate panels sharing an x-axis — same comparison, much clearer.









Note


📖 Reference
📖 R4DS §9.5 — Facets

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
Density Curves — a Smoothed Alternative



ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Length Density by Side",
    x = "Needle length (mm)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Side"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)















Tip


📖 Histogram vs. density
A density curve is a smoothed histogram, rescaled so the area under each curve sums to 1. It overlays cleanly for group comparisons — no faceting required, at the cost of hiding the raw bin counts.









Note


📖 Reference
Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics, Ch. 3 — Summary Statistics, on the shape of a distribution behind any mean and SD you report.

text: Part 4 · Mean ± SE — Plotted Directly

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
Mean ± SE — Plotted Directly



pine_mean_se_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = side)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15),
    alpha = 0.3,
    size = 2
  ) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4) +
  stat_summary(
    fun.data = mean_se,
    geom = "errorbar",
    width = 0.15,
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean ± SE Needle Length by Side",
    x = "Side of tree",
    y = "Needle length (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

pine_mean_se_plot









Two stat_summary() layers:



call
draws




fun = mean
one large point at the mean


fun.data = mean_se
error bars for ± 1 SE



stat_summary() computes the mean and SE for you, straight from the raw data — no summarize() step required first.






Warning


⚠️ Convenient, but read the fine print
“Straight from the raw data” means it used all 64 needles. Those are the naive error bars from Describing Your Data — the ones that treat 8 needles from one tree as 8 independent facts.









Note


📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 4 — Estimating with Uncertainty, on what an error bar is an estimate of.
Gotelli & Ellison, Ch. 6 — Designing Successful Field Studies, on why independence decides which rows you may average.

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
section: The error bar is a claim — make it an honest one
text:
The error bar is a claim — make it an honest one






Note


🔮 Predict first: We are about to draw the same two means, but with error bars built from the 4 tree means instead of the 64 needles. Will the dots move? Will the bars?






team_means_df <- pine_df |>
  group_by(team, side) |>
  summarize(team_mean_mm = mean(needle_length_mm), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(team_means_df, aes(x = side, y = team_mean_mm, color = side)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.08)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar",
               width = 0.15, linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(title = "Mean ± SE, computed from 4 trees",
       x = "Side of tree", y = "Mean needle length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")















Important


Same dots. Longer bars.
The means are identical (14.12 and 15.21). The SEs went from 0.49/0.46 to 1.01/0.79 — roughly double.
Each small point here is one tree, not one needle. That is the plot our design actually supports.









Tip


🖐 The habit
Before you draw an error bar, ask what one point in it represents. stat_summary() will happily compute an SE over anything you hand it — including rows that aren’t independent.

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
The Built-in Themes



pine_jitter_plot + theme_bw(base_size = 9)










theme_minimal() — light, few gridlines (what we have used so far)
theme_bw() — white background, black-and-white frame
theme_classic() — just x/y axis lines, no gridlines

A theme changes appearance only — never the data or the statistics underneath.






Warning


⚠️ The problem with the built-ins
None of them is quite publication-ready, so you end up appending ten lines of theme(axis.title = element_text(...), ...) to every single plot — and retyping them in every script, slightly differently each time.

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
section: The Themes File — Three Sizes, Written Once
text:
The Themes File — Three Sizes, Written Once


Download r_themes_for_3_sizes.R from the activity page and save it in your project folder, next to your .Rproj file.
It defines three functions, each sized for a different final output:



Function
Built for
Base font




theme_small()
~3 × 3 in — a journal panel
9 pt


theme_regular()
~7 × 7 in — a report figure
16 pt


theme_large()
~16 × 16 in — a poster
36 pt



All three give you the same publication look: white background, a black panel border, black axis lines and ticks, bold axis titles, no gridlines.






Important


Two steps, once each

Open the file and run it (Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter, or Source). Look at your Environment pane — theme_small, theme_regular, and theme_large appear as functions. That is all “running it” does: it defines them.
From then on, source() it at the top of any script that makes a figure. One line replaces the whole block of theme code you would otherwise paste into every script.






# At the top of your script,
# with library(tidyverse):
source("r_themes_for_3_sizes.R")







Note


✅ Why source() and not copy-paste
source() runs that file top to bottom, exactly as if you had typed it. Fix a margin in the themes file once and every figure in every script picks up the change the next time you run it.
Copy-pasted theme code gives you fifteen slightly different themes and no way to fix them all.









Warning


⚠️ Watch out!
source() needs the path to be right. With the file in your project root and an .Rproj open, "r_themes_for_3_sizes.R" is enough. Put it in a scripts/ folder and it becomes source("scripts/r_themes_for_3_sizes.R").

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
Using the Themes



pine_theme_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Length by Side of Tree",
    x = "Side of tree",
    y = "Needle length (mm)"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 25)) +
  theme_small() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

pine_theme_plot









It is one more + layer, exactly like theme_minimal():
+ theme_small()      # 3 × 3 in
+ theme_regular()    # 7 × 7 in
+ theme_large()      # poster






Tip


🖐 Match the theme to the size you will save
Pick the theme for the figure’s final printed size, then pass that same size to ggsave(). A theme_large() plot saved at 3 × 3 in is unreadable, and theme_small() on a poster disappears.









Note


Still your plot
Anything you add after the theme still wins — theme_small() + theme(legend.position = "none") keeps the theme and drops the legend.

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
patchwork — + for Whole Plots



install.packages("patchwork")   # once per computer


library(patchwork)

Save each plot into an object, then combine them:
plot_a + plot_b     # side by side
plot_a / plot_b     # stacked






Note


✅ Key idea
patchwork reuses the operators you already know. + puts plots beside each other, / puts one over the other — and the result is still a plot object you can save.





pine_jitter_plot + pine_mean_se_plot

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
patchwork — Building a Real Figure



combined_plot <- (pine_jitter_plot + pine_mean_se_plot) / pine_scatter_plot +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

combined_plot










Parentheses group plots, exactly like arithmetic: (a + b) / c is two on top, one across the bottom
plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") tags the panels A, B, C — what a figure caption refers to
combined_plot is one object, so ggsave() saves the whole multi-panel figure in one call







Tip


🖐 Size it for the whole figure
A three-panel figure needs roughly three panels’ worth of space. Give ggsave() a width/height for the combined plot, not for one panel.

Saving a Real Figure



# One panel, built with theme_small() — save it at the size the theme was written for
ggsave(
  "figures/pine_needle_boxplot.png",
  plot = pine_theme_plot,
  width = 3,
  height = 3,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300
)

# The three-panel patchwork figure — bigger canvas, one call
ggsave(
  "figures/pine_needle_combined.png",
  plot = combined_plot,
  width = 7,
  height = 6,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300
)







Warning


⚠️ Watch out!
ggsave() wants the filename first, then plot =. If you skip plot =, it saves whatever plot was drawn last — not necessarily the one you meant.










Note


✅ Key idea
Always set width, height, units, and dpi explicitly. Letting ggsave() guess gives you a plot sized for your screen, not for a report or a poster.









Note


📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 2 — Displaying Data, on what a figure has to carry to stand on its own in a report.
📖 R4DS §11 — Communication

text: Part 9 · Custom Colors and Legends — scale_color_manual()

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
scale_color_manual() — Choosing Your Own Colors






Tip


🚀 Advanced / extra work — ggplot’s default colors are fine for exploring data, but a real figure often needs specific colors (journal style, colorblind-safe palettes, matching a poster). This is how you take control.






ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = side)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15),
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4, color = "black") +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Side of tree",
    labels = c(shady = "Shady side", sunny = "Sunny side"),
    values = c(shady = "#2c7fb8", sunny = "#d95f0e")
  ) +
  labs(x = "Side of tree", y = "Needle length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)









Three arguments, matched by name:



Argument
Does what




name
the legend title


labels
text shown for each level


values
the actual color for each level









Note


✅ Key idea
labels and values are both named vectors, keyed by the raw values in your data (shady, sunny) — not by the pretty text you want to display. ggplot looks up each raw value and substitutes the label/color you gave it.









Tip


📖 Why these two colors?
#2c7fb8 (blue) and #d95f0e (orange) are a blue–orange pair, the safest two-colour choice for colour-vision deficiency: red–green confusion, which affects roughly 8% of men, leaves the blue–orange axis intact.
Don’t take that on faith — check any pair you invent with a simulator (the colorblindr or dichromat packages), or start from a palette that was built for it: scale_color_viridis_d() or RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(n, "Dark2").
📖 R4DS §11.4 — Scales, including the ColorBrewer palettes.

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
scale_color_manual() — Getting the Names Wrong



# Typo: "sun" instead of the real value "sunny"
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = side)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(shady = "#2c7fb8", sun = "#d95f0e")
  )








Warning


⚠️ Watch out!

Every level that appears in your data must get an entry in values

(and in labels, if you supply it), spelled exactly as it appears in the column
check with unique(pine_df$side) first if you are not sure
A missing or misspelled level draws as grey with a warning.

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
scale_fill_manual() — the fill Twin



ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Side of tree",
    labels = c(shady = "Shady side", sunny = "Sunny side"),
    values = c(shady = "#2c7fb8", sunny = "#d95f0e")
  ) +
  labs(x = "Side of tree", y = "Needle length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)















Tip


🖐 Notice
Same three arguments, same pattern — scale_fill_manual() is scale_color_manual() for the fill aesthetic instead of color. A boxplot’s box is fill; its jittered points (if you added geom_point(color = ...)) would be color. A plot can need both at once.

Wrap-up


Today you:

Built boxplots with raw points overlaid, not hidden
Wrote real axis labels, titles, and legend titles with labs() — never shipped a default column name
Mapped a third variable with color = / fill = inside aes()

Combined panels with patchwork — a + b, a / b, (a + b) / c, tagged A/B/C
Saved a real, correctly-sized figure with ggsave()
(As time allowed) Histograms, density curves, facet_wrap(), and custom colors with scale_color_manual()







Tip


🖐 Before next class
Finish the worksheet: source the themes file, build a two-panel patchwork figure with coord_cartesian() limits you chose on purpose, and save it to figures/ at 300 dpi.










Note


Where this leads
You can now import, wrangle, describe, and visualize a dataset end to end. That full pipeline — raw data → clean → summarize → visualize — is the foundation every later statistical test builds on.

Note

text: Part 2 · Boxplot Anatomy

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
Boxplot Anatomy



pine_box_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Length by Side of Tree",
    x = "Side of tree",
    y = "Needle length (mm)",
    fill = "Side"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

pine_box_plot









Boxplot anatomy:

Middle line = median
Box edges = 25th and 75th percentile (IQR)
Whiskers = 1.5 × IQR
Dots beyond whiskers = outliers

Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 2 — Displaying Data, on the boxplot and the five-number summary it draws.
📖 R4DS §9 — Layers

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
Boxplot + Raw Points






Note



🔮 Predict first: With only 8 needles per side per tree, does a boxplot alone show you everything? What might it hide?





pine_jitter_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15),
    alpha = 0.6,
    size = 2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Length by Side of Tree",
    x = "Side of tree",
    y = "Needle length (mm)",
    fill = "Side"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

pine_jitter_plot










position_jitter(width = 0.15) spreads points sideways so they don’t overlap
alpha = 0.6 — semi-transparent, so overlapping points are still visible







Tip



Always show the raw points alongside a boxplot when n is small — every point matters, and a box alone can hide a bimodal or lopsided pattern.








Note



📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 2 — Displaying Data, “How to draw a good graph,” makes exactly this argument: show the data, not only the summary.

Before labs() — Never Ship This



ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +

Important



The x-axis reads side and the y-axis reads needle_length_mm — the literal column names, not something a reader outside your lab would understand.









Warning

A plot with default column-name axes is a plot that only makes sense to you, today. Six months from now, even you may not remember what side meant.

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
section: labs() — Every Piece of Text on the Plot
text:
labs() — Every Piece of Text on the Plot



ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Length by Side of Tree",
    subtitle = "Four field teams, four trees",
    x = "Side of tree",
    y = "Needle length (mm)",
    fill = "Side",
    caption = "Data: pine_data.csv"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")









One function, five jobs:



Argument
Controls




title
main title


subtitle
smaller text under the title


x / y
axis labels


caption
small text, bottom-right


color/fill
legend title for that aesthetic









Note



✅ Key idea
labs() never touches the data or the statistics — only what a reader sees written on the plot. Change it freely.








Note



📖 Reference
📖 R4DS §11.1 — Labels

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
labs() — the Legend Title Trap



# Whichever aesthetic name you mapped, use that same name in labs()
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = team)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.15)) +
  labs(color = "Field team") # matches aes(color = team)















Warning



⚠️ Watch out!
The legend title comes from whatever you write for the aesthetic you mapped — color = "Field team" in labs() relabels a color = mapping. Write fill = "..." instead and it does nothing, because this plot never mapped fill.

section: Part 2c · Setting the Axis Limits — coord_cartesian()
text: Part 2c · Setting the Axis Limits — coord_cartesian()

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
section: coord_cartesian() — Choosing What the Reader Sees
text:
coord_cartesian() — Choosing What the Reader Sees



ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Length by Side of Tree",
    x = "Side of tree",
    y = "Needle length (mm)"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 25)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")









ggplot picks axis limits from your data. That is a fine default for exploring — and the wrong default the moment a reader has to judge how big a difference is.

coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 25)) — set the y-axis range
coord_cartesian(xlim = c(...)) — same for x
Both at once: coord_cartesian(xlim = c(...), ylim = c(...))







Note



✅ Key idea
Starting a measurement axis at zero is what keeps a 1 mm difference from looking like a canyon. Decide the limits deliberately; don’t inherit them.

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
coord_cartesian() — Both Axes at Once



pine_scatter_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm, y = needle_width_mm,
                                         color = side)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Width vs. Length",
    x = "Needle length (mm)",
    y = "Needle width (mm)",
    color = "Side"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(5, 25), ylim = c(0.4, 1.8)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

pine_scatter_plot















Tip



🖐 Notice
Two continuous axes, so both xlim = and ylim = are useful here. On the boxplot, x was a category — there is nothing to zoom.








Note



📖 Reference
📖 R4DS §11.4 — Scales

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
section: The Trap — ylim() Deletes Data, coord_cartesian() Does Not
text:
The Trap — ylim() Deletes Data, coord_cartesian() Does Not






Note



🔮 Predict first: Both plots below ask for a y-axis running 14 to 16 mm. One of them changes where the boxes are drawn. Which one, and why?





# ❌ ylim() THROWS AWAY every row outside the range first
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6) +
  ylim(14, 16) +
  labs(title = "ylim() — boxes redrawn from survivors") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")









# ✅ coord_cartesian() keeps every row and just crops the view
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(14, 16)) +
  labs(title = "coord_cartesian() — same boxes, zoomed") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")















Warning



⚠️ Watch out!
ylim(14, 16) and scale_y_continuous(limits = c(14, 16)) filter the data before the geom draws it. Every needle outside 14–16 mm is silently dropped, and the median, the quartiles, and the whiskers are all recomputed from what is left. R warns about “removed rows” and students read past it every time.
coord_cartesian() computes the statistics on all the data and then zooms the camera. The boxes do not move.








Tip



🖐 The rule
Use coord_cartesian() to zoom. Use filter() when you actually mean to remove data — on purpose, in the data step, where you can see it.








Note



📖 Worth knowing — changing the axis scale, not just its limits
Right-skewed data (a few very large values squashing everything else into a corner) is usually better read on a log axis:
+ scale_x_log10()      # the AXIS is logged; the data are untouched
That is different again from logging the data itself with mutate(log_length = log(needle_length_mm)), which changes the numbers every later calculation sees.
Nothing today needs it — our needles are not skewed. Try it on your scatterplot if you are curious, and we will come back to it when a distribution actually calls for it.

Mapping Color by Group



pine_team_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = team)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15),
    size = 2.5,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Length by Side, Colored by Team",
    x = "Side of tree",
    y = "Needle length (mm)",
    color = "Field team"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

pine_team_plot










color = team maps a third variable onto the plot — no new geom needed
ggplot auto-builds the legend and picks colors for you
Mapping inside aes() always means “vary this by data” — not “make everything this color”







Warning



⚠️ Watch out!
color = "darkblue" outside aes() sets one fixed color. color = team inside aes() maps colors to a variable. Mixing these up is one of the most common ggplot mistakes.








Note



📖 Worth knowing — where you put aes() matters too
An aes() inside ggplot() is global: every layer inherits it. An aes() inside a single geom applies to that layer only:
# global — both layers colored by side
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = side)) +
  geom_point() + stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4)

# per-layer — points colored by team, the mean drawn in plain black
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = team)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4)
Just know it exists for now — we will lean on it later, when a plot has to show raw data and a fitted model at the same time.








Note



📖 Reference
📖 R4DS §9.1 — Aesthetic mappings

Part 3b · Histograms and Density — Seeing the Whole Distribution

section: Histograms — the Shape Behind the Summary
text:
Histograms — the Shape Behind the Summary






Note



🔮 Predict first: In Describing Your Data we found the overall mean(needle_length_mm) ≈ 14.67 and the median ≈ 14.55 — nearly identical. What shape do you expect the full distribution to have — symmetric, or skewed?





ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "darkblue", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Needle Length",
    x = "Needle length (mm)",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)










binwidth sets the width of each bar in data units (here, 2mm)
Too wide hides structure; too narrow shows noise — try a few values







Tip



🖐 Try it yourself
Change binwidth = 2 to binwidth = 0.5 and to binwidth = 5. Which tells the real story?








Note



📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 2 — Displaying Data, on frequency distributions and choosing bin width.
📖 R4DS §10.3 — Variation

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
section: Histograms by Group — fill and facet_wrap() Together
text:
Histograms by Group — fill and facet_wrap() Together



ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, color = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~side, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Needle length (mm)", y = "Count", fill = "Side") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")















Note



✅ Key idea
Overlapping histograms on one panel are hard to read. Faceting stacks them into separate panels sharing an x-axis — same comparison, much clearer.








Note



📖 Reference
📖 R4DS §9.5 — Facets

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
Density Curves — a Smoothed Alternative



ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Length Density by Side",
    x = "Needle length (mm)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Side"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)















Tip



📖 Histogram vs. density
A density curve is a smoothed histogram, rescaled so the area under each curve sums to 1. It overlays cleanly for group comparisons — no faceting required, at the cost of hiding the raw bin counts.








Note



📖 Reference
Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics, Ch. 3 — Summary Statistics, on the shape of a distribution behind any mean and SD you report.

text: Part 4 · Mean ± SE — Plotted Directly

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
Mean ± SE — Plotted Directly



pine_mean_se_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = side)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15),
    alpha = 0.3,
    size = 2
  ) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4) +
  stat_summary(
    fun.data = mean_se,
    geom = "errorbar",
    width = 0.15,
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean ± SE Needle Length by Side",
    x = "Side of tree",
    y = "Needle length (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

pine_mean_se_plot









Two stat_summary() layers:



call
draws




fun = mean
one large point at the mean


fun.data = mean_se
error bars for ± 1 SE



stat_summary() computes the mean and SE for you, straight from the raw data — no summarize() step required first.






Warning



⚠️ Convenient, but read the fine print
“Straight from the raw data” means it used all 64 needles. Those are the naive error bars from Describing Your Data — the ones that treat 8 needles from one tree as 8 independent facts.








Note



📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 4 — Estimating with Uncertainty, on what an error bar is an estimate of.
Gotelli & Ellison, Ch. 6 — Designing Successful Field Studies, on why independence decides which rows you may average.

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
section: The error bar is a claim — make it an honest one
text:
The error bar is a claim — make it an honest one






Note



🔮 Predict first: We are about to draw the same two means, but with error bars built from the 4 tree means instead of the 64 needles. Will the dots move? Will the bars?





team_means_df <- pine_df |>
  group_by(team, side) |>
  summarize(team_mean_mm = mean(needle_length_mm), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(team_means_df, aes(x = side, y = team_mean_mm, color = side)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.6,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.08)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar",
               width = 0.15, linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(title = "Mean ± SE, computed from 4 trees",
       x = "Side of tree", y = "Mean needle length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")















Important



Same dots. Longer bars.
The means are identical (14.12 and 15.21). The SEs went from 0.49/0.46 to 1.01/0.79 — roughly double.
Each small point here is one tree, not one needle. That is the plot our design actually supports.








Tip



🖐 The habit
Before you draw an error bar, ask what one point in it represents. stat_summary() will happily compute an SE over anything you hand it — including rows that aren’t independent.

section: Part 6 · Themes — Write It Once, Use It Everywhere
text: Part 6 · Themes — Write It Once, Use It Everywhere

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
The Built-in Themes



pine_jitter_plot + theme_bw(base_size = 9)










theme_minimal() — light, few gridlines (what we have used so far)
theme_bw() — white background, black-and-white frame
theme_classic() — just x/y axis lines, no gridlines

A theme changes appearance only — never the data or the statistics underneath.






Warning



⚠️ The problem with the built-ins
None of them is quite publication-ready, so you end up appending ten lines of theme(axis.title = element_text(...), ...) to every single plot — and retyping them in every script, slightly differently each time.

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
section: The Themes File — Three Sizes, Written Once
text:
The Themes File — Three Sizes, Written Once


Download r_themes_for_3_sizes.R from the activity page and save it in your project folder, next to your .Rproj file.
It defines three functions, each sized for a different final output:



Function
Built for
Base font




theme_small()
~3 × 3 in — a journal panel
9 pt


theme_regular()
~7 × 7 in — a report figure
16 pt


theme_large()
~16 × 16 in — a poster
36 pt



All three give you the same publication look: white background, a black panel border, black axis lines and ticks, bold axis titles, no gridlines.






Important



Two steps, once each

Open the file and run it (Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter, or Source). Look at your Environment pane — theme_small, theme_regular, and theme_large appear as functions. That is all “running it” does: it defines them.
From then on, source() it at the top of any script that makes a figure. One line replaces the whole block of theme code you would otherwise paste into every script.





# At the top of your script,
# with library(tidyverse):
source("r_themes_for_3_sizes.R")







Note



✅ Why source() and not copy-paste
source() runs that file top to bottom, exactly as if you had typed it. Fix a margin in the themes file once and every figure in every script picks up the change the next time you run it.
Copy-pasted theme code gives you fifteen slightly different themes and no way to fix them all.








Warning



⚠️ Watch out!
source() needs the path to be right. With the file in your project root and an .Rproj open, "r_themes_for_3_sizes.R" is enough. Put it in a scripts/ folder and it becomes source("scripts/r_themes_for_3_sizes.R").

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
Using the Themes



pine_theme_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Length by Side of Tree",
    x = "Side of tree",
    y = "Needle length (mm)"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 25)) +
  theme_small() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

pine_theme_plot









It is one more + layer, exactly like theme_minimal():
+ theme_small()      # 3 × 3 in
+ theme_regular()    # 7 × 7 in
+ theme_large()      # poster






Tip



🖐 Match the theme to the size you will save
Pick the theme for the figure’s final printed size, then pass that same size to ggsave(). A theme_large() plot saved at 3 × 3 in is unreadable, and theme_small() on a poster disappears.








Note



Still your plot
Anything you add after the theme still wins — theme_small() + theme(legend.position = "none") keeps the theme and drops the legend.

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
patchwork — + for Whole Plots



install.packages("patchwork")   # once per computer


library(patchwork)

Save each plot into an object, then combine them:
plot_a + plot_b     # side by side
plot_a / plot_b     # stacked






Note



✅ Key idea
patchwork reuses the operators you already know. + puts plots beside each other, / puts one over the other — and the result is still a plot object you can save.




pine_jitter_plot + pine_mean_se_plot

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
patchwork — Building a Real Figure



combined_plot <- (pine_jitter_plot + pine_mean_se_plot) / pine_scatter_plot +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

combined_plot










Parentheses group plots, exactly like arithmetic: (a + b) / c is two on top, one across the bottom
plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") tags the panels A, B, C — what a figure caption refers to
combined_plot is one object, so ggsave() saves the whole multi-panel figure in one call







Tip



🖐 Size it for the whole figure
A three-panel figure needs roughly three panels’ worth of space. Give ggsave() a width/height for the combined plot, not for one panel.

Saving a Real Figure



# One panel, built with theme_small() — save it at the size the theme was written for
ggsave(
  "figures/pine_needle_boxplot.png",
  plot = pine_theme_plot,
  width = 3,
  height = 3,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300
)

# The three-panel patchwork figure — bigger canvas, one call
ggsave(
  "figures/pine_needle_combined.png",
  plot = combined_plot,
  width = 7,
  height = 6,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300
)







Warning



⚠️ Watch out!
ggsave() wants the filename first, then plot =. If you skip plot =, it saves whatever plot was drawn last — not necessarily the one you meant.









Note



✅ Key idea
Always set width, height, units, and dpi explicitly. Letting ggsave() guess gives you a plot sized for your screen, not for a report or a poster.








Note



📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 2 — Displaying Data, on what a figure has to carry to stand on its own in a report.
📖 R4DS §11 — Communication

text: Part 9 · Custom Colors and Legends — scale_color_manual()

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
scale_color_manual() — Choosing Your Own Colors






Tip



🚀 Advanced / extra work — ggplot’s default colors are fine for exploring data, but a real figure often needs specific colors (journal style, colorblind-safe palettes, matching a poster). This is how you take control.





ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = side)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15),
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4, color = "black") +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Side of tree",
    labels = c(shady = "Shady side", sunny = "Sunny side"),
    values = c(shady = "#2c7fb8", sunny = "#d95f0e")
  ) +
  labs(x = "Side of tree", y = "Needle length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)









Three arguments, matched by name:



Argument
Does what




name
the legend title


labels
text shown for each level


values
the actual color for each level









Note



✅ Key idea
labels and values are both named vectors, keyed by the raw values in your data (shady, sunny) — not by the pretty text you want to display. ggplot looks up each raw value and substitutes the label/color you gave it.








Tip



📖 Why these two colors?
#2c7fb8 (blue) and #d95f0e (orange) are a blue–orange pair, the safest two-colour choice for colour-vision deficiency: red–green confusion, which affects roughly 8% of men, leaves the blue–orange axis intact.
Don’t take that on faith — check any pair you invent with a simulator (the colorblindr or dichromat packages), or start from a palette that was built for it: scale_color_viridis_d() or RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(n, "Dark2").
📖 R4DS §11.4 — Scales, including the ColorBrewer palettes.

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
scale_color_manual() — Getting the Names Wrong



# Typo: "sun" instead of the real value "sunny"
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = side)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(shady = "#2c7fb8", sun = "#d95f0e")
  )








Warning



⚠️ Watch out!

Every level that appears in your data must get an entry in values

(and in labels, if you supply it), spelled exactly as it appears in the column
check with unique(pine_df$side) first if you are not sure
A missing or misspelled level draws as grey with a warning.

title: Lecture: Graphing Effectively
text:
scale_fill_manual() — the fill Twin



ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Side of tree",
    labels = c(shady = "Shady side", sunny = "Sunny side"),
    values = c(shady = "#2c7fb8", sunny = "#d95f0e")
  ) +
  labs(x = "Side of tree", y = "Needle length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)















Tip



🖐 Notice
Same three arguments, same pattern — scale_fill_manual() is scale_color_manual() for the fill aesthetic instead of color. A boxplot’s box is fill; its jittered points (if you added geom_point(color = ...)) would be color. A plot can need both at once.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Where We Left Off


Covered last time — generalized linear models:

The three elements of a GLM — distribution, predictors, link
Poisson and negative binomial for counts; overdispersion
Logistic regression and the odds ratio

Covered in week 9 — nested ANOVA, the traditional way:

Factorial vs. nested designs, and variance partitioning
Fixed vs. random effects — B nested in A
The naive (wrong) factorial model vs. aov(..., Error(...))








Note


✅ Key idea we are building on
patch nested in treat needs the right error term — MSpatch(treat), not MSresid — or the F-test for treatment is wrong.
Last week changed the distribution; this week changes the error structure. Put both together and you get glmer().









Tip


🖐 Notice
Same sea urchin dataset as week 9 — same question, same data, a different and far more flexible way to fit the model.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Part 1 · The Sea Urchin Data, Again
text: Part 1 · The Sea Urchin Data, Again

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Data Overview


treat — urchin density treatment (0 / 33 / 66 / 100%) patch — four patches nested inside each treatment, 16 in all quad — 5 replicate quadrats within every patch algae — % cover of filamentous algae, the response

## # A tibble: 4 × 4
##   treat patch  quad algae
##   <fct> <fct> <dbl> <dbl>
## 1 100%  1         1     0
## 2 100%  1         2     0
## 3 100%  1         3     0
## 4 100%  1         4     6



## # A tibble: 4 × 4
##   treat     n  mean    sd
##   <fct> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
## 1 0%       20  39.2 28.7 
## 2 33%      20  19   25.7 
## 3 66%      20  21.6 25.1 
## 4 100%     20   1.3  3.18







Note


📖 The gradient is not monotonic
39.2 → 19.0 → 21.6 → 1.3. The 33% and 66% means sit within noise of each other. That is the data, not an error — and it is part of why the treatment effect comes out non-significant.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Part 2 · Fixed, Random, and the Mixed Model
text: Part 2 · Fixed, Random, and the Mixed Model

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
What Makes an Effect “Random”?


Ask one question: do I care about these specific levels, or are they a sample of levels I could have had?










treat
patch




The levels are
0/33/66/100% density
patches 1–16


Chosen by
me, deliberately
whatever was there


Would a repeat study use the same ones?
yes
no — different patches


I want to estimate
each level’s mean
how much they vary


So it is
fixed
random










Important


The key consequence
A fixed factor with 16 levels costs you 15 parameters. A random factor with 16 levels costs you one — a single variance, σ²patch.
That is why mixed models cope with designs aov() chokes on: they are estimating far less.










Note


📖 A useful test
If you can write a sentence a reader would care about that names a specific level — “the 100% density treatment reduced algae” — it is fixed.
If the sentence would be “patch 7 happened to be lush” — nobody cares about patch 7 in particular. Random.









Warning


⚠️ You need enough levels
Estimating a variance from fewer than ~5 levels is unreliable. With 2 or 3 groups, fit them as fixed effects instead.
We have 16 patches — comfortably enough.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Reading the Random-Effects Formula


Read every random term as
\[(\ \text{what varies}\ \mid\ \text{across what}\ )\]

(1|patch) — the 1 means the intercept. Each patch gets its own baseline algae cover.
(1|treat:patch) — the same thing, just naming the group as the treatment-patch combination. Still intercept-only.
(1 + depth|patch) — this is a random slope: each patch gets its own intercept and its own slope for depth.








Warning


⚠️ (1|treat:patch) is not a random slope
Anything of the form (1|...) is random intercepts only — the 1 is the intercept. What changes between (1|patch) and (1|treat:patch) is the grouping variable, not what varies within it.
Here they are the identical model, because patch IDs are already unique (1–16) and each patch sits in one treatment. We will use (1|patch).









Tip


🖐 The rule
You only have a random slope when something other than 1 appears on the left of the |.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Fitting It



u_lmer_model <- lmer(
  algae ~ treat + (1 | patch),
  data = u_df,
  control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))

VarCorr(u_lmer_model)
##  Groups   Name        Std.Dev.
##  patch    (Intercept) 17.156  
##  Residual             17.280

fixef(u_lmer_model)
## (Intercept)      treat1      treat2      treat3 
##     20.2625     18.9375     -1.2625      1.2875


The model in words:
\[algae_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + b_{j(i)} + \epsilon_{ijk}\]

\(\mu\) — the overall mean
\(\alpha_i\) — the fixed effect of treatment i
\(b_{j(i)}\) — the random effect of patch j in treatment i, \(b \sim N(0,\ \sigma^2_{patch})\)
\(\epsilon_{ijk}\) — the residual for quadrat k, \(\epsilon \sim N(0,\ \sigma^2_{within})\)







Important


Notice what the model estimates for patch: not 16 numbers, one number — the variance those 16 patches were drawn from.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text: Part 3 · Testing the Fixed Effect

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Two Tests, Two Answers



Anova(u_lmer_model, type = 3,
      test.statistic = "F")
## Analysis of Deviance Table (Type III Wald F tests with Kenward-Roger df)
## 
## Response: algae
##                   F Df Df.res   Pr(>F)   
## (Intercept) 18.5551  1     12 0.001018 **
## treat        2.7171  3     12 0.091262 . 
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Anova(u_lmer_model, type = 3,
      test.statistic = "Chisq")
## Analysis of Deviance Table (Type III Wald chisquare tests)
## 
## Response: algae
##               Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)    
## (Intercept) 18.5551  1 0.00001651 ***
## treat        8.1513  3    0.04299 *  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The F-test (Kenward-Roger denominator df)

Accounts for the uncertainty in the estimated variance components
More conservative, better at small n
Here: F3,12 = 2.72, p = 0.091

The Wald χ²

Assumes the variance components are known, not estimated
Assumes infinite denominator df, i.e. a large sample
Here: χ²3 = 8.15, p = 0.043

χ² = F × numerator df = 2.717 × 3 = 8.15. The only difference is what goes on the bottom.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Same Model, Same Data, Opposite Conclusions
text:
Same Model, Same Data, Opposite Conclusions












Test
Statistic
p
Verdict at α = 0.05




F, Kenward-Roger df
F3,12 = 2.72
0.091
not significant

F3,12 = 2.72
0.091

0.043

Rule of thumb. Under ~100 observations or fewer than ~20 random-effect levels, use the F-test. Over ~500 observations and more than ~50 levels, χ² is fine. In between, the F-test is safer.
We have 80 observations and 16 patches. The rule picks the F-test.







Important


⚠️ Report the F-test — and say which df you used
The χ² is being over-confident. It pretends it knows σ²patch and σ²within exactly, when they were estimated from 16 patches.
The F-test agrees with week 9’s aov(Error(patch)) to four decimal places, because it is the same test.









Warning


🖐 The uncomfortable part
Run only the χ² and you report a significant effect and never know. When two defensible analyses straddle α = 0.05, say so and justify the choice — do not pick one and delete the other.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Part 4 · How the Variance Actually Gets Estimated
text: Part 4 · How the Variance Actually Gets Estimated

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
The Question This Part Answers
For three weeks, every answer came from one move: take the total sum of squares, cut it into pieces by source, divide each piece by its df to get a mean square, and form a ratio.
\[SS_{total} = SS_{treat} + SS_{patch(treat)} + SS_{within}\]
lmer() printed σ²patch = 294.3 and never showed you a sum of squares anywhere.






Important


So where did that number come from, and why is it not an SS table?
The rest of this part is the answer. It is the single biggest conceptual change between week 9 and today — bigger than the notation, bigger than the p-value.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: The Old Route — Sums of Squares and Expected Mean Squares
text:
The Old Route — Sums of Squares and Expected Mean Squares


Week 9’s table, one more time:

a_tab <- summary(aov(algae ~ treat + treat:patch,
                     data = u_df))[[1]]
round(a_tab[, c("Df", "Sum Sq", "Mean Sq")], 1)
##             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq
## treat        3  14429  4809.7
## treat:patch 12  21242  1770.2
## Residuals   64  19110   298.6

Statistical theory tells you what each mean square estimates on average — its expected mean square:
\[E[MS_{within}] = \sigma^2_{within}\] \[E[MS_{patch}] = \sigma^2_{within} + n\,\sigma^2_{patch}\]

Now set the observed equal to the expected and solve. That is all the old method is — two equations, two unknowns, no statistics at all past this point:
\[\hat\sigma^2_{within} = MS_{within}\] \[\hat\sigma^2_{patch} = \frac{MS_{patch} - MS_{within}}{n}\]

MS_patch  <- a_tab[2, "Mean Sq"]
MS_within <- a_tab[3, "Mean Sq"]
n <- 5                      # quadrats per patch

c(within = MS_within,
  patch  = (MS_patch - MS_within) / n)
##   within    patch 
## 298.6000 294.3125

This is the method of moments. It is arithmetic on a table.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: The New Route — Write Down the Variance and Search for It
text:
The New Route — Write Down the Variance and Search for It


A mixed model never builds that table. It writes the variance of the whole response vector in one matrix:
\[\mathbf{V} = \sigma^2_{patch}\,\mathbf{ZZ}^\top + \sigma^2_{within}\,\mathbf{I}\]

\(\mathbf{Z}\) says which patch each quadrat belongs to
\(\mathbf{ZZ}^\top\) is 1 for any two quadrats in the same patch, 0 otherwise
So \(\mathbf{V}\) states, directly, that two quadrats in a patch are correlated and two in different patches are not

Then it asks a completely different question:

Which pair of numbers (σ²patch, σ²within) makes the data I actually observed most likely?








Important


That is the whole switch.
Old: partition a quantity you computed (SS), then solve an algebraic identity for the variances.
New: propose a pair of variances, ask how probable the data are under them, and keep searching until that probability stops improving.
No decomposition. No table. A search over a likelihood surface.



The F-ratio idea does not disappear — it comes back at the end, when you test the fixed effect. But it is no longer how the variances are obtained.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
The Restricted Likelihood, Written Out


Eight lines, no lme4. This is literally what the optimizer is doing:

y <- u_df$algae
X <- model.matrix(~ treat, u_df)   # fixed effects
Z <- model.matrix(~ 0 + patch, u_df)   # grouping
ZZt <- Z %*% t(Z)

reml_ll <- function(v_patch, v_within) {
  V  <- v_patch * ZZt + v_within * diag(nrow(X))
  Vi <- solve(V)
  A  <- t(X) %*% Vi %*% X
  b  <- solve(A, t(X) %*% Vi %*% y)     # GLS fixed effects
  r  <- y - X %*% b
  -0.5 * as.numeric(determinant(V, log = TRUE)$modulus +
                    determinant(A, log = TRUE)$modulus +
                    t(r) %*% Vi %*% r)
}


Three pieces, each doing one job:

\(\log|\mathbf{V}|\) — penalises making the variances big, since a bigger variance spreads probability thinner
\(\mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}\) — penalises leaving big residuals, which pushes the variances up
\(\log|\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}|\) — the restricted part, the correction for having estimated the fixed effects

The answer is the pair where those forces balance.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
The Surface the Optimizer Climbs












Slice the surface at σ²within = 298.6 and you can see the whole method: the optimizer walks uphill until the slope is flat.






Warning


⚠️ Look how flat that peak is
Everything from roughly 150 to 600 sits within about one log-likelihood unit of the peak. Variance components are badly determined with only 16 groups — and that uncertainty is exactly what the Kenward-Roger F-test accounts for and the Wald χ² ignores.
This plot is the reason those two tests disagreed.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Both Routes, One Number



# route 1: moments, from the SS table
moments <- (MS_patch - MS_within) / n

# route 2: maximise the restricted likelihood
fit <- optim(c(200, 300),
             \(p) -reml_ll(p[1], p[2]),
             method = "L-BFGS-B",
             lower = c(0, 1e-6))

# route 3: what lmer() reports
lmer_vc <- as.data.frame(
  VarCorr(u_lmer_model))$vcov[1]

round(c(moments = moments,
        likelihood = fit$par[1],
        lmer = lmer_vc), 3)
##    moments likelihood       lmer 
##    294.313    294.312    294.313








Important


294.31, three ways.
They agree to within 0.001 — and the first two have nothing in common methodologically. One is algebra on a table of sums of squares; the other is a numerical search over a likelihood surface.
On a balanced design the restricted maximum-likelihood solution has a closed form, and that closed form is the moment estimator.



So week 9 was never wrong. It was a special case that happens to have a shortcut — and you have been using the shortcut without being told it was one.
Next slide: what happens when the shortcut stops existing.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Where the Two Routes Part Company
text:
Where the Two Routes Part Company


1. The moment estimator can return a negative variance.
\(MS_{patch} < MS_{within}\) is perfectly possible by chance, and then \((MS_{patch}-MS_{within})/n\) is below zero — an impossible value for a variance.

## moments    REML 
##  -1.634   0.000

REML cannot go below zero — the likelihood is only defined for non-negative variances — so it stops at the boundary and warns “boundary (singular) fit”.

2. Unbalanced data has no single n to divide by.
Thin four patches to one quadrat each, as a storm would:

##     moments, n = 5 moments, n0 = 3.95               REML 
##              198.2              250.9              256.7







Important


Three answers, and the moment estimator needs you to choose an effective n before it will give one at all. REML never asks — the likelihood already knows how many quadrats each patch has.
This is why mixed models replaced Error().

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Why REML and Not Plain ML
text:
Why REML and Not Plain ML



ml_fit <- lmer(algae ~ treat + (1 | patch),
               data = u_df, REML = FALSE,
               control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))

round(c(
  REML = as.data.frame(VarCorr(u_lmer_model))$vcov[1],
  ML   = as.data.frame(VarCorr(ml_fit))$vcov[1]), 1)
##  REML    ML 
## 294.3 205.8

Plain maximum likelihood estimates σ²patch as 205.8. REML gets 294.3. ML is biased 30% low.

You have met this bias before, in week 2.
\[s^2 = \frac{\sum(y-\bar y)^2}{n-\mathbf{1}} \quad\text{not}\quad \frac{\sum(y-\bar y)^2}{n}\]
Dividing by n under-estimates the variance because you spent one df estimating \(\bar y\). ML makes exactly that mistake, at scale: it estimates the four treatment means and then behaves as though they were known all along.






Important


REML = “restricted”: it maximises the likelihood of the data after the fixed effects have been projected out — the \(\log|\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}|\) term three slides back. That term is the \(n-1\) correction, generalised.



Use REML for variance components. Switch to ML only to compare models with different fixed effects.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Part 4 — The Short Version










Nested ANOVA (week 9)
Mixed model (today)




Starts from
the total sum of squares
the variance matrix \(\mathbf{V}\)


Core move
partition SS by source
search for the most likely variances


Variance components from
solving \(E[MS]\) equations
maximising the restricted likelihood


Needs balance?
yes, for exact tests
no


Negative variance
can happen, is meaningless
impossible — stops at 0


Unbalanced n
you must pick an effective n
handled automatically


On this dataset
σ²patch = 294.31
σ²patch = 294.31










Note


✅ The one sentence
Sums of squares divide up variation that has already been computed; likelihood proposes variances and asks how well they explain the data. On a balanced design the two land on the same number — everywhere else, only the second one still works.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Part 5 · What the Random Effect Buys You
text: Part 5 · What the Random Effect Buys You

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
The Intraclass Correlation



vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(u_lmer_model))
v_patch <- vc$vcov[vc$grp != "Residual"]
v_resid <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "Residual"]

round(c(among_patches  = v_patch,
        within_patches = v_resid,
        ICC = v_patch / (v_patch + v_resid)), 3)
##  among_patches within_patches            ICC 
##        294.313        298.600          0.496

The ICC is the share of variance living between groups — equivalently, how strongly two quadrats in the same patch resemble each other.







Important


ICC = 0.50 is the whole reason we are here
Two quadrats from the same patch are half-correlated. They are not two independent observations.
An ICC near 0 would mean patches barely matter and ordinary ANOVA would have been fine. An ICC of 0.50 means ignoring patch would have been badly wrong — and week 9’s naive model showed exactly how wrong (F = 16.1 instead of 2.7).









Tip


🖐 Use it to design the next study
With ICC = 0.50, a sixth quadrat in an existing patch buys you almost nothing. A new patch buys you a lot. The p-value could never have told you that.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Partial Pooling — What Happens to Each Patch
text:
Partial Pooling — What Happens to Each Patch


A random effect does not just adjust the p-value. It changes each patch’s estimate.
















Note


📖 New word: shrinkage
Every patch estimate is pulled toward its treatment mean. The model treats an extreme patch average as partly real signal and partly luck, and splits the difference.
Patches with fewer quadrats, or more internal scatter, get pulled further.









Tip


🖐 Why this is a feature
A patch whose 5 quadrats happened to land high is probably not that extreme — the next 5 would come back closer to average.
This is partial pooling: between treating every patch as unrelated and pretending they are all identical.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Reporting the Variance Components








Note


How to report this result
“Algal cover did not differ significantly among urchin density treatments (linear mixed model with patch as a random effect, F3,12 = 2.72, p = 0.091, Kenward-Roger denominator df). Among-patch variance was substantial (σ²patch = 294.3 vs σ²within = 298.6, ICC = 0.50), indicating strong spatial heterogeneity in algal cover.”



Both halves belong in the sentence. The fixed effect answers did the treatment do anything; the variance component answers how noisy is this reef, which is what the next person planning a study needs.







Important


⚠️ “Not significant” is not “no effect”
With σ²patch ≈ σ²within, patch-to-patch variation is as large as quadrat-to-quadrat variation. Four patches per treatment simply cannot resolve a treatment effect against that much background noise.
The honest conclusion is “this design could not detect it”, not “urchins do not affect algae.”









Tip


🖐 Where 294.3 came from
By hand from mean squares, from aov(Error(patch)), and from VarCorr() — three notations, one model. See Part 4.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text: Part 6 · Post-Hoc, Assumptions, and Reporting

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Estimated Marginal Means



u_emm <- emmeans(u_lmer_model, ~ treat)
u_emm
##  treat emmean   SE df lower.CL upper.CL
##  0%      39.2 9.41 12    18.70     59.7
##  33%     19.0 9.41 12    -1.50     39.5
##  66%     21.6 9.41 12     1.05     42.0
##  100%     1.3 9.41 12   -19.20     21.8
## 
## Degrees-of-freedom method: kenward-roger 
## Confidence level used: 0.95


Every standard error is 9.41 — identical across treatments, because the design is balanced and the SE comes from the patch stratum (4 patches per treatment), not from the 20 quadrats.






Warning


⚠️ Two of these intervals go below zero
Algae cover is a percentage. It cannot be negative.
The mixed model fixed the error structure and left the distribution alone — it still assumes normal, unbounded response. Last week you fixed the distribution and left the error structure alone. Real data often needs both: that is glmer().

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Post-Hoc Comparisons



##  treat emmean   SE df lower.CL upper.CL .group
##  100%     1.3 9.41 12   -19.20     21.8  a    
##  33%     19.0 9.41 12    -1.50     39.5  a    
##  66%     21.6 9.41 12     1.05     42.0  a    
##  0%      39.2 9.41 12    18.70     59.7  a    
## 
## Degrees-of-freedom method: kenward-roger 
## Confidence level used: 0.95 
## P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates 
## significance level used: alpha = 0.05 
## NOTE: If two or more means share the same grouping symbol,
##       then we cannot show them to be different.
##       But we also did not show them to be the same.








Important


Every treatment shares the letter a.
No pair is distinguishable. That is the correct and expected result — the omnibus F-test was already non-significant (p = 0.091), so there was nothing for a post-hoc to find.
Running post-hocs after a non-significant omnibus test is exploratory only. Report it as such, or not at all.









Note


📖 Read the pattern, not a ranking
The means run 39.2 → 19.0 → 21.6 → 1.3. The two middle treatments are effectively tied, so this is not a clean monotonic gradient. Resist the temptation to write one.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Diagnostics


















Warning


⚠️ The spread is not constant
It is tightest at the lowest fitted values and widens from there — the same heteroscedasticity the raw data showed. A mixed model fixes correlation, not unequal variance.









Tip


🖐 Use the right tool
plot() and qqnorm() were built for lm() objects. They mostly work on an lmer() fit, but DHARMa simulates from the fitted model and is the purpose-built check — that is what the activity uses.



A mixed model also assumes the random effects are normal. With 16 patches you cannot check that honestly. Say so.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Heterogeneity of Variance



leveneTest(algae ~ treat, data = u_df)
## Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
##       Df F value     Pr(>F)    
## group  3  8.1694 0.00008785 ***
##       76                       
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1








Warning


⚠️ This test ignores patch
leveneTest() has no idea the quadrats are grouped. It is testing the 80 raw values as if they were independent — the very assumption this whole lecture exists to fix. Read it as a description of the raw spread, not as a test of the mixed model.
The model’s own diagnostic is the residuals-vs-fitted plot, and DHARMa.



Variances really are unequal (the 100% treatment has SD 3.2, the 0% treatment 28.7). Quinn & Keough noted the same thing, tried transformations including arcsine, and found none that fixed it — so they analysed the untransformed data and said so. A balanced ANOVA is reasonably robust to this. Say it out loud in the methods rather than hoping nobody checks.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Visualization





















Grey — the 16 patch means. Red — the model’s treatment means and 95% intervals. The grey scatter within each treatment is σ²patch; it is why the red intervals are so wide.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text: Part 7 · Wrap-Up

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
The lmer Formula Cheat-Sheet


Read every random term as ( what varies | across what ).








Formula
Meaning




y ~ x + (1|g)
random intercept per group


y ~ x + (1 + x|g)
random intercept and slope


y ~ x + (0 + x|g)
random slope only, shared intercept


y ~ x + (1|a) + (1|b)
two crossed random factors


y ~ x + (1|a/b)
b nested in a — shorthand for (1|a) + (1|a:b)










Important


⚠️ The confusion to avoid
(1|patch) and (1|treat:patch) are both random-intercept models. The 1 is the intercept; what differs is only the grouping.










Tip


🖐 Do I need a/b here?
Only if the inner IDs restart inside each outer level (patch 1,2,3,4 in every treatment). Then R cannot tell nesting from crossing and you must write (1|treat/patch).
Our patches are numbered 1–16 across the whole study, so (1|patch) already says it.









Warning


⚠️ “boundary (singular) fit”
A variance was estimated as exactly 0 — the likelihood hit the edge of what a variance is allowed to be. It is the REML version of the moment estimator going negative (Part 4).
Simplify the random effects; do not ignore it.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Wrap-up


Today you:

Decided fixed vs random by asking whether you care about these levels or about how much they vary
Learned a random factor costs one parameter where a fixed one costs k − 1
Read (1|group) correctly, and saw it is not a random slope
Chose between the F-test (p = 0.091) and the Wald χ² (p = 0.043) — and learned why the F-test is right at 16 groups
Saw where the variance components come from: a search over a restricted likelihood, not a partition of sums of squares
Got ICC = 0.50, and saw partial pooling shrink each patch estimate toward its treatment mean








Important


✅ The one idea to keep
A mixed model does not “remove” the patch effect — it estimates it, and tests the treatment against the right amount of noise.
The old way partitioned variation that was already computed. The new way proposes variances and keeps the ones that make the data most likely. On a balanced design they agree exactly; everywhere else only the second still works.









Note


📖 Up next
glmer() — a non-normal response and a random effect. You now have both halves.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Before Next Class


Take the pine needle data, collapsed to one value per team per side (the two-stage summary from Week 3):
p_df <- pine_df |>
  group_by(team, side) |>
  summarise(needle_length_mm = mean(needle_length_mm),
            .groups = "drop")

anova(lmer(needle_length_mm ~ side + (1|team), data = p_df))
Compare F to the square of the paired-t statistic from Week 4 (t = −2.72). You should get F = 7.41, df 1 and 3, p = 0.072 — the paired t-test is this mixed model.







Tip


🚀 If you finish early
Run the same formula on the raw 64 needles instead. You get p = 0.057 and 59 denominator df, not 3.
What changed? Check VarCorr() — one variance is estimated as exactly zero and R warns “singular fit”.
You now know what that means: the likelihood walked to the edge of the parameter space, exactly as the moment estimator would have gone negative.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Readings



Gotelli & Ellison, Ch. 10 — The Analysis of Variance, for the random-effects and variance-component material this lecture rebuilds.
Quinn & Keough (2002), Experimental Design and Data Analysis for Biologists, Ch. 9 §9.1 — nested designs and expected mean squares. This is the source of today’s worked example.
Zuur, A. F., Ieno, E. N., Walker, N. J., Saveliev, A. A., & Smith, G. M. (2009). Mixed Effects Models and Extensions in Ecology with R. Springer. Ch. 5 is the standard ecological treatment of REML.
Bates, D., Mächler, M., Bolker, B., & Walker, S. (2015). Fitting linear mixed-effects models using lme4. Journal of Statistical Software, 67(1), 1–48.








Note


📖 On the dataset
The sea urchin grazing data are Andrew & Underwood’s, as analysed in Quinn & Keough Ch. 9 — the same file as week 9. The textbook PDFs are on Canvas.









Tip


🖐 Why no Whitlock & Schluter
W&S does not cover mixed models or random effects. For this topic, Gotelli, Quinn & Keough, and Zuur are the references.

Data Overview


treat — urchin density treatment (0 / 33 / 66 / 100%) patch — four patches nested inside each treatment, 16 in all quad — 5 replicate quadrats within every patch algae — % cover of filamentous algae, the response

## # A tibble: 4 × 4
