Note



📖 The gradient is not monotonic
39.2 → 19.0 → 21.6 → 1.3. The 33% and 66% means sit within noise of each other. That is the data, not an error — and it is part of why the treatment effect comes out non-significant.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Part 2 · Fixed, Random, and the Mixed Model
text: Part 2 · Fixed, Random, and the Mixed Model

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
What Makes an Effect “Random”?


Ask one question: do I care about these specific levels, or are they a sample of levels I could have had?










treat
patch




The levels are
0/33/66/100% density
patches 1–16


Chosen by
me, deliberately
whatever was there


Would a repeat study use the same ones?
yes
no — different patches


I want to estimate
each level’s mean
how much they vary


So it is
fixed
random










Important



The key consequence
A fixed factor with 16 levels costs you 15 parameters. A random factor with 16 levels costs you one — a single variance, σ²patch.
That is why mixed models cope with designs aov() chokes on: they are estimating far less.









Note



📖 A useful test
If you can write a sentence a reader would care about that names a specific level — “the 100% density treatment reduced algae” — it is fixed.
If the sentence would be “patch 7 happened to be lush” — nobody cares about patch 7 in particular. Random.








Warning



⚠️ You need enough levels
Estimating a variance from fewer than ~5 levels is unreliable. With 2 or 3 groups, fit them as fixed effects instead.
We have 16 patches — comfortably enough.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Reading the Random-Effects Formula


Read every random term as
\[(\ \text{what varies}\ \mid\ \text{across what}\ )\]

(1|patch) — the 1 means the intercept. Each patch gets its own baseline algae cover.
(1|treat:patch) — the same thing, just naming the group as the treatment-patch combination. Still intercept-only.
(1 + depth|patch) — this is a random slope: each patch gets its own intercept and its own slope for depth.








Warning



⚠️ (1|treat:patch) is not a random slope
Anything of the form (1|...) is random intercepts only — the 1 is the intercept. What changes between (1|patch) and (1|treat:patch) is the grouping variable, not what varies within it.
Here they are the identical model, because patch IDs are already unique (1–16) and each patch sits in one treatment. We will use (1|patch).








Tip



🖐 The rule
You only have a random slope when something other than 1 appears on the left of the |.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Fitting It



u_lmer_model <- lmer(
  algae ~ treat + (1 | patch),
  data = u_df,
  control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))

VarCorr(u_lmer_model)
##  Groups   Name        Std.Dev.
##  patch    (Intercept) 17.156  
##  Residual             17.280

fixef(u_lmer_model)
## (Intercept)      treat1      treat2      treat3 
##     20.2625     18.9375     -1.2625      1.2875


The model in words:
\[algae_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + b_{j(i)} + \epsilon_{ijk}\]

\(\mu\) — the overall mean
\(\alpha_i\) — the fixed effect of treatment i
\(b_{j(i)}\) — the random effect of patch j in treatment i, \(b \sim N(0,\ \sigma^2_{patch})\)
\(\epsilon_{ijk}\) — the residual for quadrat k, \(\epsilon \sim N(0,\ \sigma^2_{within})\)







Important



Notice what the model estimates for patch: not 16 numbers, one number — the variance those 16 patches were drawn from.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text: Part 3 · Testing the Fixed Effect

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Two Tests, Two Answers



Anova(u_lmer_model, type = 3,
      test.statistic = "F")
## Analysis of Deviance Table (Type III Wald F tests with Kenward-Roger df)
## 
## Response: algae
##                   F Df Df.res   Pr(>F)   
## (Intercept) 18.5551  1     12 0.001018 **
## treat        2.7171  3     12 0.091262 . 
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Anova(u_lmer_model, type = 3,
      test.statistic = "Chisq")
## Analysis of Deviance Table (Type III Wald chisquare tests)
## 
## Response: algae
##               Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)    
## (Intercept) 18.5551  1 0.00001651 ***
## treat        8.1513  3    0.04299 *  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The F-test (Kenward-Roger denominator df)

Accounts for the uncertainty in the estimated variance components
More conservative, better at small n
Here: F3,12 = 2.72, p = 0.091

The Wald χ²

Assumes the variance components are known, not estimated
Assumes infinite denominator df, i.e. a large sample
Here: χ²3 = 8.15, p = 0.043

χ² = F × numerator df = 2.717 × 3 = 8.15. The only difference is what goes on the bottom.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Same Model, Same Data, Opposite Conclusions
text:
Same Model, Same Data, Opposite Conclusions












Test
Statistic
p
Verdict at α = 0.05




F, Kenward-Roger df
F3,12 = 2.72
0.091
not significant


F, Satterthwaite df
F3,12 = 2.72
0.091
not significant


Wald χ²
χ²3 = 8.15
0.043
significant




Rule of thumb. Under ~100 observations or fewer than ~20 random-effect levels, use the F-test. Over ~500 observations and more than ~50 levels, χ² is fine. In between, the F-test is safer.
We have 80 observations and 16 patches. The rule picks the F-test.







Important



⚠️ Report the F-test — and say which df you used
The χ² is being over-confident. It pretends it knows σ²patch and σ²within exactly, when they were estimated from 16 patches.
The F-test agrees with week 9’s aov(Error(patch)) to four decimal places, because it is the same test.








Warning



🖐 The uncomfortable part
Run only the χ² and you report a significant effect and never know. When two defensible analyses straddle α = 0.05, say so and justify the choice — do not pick one and delete the other.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Part 4 · How the Variance Actually Gets Estimated
text: Part 4 · How the Variance Actually Gets Estimated

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
The Question This Part Answers
For three weeks, every answer came from one move: take the total sum of squares, cut it into pieces by source, divide each piece by its df to get a mean square, and form a ratio.
\[SS_{total} = SS_{treat} + SS_{patch(treat)} + SS_{within}\]
lmer() printed σ²patch = 294.3 and never showed you a sum of squares anywhere.






Important



So where did that number come from, and why is it not an SS table?
The rest of this part is the answer. It is the single biggest conceptual change between week 9 and today — bigger than the notation, bigger than the p-value.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: The Old Route — Sums of Squares and Expected Mean Squares
text:
The Old Route — Sums of Squares and Expected Mean Squares


Week 9’s table, one more time:

a_tab <- summary(aov(algae ~ treat + treat:patch,
                     data = u_df))[[1]]
round(a_tab[, c("Df", "Sum Sq", "Mean Sq")], 1)
##             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq
## treat        3  14429  4809.7
## treat:patch 12  21242  1770.2
## Residuals   64  19110   298.6

Statistical theory tells you what each mean square estimates on average — its expected mean square:
\[E[MS_{within}] = \sigma^2_{within}\] \[E[MS_{patch}] = \sigma^2_{within} + n\,\sigma^2_{patch}\]

Now set the observed equal to the expected and solve. That is all the old method is — two equations, two unknowns, no statistics at all past this point:
\[\hat\sigma^2_{within} = MS_{within}\] \[\hat\sigma^2_{patch} = \frac{MS_{patch} - MS_{within}}{n}\]

MS_patch  <- a_tab[2, "Mean Sq"]
MS_within <- a_tab[3, "Mean Sq"]
n <- 5                      # quadrats per patch

c(within = MS_within,
  patch  = (MS_patch - MS_within) / n)
##   within    patch 
## 298.6000 294.3125

This is the method of moments. It is arithmetic on a table.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: The New Route — Write Down the Variance and Search for It
text:
The New Route — Write Down the Variance and Search for It


A mixed model never builds that table. It writes the variance of the whole response vector in one matrix:
\[\mathbf{V} = \sigma^2_{patch}\,\mathbf{ZZ}^\top + \sigma^2_{within}\,\mathbf{I}\]

\(\mathbf{Z}\) says which patch each quadrat belongs to
\(\mathbf{ZZ}^\top\) is 1 for any two quadrats in the same patch, 0 otherwise
So \(\mathbf{V}\) states, directly, that two quadrats in a patch are correlated and two in different patches are not

Then it asks a completely different question:

Which pair of numbers (σ²patch, σ²within) makes the data I actually observed most likely?








Important



That is the whole switch.
Old: partition a quantity you computed (SS), then solve an algebraic identity for the variances.
New: propose a pair of variances, ask how probable the data are under them, and keep searching until that probability stops improving.
No decomposition. No table. A search over a likelihood surface.


The F-ratio idea does not disappear — it comes back at the end, when you test the fixed effect. But it is no longer how the variances are obtained.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
The Restricted Likelihood, Written Out


Eight lines, no lme4. This is literally what the optimizer is doing:

y <- u_df$algae
X <- model.matrix(~ treat, u_df)   # fixed effects
Z <- model.matrix(~ 0 + patch, u_df)   # grouping
ZZt <- Z %*% t(Z)

reml_ll <- function(v_patch, v_within) {
  V  <- v_patch * ZZt + v_within * diag(nrow(X))
  Vi <- solve(V)
  A  <- t(X) %*% Vi %*% X
  b  <- solve(A, t(X) %*% Vi %*% y)     # GLS fixed effects
  r  <- y - X %*% b
  -0.5 * as.numeric(determinant(V, log = TRUE)$modulus +
                    determinant(A, log = TRUE)$modulus +
                    t(r) %*% Vi %*% r)
}


Three pieces, each doing one job:

\(\log|\mathbf{V}|\) — penalises making the variances big, since a bigger variance spreads probability thinner
\(\mathbf{r}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{r}\) — penalises leaving big residuals, which pushes the variances up
\(\log|\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}|\) — the restricted part, the correction for having estimated the fixed effects

The answer is the pair where those forces balance.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
The Surface the Optimizer Climbs












Slice the surface at σ²within = 298.6 and you can see the whole method: the optimizer walks uphill until the slope is flat.






Warning



⚠️ Look how flat that peak is
Everything from roughly 150 to 600 sits within about one log-likelihood unit of the peak. Variance components are badly determined with only 16 groups — and that uncertainty is exactly what the Kenward-Roger F-test accounts for and the Wald χ² ignores.
This plot is the reason those two tests disagreed.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Both Routes, One Number



# route 1: moments, from the SS table
moments <- (MS_patch - MS_within) / n

# route 2: maximise the restricted likelihood
fit <- optim(c(200, 300),
             \(p) -reml_ll(p[1], p[2]),
             method = "L-BFGS-B",
             lower = c(0, 1e-6))

# route 3: what lmer() reports
lmer_vc <- as.data.frame(
  VarCorr(u_lmer_model))$vcov[1]

round(c(moments = moments,
        likelihood = fit$par[1],
        lmer = lmer_vc), 3)
##    moments likelihood       lmer 
##    294.313    294.312    294.313








Important



294.31, three ways.
They agree to within 0.001 — and the first two have nothing in common methodologically. One is algebra on a table of sums of squares; the other is a numerical search over a likelihood surface.
On a balanced design the restricted maximum-likelihood solution has a closed form, and that closed form is the moment estimator.


So week 9 was never wrong. It was a special case that happens to have a shortcut — and you have been using the shortcut without being told it was one.
Next slide: what happens when the shortcut stops existing.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Where the Two Routes Part Company
text:
Where the Two Routes Part Company


1. The moment estimator can return a negative variance.
\(MS_{patch} < MS_{within}\) is perfectly possible by chance, and then \((MS_{patch}-MS_{within})/n\) is below zero — an impossible value for a variance.

## moments    REML 
##  -1.634   0.000

REML cannot go below zero — the likelihood is only defined for non-negative variances — so it stops at the boundary and warns “boundary (singular) fit”.

2. Unbalanced data has no single n to divide by.
Thin four patches to one quadrat each, as a storm would:

##     moments, n = 5 moments, n0 = 3.95               REML 
##              198.2              250.9              256.7







Important



Three answers, and the moment estimator needs you to choose an effective n before it will give one at all. REML never asks — the likelihood already knows how many quadrats each patch has.
This is why mixed models replaced Error().

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Why REML and Not Plain ML
text:
Why REML and Not Plain ML



ml_fit <- lmer(algae ~ treat + (1 | patch),
               data = u_df, REML = FALSE,
               control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))

round(c(
  REML = as.data.frame(VarCorr(u_lmer_model))$vcov[1],
  ML   = as.data.frame(VarCorr(ml_fit))$vcov[1]), 1)
##  REML    ML 
## 294.3 205.8

Plain maximum likelihood estimates σ²patch as 205.8. REML gets 294.3. ML is biased 30% low.

You have met this bias before, in week 2.
\[s^2 = \frac{\sum(y-\bar y)^2}{n-\mathbf{1}} \quad\text{not}\quad \frac{\sum(y-\bar y)^2}{n}\]
Dividing by n under-estimates the variance because you spent one df estimating \(\bar y\). ML makes exactly that mistake, at scale: it estimates the four treatment means and then behaves as though they were known all along.






Important



REML = “restricted”: it maximises the likelihood of the data after the fixed effects have been projected out — the \(\log|\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}|\) term three slides back. That term is the \(n-1\) correction, generalised.


Use REML for variance components. Switch to ML only to compare models with different fixed effects.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Part 4 — The Short Version










Nested ANOVA (week 9)
Mixed model (today)




Starts from
the total sum of squares
the variance matrix \(\mathbf{V}\)


Core move
partition SS by source
search for the most likely variances


Variance components from
solving \(E[MS]\) equations
maximising the restricted likelihood


Needs balance?
yes, for exact tests
no


Negative variance
can happen, is meaningless
impossible — stops at 0


Unbalanced n
you must pick an effective n
handled automatically


On this dataset
σ²patch = 294.31
σ²patch = 294.31










Note



✅ The one sentence
Sums of squares divide up variation that has already been computed; likelihood proposes variances and asks how well they explain the data. On a balanced design the two land on the same number — everywhere else, only the second one still works.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Part 5 · What the Random Effect Buys You
text: Part 5 · What the Random Effect Buys You

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
The Intraclass Correlation



vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(u_lmer_model))
v_patch <- vc$vcov[vc$grp != "Residual"]
v_resid <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "Residual"]

round(c(among_patches  = v_patch,
        within_patches = v_resid,
        ICC = v_patch / (v_patch + v_resid)), 3)
##  among_patches within_patches            ICC 
##        294.313        298.600          0.496

The ICC is the share of variance living between groups — equivalently, how strongly two quadrats in the same patch resemble each other.







Important



ICC = 0.50 is the whole reason we are here
Two quadrats from the same patch are half-correlated. They are not two independent observations.
An ICC near 0 would mean patches barely matter and ordinary ANOVA would have been fine. An ICC of 0.50 means ignoring patch would have been badly wrong — and week 9’s naive model showed exactly how wrong (F = 16.1 instead of 2.7).








Tip



🖐 Use it to design the next study
With ICC = 0.50, a sixth quadrat in an existing patch buys you almost nothing. A new patch buys you a lot. The p-value could never have told you that.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
section: Partial Pooling — What Happens to Each Patch
text:
Partial Pooling — What Happens to Each Patch


A random effect does not just adjust the p-value. It changes each patch’s estimate.
















Note



📖 New word: shrinkage
Every patch estimate is pulled toward its treatment mean. The model treats an extreme patch average as partly real signal and partly luck, and splits the difference.
Patches with fewer quadrats, or more internal scatter, get pulled further.








Tip



🖐 Why this is a feature
A patch whose 5 quadrats happened to land high is probably not that extreme — the next 5 would come back closer to average.
This is partial pooling: between treating every patch as unrelated and pretending they are all identical.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Reporting the Variance Components








Note



How to report this result
“Algal cover did not differ significantly among urchin density treatments (linear mixed model with patch as a random effect, F3,12 = 2.72, p = 0.091, Kenward-Roger denominator df). Among-patch variance was substantial (σ²patch = 294.3 vs σ²within = 298.6, ICC = 0.50), indicating strong spatial heterogeneity in algal cover.”


Both halves belong in the sentence. The fixed effect answers did the treatment do anything; the variance component answers how noisy is this reef, which is what the next person planning a study needs.







Important



⚠️ “Not significant” is not “no effect”
With σ²patch ≈ σ²within, patch-to-patch variation is as large as quadrat-to-quadrat variation. Four patches per treatment simply cannot resolve a treatment effect against that much background noise.
The honest conclusion is “this design could not detect it”, not “urchins do not affect algae.”








Tip



🖐 Where 294.3 came from
By hand from mean squares, from aov(Error(patch)), and from VarCorr() — three notations, one model. See Part 4.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text: Part 6 · Post-Hoc, Assumptions, and Reporting

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Estimated Marginal Means



u_emm <- emmeans(u_lmer_model, ~ treat)
u_emm
##  treat emmean   SE df lower.CL upper.CL
##  0%      39.2 9.41 12    18.70     59.7
##  33%     19.0 9.41 12    -1.50     39.5
##  66%     21.6 9.41 12     1.05     42.0
##  100%     1.3 9.41 12   -19.20     21.8
## 
## Degrees-of-freedom method: kenward-roger 
## Confidence level used: 0.95


Every standard error is 9.41 — identical across treatments, because the design is balanced and the SE comes from the patch stratum (4 patches per treatment), not from the 20 quadrats.






Warning



⚠️ Two of these intervals go below zero
Algae cover is a percentage. It cannot be negative.
The mixed model fixed the error structure and left the distribution alone — it still assumes normal, unbounded response. Last week you fixed the distribution and left the error structure alone. Real data often needs both: that is glmer().

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Post-Hoc Comparisons



##  treat emmean   SE df lower.CL upper.CL .group
##  100%     1.3 9.41 12   -19.20     21.8  a    
##  33%     19.0 9.41 12    -1.50     39.5  a    
##  66%     21.6 9.41 12     1.05     42.0  a    
##  0%      39.2 9.41 12    18.70     59.7  a    
## 
## Degrees-of-freedom method: kenward-roger 
## Confidence level used: 0.95 
## P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates 
## significance level used: alpha = 0.05 
## NOTE: If two or more means share the same grouping symbol,
##       then we cannot show them to be different.
##       But we also did not show them to be the same.








Important



Every treatment shares the letter a.
No pair is distinguishable. That is the correct and expected result — the omnibus F-test was already non-significant (p = 0.091), so there was nothing for a post-hoc to find.
Running post-hocs after a non-significant omnibus test is exploratory only. Report it as such, or not at all.








Note



📖 Read the pattern, not a ranking
The means run 39.2 → 19.0 → 21.6 → 1.3. The two middle treatments are effectively tied, so this is not a clean monotonic gradient. Resist the temptation to write one.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Diagnostics


















Warning



⚠️ The spread is not constant
It is tightest at the lowest fitted values and widens from there — the same heteroscedasticity the raw data showed. A mixed model fixes correlation, not unequal variance.








Tip



🖐 Use the right tool
plot() and qqnorm() were built for lm() objects. They mostly work on an lmer() fit, but DHARMa simulates from the fitted model and is the purpose-built check — that is what the activity uses.


A mixed model also assumes the random effects are normal. With 16 patches you cannot check that honestly. Say so.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Heterogeneity of Variance



leveneTest(algae ~ treat, data = u_df)
## Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
##       Df F value     Pr(>F)    
## group  3  8.1694 0.00008785 ***
##       76                       
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1








Warning



⚠️ This test ignores patch
leveneTest() has no idea the quadrats are grouped. It is testing the 80 raw values as if they were independent — the very assumption this whole lecture exists to fix. Read it as a description of the raw spread, not as a test of the mixed model.
The model’s own diagnostic is the residuals-vs-fitted plot, and DHARMa.


Variances really are unequal (the 100% treatment has SD 3.2, the 0% treatment 28.7). Quinn & Keough noted the same thing, tried transformations including arcsine, and found none that fixed it — so they analysed the untransformed data and said so. A balanced ANOVA is reasonably robust to this. Say it out loud in the methods rather than hoping nobody checks.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Visualization





















Grey — the 16 patch means. Red — the model’s treatment means and 95% intervals. The grey scatter within each treatment is σ²patch; it is why the red intervals are so wide.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text: Part 7 · Wrap-Up

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
The lmer Formula Cheat-Sheet


Read every random term as ( what varies | across what ).








Formula
Meaning




y ~ x + (1|g)
random intercept per group


y ~ x + (1 + x|g)
random intercept and slope


y ~ x + (0 + x|g)
random slope only, shared intercept


y ~ x + (1|a) + (1|b)
two crossed random factors


y ~ x + (1|a/b)
b nested in a — shorthand for (1|a) + (1|a:b)










Important



⚠️ The confusion to avoid
(1|patch) and (1|treat:patch) are both random-intercept models. The 1 is the intercept; what differs is only the grouping.









Tip



🖐 Do I need a/b here?
Only if the inner IDs restart inside each outer level (patch 1,2,3,4 in every treatment). Then R cannot tell nesting from crossing and you must write (1|treat/patch).
Our patches are numbered 1–16 across the whole study, so (1|patch) already says it.








Warning



⚠️ “boundary (singular) fit”
A variance was estimated as exactly 0 — the likelihood hit the edge of what a variance is allowed to be. It is the REML version of the moment estimator going negative (Part 4).
Simplify the random effects; do not ignore it.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Wrap-up


Today you:

Decided fixed vs random by asking whether you care about these levels or about how much they vary
Learned a random factor costs one parameter where a fixed one costs k − 1
Read (1|group) correctly, and saw it is not a random slope
Chose between the F-test (p = 0.091) and the Wald χ² (p = 0.043) — and learned why the F-test is right at 16 groups
Saw where the variance components come from: a search over a restricted likelihood, not a partition of sums of squares
Got ICC = 0.50, and saw partial pooling shrink each patch estimate toward its treatment mean








Important



✅ The one idea to keep
A mixed model does not “remove” the patch effect — it estimates it, and tests the treatment against the right amount of noise.
The old way partitioned variation that was already computed. The new way proposes variances and keeps the ones that make the data most likely. On a balanced design they agree exactly; everywhere else only the second still works.








Note



📖 Up next
glmer() — a non-normal response and a random effect. You now have both halves.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Before Next Class


Take the pine needle data, collapsed to one value per team per side (the two-stage summary from Week 3):
p_df <- pine_df |>
  group_by(team, side) |>
  summarise(needle_length_mm = mean(needle_length_mm),
            .groups = "drop")

anova(lmer(needle_length_mm ~ side + (1|team), data = p_df))
Compare F to the square of the paired-t statistic from Week 4 (t = −2.72). You should get F = 7.41, df 1 and 3, p = 0.072 — the paired t-test is this mixed model.







Tip



🚀 If you finish early
Run the same formula on the raw 64 needles instead. You get p = 0.057 and 59 denominator df, not 3.
What changed? Check VarCorr() — one variance is estimated as exactly zero and R warns “singular fit”.
You now know what that means: the likelihood walked to the edge of the parameter space, exactly as the moment estimator would have gone negative.

title: Lecture: Linear Mixed Models
text:
Readings



Gotelli & Ellison, Ch. 10 — The Analysis of Variance, for the random-effects and variance-component material this lecture rebuilds.
Quinn & Keough (2002), Experimental Design and Data Analysis for Biologists, Ch. 9 §9.1 — nested designs and expected mean squares. This is the source of today’s worked example.
Zuur, A. F., Ieno, E. N., Walker, N. J., Saveliev, A. A., & Smith, G. M. (2009). Mixed Effects Models and Extensions in Ecology with R. Springer. Ch. 5 is the standard ecological treatment of REML.
Bates, D., Mächler, M., Bolker, B., & Walker, S. (2015). Fitting linear mixed-effects models using lme4. Journal of Statistical Software, 67(1), 1–48.








Note



📖 On the dataset
The sea urchin grazing data are Andrew & Underwood’s, as analysed in Quinn & Keough Ch. 9 — the same file as week 9. The textbook PDFs are on Canvas.








Tip



🖐 Why no Whitlock & Schluter
W&S does not cover mixed models or random effects. For this topic, Gotelli, Quinn & Keough, and Zuur are the references.

One continuous predictor, one continuous response

A simple regression has one predictor and one partition of variance. Today we add more predictors.
The logic barely changes. The bookkeeping does — and so does what each slope means.

section: The Study · Birds in Fragmented Forest
text:
The Study · Birds in Fragmented Forest


Loyn (1987) surveyed 56 remnant forest patches in Victoria, Australia, and counted the birds in each one. For every patch he also recorded six things that might explain the count.
Small patches, isolated patches, recently cut-off patches and heavily grazed patches are all candidates — and they are not independent of each other.





Column
What it is




abundance
birds per patch (the response)


area_ha
patch area


dist_m
distance to nearest patch


dist_larger_m
distance to nearest larger patch


year_isolated
year the patch was cut off


grazing
grazing intensity, 1–5


altitude_m
elevation

Reading the Data In



bird_df <- read_csv("data/loyn_birds.csv") %>%
  mutate(log_area        = log10(area_ha),
         log_dist        = log10(dist_m),

grazing_class
The same grazing intensity as a word rather than a number. Part 7 is about what changes when you use it.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: When Do We Need More Than One Predictor?
text:
When Do We Need More Than One Predictor?


Bird abundance in a patch plausibly depends on all six of those predictors at once, and they are not independent of each other — small patches tend to be grazed harder, and isolated patches tend to be older.
Fitting one predictor at a time cannot answer “does area matter once grazing is accounted for.”

Predictors all continuous → multiple regression
A mix of continuous and categorical → still multiple regression, with dummy variables






Continuous X
Categorical X




Continuous Y
Regression
ANOVA


Categorical Y
Logistic regression
Contingency tables

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
One Predictor at a Time


Start the way you would have last week — fit each predictor on its own.


# A tibble: 6 × 3
  predictor         slope        p
  <chr>             <dbl>    <dbl>
1 log_area         9.78   7.18e-11
2 log_dist         3.29   3.52e- 1
3 log_dist_larger  2.21   3.86e- 1
4 year_isolated    0.211  7.68e- 5
5 grazing         -4.98   6.90e- 9
6 altitude_m       0.0952 3.32e- 3



Four of the six are significant on their own, two of them overwhelmingly.
Grazing has the most quotable effect: every extra step of grazing intensity costs about 5 birds, at p = 6.90e-09. Area is the better-supported one — smaller p, more variance explained.






Warning


⚠️ Hold that thought
Every one of these fits ignores the other five predictors entirely.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · Which Predictors Will Survive?


We are about to put all six predictors into one model together.
What do you expect to happen?
(a) All four significant predictors stay significant — they were each real
(b) Roughly the same four stay, but with smaller slopes
(c) Only one or two survive, and at least one strong predictor becomes non-significant
(d) Nothing survives — with six predictors and 56 patches there is not enough data






Warning


✍️ Write your letter down, then vote.










Note


The question to ask
How much of what grazing “explains” on its own is really being explained by patch area?
Small patches are grazed harder. Look back at the table — is grazing telling you something area was not already telling you?

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
From a Line to a (Hyper)plane


With one predictor we fit a line through a scatterplot.
With two, we fit a plane through a cloud — here, bird abundance over log patch area and grazing intensity.
With three or more it is a hyperplane, which you cannot draw but can still fit.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 2 · The Multiple Regression Model

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
The Multiple Regression Model


For i = 1 to n observations and p predictors:
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \dots + \beta_p x_{ip} + \epsilon_i\]

\(y_i\) — the response for observation i
\(\beta_0\) — the intercept, the mean of Y when every predictor is 0
\(\beta_1 \dots \beta_p\) — the partial regression slopes
\(\epsilon_i\) — the error, estimated by the residual \(y_i - \hat{y}_i\)








Note


✅ Key idea — what “partial” means
A partial slope is the change in Y per one-unit change in that predictor while every other predictor is held constant.
It is a conditional statement. Change what else is in the model and you have changed the condition — so the number is allowed to change too.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: The Full Model · The Answer to the Vote
text:
The Full Model · The Answer to the Vote



full_model <- lm(abundance ~ log_area + log_dist +
                   log_dist_larger + year_isolated +
                   grazing + altitude_m,
                 data = bird_df)

summary(full_model)


Call:
lm(formula = abundance ~ log_area + log_dist + log_dist_larger + 
    year_isolated + grazing + altitude_m, data = bird_df)

Residuals:

-15.6506  -2.9390   0.5289   2.5353  15.2842 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)     -125.69725   91.69228  -1.371   0.1767    
log_area           7.47023    1.46489   5.099 5.49e-06 ***
log_dist          -0.90696    2.67572  -0.339   0.7361    
log_dist_larger   -0.64842    2.12270  -0.305   0.7613    
year_isolated      0.07387    0.04520   1.634   0.1086

Important


✅ The answer is (c).
Four predictors were significant alone. In the model together, only log_area survives (p < 0.001).
Grazing has gone from a slope of -4.98 (p = 6.90e-09) to -1.67 (p = 0.0791) — most of what grazing appeared to explain was patch area wearing a different hat.
Year of isolation and altitude have gone the same way.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Why Not Just Regress Y on Each X Separately?
text:
Why Not Just Regress Y on Each X Separately?


Each simple regression asks “does this predictor track abundance?” The multiple regression asks “does it track abundance among patches that are otherwise alike?”
Those are different questions, and they can have different answers.









Predictor
Alone
In the full model




log area
9.78
7.47


grazing
-4.98
-1.67


year isolated
0.211
0.074


altitude
0.095
0.02











Warning


⚠️ Neither number is “wrong”
If you want to predict bird abundance from grazing alone, -4.98 is the right slope to use.
If you want to claim grazing has an effect beyond the fact that grazed patches are small, -1.67 is the number you have to defend — and here you cannot.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Estimation and Prediction


Estimation. Ordinary least squares again: choose the coefficients that minimise \(\sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\). With several predictors this is a set of simultaneous equations solved with matrix algebra — lm() does it instantly, and what matters is knowing what it minimises.
Prediction. Substitute new values for every predictor.

More observations → narrower intervals
More predictors → wider intervals
Stay inside the range of every predictor








Warning


⚠️ Extrapolation is worse here
In simple regression you only have to stay inside one range. Here you have to stay inside the data cloud — and a combination can be far outside it even when each predictor separately looks ordinary.
There are no 1000-ha patches under intense grazing in these data. The model will still happily predict one.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 3 · ANOVA for Multiple Regression

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Partitioning Variance — Sums of Squares


Exactly the partition from last week, with p predictors instead of one:
\[SS_{total} = SS_{regression} + SS_{residual}\]

\(SS_{regression}\) — variation the model explains
\(SS_{residual}\) — variation it does not
Regression df is now p, not 1






Source
SS
df
MS




Regression
\(\sum (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2\)
\(p\)
SS/df


Residual
\(\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\)
\(n-p-1\)
SS/df


Total
\(\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2\)
\(n-1\)






Mean squares are variance estimators, so they do not grow with n
which is why the F-ratio is built from Mean Squares and NOT from the Sums of Squares directly.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Hypotheses — the “Basic” Test


The overall F-test at the bottom of summary() tests one null:
\[H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \dots = \beta_p = 0\]

If it is true, \(MS_{regression}\) and \(MS_{residual}\) estimate the same variance and F ≈ 1
If any β is non-zero, \(MS_{regression}\) is inflated and F > 1

It tells you the model as a whole explains something. It does not tell you which predictor did the work.







Warning


⚠️ A significant overall F with nothing significant inside it
This happens, and it is the classic signature of collinearity: the predictors jointly explain a lot, but they are so tangled that no individual slope can be pinned down.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Hypotheses — Testing One Predictor


To ask whether one specific β is zero, fit the model with and without it and compare:
\[SS_{extra} = SS_{regression}^{full} - SS_{regression}^{reduced}\]
\[F_{q,\,n-p-1} = \frac{SS_{extra}/q}{MS_{residual}^{full}}\]
where q is how many predictors you dropped — q = 1 for a single predictor, q = 4 below.

reduced_model <- lm(abundance ~ log_area + grazing,
                    data = bird_df)

anova(reduced_model, full_model)

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: abundance ~ log_area + grazing
Model 2: abundance ~ log_area + log_dist + log_dist_larger + year_isolated + 
    grazing + altitude_m
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq     F Pr(>F)
1     53 2200.9                          
2     49 1996.8  4    204.09 1.252 0.3015



Dropping four predictors at once — distance, distance to a larger patch, year of isolation and altitude — costs nothing detectable (p = 0.302).






Tip


🖐 You rarely run this by hand
The t-test beside each coefficient in summary() answers the same question for a single predictor. Use anova() when you want to drop a group of predictors at once.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Explained Variance


\[R^2 = \frac{SS_{regression}}{SS_{total}} = 1 - \frac{SS_{residual}}{SS_{total}}\]
For the reduced model: \(\dfrac{4137}{6338}\) = 0.653
The six-predictor model manages 0.685 — higher, as it must be.







Warning


⚠️ Watch out

R² always rises when you add a predictor, even a useless one
So R² cannot be used to compare models with different numbers of predictors
R² from models with differently transformed Y are not comparable at all




That is why adjusted R² and AIC exist, and we come back to them in Part 8.

text: Part 4 · Assumptions and Diagnostics

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: First: Does a Predictor Need a Transform?
text:
First: Does a Predictor Need a Transform?


Patch area runs from 0.1 ha to 1,771 ha — four orders of magnitude. Fitted raw, it behaves exactly like last week’s homework:










raw area_ha
log10(area_ha)




slope

9.78

0.014

Every model in this lecture uses log_area, and the diagnostics are why.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Assumptions and Diagnostics — Outliers



Fixed X values — unrealistic in field data, but the working assumption
No overly influential points — check leverage and influence with Cook’s distance
A point can be extreme in Y, extreme in X, or extreme in the combination; only the third kind is uniquely a multiple-regression problem

Largest Cook’s distance here is 0.2 — nothing near the usual threshold of 1.


plot(reduced_model, which = 4)

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Assumptions and Diagnostics — Residuals


Normality, equal variance and independence — all read off the residuals, exactly as last week.

shapiro.test(residuals(reduced_model))


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  residuals(reduced_model)
W = 0.98422, p-value = 0.6728


Distribution and variance problems are usually fixed by transforming Y, or a predictor, before anything more exotic.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Assumptions — Sample Size and Added-Variable Plots
text:
Assumptions — Sample Size and Added-Variable Plots



More observations than predictors — a common rule of thumb is 10 observations per predictor. Six predictors would want 60; we have 56, so the full model is already at the edge
Predictors not collinear — Part 5
Each X linear in Y after accounting for the others — this is what an added-variable plot shows, and it is the multiple-regression version of “plot your data first”

avPlots(reduced_model)










Each panel is Y and one X after the other predictor’s effect has been removed from both.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 5 · Collinearity

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Collinearity — the Problem


Predictors in field data are almost never independent. Here, small patches are grazed harder — r = -0.56.
When predictors overlap:

Parameter estimates become unstable — one changed value can move them a lot
Standard errors inflate, so slopes lose significance
The model can fit well while no single slope is trustworthy




                log_area log_dist log_dist_larger year_isolated grazing
log_area            1.00     0.30            0.38          0.28   -0.56
log_dist            0.30     1.00            0.60         -0.02   -0.14
log_dist_larger     0.38     0.60            1.00         -0.16   -0.03
year_isolated       0.28    -0.02           -0.16          1.00   -0.64
grazing            -0.56    -0.14           -0.03         -0.64    1.00
altitude_m          0.28    -0.22           -0.27          0.23   -0.41
                altitude_m
log_area              0.28
log_dist             -0.22
log_dist_larger      -0.27
year_isolated         0.23
grazing              -0.41
altitude_m            1.00

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Collinearity — Detecting It


Variance Inflation Factors:
\[VIF_{X_j} = \frac{1}{1 - R^2_j}\]
where \(R^2_j\) comes from regressing \(X_j\) on all the other predictors — not from a pairwise correlation. (With two predictors they coincide; with more they do not.)

Rule of thumb: VIF > 10 is bad; some authors use > 5
Simplest fix: drop predictors that are measuring the same thing



vif(full_model)

       log_area        log_dist log_dist_larger   year_isolated         grazing 
       1.911514        1.654553        2.009749        1.804769        2.524814 
     altitude_m 
       1.467937 








Note


✅ Key idea
A high VIF does not mean the model is wrong. It means you cannot trust the individual partial slopes, even when the model as a whole fits well.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · The Slope That Changed Its Mind
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · The Slope That Changed Its Mind


Grazing went from -4.98 on its own to -1.67 in the full model, and lost its significance. The VIFs are all under 3.
What is the right thing to say about grazing?
(a) Grazing has no effect on bird abundance
(b) The effect of grazing is real but small — the full model estimates it better
(c) Grazing and patch area explain overlapping variation, and these data cannot cleanly separate them
(d) The full model is broken by collinearity and should be discarded






Warning


✍️ One letter. Write it down, then argue it with your neighbour.










Note


The question to ask
Is this a statement about the world, or a statement about what this dataset can resolve?

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: What the Data Can and Cannot Separate
text:
What the Data Can and Cannot Separate








Important


✅ The answer is (c).
Grazing and area are correlated at r = -0.56. The heavily grazed patches in this dataset are also the small ones, so no analysis can tell you which of the two is doing the work.
(a) overstates it — a non-significant partial slope is not evidence of no effect. (b) is the common mistake: the full model is not “better”, it answers a different, conditional question. (d) is wrong too — VIFs under 3 are mild, and the model predicts perfectly well. It just cannot apportion credit.










Tip


🖐 What would settle it
Find, or create, patches that break the correlation: large heavily grazed patches and small lightly grazed ones.
That is a design problem, not an analysis problem — which is where this course started.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 6 · Interactions

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Interactions — Additive vs. Multiplicative


So far every model has been additive — the effect of area is the same at every grazing level.
An interaction says the effect of one predictor depends on the level of another:
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_{1} + \beta_2X_{2} + \epsilon_i\] \[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_{1} + \beta_2X_{2} + \beta_3X_{1}X_{2} + \epsilon_i\]
An interaction term is just another predictor: the product of two others, with its own coefficient.







Note


✅ Key idea
Additive: parallel lines.
Interactive: lines with different slopes — the fitted surface is no longer flat.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Interactions — Fitting One



interaction_model <- lm(abundance ~ log_area * grazing,
                        data = bird_df)

summary(interaction_model)$coefficients

                  Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)      26.558079  3.3576293  7.909771 1.768256e-10
log_area          2.112005  2.0375755  1.036528 3.047520e-01
grazing          -4.547139  0.8850592 -5.137667 4.246998e-06
log_area:grazing  2.142303  0.7358161  2.911465 5.287173e-03



The interaction is significant (p = 0.00529), and a * b expands to a + b + a:b automatically.
What it means: patch area matters more where grazing is heavy. In lightly grazed country a small patch still holds birds; under heavy grazing only the big patches do.






Warning


⚠️ You cannot read the main effects the same way any more
With an interaction in the model, the log_area coefficient is the slope when grazing = 0 — a value that does not exist in these data.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Interactions — the Cost



Parameter proliferation. Every predictor you add roughly doubles the number of possible terms — six predictors with all interactions is 64 terms, and you have 56 patches
Interpretation gets harder, as the slide before shows
Include an interaction when it makes biological sense, not because it might be significant

“Does fragmentation hurt more where grazing is heavy” is a real hypothesis. That is why this one belongs.







Warning


⚠️ Watch out
Test enough interactions and one will reach p < 0.05 by chance. With six predictors there are 15 two-way interactions alone — at α = 0.05 you expect roughly one false positive just from testing them all.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 7 · Factors and Dummy Variables

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Categorical Predictors Become Dummy Variables


So far grazing has been a number, 1 to 5, which forces every step to have the same effect. That is a strong assumption — is the jump from light to moderate really the same size as moderate to heavy?
Treat it as a category instead and the model estimates each level separately. A categorical predictor with k levels becomes k − 1 dummy variables, each 0 or 1.
One level gets no dummy at all. That is the reference level, and every other coefficient is a comparison against it.


count(bird_df, grazing, grazing_class)

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  grazing grazing_class     n
    <dbl> <chr>         <int>
1       1 minimal          13
2       2 light             8
3       3 moderate         15
4       4 heavy             7
5       5 intense          13

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: R Picks the Reference Level for You — Alphabetically
text:
R Picks the Reference Level for You — Alphabetically



bird_df <- bird_df %>%
  mutate(grazing_class = factor(grazing_class))

levels(bird_df$grazing_class)

[1] "heavy"    "intense"  "light"    "minimal"  "moderate"


A character column becomes a factor in alphabetical order, so the reference level here is heavy — the fourth of five grazing intensities, chosen by spelling.



                      Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)              14.12       2.49    5.68     0.00
log_area                  7.25       1.26    5.77     0.00
grazing_classintense    -10.30       2.84   -3.62     0.00
grazing_classlight        1.97       3.05    0.65     0.52
grazing_classminimal      1.59       2.98    0.53     0.60
grazing_classmoderate     1.40       2.70    0.52     0.61


Every grazing coefficient is now “compared with heavy grazing,” which is a comparison nobody asked for.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: What lm() Actually Fits · the Dummy Columns
text:
What lm() Actually Fits · the Dummy Columns


factor() did not put any zeros and ones in your data — the column still reads minimal, light, heavy. The 0/1s get built when the model is fit, by model.matrix():

dummies <- model.matrix(~ grazing_class, data = bird_df)
colnames(dummies) <- str_remove(colnames(dummies), "grazing_class")

one_each <- match(levels(bird_df$grazing_class), bird_df$grazing_class)
cbind(class = levels(bird_df$grazing_class), as.data.frame(dummies[one_each, ]))

      class (Intercept) intense light minimal moderate
9     heavy           1       0     0       0        0
2   intense           1       1     0       0        0
1     light           1       0     1       0        0
14  minimal           1       0     0       1        0
4  moderate           1       0     0       0        1


One site per class. That matrix is what least squares actually solves — lm() never sees the word “heavy.”

Each dummy is a yes/no switch: is this site light? A site belongs to exactly one class, so exactly one switch is on per row — or none at all.
Look at the heavy row: all four switches are 0, and only the intercept column of 1s is left. heavy is not missing from the model — it is the row where nothing is switched on. The reference level is the intercept, which is why 5 levels need only 4 dummies.






Warning


⚠️ Why not a fifth dummy
Five switches would sum to 1 in every single row — exactly the intercept column. The model could not tell them apart, and R would print NA: the same perfect aliasing as the deer-mouse brothers.
Dropping a level is not a choice. It is arithmetic.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · Which Level Should Be the Reference?
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · Which Level Should Be the Reference?


The five grazing classes are minimal, light, moderate, heavy, intense.
Which should be the reference level, and why?
(a) heavy — leave R’s default alone; the choice does not affect the model
(b) intense — the most extreme level makes the biggest contrasts
(c) minimal — the least-disturbed level, so every coefficient reads as the cost of adding grazing
(d) It does not matter, because R² and the F-test are identical either way






Warning


✍️ Careful — two of these are true statements. Only one is the right decision.










Note


The question to ask
Which comparison do I want to read straight off the output?

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Making the Control the Reference · fct_relevel()
text:
Making the Control the Reference · fct_relevel()








Important


✅ The answer is (c).

is true — the fit, R², F and the ANOVA table are identical whichever level is the reference. But that is not a reason to accept a bad default: the coefficients are what people read, and they should answer the question you asked.

minimal grazing is the closest thing this observational study has to a control.



Name the control. That is the whole call.

bird_df <- bird_df %>%
  mutate(grazing_class =
           fct_relevel(grazing_class, "minimal"))

levels(bird_df$grazing_class)

[1] "minimal"  "heavy"    "intense"  "light"    "moderate"



fct_relevel() moves the levels you name to the front and leaves the rest where they were. Name one level and it becomes level 1 — the reference.
minimal is now first. The other four are still in alphabetical order behind it, and that is fine: only the first level decides the reference.






Tip


🖐 The habit to build
One line, every time a factor enters a model:
fct_relevel(treatment, "control")
Not factor() and hope. Not relevel-it-later. Set it where you make the factor.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Naming All Five · Reference and Display Order
text:
Naming All Five · Reference and Display Order


Naming one level fixed the reference. Name all five and you also fix the order they print and plot in — light → intense, the way the gradient actually runs.

bird_df <- bird_df %>%
  mutate(grazing_class = fct_relevel(
    grazing_class,
    "minimal", "light", "moderate", "heavy", "intense"))

levels(bird_df$grazing_class)

[1] "minimal"  "light"    "moderate" "heavy"    "intense" 









Note


✅ Both versions fit the same model
Same reference, so same R², same F, same fitted values — only the order of the coefficient rows changes.
The reason to name all five anyway: that order becomes your legend order in every figure you draw from this column.



The activity ends by checking exactly this — if the legend runs minimal → intense instead of alphabetically, the relevel worked.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Same Model, Same F, a Readable Story
text:
Same Model, Same F, a Readable Story



grazing_model <- lm(abundance ~ log_area + grazing_class,
                    data = bird_df)

summary(grazing_model)$coefficients %>% round(2)

                      Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)              15.72       2.77    5.68     0.00
log_area                  7.25       1.26    5.77     0.00
grazing_classlight        0.38       2.91    0.13     0.90
grazing_classmoderate    -0.19       2.55   -0.07     0.94
grazing_classheavy       -1.59       2.98   -0.53     0.60
grazing_classintense    -11.89       2.93   -4.06     0.00



Now every coefficient is a comparison with minimal grazing, and the pattern is obvious:

light, moderate and heavy are all indistinguishable from minimal
intense costs about 11.9 birds, p < 0.001

Grazing is a threshold, not a gradient — and fitting it as the number 1–5 hid that completely, averaging the effect into -2.85 birds per step.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Adding the Coefficients Up


A factor coefficient is a piece of an equation, not a mean on its own. To get a group’s prediction, start at the intercept and add the one switch that is on:
\[\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1(\text{log\_area}) + b_L L + b_M M + b_H H + b_I I\]
Hold area at its average and add them up — the c(0, ...) is the reference level, minimal’s dummy:

b  <- coef(grazing_model)
la <- mean(bird_df$log_area)

group_fit <- b[1] + b[2] * la + c(0, b[3:6])
names(group_fit) <- levels(bird_df$grazing_class)
round(group_fit, 1)

 minimal    light moderate    heavy  intense 
    22.5     22.9     22.3     20.9     10.6 


minimal is 15.72 + 7.25(0.93) = 22.5 birds; intense is that same number 11.89 lower. Every class is the reference prediction plus its own contrast.







Important


✅ This is where ANOVA starts
Drop the continuous predictor and the \(b_1\) term disappears. Then

intercept = the reference group’s mean
intercept + contrast = any other group’s mean

One-way ANOVA is this slide with no log_area column — same dummy coding, same addition.









Note


🧭 Adjusted, not raw
Raw minimal is 28.6 birds, not 22.5 — ungrazed patches are also the big ones, and holding area constant takes that credit back. That gap is ANCOVA.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Why This Matters Even More in ANOVA
text:
Why This Matters Even More in ANOVA


With only continuous predictors there is no reference level at all — every slope is “per unit of X” and nothing is being compared with anything.
The moment a factor enters the model, every coefficient becomes a contrast against the reference, and that is the whole structure of the next five weeks:

One-way ANOVA — treatment means against a control
Two-way ANOVA — main effects read at the other factor’s reference level
ANCOVA — separate intercepts, all relative to one group








Important


✅ The rule to carry forward
factor() gives you alphabetical order. Alphabetical order is almost never the order your experiment was designed in.
Set the control as the first level, every time, and your model output reads as “what each treatment did to the control” without any further work.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 8 · Comparing Models

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Comparing Models — the Problem



Which predictors should be in the model?
Occam’s razor: the best model balances fit against complexity
Overfitting: a high R² bought with useless predictors — which is why R² alone cannot choose between models

anova() needs the models to be nested — one model’s predictors a subset of the other’s. AIC does not, which is why it can rank “area only” against “grazing only”; it only needs the same response and the same rows.







Note


📖 Reference
Quinn & Keough, Ch. 6, works through exactly this dataset. Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 17, covers model comparison for regression.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Comparing Models — Penalizing Complexity


Two ways to charge a model for its predictors:
\[\text{Adjusted } R^2 = 1 - \frac{SS_{Residual}/(n - p - 1)}{SS_{Total}/(n - 1)}\]
\[\text{AIC} = n\ln(SS_{Residual}) + 2(p + 1) - n\ln(n)\]

Higher adjusted R² is better
Lower AIC is better
AIC is comparative only — the number on its own means nothing, and models must be fitted to the same rows
This is Quinn & Keough’s form; AIC() in R adds a constant, so the printed values differ from the formula while every ΔAIC is identical








Warning


⚠️ The NA trap
If one predictor has missing values, lm() silently drops those rows. Two models fitted to different numbers of rows cannot be compared by AIC, and R will not warn you.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Comparing Models — How to Search



Fit all possible models and compare — fine with a few predictors, hopeless with many
Automated stepwise selection adds or removes terms by partial F or AIC
We use manual backward selection: start full, drop what earns nothing, stop when dropping hurts








Warning


⚠️ Stepwise selection is controversial
It inflates R², biases p-values, and knows nothing about biology. A small set of models you can justify beats an automated search over all of them.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Comparing Models — Putting It Together



model_comparison <- tibble(
  model = c("all six predictors",
            "log_area + grazing",
            "log_area only",
            "grazing only"),
  adj_r2 = c(summary(full_model)$adj.r.squared,
             summary(reduced_model)$adj.r.squared,
             summary(lm(abundance ~ log_area, bird_df))$adj.r.squared,
             summary(lm(abundance ~ grazing, bird_df))$adj.r.squared),
  AIC = c(AIC(full_model),
          AIC(reduced_model),
          AIC(lm(abundance ~ log_area, bird_df)),
          AIC(lm(abundance ~ grazing, bird_df)))
) %>%
  mutate(delta_AIC = AIC - min(AIC)) %>%
  arrange(AIC)

model_comparison

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  model              adj_r2   AIC delta_AIC
  <chr>               <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 log_area + grazing  0.640  373.      0   
2 all six predictors  0.646  375.      2.55
3 log_area only       0.539  385.     12.8 
4 grazing only        0.456  395.     22.1 









Important


✅ The two-predictor model wins
It has the lowest AIC and essentially the same adjusted R² as the full model — with four fewer predictors.
A ΔAIC above about 2 is usually treated as a real difference, so the full model’s extra terms are not paying for themselves.



The anova() test in Part 3 said the same thing. Two routes, one answer.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 9 · Relative Importance of Predictors

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
How Important Is Each Predictor?


Three standard approaches, and they answer slightly different questions:

F- or t-tests on the partial slopes
Coefficient of partial determination — the variance a predictor adds
Standardized partial slopes — every predictor in SD units

None of them is “the” right answer.







Warning


⚠️ Why the raw slopes cannot be compared
log_area has a slope of 6.89 and grazing -2.85.
One is “birds per tenfold increase in area,” the other is “birds per step of grazing intensity.” Comparing those two numbers is comparing metres with kilograms.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Approaches 1 and 2 — Partial F and Partial R²
text:
Approaches 1 and 2 — Partial F and Partial R²



Anova(reduced_model, type = "II")

Anova Table (Type II tests)

Response: abundance
          Sum Sq Df F value    Pr(>F)    
log_area  1184.6  1  28.527 1.977e-06 ***
grazing    666.0  1  16.038 0.0001946 ***
Residuals 2200.9 53                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Partial η² = \(\dfrac{SS_{predictor}}{SS_{predictor} + SS_{residual}}\) — variance explained after controlling for the other predictor.











log_area
grazing




partial η²
0.35
0.232


ΔR²
0.187
0.105




ΔR² is what the model’s R² would lose if you dropped that predictor — its unique contribution.
Both say area is the stronger of the two.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Approach 3 — Standardized Partial Slopes


Rescale every variable to mean 0 and SD 1, and the slopes become directly comparable: “SDs of Y per SD of X.”

bird_z <- bird_df %>%
  mutate(across(c(abundance, log_area, grazing),
                ~ as.numeric(scale(.))))

lm(abundance ~ log_area + grazing, data = bird_z) %>%
  coef() %>% round(3)

(Intercept)    log_area     grazing 
      0.000       0.521      -0.391 



log_area 0.52 versus grazing -0.39 — area is about 1.3× the influence of grazing per standard deviation.






Note


✅ All three agree here
Partial F, partial R² and standardized slopes all rank area above grazing. When they disagree, that is worth reporting — it usually means the predictors are tangled.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Partial η² and ΔR² — What to Keep, What to Toss
text:
Partial η² and ΔR² — What to Keep, What to Toss


Run both on the full model and every predictor is ranked at once.

anova_full  <- Anova(full_model, type = "II")
ss_res_full <- sum(residuals(full_model)^2)

tibble(predictor = rownames(anova_full),
       SS        = anova_full[, "Sum Sq"]) %>%
  filter(predictor != "Residuals") %>%
  mutate(pEta2 = SS / (SS + ss_res_full),
         dR2   = SS / ss_tot) %>%
  arrange(desc(pEta2))

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  predictor            SS   pEta2      dR2
  <chr>             <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>
1 log_area        1060.   0.347   0.167   
2 grazing          131.   0.0616  0.0207  
3 year_isolated    109.   0.0517  0.0172  
4 altitude_m        27.0  0.0133  0.00426 
5 log_dist           4.68 0.00234 0.000739
6 log_dist_larger    3.80 0.00190 0.000600



log_area carries pη² = 0.35 — 5.6× the next predictor.
The two distance predictors sit at 0.002. That is nothing.






Note


✅ Two columns, two questions
pη² ranks the predictors. ΔR² says what each one uniquely buys — what R² would lose if you dropped it.



A fourth route to the same answer the vote, the t-tests and AIC already gave you.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: The Trap in the ΔR² Column
text:
The Trap in the ΔR² Column


Add up the ΔR² column: 0.211.
The model’s R² is 0.685.
So where did the other 0.47 of explained variance go?
It is real, and it is shared. ΔR² only counts the variance a predictor explains that nothing else can. Variance that two collinear predictors could each account for belongs to neither of them, so it appears in R² and in no row of this table.







Important


⚠️ Do not toss on pη² alone
A predictor can have a tiny pη² for two completely different reasons:

It genuinely does nothing — toss it
It is tangled with a predictor already in the model — vif() from Part 5 is how you tell the difference

Drop it for reason 2 and you have not learned it has no effect — only that these data cannot separate it from its partner.









Note


✅ How to use these
pη² to rank, ΔR² to see what each predictor uniquely buys you, vif() to decide whether a small value means “useless” or “redundant.”

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Wrap-up
Today you:

Extended the regression line to a plane, and fitted 56 forest patches against six predictors at once
Watched four predictors that were significant alone collapse to one in the model together
Read a partial slope as a conditional statement, and saw that neither it nor the simple slope is “wrong”
Tested groups of predictors with anova(reduced, full) and single ones with the t-tests in summary()
Diagnosed collinearity with vif(), and learned to say “these data cannot separate them” instead of “it has no effect”
Fitted a real interaction — fragmentation costs more where grazing is heavy
Turned a categorical predictor into dummy variables, and set the reference level on purpose with fct_relevel()
Compared models with adjusted R² and AIC, and ranked predictors by partial η², ΔR² and standardized slopes to decide what to keep

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: The Three Things to Carry Out of Here
text:
The Three Things to Carry Out of Here








Important


⚠️ R² always rises
Adding predictors can only increase plain R². Adjusted R² and AIC exist precisely because “explains more variance” is not the same as “is a better model.”









Note


✅ A partial slope is conditional
“What does area do among patches grazed the same amount?” Change what else is in the model and you have changed the question.










Important


✅ Set your reference level
factor() sorts alphabetically. Your control is almost never first alphabetically — use fct_relevel() and make the output say what you meant.
This is the habit that makes every ANOVA from Week 8 onward readable.









Note


Up next — Analysis of Variance
What happens when every predictor is categorical, and why ANOVA and regression are the same machinery in different clothes.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: The Study · Birds in Fragmented Forest
text:
The Study · Birds in Fragmented Forest


Loyn (1987) surveyed 56 remnant forest patches in Victoria, Australia, and counted the birds in each one. For every patch he also recorded six things that might explain the count.
Small patches, isolated patches, recently cut-off patches and heavily grazed patches are all candidates — and they are not independent of each other.





Column
What it is




abundance
birds per patch (the response)


area_ha
patch area


dist_m
distance to nearest patch


dist_larger_m
distance to nearest larger patch


year_isolated
year the patch was cut off


grazing
grazing intensity, 1–5


altitude_m
elevation

text:
Reading the Data In



bird_df <- read_csv("data/loyn_birds.csv") %>%
  mutate(log_area        = log10(area_ha),
         log_dist        = log10(dist_m),
         log_dist_larger = log10(dist_larger_m))

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: When Do We Need More Than One Predictor?
text:
When Do We Need More Than One Predictor?


Bird abundance in a patch plausibly depends on all six of those predictors at once, and they are not independent of each other — small patches tend to be grazed harder, and isolated patches tend to be older.
Fitting one predictor at a time cannot answer “does area matter once grazing is accounted for.”

Predictors all continuous → multiple regression
A mix of continuous and categorical → still multiple regression, with dummy variables






Continuous X
Categorical X




Continuous Y
Regression
ANOVA


Categorical Y
Logistic regression
Contingency tables

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
One Predictor at a Time


Start the way you would have last week — fit each predictor on its own.


# A tibble: 6 × 3
  predictor         slope        p
  <chr>             <dbl>    <dbl>
1 log_area         9.78   7.18e-11
2 log_dist         3.29   3.52e- 1
3 log_dist_larger  2.21   3.86e- 1
4 year_isolated    0.211  7.68e- 5
5 grazing         -4.98   6.90e- 9
6 altitude_m       0.0952 3.32e- 3



Four of the six are significant on their own, two of them overwhelmingly.
Grazing has the most quotable effect: every extra step of grazing intensity costs about 5 birds, at p = 6.90e-09. Area is the better-supported one — smaller p, more variance explained.






Warning



⚠️ Hold that thought
Every one of these fits ignores the other five predictors entirely.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · Which Predictors Will Survive?


We are about to put all six predictors into one model together.
What do you expect to happen?
(a) All four significant predictors stay significant — they were each real
(b) Roughly the same four stay, but with smaller slopes
(c) Only one or two survive, and at least one strong predictor becomes non-significant
(d) Nothing survives — with six predictors and 56 patches there is not enough data






Warning



✍️ Write your letter down, then vote.









Note



The question to ask
How much of what grazing “explains” on its own is really being explained by patch area?
Small patches are grazed harder. Look back at the table — is grazing telling you something area was not already telling you?

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
From a Line to a (Hyper)plane


With one predictor we fit a line through a scatterplot.
With two, we fit a plane through a cloud — here, bird abundance over log patch area and grazing intensity.
With three or more it is a hyperplane, which you cannot draw but can still fit.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 2 · The Multiple Regression Model

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
The Multiple Regression Model


For i = 1 to n observations and p predictors:
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \dots + \beta_p x_{ip} + \epsilon_i\]

\(y_i\) — the response for observation i
\(\beta_0\) — the intercept, the mean of Y when every predictor is 0
\(\beta_1 \dots \beta_p\) — the partial regression slopes
\(\epsilon_i\) — the error, estimated by the residual \(y_i - \hat{y}_i\)








Note



✅ Key idea — what “partial” means
A partial slope is the change in Y per one-unit change in that predictor while every other predictor is held constant.
It is a conditional statement. Change what else is in the model and you have changed the condition — so the number is allowed to change too.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: The Full Model · The Answer to the Vote
text:
The Full Model · The Answer to the Vote



full_model <- lm(abundance ~ log_area + log_dist +
                   log_dist_larger + year_isolated +
                   grazing + altitude_m,
                 data = bird_df)

summary(full_model)


Call:

    year_isolated + grazing + altitude_m, data = bird_df)

(Intercept)     -125.69725   91.69228  -1.371   0.1767    
log_area           7.47023    1.46489   5.099 5.49e-06 ***
log_dist          -0.90696    2.67572  -0.339   0.7361    
log_dist_larger   -0.64842    2.12270  -0.305   0.7613    
year_isolated      0.07387    0.04520   1.634   0.1086

Important

Four predictors were significant alone. In the model together, only log_area survives (p < 0.001).
Grazing has gone from a slope of -4.98 (p = 6.90e-09) to -1.67 (p = 0.0791) — most of what grazing appeared to explain was patch area wearing a different hat.
Year of isolation and altitude have gone the same way.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Why Not Just Regress Y on Each X Separately?
text:
Why Not Just Regress Y on Each X Separately?


Each simple regression asks “does this predictor track abundance?” The multiple regression asks “does it track abundance among patches that are otherwise alike?”
Those are different questions, and they can have different answers.









Predictor
Alone
In the full model




log area
9.78
7.47


grazing
-4.98
-1.67


year isolated
0.211
0.074


altitude
0.095
0.02











Warning



⚠️ Neither number is “wrong”
If you want to predict bird abundance from grazing alone, -4.98 is the right slope to use.
If you want to claim grazing has an effect beyond the fact that grazed patches are small, -1.67 is the number you have to defend — and here you cannot.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Estimation and Prediction


Estimation. Ordinary least squares again: choose the coefficients that minimise \(\sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\). With several predictors this is a set of simultaneous equations solved with matrix algebra — lm() does it instantly, and what matters is knowing what it minimises.
Prediction. Substitute new values for every predictor.

More observations → narrower intervals
More predictors → wider intervals
Stay inside the range of every predictor








Warning



⚠️ Extrapolation is worse here
In simple regression you only have to stay inside one range. Here you have to stay inside the data cloud — and a combination can be far outside it even when each predictor separately looks ordinary.
There are no 1000-ha patches under intense grazing in these data. The model will still happily predict one.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 3 · ANOVA for Multiple Regression

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Partitioning Variance — Sums of Squares


Exactly the partition from last week, with p predictors instead of one:
\[SS_{total} = SS_{regression} + SS_{residual}\]

\(SS_{regression}\) — variation the model explains
\(SS_{residual}\) — variation it does not
Regression df is now p, not 1






Source
SS
df
MS




Regression
\(\sum (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2\)
\(p\)
SS/df


Residual
\(\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\)
\(n-p-1\)
SS/df


Total
\(\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2\)
\(n-1\)






Mean squares are variance estimators, so they do not grow with n
which is why the F-ratio is built from Mean Squares and NOT from the Sums of Squares directly.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Hypotheses — the “Basic” Test


The overall F-test at the bottom of summary() tests one null:
\[H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \dots = \beta_p = 0\]

If it is true, \(MS_{regression}\) and \(MS_{residual}\) estimate the same variance and F ≈ 1
If any β is non-zero, \(MS_{regression}\) is inflated and F > 1

It tells you the model as a whole explains something. It does not tell you which predictor did the work.







Warning



⚠️ A significant overall F with nothing significant inside it
This happens, and it is the classic signature of collinearity: the predictors jointly explain a lot, but they are so tangled that no individual slope can be pinned down.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Hypotheses — Testing One Predictor


To ask whether one specific β is zero, fit the model with and without it and compare:
\[SS_{extra} = SS_{regression}^{full} - SS_{regression}^{reduced}\]
\[F_{q,\,n-p-1} = \frac{SS_{extra}/q}{MS_{residual}^{full}}\]
where q is how many predictors you dropped — q = 1 for a single predictor, q = 4 below.

reduced_model <- lm(abundance ~ log_area + grazing,
                    data = bird_df)

anova(reduced_model, full_model)

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: abundance ~ log_area + grazing
Model 2: abundance ~ log_area + log_dist + log_dist_larger + year_isolated + 
    grazing + altitude_m
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq     F Pr(>F)
1     53 2200.9                          
2     49 1996.8  4    204.09 1.252 0.3015



Dropping four predictors at once — distance, distance to a larger patch, year of isolation and altitude — costs nothing detectable (p = 0.302).






Tip



🖐 You rarely run this by hand
The t-test beside each coefficient in summary() answers the same question for a single predictor. Use anova() when you want to drop a group of predictors at once.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Explained Variance


\[R^2 = \frac{SS_{regression}}{SS_{total}} = 1 - \frac{SS_{residual}}{SS_{total}}\]
For the reduced model: \(\dfrac{4137}{6338}\) = 0.653
The six-predictor model manages 0.685 — higher, as it must be.







Warning



⚠️ Watch out

R² always rises when you add a predictor, even a useless one
So R² cannot be used to compare models with different numbers of predictors
R² from models with differently transformed Y are not comparable at all



That is why adjusted R² and AIC exist, and we come back to them in Part 8.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 4 · Assumptions and Diagnostics

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: First: Does a Predictor Need a Transform?
text:
First: Does a Predictor Need a Transform?


Patch area runs from 0.1 ha to 1,771 ha — four orders of magnitude. Fitted raw, it behaves exactly like last week’s homework:










raw area_ha
log10(area_ha)




slope
0.0103
9.78


R²
0.066
0.548


Shapiro on residuals
0.014
0.0831




Every model in this lecture uses log_area, and the diagnostics are why.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Assumptions and Diagnostics — Outliers



Fixed X values — unrealistic in field data, but the working assumption
No overly influential points — check leverage and influence with Cook’s distance
A point can be extreme in Y, extreme in X, or extreme in the combination; only the third kind is uniquely a multiple-regression problem

Largest Cook’s distance here is 0.2 — nothing near the usual threshold of 1.


plot(reduced_model, which = 4)

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Assumptions and Diagnostics — Residuals


Normality, equal variance and independence — all read off the residuals, exactly as last week.

shapiro.test(residuals(reduced_model))


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  residuals(reduced_model)
W = 0.98422, p-value = 0.6728


Distribution and variance problems are usually fixed by transforming Y, or a predictor, before anything more exotic.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Assumptions — Sample Size and Added-Variable Plots
text:
Assumptions — Sample Size and Added-Variable Plots



More observations than predictors — a common rule of thumb is 10 observations per predictor. Six predictors would want 60; we have 56, so the full model is already at the edge
Predictors not collinear — Part 5
Each X linear in Y after accounting for the others — this is what an added-variable plot shows, and it is the multiple-regression version of “plot your data first”

avPlots(reduced_model)










Each panel is Y and one X after the other predictor’s effect has been removed from both.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 5 · Collinearity

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Collinearity — the Problem


Predictors in field data are almost never independent. Here, small patches are grazed harder — r = -0.56.
When predictors overlap:

Parameter estimates become unstable — one changed value can move them a lot
Standard errors inflate, so slopes lose significance
The model can fit well while no single slope is trustworthy




                log_area log_dist log_dist_larger year_isolated grazing
log_area            1.00     0.30            0.38          0.28   -0.56
log_dist            0.30     1.00            0.60         -0.02   -0.14
log_dist_larger     0.38     0.60            1.00         -0.16   -0.03
year_isolated       0.28    -0.02           -0.16          1.00   -0.64
grazing            -0.56    -0.14           -0.03         -0.64    1.00
altitude_m          0.28    -0.22           -0.27          0.23   -0.41
                altitude_m
log_area              0.28
log_dist             -0.22
log_dist_larger      -0.27
year_isolated         0.23
grazing              -0.41
altitude_m            1.00

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Collinearity — Detecting It


Variance Inflation Factors:
\[VIF_{X_j} = \frac{1}{1 - R^2_j}\]
where \(R^2_j\) comes from regressing \(X_j\) on all the other predictors — not from a pairwise correlation. (With two predictors they coincide; with more they do not.)

Rule of thumb: VIF > 10 is bad; some authors use > 5
Simplest fix: drop predictors that are measuring the same thing



vif(full_model)

       log_area        log_dist log_dist_larger   year_isolated         grazing 
       1.911514        1.654553        2.009749        1.804769        2.524814 
     altitude_m 
       1.467937 








Note



✅ Key idea
A high VIF does not mean the model is wrong. It means you cannot trust the individual partial slopes, even when the model as a whole fits well.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · The Slope That Changed Its Mind
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · The Slope That Changed Its Mind


Grazing went from -4.98 on its own to -1.67 in the full model, and lost its significance. The VIFs are all under 3.
What is the right thing to say about grazing?
(a) Grazing has no effect on bird abundance
(b) The effect of grazing is real but small — the full model estimates it better
