(c) Grazing and patch area explain overlapping variation, and these data cannot cleanly separate them
(d) The full model is broken by collinearity and should be discarded






Warning



✍️ One letter. Write it down, then argue it with your neighbour.









Note



The question to ask
Is this a statement about the world, or a statement about what this dataset can resolve?

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: What the Data Can and Cannot Separate
text:
What the Data Can and Cannot Separate








Important



✅ The answer is (c).
Grazing and area are correlated at r = -0.56. The heavily grazed patches in this dataset are also the small ones, so no analysis can tell you which of the two is doing the work.
(a) overstates it — a non-significant partial slope is not evidence of no effect. (b) is the common mistake: the full model is not “better”, it answers a different, conditional question. (d) is wrong too — VIFs under 3 are mild, and the model predicts perfectly well. It just cannot apportion credit.









Tip



🖐 What would settle it
Find, or create, patches that break the correlation: large heavily grazed patches and small lightly grazed ones.
That is a design problem, not an analysis problem — which is where this course started.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 6 · Interactions

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Interactions — Additive vs. Multiplicative


So far every model has been additive — the effect of area is the same at every grazing level.
An interaction says the effect of one predictor depends on the level of another:
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_{1} + \beta_2X_{2} + \epsilon_i\] \[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_{1} + \beta_2X_{2} + \beta_3X_{1}X_{2} + \epsilon_i\]
An interaction term is just another predictor: the product of two others, with its own coefficient.







Note



✅ Key idea
Additive: parallel lines.
Interactive: lines with different slopes — the fitted surface is no longer flat.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Interactions — Fitting One



interaction_model <- lm(abundance ~ log_area * grazing,
                        data = bird_df)

summary(interaction_model)$coefficients

                  Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)      26.558079  3.3576293  7.909771 1.768256e-10
log_area          2.112005  2.0375755  1.036528 3.047520e-01
grazing          -4.547139  0.8850592 -5.137667 4.246998e-06
log_area:grazing  2.142303  0.7358161  2.911465 5.287173e-03



The interaction is significant (p = 0.00529), and a * b expands to a + b + a:b automatically.
What it means: patch area matters more where grazing is heavy. In lightly grazed country a small patch still holds birds; under heavy grazing only the big patches do.






Warning



⚠️ You cannot read the main effects the same way any more
With an interaction in the model, the log_area coefficient is the slope when grazing = 0 — a value that does not exist in these data.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Interactions — the Cost



Parameter proliferation. Every predictor you add roughly doubles the number of possible terms — six predictors with all interactions is 64 terms, and you have 56 patches
Interpretation gets harder, as the slide before shows
Include an interaction when it makes biological sense, not because it might be significant

“Does fragmentation hurt more where grazing is heavy” is a real hypothesis. That is why this one belongs.







Warning



⚠️ Watch out
Test enough interactions and one will reach p < 0.05 by chance. With six predictors there are 15 two-way interactions alone — at α = 0.05 you expect roughly one false positive just from testing them all.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 7 · Factors and Dummy Variables

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Categorical Predictors Become Dummy Variables


So far grazing has been a number, 1 to 5, which forces every step to have the same effect. That is a strong assumption — is the jump from light to moderate really the same size as moderate to heavy?
Treat it as a category instead and the model estimates each level separately. A categorical predictor with k levels becomes k − 1 dummy variables, each 0 or 1.
One level gets no dummy at all. That is the reference level, and every other coefficient is a comparison against it.


count(bird_df, grazing, grazing_class)

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  grazing grazing_class     n
    <dbl> <chr>         <int>
1       1 minimal          13
2       2 light             8
3       3 moderate         15
4       4 heavy             7
5       5 intense          13

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: R Picks the Reference Level for You — Alphabetically
text:
R Picks the Reference Level for You — Alphabetically



bird_df <- bird_df %>%
  mutate(grazing_class = factor(grazing_class))

levels(bird_df$grazing_class)

[1] "heavy"    "intense"  "light"    "minimal"  "moderate"


A character column becomes a factor in alphabetical order, so the reference level here is heavy — the fourth of five grazing intensities, chosen by spelling.



                      Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)              14.12       2.49    5.68     0.00
log_area                  7.25       1.26    5.77     0.00
grazing_classintense    -10.30       2.84   -3.62     0.00
grazing_classlight        1.97       3.05    0.65     0.52
grazing_classminimal      1.59       2.98    0.53     0.60
grazing_classmoderate     1.40       2.70    0.52     0.61


Every grazing coefficient is now “compared with heavy grazing,” which is a comparison nobody asked for.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: What lm() Actually Fits · the Dummy Columns
text:
What lm() Actually Fits · the Dummy Columns


factor() did not put any zeros and ones in your data — the column still reads minimal, light, heavy. The 0/1s get built when the model is fit, by model.matrix():

dummies <- model.matrix(~ grazing_class, data = bird_df)
colnames(dummies) <- str_remove(colnames(dummies), "grazing_class")

one_each <- match(levels(bird_df$grazing_class), bird_df$grazing_class)
cbind(class = levels(bird_df$grazing_class), as.data.frame(dummies[one_each, ]))

      class (Intercept) intense light minimal moderate
9     heavy           1       0     0       0        0
2   intense           1       1     0       0        0
1     light           1       0     1       0        0
14  minimal           1       0     0       1        0
4  moderate           1       0     0       0        1


One site per class. That matrix is what least squares actually solves — lm() never sees the word “heavy.”

Each dummy is a yes/no switch: is this site light? A site belongs to exactly one class, so exactly one switch is on per row — or none at all.
Look at the heavy row: all four switches are 0, and only the intercept column of 1s is left. heavy is not missing from the model — it is the row where nothing is switched on. The reference level is the intercept, which is why 5 levels need only 4 dummies.






Warning



⚠️ Why not a fifth dummy
Five switches would sum to 1 in every single row — exactly the intercept column. The model could not tell them apart, and R would print NA: the same perfect aliasing as the deer-mouse brothers.
Dropping a level is not a choice. It is arithmetic.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: 🗳️ DECIDE · Which Level Should Be the Reference?
text:
🗳️ DECIDE · Which Level Should Be the Reference?


The five grazing classes are minimal, light, moderate, heavy, intense.
Which should be the reference level, and why?
(a) heavy — leave R’s default alone; the choice does not affect the model
(b) intense — the most extreme level makes the biggest contrasts
(c) minimal — the least-disturbed level, so every coefficient reads as the cost of adding grazing
(d) It does not matter, because R² and the F-test are identical either way






Warning



✍️ Careful — two of these are true statements. Only one is the right decision.









Note



The question to ask
Which comparison do I want to read straight off the output?

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Making the Control the Reference · fct_relevel()
text:
Making the Control the Reference · fct_relevel()








Important



✅ The answer is (c).

is true — the fit, R², F and the ANOVA table are identical whichever level is the reference. But that is not a reason to accept a bad default: the coefficients are what people read, and they should answer the question you asked.

minimal grazing is the closest thing this observational study has to a control.


Name the control. That is the whole call.

bird_df <- bird_df %>%
  mutate(grazing_class =
           fct_relevel(grazing_class, "minimal"))

levels(bird_df$grazing_class)

[1] "minimal"  "heavy"    "intense"  "light"    "moderate"



fct_relevel() moves the levels you name to the front and leaves the rest where they were. Name one level and it becomes level 1 — the reference.
minimal is now first. The other four are still in alphabetical order behind it, and that is fine: only the first level decides the reference.






Tip



🖐 The habit to build
One line, every time a factor enters a model:
fct_relevel(treatment, "control")
Not factor() and hope. Not relevel-it-later. Set it where you make the factor.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Naming All Five · Reference and Display Order
text:
Naming All Five · Reference and Display Order


Naming one level fixed the reference. Name all five and you also fix the order they print and plot in — light → intense, the way the gradient actually runs.

bird_df <- bird_df %>%
  mutate(grazing_class = fct_relevel(
    grazing_class,
    "minimal", "light", "moderate", "heavy", "intense"))

levels(bird_df$grazing_class)

[1] "minimal"  "light"    "moderate" "heavy"    "intense" 









Note



✅ Both versions fit the same model
Same reference, so same R², same F, same fitted values — only the order of the coefficient rows changes.
The reason to name all five anyway: that order becomes your legend order in every figure you draw from this column.


The activity ends by checking exactly this — if the legend runs minimal → intense instead of alphabetically, the relevel worked.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Same Model, Same F, a Readable Story
text:
Same Model, Same F, a Readable Story



grazing_model <- lm(abundance ~ log_area + grazing_class,
                    data = bird_df)

summary(grazing_model)$coefficients %>% round(2)

                      Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)              15.72       2.77    5.68     0.00
log_area                  7.25       1.26    5.77     0.00
grazing_classlight        0.38       2.91    0.13     0.90
grazing_classmoderate    -0.19       2.55   -0.07     0.94
grazing_classheavy       -1.59       2.98   -0.53     0.60
grazing_classintense    -11.89       2.93   -4.06     0.00



Now every coefficient is a comparison with minimal grazing, and the pattern is obvious:

light, moderate and heavy are all indistinguishable from minimal
intense costs about 11.9 birds, p < 0.001

Grazing is a threshold, not a gradient — and fitting it as the number 1–5 hid that completely, averaging the effect into -2.85 birds per step.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Adding the Coefficients Up


A factor coefficient is a piece of an equation, not a mean on its own. To get a group’s prediction, start at the intercept and add the one switch that is on:
\[\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1(\text{log\_area}) + b_L L + b_M M + b_H H + b_I I\]
Hold area at its average and add them up — the c(0, ...) is the reference level, minimal’s dummy:

b  <- coef(grazing_model)
la <- mean(bird_df$log_area)

group_fit <- b[1] + b[2] * la + c(0, b[3:6])
names(group_fit) <- levels(bird_df$grazing_class)
round(group_fit, 1)

 minimal    light moderate    heavy  intense 
    22.5     22.9     22.3     20.9     10.6 


minimal is 15.72 + 7.25(0.93) = 22.5 birds; intense is that same number 11.89 lower. Every class is the reference prediction plus its own contrast.







Important



✅ This is where ANOVA starts
Drop the continuous predictor and the \(b_1\) term disappears. Then

intercept = the reference group’s mean
intercept + contrast = any other group’s mean

One-way ANOVA is this slide with no log_area column — same dummy coding, same addition.








Note



🧭 Adjusted, not raw
Raw minimal is 28.6 birds, not 22.5 — ungrazed patches are also the big ones, and holding area constant takes that credit back. That gap is ANCOVA.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Why This Matters Even More in ANOVA
text:
Why This Matters Even More in ANOVA


With only continuous predictors there is no reference level at all — every slope is “per unit of X” and nothing is being compared with anything.
The moment a factor enters the model, every coefficient becomes a contrast against the reference, and that is the whole structure of the next five weeks:

One-way ANOVA — treatment means against a control
Two-way ANOVA — main effects read at the other factor’s reference level
ANCOVA — separate intercepts, all relative to one group








Important



✅ The rule to carry forward
factor() gives you alphabetical order. Alphabetical order is almost never the order your experiment was designed in.
Set the control as the first level, every time, and your model output reads as “what each treatment did to the control” without any further work.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 8 · Comparing Models

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Comparing Models — the Problem



Which predictors should be in the model?
Occam’s razor: the best model balances fit against complexity
Overfitting: a high R² bought with useless predictors — which is why R² alone cannot choose between models

anova() needs the models to be nested — one model’s predictors a subset of the other’s. AIC does not, which is why it can rank “area only” against “grazing only”; it only needs the same response and the same rows.







Note



📖 Reference
Quinn & Keough, Ch. 6, works through exactly this dataset. Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 17, covers model comparison for regression.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Comparing Models — Penalizing Complexity


Two ways to charge a model for its predictors:
\[\text{Adjusted } R^2 = 1 - \frac{SS_{Residual}/(n - p - 1)}{SS_{Total}/(n - 1)}\]
\[\text{AIC} = n\ln(SS_{Residual}) + 2(p + 1) - n\ln(n)\]

Higher adjusted R² is better
Lower AIC is better
AIC is comparative only — the number on its own means nothing, and models must be fitted to the same rows
This is Quinn & Keough’s form; AIC() in R adds a constant, so the printed values differ from the formula while every ΔAIC is identical








Warning



⚠️ The NA trap
If one predictor has missing values, lm() silently drops those rows. Two models fitted to different numbers of rows cannot be compared by AIC, and R will not warn you.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Comparing Models — How to Search



Fit all possible models and compare — fine with a few predictors, hopeless with many
Automated stepwise selection adds or removes terms by partial F or AIC
We use manual backward selection: start full, drop what earns nothing, stop when dropping hurts








Warning



⚠️ Stepwise selection is controversial
It inflates R², biases p-values, and knows nothing about biology. A small set of models you can justify beats an automated search over all of them.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Comparing Models — Putting It Together



model_comparison <- tibble(
  model = c("all six predictors",
            "log_area + grazing",
            "log_area only",
            "grazing only"),
  adj_r2 = c(summary(full_model)$adj.r.squared,
             summary(reduced_model)$adj.r.squared,
             summary(lm(abundance ~ log_area, bird_df))$adj.r.squared,
             summary(lm(abundance ~ grazing, bird_df))$adj.r.squared),
  AIC = c(AIC(full_model),
          AIC(reduced_model),
          AIC(lm(abundance ~ log_area, bird_df)),
          AIC(lm(abundance ~ grazing, bird_df)))
) %>%
  mutate(delta_AIC = AIC - min(AIC)) %>%
  arrange(AIC)

model_comparison

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  model              adj_r2   AIC delta_AIC
  <chr>               <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
1 log_area + grazing  0.640  373.      0   
2 all six predictors  0.646  375.      2.55
3 log_area only       0.539  385.     12.8 
4 grazing only        0.456  395.     22.1 









Important



✅ The two-predictor model wins
It has the lowest AIC and essentially the same adjusted R² as the full model — with four fewer predictors.
A ΔAIC above about 2 is usually treated as a real difference, so the full model’s extra terms are not paying for themselves.


The anova() test in Part 3 said the same thing. Two routes, one answer.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text: Part 9 · Relative Importance of Predictors

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
How Important Is Each Predictor?


Three standard approaches, and they answer slightly different questions:

F- or t-tests on the partial slopes
Coefficient of partial determination — the variance a predictor adds
Standardized partial slopes — every predictor in SD units

None of them is “the” right answer.







Warning



⚠️ Why the raw slopes cannot be compared
log_area has a slope of 6.89 and grazing -2.85.
One is “birds per tenfold increase in area,” the other is “birds per step of grazing intensity.” Comparing those two numbers is comparing metres with kilograms.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Approaches 1 and 2 — Partial F and Partial R²
text:
Approaches 1 and 2 — Partial F and Partial R²



Anova(reduced_model, type = "II")

Anova Table (Type II tests)

Response: abundance
          Sum Sq Df F value    Pr(>F)    
log_area  1184.6  1  28.527 1.977e-06 ***
grazing    666.0  1  16.038 0.0001946 ***
Residuals 2200.9 53                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Partial η² = \(\dfrac{SS_{predictor}}{SS_{predictor} + SS_{residual}}\) — variance explained after controlling for the other predictor.











log_area
grazing




partial η²
0.35
0.232


ΔR²
0.187
0.105




ΔR² is what the model’s R² would lose if you dropped that predictor — its unique contribution.
Both say area is the stronger of the two.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Approach 3 — Standardized Partial Slopes


Rescale every variable to mean 0 and SD 1, and the slopes become directly comparable: “SDs of Y per SD of X.”

bird_z <- bird_df %>%
  mutate(across(c(abundance, log_area, grazing),
                ~ as.numeric(scale(.))))

lm(abundance ~ log_area + grazing, data = bird_z) %>%
  coef() %>% round(3)

(Intercept)    log_area     grazing 
      0.000       0.521      -0.391 



log_area 0.52 versus grazing -0.39 — area is about 1.3× the influence of grazing per standard deviation.






Note



✅ All three agree here
Partial F, partial R² and standardized slopes all rank area above grazing. When they disagree, that is worth reporting — it usually means the predictors are tangled.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: Partial η² and ΔR² — What to Keep, What to Toss
text:
Partial η² and ΔR² — What to Keep, What to Toss


Run both on the full model and every predictor is ranked at once.

anova_full  <- Anova(full_model, type = "II")
ss_res_full <- sum(residuals(full_model)^2)

tibble(predictor = rownames(anova_full),
       SS        = anova_full[, "Sum Sq"]) %>%
  filter(predictor != "Residuals") %>%
  mutate(pEta2 = SS / (SS + ss_res_full),
         dR2   = SS / ss_tot) %>%
  arrange(desc(pEta2))

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  predictor            SS   pEta2      dR2
  <chr>             <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>
1 log_area        1060.   0.347   0.167   
2 grazing          131.   0.0616  0.0207  
3 year_isolated    109.   0.0517  0.0172  
4 altitude_m        27.0  0.0133  0.00426 
5 log_dist           4.68 0.00234 0.000739
6 log_dist_larger    3.80 0.00190 0.000600



log_area carries pη² = 0.35 — 5.6× the next predictor.
The two distance predictors sit at 0.002. That is nothing.






Note



✅ Two columns, two questions
pη² ranks the predictors. ΔR² says what each one uniquely buys — what R² would lose if you dropped it.


A fourth route to the same answer the vote, the t-tests and AIC already gave you.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: The Trap in the ΔR² Column
text:
The Trap in the ΔR² Column


Add up the ΔR² column: 0.211.
The model’s R² is 0.685.
So where did the other 0.47 of explained variance go?
It is real, and it is shared. ΔR² only counts the variance a predictor explains that nothing else can. Variance that two collinear predictors could each account for belongs to neither of them, so it appears in R² and in no row of this table.







Important



⚠️ Do not toss on pη² alone
A predictor can have a tiny pη² for two completely different reasons:

It genuinely does nothing — toss it
It is tangled with a predictor already in the model — vif() from Part 5 is how you tell the difference

Drop it for reason 2 and you have not learned it has no effect — only that these data cannot separate it from its partner.








Note



✅ How to use these
pη² to rank, ΔR² to see what each predictor uniquely buys you, vif() to decide whether a small value means “useless” or “redundant.”

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Wrap-up
Today you:

Extended the regression line to a plane, and fitted 56 forest patches against six predictors at once
Watched four predictors that were significant alone collapse to one in the model together
Read a partial slope as a conditional statement, and saw that neither it nor the simple slope is “wrong”
Tested groups of predictors with anova(reduced, full) and single ones with the t-tests in summary()
Diagnosed collinearity with vif(), and learned to say “these data cannot separate them” instead of “it has no effect”
Fitted a real interaction — fragmentation costs more where grazing is heavy
Turned a categorical predictor into dummy variables, and set the reference level on purpose with fct_relevel()
Compared models with adjusted R² and AIC, and ranked predictors by partial η², ΔR² and standardized slopes to decide what to keep

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
section: The Three Things to Carry Out of Here
text:
The Three Things to Carry Out of Here








Important



⚠️ R² always rises
Adding predictors can only increase plain R². Adjusted R² and AIC exist precisely because “explains more variance” is not the same as “is a better model.”








Note



✅ A partial slope is conditional
“What does area do among patches grazed the same amount?” Change what else is in the model and you have changed the question.









Important



✅ Set your reference level
factor() sorts alphabetically. Your control is almost never first alphabetically — use fct_relevel() and make the output say what you meant.
This is the habit that makes every ANOVA from Week 8 onward readable.








Note



Up next — Analysis of Variance
What happens when every predictor is categorical, and why ANOVA and regression are the same machinery in different clothes.

title: Lecture: Multiple Regression
text:
Readings

Quinn, G. P., & Keough, M. J. (2002). Experimental Design and Data Analysis for Biologists, Ch. 6 — Multiple and Complex Regression. This lecture follows their Box 6-2 analysis of the Loyn data.
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 17 — Regression.
Gotelli & Ellison, Ch. 9 — Regression.
Loyn, R. H. (1987). Effects of patch area and habitat on bird abundances, species numbers and tree health in fragmented Victorian forests. In Nature Conservation: The Role of Remnants of Native Vegetation. Surrey Beatty & Sons.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text: Part 1 · Why Multivariate Data?

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Where We Have Been


One response variable at a time

Everything from t-tests through ANCOVA and mixed models shared one structure:

One response variable, y
One or more predictors
Partition the variance in y

That works when the biology really is about one number — lifespan, mass, count, survival.


But ecology is rarely one number

A plant is its whole shape: height and mouth and tube and wing and mass.
A stream site is its whole fish community: 27 species at once.
Running 10 separate ANOVAs on 10 traits:

inflates the family-wise error rate,
and still never tells you how the traits go together.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Introduction to Multivariate Analysis


What multivariate methods do

Take many correlated variables measured on the same objects and ask:

Which objects resemble which?
What are the main axes of variation?
Do groups differ in their overall multivariate makeup?

Three jobs, in order, and this lecture is a map of all three:

Put variables on a common footing — standardization
Turn objects into resemblances — distance / dissimilarity
Draw the resemblances in 2-D — ordination








Note


Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics, Ch. 12 — The Analysis of Multivariate Data — is the core reference for this lecture.




Darlingtonia californica (cobra lily)



Photo of a cobra lily (Darlingtonia californica) showing its hooded, pitcher-shaped leaves and forked, tongue-like appendages, the carnivorous plant whose morphology this lecture’s PCA example analyzes.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Our First Dataset: Darlingtonia


Cobra lily morphology

87 plants from 4 sites in the Siskiyou Mountains of Oregon, 10 variables each.
Morphology (mm): height, mouth_diam, tube_diam, keel_diam, wing1_length, wing2_length, wingsprea
Biomass (g): hoodmass_g, tubemass_g, wingmass_g
Sites: TJH (T.J. Howell’s Fen) · DG (Day’s Gulch) · LEH (L.E. Hunter’s Fen) · HD (High Divide)


## # A tibble: 4 × 2
##   site  n_plants
##   <chr>    <int>
## 1 DG          25
## 2 HD          12
## 3 LEH         25
## 4 TJH         25


Pitcher structure showing the measured features



Vintage-style line illustration of three Darlingtonia pitcher-leaf structures with their hooded tops, tube bodies, and forked wing appendages labeled by shape, showing the plant parts behind variables like height, mouth diameter, tube diameter, and wing length/spread used in the PCA.



All continuous, all positive, mostly correlated — the classic setting for PCA.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
section: Our Second Dataset: Doubs River Fish
text:
Our Second Dataset: Doubs River Fish


A very different kind of multivariate data

29 sites along the Doubs River (France), 27 fish species, abundance counts.
Sites are ordered upstream → downstream, so there is a real environmental gradient to recover.
The structural difference that matters:

52.1% of the entries are zeros.
Species richness ranges from 1 to 26 species per site.

Count data, shared absences, wildly different totals. This is why Euclidean distance is not always the right answer.



## # A tibble: 6 × 7
##    site   CHA   TRU   VAI   LOC   GAR   ABL
##   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
## 1     1     0     3     0     0     0     0
## 2     2     0     5     4     3     0     0
## 3    14     3     4     4     5     0     0
## 4    15     2     3     3     5     1     0
## 5    28     0     1     1     1     5     5
## 6    29     0     0     0     0     5     5


Site 1 holds a single species (3 brown trout).
Site 29 holds 26.
Nothing in a t-test or an ANOVA handles a response like this.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
📥 Download the Data
📥 darlingtonia.csv 📥 DoubsSpe.csv 📥 DoubsEnv.csv
Loading both datasets

darlingtonia <- read_csv("data/darlingtonia.csv")

doubs_spe <- read_csv("data/DoubsSpe.csv") %>% rename(site = 1)
doubs_env <- read_csv("data/DoubsEnv.csv") %>% rename(site = 1)

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Exploring the Raw Darlingtonia Data


Always look first

Check for outliers, examine distributions, look for patterns by site, understand the scales.
Key observations:

Variables measured in different units (mm vs. g)
Height is in the hundreds; wing mass is in hundredths
We will have to standardize before we can combine them

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text: Part 2 · Standardization

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
The Problem of Different Scales


Why standardization matters

Variables with larger numbers dominate any distance you compute.
In this data:


## # A tibble: 1 × 3
##   sd_height sd_wingmass ratio
##       <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>
## 1      101.       0.102  986.


Height varies about 990× more than wing mass does. In a raw Euclidean distance, wing mass contributes essentially nothing.
That is an accident of units, not biology.


Z-score standardization

\(Z = \dfrac{Y_i - \bar{Y}}{s}\)
Each variable becomes:

Mean = 0
Standard deviation = 1
Units = “standard deviations from the mean”

Every variable now gets an equal vote.


darl_numeric <- darlingtonia %>%
  dplyr::select(-site)

darl_scaled <- scale(darl_numeric)

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Standardization in Pictures












When not to standardize

Same units, and the differences in spread are real biology.

Ten lengths all in mm, where “this trait varies more” is the finding — standardizing would erase it.

Species abundance data. Standardizing each species to mean 0 turns absences into negative numbers, and most dissimilarity measures for community data are undefined for negatives.

Community data gets transformed (square-root, Hellinger) rather than z-scored. More on that in week 15.

The question to ask is always: do I want these variables to have equal influence?

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text: Part 3 · Distance and Dissimilarity

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Euclidean Distance Between Two Objects


How different are two plants?

Two variables (height, mouth diameter):

\(d_{i,j} = \sqrt{(y_{i,1} - y_{j,1})^2 + (y_{i,2} - y_{j,2})^2}\)

p variables:

\(d_{i,j} = \sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^{p}(y_{i,k} - y_{j,k})^2}\)

The Pythagorean theorem, extended to as many dimensions as you have variables.
Always compute it on standardized values — otherwise you are measuring your unit choices, not your plants.



# distance between plants 1 and 2
# on the STANDARDIZED data
z <- scale(darl_numeric)

round(sqrt(sum((z[1, ] - z[2, ])^2)), 2)
## [1] 5.79

# same thing, via dist()
round(as.matrix(dist(z))[1, 2], 2)
## [1] 5.79


5.79 standard deviations apart across all 10 traits.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
The Dissimilarity Matrix


The hub of everything that follows

dist() returns one number for every pair of objects: an n × n dissimilarity matrix.
With 87 plants that is 3,741 pairwise distances.
Why it matters: PCoA, NMDS, cluster analysis, PERMANOVA and ANOSIM all start from this matrix and nothing else.

Choose the metric well and everything downstream is sensible.
Choose it badly and no amount of clever plotting rescues you.




d_darl <- dist(z)          # Euclidean

# the corner of the matrix
round(as.matrix(d_darl)[1:5, 1:5], 2)
##      1    2    3    4    5
## 1 0.00 5.79 3.50 2.36 3.73
## 2 5.79 0.00 3.27 4.74 3.78
## 3 3.50 3.27 0.00 2.40 2.03
## 4 2.36 4.74 2.40 0.00 3.45
## 5 3.73 3.78 2.03 3.45 0.00


Symmetric, zero on the diagonal, and that is all an ordination method ever sees.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Not All Distances Are Euclidean
Four metrics you will meet in this course










Metric
Formula idea
Data it suits
Range




Euclidean
straight-line distance
continuous, standardized, few zeros
0 → ∞


Manhattan
sum of absolute differences
continuous, less outlier-sensitive
0 → ∞


Bray–Curtis
shared abundance / total abundance
species abundance counts
0 → 1


Jaccard
shared species / total species
presence–absence
0 → 1





Euclidean and Manhattan are metric distances — they obey the triangle inequality and can be drawn in a real coordinate space.
Bray–Curtis and Jaccard are semi-metric dissimilarities — bounded at 1 (= “share nothing”), which is exactly what you want for communities, but which breaks the geometry PCA relies on.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
The Double-Zero Problem


Why community data needs Bray–Curtis

Doubs site 1 holds one species. Site 29 holds 26. They share nothing.
Euclidean distance counts all the species that are absent from both sites as evidence of similarity — two barren sites look like twins.
Ecologically that is nonsense: a species can be absent for a dozen unrelated reasons.
Bray–Curtis ignores double zeros entirely and returns 1 for two sites with nothing in common.



# sites 1 and 29 share no species
e <- as.matrix(vegdist(doubs_mat,
                       method = "euclidean"))
b <- as.matrix(vegdist(doubs_mat,
                       method = "bray"))

c(euclidean = round(e[1, 29], 2),
  bray      = round(b[1, 29], 3))
## euclidean      bray 
##      20.4       1.0


Bray–Curtis says 1.0 — maximally different, which is correct.
Euclidean returns a number with no upper bound and no interpretation.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Choosing a Distance Metric


Decision rules

Continuous traits, environmental variables, few zeros

→ standardize, then Euclidean
→ PCA is available to you

Species abundances with many zeros

→ transform, then Bray–Curtis
→ PCA is not appropriate; use NMDS or PCoA

Presence–absence

→ Jaccard (or Sørensen)

Outlier-heavy continuous data

→ Manhattan, which does not square the differences




# same data, three metrics, first pair
round(c(
  euclidean = vegdist(doubs_mat,
                 method = "euclidean")[1],
  manhattan = vegdist(doubs_mat,
                 method = "manhattan")[1],
  bray      = vegdist(doubs_mat,
                 method = "bray")[1],
  jaccard   = vegdist(doubs_mat > 0,
                 method = "jaccard")[1]), 3)
## euclidean manhattan      bray   jaccard 
##     5.385     9.000     0.600     0.667







Important


The metric is a modelling decision, not a default. It encodes what you mean by “different”.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text: Part 4 · Ordination — The Big Picture

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
What Ordination Does


Many dimensions → a readable map

You have 10 variables, so each plant is a point in 10-dimensional space. Nobody can see that.
Ordination finds a 2-D (or 3-D) map in which objects that were close in the full space are still close on the page.
It is a lossy summary. Some information is always thrown away; the honest report always says how much.
The word means “putting in order” — arranging objects along axes.





Scatterplot of a correlated two-variable Gaussian point cloud with two perpendicular black arrows overlaid, the longer arrow pointing along the direction of greatest spread (the first principal axis) and the shorter arrow perpendicular to it (the second), illustrating how PCA finds new axes aligned with the directions of maximum variance.


Reducing 2 variables to 1 principal axis: the new axis points along the direction of greatest spread.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
The Map of Ordination Methods











Method
Starts from
Distance implied
How it solves
Where in this course




PCA
raw / standardized variables
Euclidean only
eigen-decomposition
Week 14


PCoA
any dissimilarity matrix
whatever you chose
eigen-decomposition
named only


CA / DCA
species count table
chi-square
eigen-decomposition
named only


NMDS
any dissimilarity matrix
whatever you chose
iterative, rank-based
Week 15


Cluster
any dissimilarity matrix
whatever you chose
agglomerative joining
Week 15





The top block is eigenanalysis: one exact answer, axes ranked by variance explained, and you can read loadings off them.
NMDS is different: it preserves only the rank order of the dissimilarities, solves by iteration, and has no “% variance explained” — it has stress instead.
Cluster analysis answers a different question entirely: not “where does each object sit?” but “which objects group together?”

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Eigenanalysis vs. Iteration


Eigen methods (PCA, PCoA, CA)

Find axes by decomposing the correlation or distance structure directly.
Give you:

an exact, reproducible answer
axes ordered by variance explained
loadings: how each variable builds each axis

But they assume the distance is Euclidean-like and the relationships are linear.


NMDS

Does not decompose anything. It searches: shuffle the points, measure how badly the map distorts the rank order of distances, repeat.
Gives you:

a map honouring any dissimilarity you like
no linearity assumption
stress as the goodness-of-fit

But: no loadings, axes are arbitrary, and a different random start can give a rotated answer.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text: Part 5 · A First Ordination — PCA

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
PCA in One Slide


The idea

PCA builds new variables (components) that are:

Linear combinations of the original variables
Uncorrelated with each other
Ordered by how much variance they capture

For plant i on component k:

\(Z_{ik} = a_{k1}Y_{i1} + a_{k2}Y_{i2} + \ldots + a_{kp}Y_{ip}\)
\(a_{kj}\) = the loading of variable j on component k
\(Z_{ik}\) = the score of plant i on component k

PC1 takes as much variance as any single axis can; PC2 takes as much of what is left as possible, at right angles to PC1; and so on.


Running it

pca_result <- prcomp(darl_numeric,
                     center = TRUE,
                     scale. = TRUE)


center = TRUE → mean 0
scale. = TRUE → SD 1 (note the dot)
Together those two arguments are the standardization from Part 2.







Note


Next week we open the box: eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and what prcomp() is actually solving.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Do the Variables Even Correlate?


PCA only helps if they do

PCA earns its keep by collapsing redundancy. If the variables are already uncorrelated, there is no redundancy to collapse and the components are just the original variables, reordered.
Here the strongest pairs are:


## # A tibble: 4 × 2
##   pair                            r
##   <chr>                       <dbl>
## 1 height ~ tubemass_g         0.843
## 2 wing1_length ~ wing2_length 0.836
## 3 hoodmass_g ~ wingmass_g     0.803
## 4 wing1_length ~ wingmass_g   0.764

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
How Much Did We Capture?


Variance explained

## # A tibble: 6 × 4
##   PC    Eigenvalue Percent Cumulative
##   <chr>      <dbl>   <dbl>      <dbl>
## 1 PC1        4.99     49.9       49.9
## 2 PC2        1.77     17.7       67.5
## 3 PC3        1.53     15.3       82.8
## 4 PC4        0.573     5.7       88.5
## 5 PC5        0.352     3.5       92  
## 6 PC6        0.261     2.6       94.6


PC1 = 49.9%, PC2 = 17.7%, PC3 = 15.3%
First three together: 82.8% of all variation in 10 variables, in 3 numbers.












The elbow after PC3 is the usual cue to stop.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Reading the Loadings


What loads where

##                 PC1    PC2    PC3
## height       -0.278 -0.449  0.198
## mouth_diam   -0.369 -0.110  0.214
## tube_diam     0.040 -0.602 -0.390
## keel_diam     0.202 -0.491 -0.328
## wing1_length -0.375  0.171 -0.280
## wing2_length -0.342  0.131 -0.415
## wingsprea    -0.239  0.156 -0.549
## hoodmass_g   -0.385 -0.057  0.185
## tubemass_g   -0.355 -0.320  0.263
## wingmass_g   -0.393  0.080 -0.007


Rules of thumb

Loadings beyond ±0.3 are worth discussing; beyond ±0.5 they dominate the axis.
Near zero means the variable has nothing to say about that axis.
PC1: nearly every variable loads in the same direction with similar magnitude → a general size axis.
PC2: tube_diam and keel_diam stand apart from the rest → tube girth.
PC3: wingsprea and wing2_length dominate → a wing axis.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
section: ⚠️ The Sign of a Component Is Arbitrary
text:
⚠️ The Sign of a Component Is Arbitrary


This trips up every student once

On this run, every PC1 loading is negative. Run the same code on a different machine, or drop one plant, and they may all come back positive.
Both answers are equally correct. An eigenvector defines a line, and a line has no preferred end. Multiplying a whole component — loadings and scores — by −1 changes nothing:

the variance explained is identical
the distances between points are identical
the biology is identical

What you must never do is flip the loadings and not the scores.



# PC1 loadings are all negative here,
# so a HIGH PC1 score = a SMALL plant
round(pca_result$rotation[1:4, 1], 3)
##     height mouth_diam  tube_diam  keel_diam 
##     -0.278     -0.369      0.040      0.202

# flipping is legal and changes nothing
flip <- -pca_result$x[, 1]
round(c(var_original = var(pca_result$x[, 1]),
        var_flipped  = var(flip)), 3)
## var_original  var_flipped 
##        4.987        4.987

Always check the sign before you write a sentence such as “site X has higher PC1”. Say what it means biologically, not just which way the number went.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
PC1: A Size Axis












Interpretation

Eight of ten variables load together between about −0.24 and −0.39: height, mouth, both wings, wing spread, and all three masses.
Only keel_diam (0.202) and tube_diam (0.04) sit apart.
Biological meaning: bigger plants are bigger in nearly every way. PC1 is general size.
Because the loadings are negative on this run:

low PC1 score → large plant
high PC1 score → small plant

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
PC2 and PC3: Shape Axes












What these axes are

PC2 (17.7%) — tube girth. tube_diam (-0.6) and keel_diam (-0.49) dominate, with height also loading. A plant can be tall and thin-tubed, or short and fat-tubed, at any overall size.
PC3 (15.3%) — wings. wingsprea (-0.55) and wing2_length (-0.42) dominate. How far the trap’s forked appendages spread, independent of size and tube girth.
This is PCA doing its job: three independent descriptions of shape, out of ten entangled measurements.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
section: Scores: Putting the Plants on the Map
text:
Scores: Putting the Plants on the Map


What scores are

A score is one plant’s value on one component — its coordinate in the new space.
pca_result$x holds them, one row per plant.


## # A tibble: 6 × 5
##   plant_id site    PC1   PC2   PC3
##      <int> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
## 1        1 TJH   -1.92  0.08  1.53
## 2        2 TJH    3.35  1.53  0.75
## 3        3 TJH    0.92 -0.03  0.25
## 4        4 TJH   -0.98  0.24 -0.24
## 5        5 TJH    1.15 -1.02  1.54
## 6        6 TJH   -1.37 -0.61  0.85












This is an ordination: plants ordered along interpretable axes.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
The Biplot


Reading it

Points = plants (scores). Arrows = variables (loadings).
Arrow length = how strongly that variable is represented in this plane.
Angle between arrows = correlation: small angle → positively correlated; 90° → uncorrelated; 180° → negatively correlated.
A plant lying out along an arrow is high in that variable.
HD plants sit to the right — and because PC1 loadings are negative, right means small. HD grows the smallest plants.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text: Part 6 · A First NMDS

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
section: Why the Fish Data Needs a Different Tool
text:
Why the Fish Data Needs a Different Tool


PCA would be the wrong choice here

52.1% zeros, counts spanning orders of magnitude, and a strong non-linear gradient from headwater to lowland.
PCA would impose Euclidean distance, treat shared absences as similarity, and spread the sites along a meaningless horseshoe.
NMDS instead:

Compute Bray–Curtis dissimilarities.
Drop the sites onto a 2-D map at random.
Nudge them until the rank order of map distances matches the rank order of real dissimilarities as closely as possible.
Report stress — how badly it still fails.




nmds <- metaMDS(doubs_mat,
                distance = "bray",
                k = 2, trymax = 50,
                trace = 0)


round(nmds$stress, 3)
## [1] 0.074


Stress rules of thumb: < 0.05 excellent · < 0.1 good · < 0.2 usable · > 0.3 meaningless.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
The NMDS Map












What to notice

Sites arrange along a gradient, in roughly their real upstream-to-downstream order — which NMDS was never told.
Stress = 0.074: a good 2-D fit.
The axes mean nothing. No variance explained, no loadings; the map can be rotated or reflected freely.
Contrast the PCA biplot, whose axes carried percentages and whose arrows carried meaning.







Note


Week 15 takes this apart properly: the algorithm, Shepard diagrams, choosing k, and fitting environmental vectors.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text: Part 7 · Testing Group Differences

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Do the Sites Actually Differ?


Route 1 — ANOVA on component scores

PC scores are ordinary continuous variables, and they are uncorrelated with one another by construction — so you may put them straight into the ANOVA you already know.
One test per component, each answering a different question about shape.


map_dfr(c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3"), \(k) {
  a <- summary(aov(pc_scores[[k]] ~ pc_scores$site))[[1]]
  tibble(PC = k, F = round(a[1, 4], 2),
         p = signif(a[1, 5], 3))
})
## # A tibble: 3 × 3
##   PC        F          p
##   <chr> <dbl>      <dbl>
## 1 PC1    11.3 0.00000275
## 2 PC2     4.6 0.00502   
## 3 PC3    13.8 0.00000022


What it says

All three components differ significantly among sites.
Sites differ in size (PC1), in tube girth (PC2) and in wing spread (PC3) — the sites are not simply scaled versions of one another.
The caveat: this is three tests on three axes chosen by the data themselves. It is a reasonable description, not a clean confirmatory test.







Warning


PCA was run on all 87 plants at once, ignoring site. The components are therefore not independent of the grouping you then test. Treat these p-values as exploratory.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Which Sites Differ, and How?



##  site emmean    SE df lower.CL upper.CL .group
##  DG   -1.024 0.383 83   -1.786   -0.262  a    
##  LEH  -0.659 0.383 83   -1.421    0.103  ab   
##  TJH   0.423 0.383 83   -0.339    1.185   b   
##  HD    2.626 0.553 83    1.526    3.726    c  
## 
## Confidence level used: 0.95 
## P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates 
## significance level used: alpha = 0.05 
## NOTE: If two or more means share the same grouping symbol,
##       then we cannot show them to be different.
##       But we also did not show them to be the same.


Reading it in biology, not in numbers

HD sits alone in its own group with the highest PC1 score.
PC1 loadings are negative, so a high score means a small plant: HD grows the smallest cobra lilies, and significantly so.
DG sits at the other end — the largest plants.
LEH and TJH overlap in the middle.







Important


This is the sign trap in action. “HD has the highest PC1” and “HD has the smallest plants” are the same sentence. Always translate before you write.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
section: Route 2 — PERMANOVA on the Distance Matrix
text:
Route 2 — PERMANOVA on the Distance Matrix


Test the whole community at once

PERMANOVA skips the ordination entirely: it partitions the dissimilarity matrix directly and gets its p-value by permuting group labels.
One test on all 10 variables at once, instead of one per component.


adonis2(darl_scaled ~ site,
        data   = darlingtonia,
        method = "euclidean")
## Permutation test for adonis under reduced model
## Permutation: free
## Number of permutations: 999
## 
## adonis2(formula = darl_scaled ~ site, data = darlingtonia, method = "euclidean")
##          Df SumOfSqs      R2      F Pr(>F)    
## Model     3    213.7 0.24849 9.1483  0.001 ***
## Residual 83    646.3 0.75151                  
## Total    86    860.0 1.00000                  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Why it is worth knowing now

No normality assumption, no multivariate normality, no equal covariance matrices.
Works on any dissimilarity you can justify — which is why it is the natural partner to NMDS.
R2 is the fraction of total dissimilarity attributable to site — read it like an ANOVA’s \(\eta^2\).

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
PERMANOVA’s One Real Assumption


Equal dispersion

A significant PERMANOVA means groups differ in centroid (location) or merely in spread (dispersion).
betadisper() tells them apart.


disp <- betadisper(
  vegdist(darl_scaled, method = "euclidean"),
  darlingtonia$site)

anova(disp)
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Response: Distances
##           Df  Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)  
## Groups     3  11.629  3.8762   2.743 0.04828 *
## Residuals 83 117.290  1.4131                  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Reading the two together

Significant PERMANOVA + non-significant dispersion → groups genuinely sit in different places. Clean result.
Both significant → the location difference may be partly a spread difference. Say so.


round(tapply(disp$distances,
             darlingtonia$site, mean), 2)
##   DG   HD  LEH  TJH 
## 2.17 1.98 2.98 2.44


Here both are significant: LEH is the most variable. The site effect is strong enough (R² = 0.25) that it is not only dispersion — but an honest write-up mentions it.







Note


Week 15 develops PERMANOVA and ANOSIM in full on the Doubs data.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
section: Part 8 · Choosing a Method and Wrapping Up
text: Part 8 · Choosing a Method and Wrapping Up

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
A Decision Guide









Your data
Your question
Use




Continuous traits, correlated, few zeros
What are the main axes of variation?
PCA (week 14)


Species counts, many zeros
How do communities arrange along a gradient?
NMDS (week 15)


Any dissimilarity matrix
Which objects group together?
Cluster analysis (week 15)


Any dissimilarity matrix
Do my groups differ?
PERMANOVA / ANOSIM (week 15)


Continuous, multivariate normal
Do groups differ, parametrically?
MANOVA


Categorical variables
Same questions, categorical data
CA / MCA





Two questions settle almost every case:

What kind of data is it? → fixes the distance metric.
Description or test? → fixes ordination vs. PERMANOVA.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
section: Assumptions and Things That Go Wrong
text:
Assumptions and Things That Go Wrong


Check before you ordinate

Sample size: at least 3× as many objects as variables; 50+ is comfortable. We have 87 plants and 10 variables.
Correlation: if nothing correlates, PCA has nothing to collapse. KMO() gives a sampling-adequacy score; ours is 0.76 (> 0.6 acceptable, > 0.8 good).
Linearity: eigen methods see only linear relationships.
Outliers: one extreme object can define an entire component.


Common mistakes

❌ Not standardizing variables with different units
❌ Euclidean distance on species counts
❌ Reading meaning into a sign flip
❌ Interpreting components that explain 3% of the variance
❌ Quoting “% variance explained” for an NMDS — it has none
❌ Calling a significant PERMANOVA a centroid difference without checking dispersion
❌ Treating an exploratory ordination as a confirmatory test

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Reporting Multivariate Results


Methods

“Ten morphological and biomass variables measured on 87 Darlingtonia californica plants from four sites were standardized to zero mean and unit variance and subjected to principal component analysis (prcomp(), R 4.6.1). Components with eigenvalues > 1 were retained. Site differences were tested with PERMANOVA on Euclidean distances (vegan::adonis2(), 999 permutations), with homogeneity of multivariate dispersion checked using betadisper().”


Results — always state

% variance for every component you interpret
Loadings for the retained components
The biological reading of each axis, sign resolved
The test result with its dispersion check

Never report

All 10 components when 3 are meaningful
Loadings below |0.3|
Raw eigenvalues in place of percentages
Every individual score

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Summary


What we did today

Standardized 10 variables onto a common footing, because units are not biology.
Built a dissimilarity matrix and learned that the choice of metric — Euclidean, Manhattan, Bray–Curtis, Jaccard — is the modelling decision.
Saw the map of ordination methods and where each one lives in this course.
Ran a PCA: 10 variables → 82.8% of the variation in three interpretable axes (size, tube girth, wings).
Ran an NMDS on fish counts and recovered a river gradient at stress = 0.074.


What to carry forward

The distance matrix is the hub. Everything downstream reads from it.
Component signs are arbitrary — translate into biology before you write a sentence.
Ordination describes; PERMANOVA tests. Do not confuse them.
Next week: what prcomp() is actually solving — eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and PCA in full.
Week 15: NMDS, cluster analysis, PERMANOVA and ANOSIM in full.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Readings

Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics, Ch. 12 — The Analysis of Multivariate Data
Quinn & Keough, Experimental Design and Data Analysis for Biologists, Ch. 15 (introduction to multivariate analyses) and Ch. 16 (multivariate analysis of variance and discriminant analysis)
Whitlock & Schluter does not cover multivariate methods.

Data sources

Darlingtonia: Ellison, A.M. & Farnsworth, E.J. — cobra lily morphology from four sites in the Siskiyou Mountains, Oregon; distributed with Gotelli & Ellison.
Doubs River fish: Verneaux, J. (1973), as distributed in Borcard, Gillet & Legendre, Numerical Ecology with R.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Where We Have Been



One response variable at a time

Everything from t-tests through ANCOVA and mixed models shared one structure:

One response variable, y
One or more predictors
Partition the variance in y

That works when the biology really is about one number — lifespan, mass, count, survival.




But ecology is rarely one number

A plant is its whole shape: height and mouth and tube and wing and mass.
A stream site is its whole fish community: 27 species at once.
Running 10 separate ANOVAs on 10 traits:

inflates the family-wise error rate,
and still never tells you how the traits go together.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Introduction to Multivariate Analysis



What multivariate methods do

Take many correlated variables measured on the same objects and ask:

Which objects resemble which?
What are the main axes of variation?
Do groups differ in their overall multivariate makeup?

Three jobs, in order, and this lecture is a map of all three:

Put variables on a common footing — standardization
Turn objects into resemblances — distance / dissimilarity
Draw the resemblances in 2-D — ordination








Note



Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics, Ch. 12 — The Analysis of Multivariate Data — is the core reference for this lecture.




Darlingtonia californica (cobra lily)



Photo of a cobra lily (Darlingtonia californica) showing its hooded, pitcher-shaped leaves and forked, tongue-like appendages, the carnivorous plant whose morphology this lecture’s PCA example analyzes.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Our First Dataset: Darlingtonia



Cobra lily morphology

87 plants from 4 sites in the Siskiyou Mountains of Oregon, 10 variables each.
Morphology (mm): height, mouth_diam, tube_diam, keel_diam, wing1_length, wing2_length, wingsprea
Biomass (g): hoodmass_g, tubemass_g, wingmass_g
Sites: TJH (T.J. Howell’s Fen) · DG (Day’s Gulch) · LEH (L.E. Hunter’s Fen) · HD (High Divide)


## # A tibble: 4 × 2
##   site  n_plants
##   <chr>    <int>
## 1 DG          25
## 2 HD          12
## 3 LEH         25
## 4 TJH         25



Pitcher structure showing the measured features



Vintage-style line illustration of three Darlingtonia pitcher-leaf structures with their hooded tops, tube bodies, and forked wing appendages labeled by shape, showing the plant parts behind variables like height, mouth diameter, tube diameter, and wing length/spread used in the PCA.



All continuous, all positive, mostly correlated — the classic setting for PCA.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
section: Our Second Dataset: Doubs River Fish
text:
Our Second Dataset: Doubs River Fish



A very different kind of multivariate data

29 sites along the Doubs River (France), 27 fish species, abundance counts.
Sites are ordered upstream → downstream, so there is a real environmental gradient to recover.
The structural difference that matters:

52.1% of the entries are zeros.
Species richness ranges from 1 to 26 species per site.

Count data, shared absences, wildly different totals. This is why Euclidean distance is not always the right answer.




## # A tibble: 6 × 7
##    site   CHA   TRU   VAI   LOC   GAR   ABL
##   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
## 1     1     0     3     0     0     0     0
## 2     2     0     5     4     3     0     0
## 3    14     3     4     4     5     0     0
## 4    15     2     3     3     5     1     0
## 5    28     0     1     1     1     5     5
## 6    29     0     0     0     0     5     5


Site 1 holds a single species (3 brown trout).
Site 29 holds 26.
Nothing in a t-test or an ANOVA handles a response like this.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
📥 Download the Data
📥 darlingtonia.csv 📥 DoubsSpe.csv 📥 DoubsEnv.csv

Loading both datasets

darlingtonia <- read_csv("data/darlingtonia.csv")

doubs_spe <- read_csv("data/DoubsSpe.csv") %>% rename(site = 1)
doubs_env <- read_csv("data/DoubsEnv.csv") %>% rename(site = 1)

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Exploring the Raw Darlingtonia Data



Always look first

Check for outliers, examine distributions, look for patterns by site, understand the scales.
Key observations:

Variables measured in different units (mm vs. g)
Height is in the hundreds; wing mass is in hundredths
We will have to standardize before we can combine them

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text: Part 2 · Standardization

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
The Problem of Different Scales



Why standardization matters

Variables with larger numbers dominate any distance you compute.
In this data:


## # A tibble: 1 × 3
##   sd_height sd_wingmass ratio
##       <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>
## 1      101.       0.102  986.


Height varies about 990× more than wing mass does. In a raw Euclidean distance, wing mass contributes essentially nothing.
That is an accident of units, not biology.




Z-score standardization

\(Z = \dfrac{Y_i - \bar{Y}}{s}\)
Each variable becomes:

Mean = 0
Standard deviation = 1
Units = “standard deviations from the mean”

Every variable now gets an equal vote.


darl_numeric <- darlingtonia %>%
  dplyr::select(-site)

darl_scaled <- scale(darl_numeric)

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Standardization in Pictures













When not to standardize

Same units, and the differences in spread are real biology.

Ten lengths all in mm, where “this trait varies more” is the finding — standardizing would erase it.

Species abundance data. Standardizing each species to mean 0 turns absences into negative numbers, and most dissimilarity measures for community data are undefined for negatives.

Community data gets transformed (square-root, Hellinger) rather than z-scored. More on that in week 15.

The question to ask is always: do I want these variables to have equal influence?

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text: Part 3 · Distance and Dissimilarity

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Euclidean Distance Between Two Objects



How different are two plants?

Two variables (height, mouth diameter):

\(d_{i,j} = \sqrt{(y_{i,1} - y_{j,1})^2 + (y_{i,2} - y_{j,2})^2}\)

p variables:

\(d_{i,j} = \sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^{p}(y_{i,k} - y_{j,k})^2}\)

The Pythagorean theorem, extended to as many dimensions as you have variables.
Always compute it on standardized values — otherwise you are measuring your unit choices, not your plants.




# distance between plants 1 and 2
# on the STANDARDIZED data
z <- scale(darl_numeric)

round(sqrt(sum((z[1, ] - z[2, ])^2)), 2)
## [1] 5.79

# same thing, via dist()
round(as.matrix(dist(z))[1, 2], 2)
## [1] 5.79


5.79 standard deviations apart across all 10 traits.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
The Dissimilarity Matrix



The hub of everything that follows

dist() returns one number for every pair of objects: an n × n dissimilarity matrix.
With 87 plants that is 3,741 pairwise distances.
Why it matters: PCoA, NMDS, cluster analysis, PERMANOVA and ANOSIM all start from this matrix and nothing else.

Choose the metric well and everything downstream is sensible.
Choose it badly and no amount of clever plotting rescues you.





d_darl <- dist(z)          # Euclidean

# the corner of the matrix
round(as.matrix(d_darl)[1:5, 1:5], 2)
##      1    2    3    4    5
## 1 0.00 5.79 3.50 2.36 3.73
## 2 5.79 0.00 3.27 4.74 3.78
## 3 3.50 3.27 0.00 2.40 2.03
## 4 2.36 4.74 2.40 0.00 3.45
## 5 3.73 3.78 2.03 3.45 0.00


Symmetric, zero on the diagonal, and that is all an ordination method ever sees.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Not All Distances Are Euclidean

Four metrics you will meet in this course










Metric
Formula idea
Data it suits
Range




Euclidean
straight-line distance
continuous, standardized, few zeros
0 → ∞


Manhattan
sum of absolute differences
continuous, less outlier-sensitive
0 → ∞


Bray–Curtis
shared abundance / total abundance
species abundance counts
0 → 1


Jaccard
shared species / total species
presence–absence
0 → 1





Euclidean and Manhattan are metric distances — they obey the triangle inequality and can be drawn in a real coordinate space.
Bray–Curtis and Jaccard are semi-metric dissimilarities — bounded at 1 (= “share nothing”), which is exactly what you want for communities, but which breaks the geometry PCA relies on.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
The Double-Zero Problem



Why community data needs Bray–Curtis

Doubs site 1 holds one species. Site 29 holds 26. They share nothing.
Euclidean distance counts all the species that are absent from both sites as evidence of similarity — two barren sites look like twins.
Ecologically that is nonsense: a species can be absent for a dozen unrelated reasons.
Bray–Curtis ignores double zeros entirely and returns 1 for two sites with nothing in common.




# sites 1 and 29 share no species
e <- as.matrix(vegdist(doubs_mat,
                       method = "euclidean"))
b <- as.matrix(vegdist(doubs_mat,
                       method = "bray"))

c(euclidean = round(e[1, 29], 2),
  bray      = round(b[1, 29], 3))
## euclidean      bray 
##      20.4       1.0


Bray–Curtis says 1.0 — maximally different, which is correct.
Euclidean returns a number with no upper bound and no interpretation.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Choosing a Distance Metric



Decision rules

Continuous traits, environmental variables, few zeros

→ standardize, then Euclidean
→ PCA is available to you

Species abundances with many zeros

→ transform, then Bray–Curtis
→ PCA is not appropriate; use NMDS or PCoA

Presence–absence

→ Jaccard (or Sørensen)

Outlier-heavy continuous data

→ Manhattan, which does not square the differences





# same data, three metrics, first pair
round(c(
  euclidean = vegdist(doubs_mat,
                 method = "euclidean")[1],
  manhattan = vegdist(doubs_mat,
                 method = "manhattan")[1],
  bray      = vegdist(doubs_mat,
                 method = "bray")[1],
  jaccard   = vegdist(doubs_mat > 0,
                 method = "jaccard")[1]), 3)
## euclidean manhattan      bray   jaccard 
##     5.385     9.000     0.600     0.667







Important



The metric is a modelling decision, not a default. It encodes what you mean by “different”.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text: Part 4 · Ordination — The Big Picture

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
What Ordination Does



Many dimensions → a readable map

You have 10 variables, so each plant is a point in 10-dimensional space. Nobody can see that.
Ordination finds a 2-D (or 3-D) map in which objects that were close in the full space are still close on the page.
It is a lossy summary. Some information is always thrown away; the honest report always says how much.
The word means “putting in order” — arranging objects along axes.






Scatterplot of a correlated two-variable Gaussian point cloud with two perpendicular black arrows overlaid, the longer arrow pointing along the direction of greatest spread (the first principal axis) and the shorter arrow perpendicular to it (the second), illustrating how PCA finds new axes aligned with the directions of maximum variance.


Reducing 2 variables to 1 principal axis: the new axis points along the direction of greatest spread.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
The Map of Ordination Methods











Method
Starts from
Distance implied
How it solves
Where in this course




PCA
raw / standardized variables
Euclidean only
eigen-decomposition
Week 14


PCoA
any dissimilarity matrix
whatever you chose
eigen-decomposition
named only


CA / DCA
species count table
chi-square
eigen-decomposition
named only


NMDS
any dissimilarity matrix
whatever you chose
iterative, rank-based
Week 15


Cluster
any dissimilarity matrix
whatever you chose
agglomerative joining
Week 15





The top block is eigenanalysis: one exact answer, axes ranked by variance explained, and you can read loadings off them.
NMDS is different: it preserves only the rank order of the dissimilarities, solves by iteration, and has no “% variance explained” — it has stress instead.
Cluster analysis answers a different question entirely: not “where does each object sit?” but “which objects group together?”

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Eigenanalysis vs. Iteration



Eigen methods (PCA, PCoA, CA)

Find axes by decomposing the correlation or distance structure directly.
Give you:

an exact, reproducible answer
axes ordered by variance explained
loadings: how each variable builds each axis

But they assume the distance is Euclidean-like and the relationships are linear.




NMDS

Does not decompose anything. It searches: shuffle the points, measure how badly the map distorts the rank order of distances, repeat.
Gives you:

a map honouring any dissimilarity you like
no linearity assumption
stress as the goodness-of-fit

But: no loadings, axes are arbitrary, and a different random start can give a rotated answer.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text: Part 5 · A First Ordination — PCA

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
PCA in One Slide



The idea

PCA builds new variables (components) that are:

Linear combinations of the original variables
Uncorrelated with each other
Ordered by how much variance they capture

For plant i on component k:

\(Z_{ik} = a_{k1}Y_{i1} + a_{k2}Y_{i2} + \ldots + a_{kp}Y_{ip}\)
\(a_{kj}\) = the loading of variable j on component k
\(Z_{ik}\) = the score of plant i on component k

PC1 takes as much variance as any single axis can; PC2 takes as much of what is left as possible, at right angles to PC1; and so on.




Running it

pca_result <- prcomp(darl_numeric,
                     center = TRUE,
                     scale. = TRUE)


center = TRUE → mean 0
scale. = TRUE → SD 1 (note the dot)
Together those two arguments are the standardization from Part 2.







Note



Next week we open the box: eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and what prcomp() is actually solving.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Do the Variables Even Correlate?



PCA only helps if they do

PCA earns its keep by collapsing redundancy. If the variables are already uncorrelated, there is no redundancy to collapse and the components are just the original variables, reordered.
Here the strongest pairs are:


## # A tibble: 4 × 2
##   pair                            r
##   <chr>                       <dbl>
## 1 height ~ tubemass_g         0.843
## 2 wing1_length ~ wing2_length 0.836
## 3 hoodmass_g ~ wingmass_g     0.803
## 4 wing1_length ~ wingmass_g   0.764

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
How Much Did We Capture?



Variance explained

## # A tibble: 6 × 4
##   PC    Eigenvalue Percent Cumulative
##   <chr>      <dbl>   <dbl>      <dbl>
## 1 PC1        4.99     49.9       49.9
## 2 PC2        1.77     17.7       67.5
## 3 PC3        1.53     15.3       82.8
## 4 PC4        0.573     5.7       88.5
## 5 PC5        0.352     3.5       92  
## 6 PC6        0.261     2.6       94.6


PC1 = 49.9%, PC2 = 17.7%, PC3 = 15.3%
First three together: 82.8% of all variation in 10 variables, in 3 numbers.













The elbow after PC3 is the usual cue to stop.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Reading the Loadings



What loads where

##                 PC1    PC2    PC3
## height       -0.278 -0.449  0.198
## mouth_diam   -0.369 -0.110  0.214
## tube_diam     0.040 -0.602 -0.390
## keel_diam     0.202 -0.491 -0.328
## wing1_length -0.375  0.171 -0.280
## wing2_length -0.342  0.131 -0.415
## wingsprea    -0.239  0.156 -0.549
## hoodmass_g   -0.385 -0.057  0.185
## tubemass_g   -0.355 -0.320  0.263
## wingmass_g   -0.393  0.080 -0.007




Rules of thumb

Loadings beyond ±0.3 are worth discussing; beyond ±0.5 they dominate the axis.
Near zero means the variable has nothing to say about that axis.
PC1: nearly every variable loads in the same direction with similar magnitude → a general size axis.
PC2: tube_diam and keel_diam stand apart from the rest → tube girth.
PC3: wingsprea and wing2_length dominate → a wing axis.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
section: ⚠️ The Sign of a Component Is Arbitrary
text:
⚠️ The Sign of a Component Is Arbitrary



This trips up every student once

On this run, every PC1 loading is negative. Run the same code on a different machine, or drop one plant, and they may all come back positive.
Both answers are equally correct. An eigenvector defines a line, and a line has no preferred end. Multiplying a whole component — loadings and scores — by −1 changes nothing:

the variance explained is identical
the distances between points are identical
the biology is identical

What you must never do is flip the loadings and not the scores.




# PC1 loadings are all negative here,
# so a HIGH PC1 score = a SMALL plant
round(pca_result$rotation[1:4, 1], 3)
##     height mouth_diam  tube_diam  keel_diam 
##     -0.278     -0.369      0.040      0.202

# flipping is legal and changes nothing
flip <- -pca_result$x[, 1]
round(c(var_original = var(pca_result$x[, 1]),
        var_flipped  = var(flip)), 3)
## var_original  var_flipped 
##        4.987        4.987

Always check the sign before you write a sentence such as “site X has higher PC1”. Say what it means biologically, not just which way the number went.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
PC1: A Size Axis













Interpretation

Eight of ten variables load together between about −0.24 and −0.39: height, mouth, both wings, wing spread, and all three masses.
Only keel_diam (0.202) and tube_diam (0.04) sit apart.
Biological meaning: bigger plants are bigger in nearly every way. PC1 is general size.
Because the loadings are negative on this run:

low PC1 score → large plant
high PC1 score → small plant

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
PC2 and PC3: Shape Axes













What these axes are

PC2 (17.7%) — tube girth. tube_diam (-0.6) and keel_diam (-0.49) dominate, with height also loading. A plant can be tall and thin-tubed, or short and fat-tubed, at any overall size.
PC3 (15.3%) — wings. wingsprea (-0.55) and wing2_length (-0.42) dominate. How far the trap’s forked appendages spread, independent of size and tube girth.
This is PCA doing its job: three independent descriptions of shape, out of ten entangled measurements.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
section: Scores: Putting the Plants on the Map
text:
Scores: Putting the Plants on the Map



What scores are

A score is one plant’s value on one component — its coordinate in the new space.
pca_result$x holds them, one row per plant.


## # A tibble: 6 × 5
##   plant_id site    PC1   PC2   PC3
##      <int> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
## 1        1 TJH   -1.92  0.08  1.53
## 2        2 TJH    3.35  1.53  0.75
## 3        3 TJH    0.92 -0.03  0.25
## 4        4 TJH   -0.98  0.24 -0.24
## 5        5 TJH    1.15 -1.02  1.54
## 6        6 TJH   -1.37 -0.61  0.85













This is an ordination: plants ordered along interpretable axes.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
The Biplot



Reading it

Points = plants (scores). Arrows = variables (loadings).
Arrow length = how strongly that variable is represented in this plane.
Angle between arrows = correlation: small angle → positively correlated; 90° → uncorrelated; 180° → negatively correlated.
A plant lying out along an arrow is high in that variable.
HD plants sit to the right — and because PC1 loadings are negative, right means small. HD grows the smallest plants.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text: Part 6 · A First NMDS

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
section: Why the Fish Data Needs a Different Tool
text:
Why the Fish Data Needs a Different Tool



PCA would be the wrong choice here

52.1% zeros, counts spanning orders of magnitude, and a strong non-linear gradient from headwater to lowland.
PCA would impose Euclidean distance, treat shared absences as similarity, and spread the sites along a meaningless horseshoe.
NMDS instead:

Compute Bray–Curtis dissimilarities.
Drop the sites onto a 2-D map at random.
Nudge them until the rank order of map distances matches the rank order of real dissimilarities as closely as possible.
Report stress — how badly it still fails.





nmds <- metaMDS(doubs_mat,
                distance = "bray",
                k = 2, trymax = 50,
                trace = 0)


round(nmds$stress, 3)
## [1] 0.074


Stress rules of thumb: < 0.05 excellent · < 0.1 good · < 0.2 usable · > 0.3 meaningless.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
The NMDS Map













What to notice

Sites arrange along a gradient, in roughly their real upstream-to-downstream order — which NMDS was never told.
Stress = 0.074: a good 2-D fit.
The axes mean nothing. No variance explained, no loadings; the map can be rotated or reflected freely.
Contrast the PCA biplot, whose axes carried percentages and whose arrows carried meaning.







Note



Week 15 takes this apart properly: the algorithm, Shepard diagrams, choosing k, and fitting environmental vectors.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text: Part 7 · Testing Group Differences

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Do the Sites Actually Differ?



Route 1 — ANOVA on component scores

PC scores are ordinary continuous variables, and they are uncorrelated with one another by construction — so you may put them straight into the ANOVA you already know.
One test per component, each answering a different question about shape.


map_dfr(c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3"), \(k) {
  a <- summary(aov(pc_scores[[k]] ~ pc_scores$site))[[1]]
  tibble(PC = k, F = round(a[1, 4], 2),
         p = signif(a[1, 5], 3))
})
## # A tibble: 3 × 3
##   PC        F          p
##   <chr> <dbl>      <dbl>
## 1 PC1    11.3 0.00000275
## 2 PC2     4.6 0.00502   
## 3 PC3    13.8 0.00000022




What it says

All three components differ significantly among sites.
Sites differ in size (PC1), in tube girth (PC2) and in wing spread (PC3) — the sites are not simply scaled versions of one another.
The caveat: this is three tests on three axes chosen by the data themselves. It is a reasonable description, not a clean confirmatory test.







Warning



PCA was run on all 87 plants at once, ignoring site. The components are therefore not independent of the grouping you then test. Treat these p-values as exploratory.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Which Sites Differ, and How?



##  site emmean    SE df lower.CL upper.CL .group
##  DG   -1.024 0.383 83   -1.786   -0.262  a    
##  LEH  -0.659 0.383 83   -1.421    0.103  ab   
##  TJH   0.423 0.383 83   -0.339    1.185   b   
##  HD    2.626 0.553 83    1.526    3.726    c  
## 
## Confidence level used: 0.95 
## P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates 
## significance level used: alpha = 0.05 
## NOTE: If two or more means share the same grouping symbol,
##       then we cannot show them to be different.
##       But we also did not show them to be the same.



Reading it in biology, not in numbers

HD sits alone in its own group with the highest PC1 score.
PC1 loadings are negative, so a high score means a small plant: HD grows the smallest cobra lilies, and significantly so.
DG sits at the other end — the largest plants.
LEH and TJH overlap in the middle.







Important



This is the sign trap in action. “HD has the highest PC1” and “HD has the smallest plants” are the same sentence. Always translate before you write.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
section: Route 2 — PERMANOVA on the Distance Matrix
text:
Route 2 — PERMANOVA on the Distance Matrix



Test the whole community at once

PERMANOVA skips the ordination entirely: it partitions the dissimilarity matrix directly and gets its p-value by permuting group labels.
One test on all 10 variables at once, instead of one per component.


adonis2(darl_scaled ~ site,
        data   = darlingtonia,
        method = "euclidean")
## Permutation test for adonis under reduced model
## Permutation: free
## Number of permutations: 999
## 
## adonis2(formula = darl_scaled ~ site, data = darlingtonia, method = "euclidean")
##          Df SumOfSqs      R2      F Pr(>F)    
## Model     3    213.7 0.24849 9.1483  0.001 ***
## Residual 83    646.3 0.75151                  
## Total    86    860.0 1.00000                  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




Why it is worth knowing now

No normality assumption, no multivariate normality, no equal covariance matrices.
Works on any dissimilarity you can justify — which is why it is the natural partner to NMDS.
R2 is the fraction of total dissimilarity attributable to site — read it like an ANOVA’s \(\eta^2\).

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
PERMANOVA’s One Real Assumption



Equal dispersion

A significant PERMANOVA means groups differ in centroid (location) or merely in spread (dispersion).
betadisper() tells them apart.


disp <- betadisper(
  vegdist(darl_scaled, method = "euclidean"),
  darlingtonia$site)

anova(disp)
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Response: Distances
##           Df  Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)  
## Groups     3  11.629  3.8762   2.743 0.04828 *
## Residuals 83 117.290  1.4131                  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




Reading the two together

Significant PERMANOVA + non-significant dispersion → groups genuinely sit in different places. Clean result.
Both significant → the location difference may be partly a spread difference. Say so.


round(tapply(disp$distances,
             darlingtonia$site, mean), 2)
##   DG   HD  LEH  TJH 
## 2.17 1.98 2.98 2.44
