Here both are significant: LEH is the most variable. The site effect is strong enough (R² = 0.25) that it is not only dispersion — but an honest write-up mentions it.







Note



Week 15 develops PERMANOVA and ANOSIM in full on the Doubs data.

A Decision Guide









Your data
Your question
Use




Continuous traits, correlated, few zeros
What are the main axes of variation?
PCA (week 14)


Species counts, many zeros
How do communities arrange along a gradient?
NMDS (week 15)


Any dissimilarity matrix
Which objects group together?
Cluster analysis (week 15)


Any dissimilarity matrix

PERMANOVA / ANOSIM (week 15)


Continuous, multivariate normal
Do groups differ, parametrically?
MANOVA


Categorical variables
Same questions, categorical data
CA / MCA





Two questions settle almost every case:

What kind of data is it? → fixes the distance metric.
Description or test? → fixes ordination vs. PERMANOVA.

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
section: Assumptions and Things That Go Wrong
text:
Assumptions and Things That Go Wrong



Check before you ordinate

Sample size: at least 3× as many objects as variables; 50+ is comfortable. We have 87 plants and 10 variables.
Correlation: if nothing correlates, PCA has nothing to collapse. KMO() gives a sampling-adequacy score; ours is 0.76 (> 0.6 acceptable, > 0.8 good).
Linearity: eigen methods see only linear relationships.
Outliers: one extreme object can define an entire component.




Common mistakes

❌ Not standardizing variables with different units
❌ Euclidean distance on species counts
❌ Reading meaning into a sign flip
❌ Interpreting components that explain 3% of the variance
❌ Quoting “% variance explained” for an NMDS — it has none
❌ Calling a significant PERMANOVA a centroid difference without checking dispersion
❌ Treating an exploratory ordination as a confirmatory test

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Reporting Multivariate Results



Methods

“Ten morphological and biomass variables measured on 87 Darlingtonia californica plants from four sites were standardized to zero mean and unit variance and subjected to principal component analysis (prcomp(), R 4.6.1). Components with eigenvalues > 1 were retained. Site differences were tested with PERMANOVA on Euclidean distances (vegan::adonis2(), 999 permutations), with homogeneity of multivariate dispersion checked using betadisper().”




Results — always state

% variance for every component you interpret
Loadings for the retained components
The biological reading of each axis, sign resolved
The test result with its dispersion check



Never report

All 10 components when 3 are meaningful
Loadings below |0.3|
Raw eigenvalues in place of percentages
Every individual score

title: Lecture: Multivariate Statistics
text:
Summary



What we did today

Standardized 10 variables onto a common footing, because units are not biology.
Built a dissimilarity matrix and learned that the choice of metric — Euclidean, Manhattan, Bray–Curtis, Jaccard — is the modelling decision.
Saw the map of ordination methods and where each one lives in this course.
Ran a PCA: 10 variables → 82.8% of the variation in three interpretable axes (size, tube girth, wings).
Ran an NMDS on fish counts and recovered a river gradient at stress = 0.074.




What to carry forward

The distance matrix is the hub. Everything downstream reads from it.
Component signs are arbitrary — translate into biology before you write a sentence.
Ordination describes; PERMANOVA tests. Do not confuse them.
Next week: what prcomp() is actually solving — eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and PCA in full.
Week 15: NMDS, cluster analysis, PERMANOVA and ANOSIM in full.

Whitlock & Schluter does not cover multivariate methods.

both fixed — rare

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text: Part 4 · The Nested Design Model

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Nested Design: Linear Model Structure


Consider a nested design with:

p levels of factor A (i = 1…p) — e.g., 4 grazing levels
q levels of factor B (j = 1…q), nested within each level of A — e.g., 4 different patches per grazing level
n replicates (k = 1…n) in each combination of A and B — e.g., 5 replicate quadrats in each patch in each grazing level

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: Calculating Means in a Nested Design
text:
Calculating Means in a Nested Design


We can calculate several means:

Overall mean (across all levels of A and B) = \(\bar{y}\)
A mean for each level of A (across all levels of B in that A) = \(\bar{y}_i\)
A mean for each level of B within each A = \(\bar{y}_{j(i)}\)

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text: Nested Design Means, Visualized

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
The Nested Design Linear Model


\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_{j(i)} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]

\(y_{ijk}\) is the response variable — the value of the k-th replicate in the j-th level of B in the i-th level of A (e.g., algal biomass in the 3rd quadrat, in the 2nd patch, in the low-grazing treatment)
\(\mu\) is the overall mean (overall average algal biomass)








Tip


🖐 Notice
This looks almost identical to the two-way ANOVA model — the difference is entirely in the subscript: \(\beta_{j(i)}\), not \(\beta_j\). B only exists inside a specific A.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: Fixed and Random Effects in the Nested Model
text:
Fixed and Random Effects in the Nested Model


\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_{j(i)} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]

\(\alpha_i\) is the fixed effect of factor A — the difference between the average biomass in all low-grazing-level quadrats and the overall mean
\(\beta_{j(i)}\) is the random effect of factor B nested within factor A — usually a random variable measuring variance among all possible levels of B within each level of A (variance among all possible patches that could have been used in the low-grazing treatment)








Note


✅ Key idea
B being random is the whole point of nesting: you don’t care about these specific patches — you care about patch-to-patch variability in general.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: The Error Term in the Nested Model
text:
The Error Term in the Nested Model


\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_{j(i)} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]

\(\varepsilon_{ijk}\) is the error term — the unexplained variance associated with the k-th replicate in the j-th level of B in the i-th level of A
\(\alpha_i\) is the effect of the i-th level of A: \(\mu_i - \mu\)
\(\varepsilon_{ijk}\): the difference between the observed algal biomass in the 3rd quadrat in the 2nd patch in the low-grazing treatment, and the predicted biomass (the average biomass in that 2nd patch in the low-grazing treatment)








Tip


🖐 Notice
The residual is measured against the cell mean (this specific patch), not the treatment mean — that’s what makes it “nested,” arithmetically.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text: Part 5 · Partitioning Variance

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: Analysis of Variance: Residual and Total
text:
Analysis of Variance: Residual and Total



\(SS_{resid}\) is the difference between each observation and the mean for its level of factor B, summed over all observations
\(SS_{total} = SS_A + SS_B + SS_{resid}\)
SS can be turned into MS by dividing by the appropriate df

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Analysis of Variance: SSA


As before, we partition the variance in the response variable using SS. \(SS_A\) is the SS of differences between the mean in each level of A and the overall mean.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Analysis of Variance: SSB


\(SS_B\) is the SS of the difference between the mean in each level of B and the mean of the corresponding level of A, summed across all levels of A.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text: The Nested ANOVA Table

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text: Part 6 · Hypotheses and Assumptions

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Null Hypotheses: Factor A


Two hypotheses are tested on values of MS. 1. No effects of factor A — assuming A is fixed:

\(H_0(A)\): \(\mu_1 = \mu_2 = ... = \mu_i = \mu\)
Same as in 1-factor ANOVA, using means from B factors nested within each level of A
(no difference in algal biomass across all grazing levels: \(\mu_{none} = \mu_{low} = \mu_{med} = \mu_{high}\))

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Null Hypotheses: Factor B


2. No effects of factor B nested in A — assuming B is random:

\(H_0(B)\): \(\sigma^2_\beta = 0\) (no variance added due to differences between all possible levels of B)
(no variance added due to differences between patches)

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Conclusions from the Analysis


Conclusion:
“Significant variation between replicate patches within each treatment, but no significant difference in the amount of filamentous algae between treatments.”

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Unbalanced Nested Designs


Unequal sample sizes can arise from:

An uneven number of B levels within each A
An uneven number of replicates within each level of B

The second kind is the one that bites. Patch means stop being equally precise, so:

aov(Error(...)) loses its exact F-tests
averaging to patch means stops being equivalent to the nested test
you can no longer weight patches by their precision without \(\sigma^2_{within}\)

The principled fix is a mixed model — Week 11.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Nested Design Assumptions


As usual, we assume: equal variance, normality, no outliers, independence of observations.
Equal variance + normality need to be assessed at both levels:

Since means for each level of B within each A are used for the H-test about A, need to assess whether those means meet normality and equal variance
Examine residuals for the H-test about B
Transformations can be used








Warning


⚠️ Watch out!
This is the part people most often get wrong: checking assumptions on the raw data isn’t enough for a nested design — you need to check them at the level each hypothesis test actually operates on.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Manual Nested ANOVA — Setting Up


In this experimental design, patch is nested within treat because each patch received only one treatment level — a hierarchical design where the effect of patches must be considered within each treatment (Quinn & Keough 2002).
We’ll use a traditional nested ANOVA. You could make this easy by averaging algae per patch and running a one-way ANOVA on the 16 patch means. On a perfectly balanced design that gives the identical F, df and p — but it throws away the within-patch variance, and the moment the design stops being balanced that shortcut starts costing you. We come back to both halves of this at the end of the lecture.
This first attempt is really a regular factorial ANOVA — not appropriate, since it’s pseudoreplicated. Also, the F-value for Treat is using \(MS_{resid}\) when it should use \(MS_{treat:patch}\).


u_fact_model <- aov(algae ~ treat + treat:patch, data = u_df)
cat("Factorial model summary:\n\n")
## Factorial model summary:
summary(u_fact_model)
##             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value       Pr(>F)    
## treat        3  14429    4810  16.108 0.0000000658 ***
## treat:patch 12  21242    1770   5.928 0.0000008323 ***
## Residuals   64  19110     299                         
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: Why the Factorial ANOVA Is Not Correct
text:
Why the Factorial ANOVA Is Not Correct



We can correct this by specifying the error term
The MS needed for the F-value is really MS(patch nested in treatment), because those are the true replicates
We can specify that — the problem is this approach can’t really handle unbalanced designs



# Error(patch) -- not Error(treat:patch). Patch IDs are already unique
# (1-16) and each patch sits in exactly one treatment, so naming the patch
# alone is enough. Writing treat:patch asks for 4 x 16 = 64 combinations
# when only 16 exist, which makes R warn "Error() model is singular".
# Both give identical numbers; this one does it without the warning.
u_nested_model <- aov(algae ~ treat + Error(patch), data = u_df)
cat("Correctly specified nested ANOVA:\n\n")
## Correctly specified nested ANOVA:
summary(u_nested_model)
## 
## Error: patch
##           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)  
## treat      3  14429    4810   2.717 0.0913 .
## Residuals 12  21242    1770                 
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Error: Within
##           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
## Residuals 64  19110   298.6

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Same Numerator, Different Denominator


Both models used the same 80 quadrats and produced the same sums of squares. Only the F-test’s denominator changed:











MS treat
÷ MS error
= F
p




Naive factorial
4810
÷ 299 (quadrats)
16.11
0.00000007


Nested
4810
÷ 1770 (patches)
2.72
0.091









Important


The p-value moved by six orders of magnitude.
The naive model tested the treatment against variation between quadrats within a patch — but quadrats are not what we assigned treatments to. Patches are. 80 quadrats, but only 16 patches: 12 denominator df, not 64.










Note


✅ How to find the right denominator
Ask: what did I randomly assign the treatment to?
That unit — patch here — supplies the error term. Everything measured inside it is a subsample, and subsamples tell you about measurement noise, not about treatment effects.









Tip


🖐 Notice MS(patch) is large
1770 vs 299 — patches genuinely differ from one another. That variability is real biology, and the nested model makes you pay for it. The naive model pretended it was not there.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: Where You Have Seen This Before
text:
Where You Have Seen This Before


This is the pine needle problem again, one level up:




Our pine study
This urchin study




8 needles per side
5 quadrats per patch


within one tree
within one patch


4 trees are the replicates
16 patches are the replicates


64 rows, n = 4
80 rows, n = 16




In Week 1 we solved it by averaging each tree to one number. That works, and it is honest.






Note


✅ Key idea
Averaging throws the subsamples away. Nesting uses them — to estimate how noisy your measurements are — while still refusing to count them as replicates. On a balanced design the treatment test comes out the same either way; the variance components never do, and once the design is unbalanced neither does the test.










Warning


⚠️ The limit of aov(Error(...))
This syntax needs a (near-)balanced design. Ours is perfectly balanced — 4 patches per treatment, 5 quadrats per patch — so it works.
Real data usually is not. That is the problem mixed models solve, and it is where we go next.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: How Do I Know If My Design Is Nested?
text:
How Do I Know If My Design Is Nested?


Three questions, in order. Ask them of your own data before you fit anything.
1. What did I apply the treatment to? → Whole patches. Not quadrats.
2. Does every level of B appear under every level of A? → Patch 7 only ever received the 66% density. It cannot appear under 100%. → No ⇒ nested. (Yes ⇒ crossed/factorial.)
3. How many of those units do I have per treatment? → 4 patches, not 20 quadrats. That is your n.






Important


The answer to Q1 is your error term.
aov(algae ~ treat + Error(patch), data = u_df)
#                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^
#                   the thing treatments were assigned to










Tip


🖐 A quick tell
If two rows of your data share a value for the thing you randomized, they are not independent replicates of it.
Two quadrats in patch 3 share patch 3. Two needles on one tree share that tree.









Warning


⚠️ Nested factors are random
We are not asking “is patch 7 different from patch 12?” — those specific patches are of no interest. They are a sample of possible patches, so patch enters as a random effect.
The factor above it (treat) is fixed: those four densities are exactly the ones we care about.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: Part 9 · Post-Hoc, and What the Test Really Is
text: Part 9 · Post-Hoc, and What the Test Really Is

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Post-Hoc on a Nested Model



u_emm <- emmeans(u_nested_model, ~ treat)
u_emm
##  treat emmean   SE df lower.CL upper.CL
##  0%      39.2 9.41 12    18.70     59.7
##  33%     19.0 9.41 12    -1.50     39.5
##  66%     21.6 9.41 12     1.05     42.0
##  100%     1.3 9.41 12   -19.20     21.8
## 
## Warning: EMMs are biased unless design is perfectly balanced 
## Confidence level used: 0.95

multcomp::cld(u_emm, Letters = letters)
##  treat emmean   SE df lower.CL upper.CL .group
##  100%     1.3 9.41 12   -19.20     21.8  a    
##  33%     19.0 9.41 12    -1.50     39.5  a    
##  66%     21.6 9.41 12     1.05     42.0  a    
##  0%      39.2 9.41 12    18.70     59.7  a    
## 
## Warning: EMMs are biased unless design is perfectly balanced 
## Confidence level used: 0.95 
## P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates 
## significance level used: alpha = 0.05 
## NOTE: If two or more means share the same grouping symbol,
##       then we cannot show them to be different.
##       But we also did not show them to be the same.


Means from 1.3 % to 39.2 % — a thirty-fold spread — and every one of them shares the letter a.
The SE is 9.41 on every mean, and it comes from \(MS_{B(A)}\), the patch stratum. With only 4 patches per treatment there is simply not enough replication to separate them.






Warning


⚠️ emmeans will warn you
“EMMs are biased unless design is perfectly balanced.” Ours is balanced — 4 patches per treatment, 5 quadrats per patch — so read past it. The warning fires on any aovlist object.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: The Nested F Is a One-Way ANOVA on the Patch Means — If Balanced
text:
The Nested F Is a One-Way ANOVA on the Patch Means — If Balanced



# Collapse all 80 quadrats to the 16 patch means ...
patch_df <- u_df %>%
  group_by(treat, patch) %>%
  summarise(mean_algae = mean(algae), .groups = "drop")

# ... and run an ordinary one-way ANOVA on those 16 rows
summary(aov(mean_algae ~ treat, data = patch_df))
##             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)  
## treat        3   2886   961.9   2.717 0.0913 .
## Residuals   12   4248   354.0                 
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


F = 2.717 on 3 and 12 df, p = 0.091 — identical to the nested model, to every digit. The SS are exactly one fifth, and dividing numerator and denominator by the same 5 leaves F untouched.






Note


✅ What the subsamples bought you
Not df for the treatment test — that was 12 either way. They made each patch’s value more precise, and let you estimate the within-patch variance. For power against the treatment you need more patches: twenty quadrats in four patches is still n = 4.









Important


⚠️ All of this depends on BALANCE — 5 quadrats in every patch. Change that and the equality breaks. Next slide.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: …And Why Averaging Breaks When You Are Not
text:
…And Why Averaging Breaks When You Are Not



# a storm scours all but one quadrat in four patches
thin_df <- u_df %>%
  filter(!(patch %in% c(2, 6, 10, 14) & quad > 1))

# nested ANOVA on the thinned data
summary(aov(algae ~ treat + Error(patch), thin_df))[[1]]
##           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
## treat      3   8837    2946    2.25  0.135
## Residuals 12  15713    1309

# the patch-mean shortcut, same data
pm <- thin_df %>% group_by(treat, patch) %>%
  summarise(m = mean(algae), .groups = "drop")
anova(aov(m ~ treat, pm))
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Response: m
##           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)  
## treat      3 3174.1  1058.0  2.9628 0.07493 .
## Residuals 12 4285.2   357.1                  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1







nested aov
patch means




balanced
F=2.72, p=0.091
F=2.72, p=0.091


unbalanced
F=2.25, p=0.135
F=2.96, p=0.075




Same data — and the shortcut is now the most optimistic.






Important


⚠️ The patch means are no longer equally precise
\[\operatorname{Var}(\bar y_j) = \sigma^2_{patch} + \frac{\sigma^2_{within}}{n_j}\]
A patch with 1 quadrat is far noisier than one with 5 — but the ANOVA on the means treats them as interchangeable, violating its own equal-variance assumption by construction.
To weight them you need \(\sigma^2_{within}\) — which averaging already threw away. That is the cost of losing sight of the variance inside the nested groups.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Reporting a Nested ANOVA








Note


How to report this result
“Algal cover did not differ significantly among urchin density treatments (nested ANOVA, F₃,₁₂ = 2.72, p = 0.091), with patches treated as a random factor nested within treatment. Variation among patches within treatments was substantial, accounting for approximately 50% of the total variance (σ²_patch = 294, σ²_within = 299; n = 4 patches per treatment, 5 quadrats per patch).”



The three things people get wrong:

The df. It is F(3, 12) — from the patch stratum, not the 64 on the “Within” line. F(3, 64) is the wrong test.
Silence about the nesting. Say “nested” and name the random factor; “F = 2.72” alone tells a reader nothing.
Throwing away the patch variance. It is a result, not a nuisance — here it is half the story.



# Variance components, straight from
# the two mean squares
MS_patch  <- 1770.2   # Error: patch
MS_within <- 298.6    # Error: Within
n_quad    <- 5        # quadrats per patch

var_patch  <- (MS_patch - MS_within) / n_quad
var_within <- MS_within

cat("among patches:", round(var_patch, 1), "
")
## among patches: 294.3
cat("within patch: ", round(var_within, 1), "
")
## within patch:  298.6
cat("% among patches:",
    round(100 * var_patch /
          (var_patch + var_within), 1), "%
")
## % among patches: 49.6 %







Tip


🖐 Half the variance is between patches
Ignore that and you are pretending 80 quadrats are 80 independent observations. They are closer to 16.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Wrap-up — What You Did Today



Told a nested design from a crossed one, and learned the three questions that decide it
Found the right error term by asking what the treatment was applied to
Watched the same 80 quadrats give F = 16.11 (p < 0.0000001) the wrong way and F = 2.72 (p = 0.091) the right way
Proved the nested F is just a one-way ANOVA on the 16 patch means — and watched that equality fall apart the moment the design went unbalanced
Estimated variance components — half the variation lives between patches
Reported it with the correct degrees of freedom








Important


⚠️ The mistake this lecture exists to prevent
Using the residual mean square as your denominator when the treatment was applied to something coarser than a single measurement.
It inflates F, shrinks p, and it is the most common error in ecological field experiments (Hurlbert 1984).

Take a dataset you actually care about — yours, or one from a paper — and answer the three questions from “How Do I Know If My Design Is Nested?”.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text: Part 4 · The Nested Design Model

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Nested Design: Linear Model Structure


Consider a nested design with:

p levels of factor A (i = 1…p) — e.g., 4 grazing levels
q levels of factor B (j = 1…q), nested within each level of A — e.g., 4 different patches per grazing level
n replicates (k = 1…n) in each combination of A and B — e.g., 5 replicate quadrats in each patch in each grazing level

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: Calculating Means in a Nested Design
text:
Calculating Means in a Nested Design


We can calculate several means:

Overall mean (across all levels of A and B) = \(\bar{y}\)
A mean for each level of A (across all levels of B in that A) = \(\bar{y}_i\)
A mean for each level of B within each A = \(\bar{y}_{j(i)}\)

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text: Nested Design Means, Visualized

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
The Nested Design Linear Model


\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_{j(i)} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]

\(y_{ijk}\) is the response variable — the value of the k-th replicate in the j-th level of B in the i-th level of A (e.g., algal biomass in the 3rd quadrat, in the 2nd patch, in the low-grazing treatment)
\(\mu\) is the overall mean (overall average algal biomass)








Tip



🖐 Notice
This looks almost identical to the two-way ANOVA model — the difference is entirely in the subscript: \(\beta_{j(i)}\), not \(\beta_j\). B only exists inside a specific A.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: Fixed and Random Effects in the Nested Model
text:
Fixed and Random Effects in the Nested Model


\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_{j(i)} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]

\(\alpha_i\) is the fixed effect of factor A — the difference between the average biomass in all low-grazing-level quadrats and the overall mean
\(\beta_{j(i)}\) is the random effect of factor B nested within factor A — usually a random variable measuring variance among all possible levels of B within each level of A (variance among all possible patches that could have been used in the low-grazing treatment)








Note



✅ Key idea
B being random is the whole point of nesting: you don’t care about these specific patches — you care about patch-to-patch variability in general.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: The Error Term in the Nested Model
text:
The Error Term in the Nested Model


\[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_{j(i)} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]

\(\varepsilon_{ijk}\) is the error term — the unexplained variance associated with the k-th replicate in the j-th level of B in the i-th level of A
\(\alpha_i\) is the effect of the i-th level of A: \(\mu_i - \mu\)
\(\varepsilon_{ijk}\): the difference between the observed algal biomass in the 3rd quadrat in the 2nd patch in the low-grazing treatment, and the predicted biomass (the average biomass in that 2nd patch in the low-grazing treatment)








Tip



🖐 Notice
The residual is measured against the cell mean (this specific patch), not the treatment mean — that’s what makes it “nested,” arithmetically.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text: Part 5 · Partitioning Variance

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: Analysis of Variance: Residual and Total
text:
Analysis of Variance: Residual and Total



\(SS_{resid}\) is the difference between each observation and the mean for its level of factor B, summed over all observations
\(SS_{total} = SS_A + SS_B + SS_{resid}\)
SS can be turned into MS by dividing by the appropriate df

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Analysis of Variance: SSA


As before, we partition the variance in the response variable using SS. \(SS_A\) is the SS of differences between the mean in each level of A and the overall mean.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Analysis of Variance: SSB


\(SS_B\) is the SS of the difference between the mean in each level of B and the mean of the corresponding level of A, summed across all levels of A.

text: Part 6 · Hypotheses and Assumptions

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Null Hypotheses: Factor A


Two hypotheses are tested on values of MS. 1. No effects of factor A — assuming A is fixed:

\(H_0(A)\): \(\mu_1 = \mu_2 = ... = \mu_i = \mu\)
Same as in 1-factor ANOVA, using means from B factors nested within each level of A
(no difference in algal biomass across all grazing levels: \(\mu_{none} = \mu_{low} = \mu_{med} = \mu_{high}\))

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Null Hypotheses: Factor B


2. No effects of factor B nested in A — assuming B is random:

\(H_0(B)\): \(\sigma^2_\beta = 0\) (no variance added due to differences between all possible levels of B)
(no variance added due to differences between patches)

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Conclusions from the Analysis


Conclusion:
“Significant variation between replicate patches within each treatment, but no significant difference in the amount of filamentous algae between treatments.”

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Unbalanced Nested Designs


Unequal sample sizes can arise from:

An uneven number of B levels within each A
An uneven number of replicates within each level of B

The second kind is the one that bites. Patch means stop being equally precise, so:

aov(Error(...)) loses its exact F-tests
averaging to patch means stops being equivalent to the nested test
you can no longer weight patches by their precision without \(\sigma^2_{within}\)

The principled fix is a mixed model — Week 11.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Nested Design Assumptions


As usual, we assume: equal variance, normality, no outliers, independence of observations.
Equal variance + normality need to be assessed at both levels:

Since means for each level of B within each A are used for the H-test about A, need to assess whether those means meet normality and equal variance
Examine residuals for the H-test about B
Transformations can be used








Warning



⚠️ Watch out!
This is the part people most often get wrong: checking assumptions on the raw data isn’t enough for a nested design — you need to check them at the level each hypothesis test actually operates on.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Manual Nested ANOVA — Setting Up


In this experimental design, patch is nested within treat because each patch received only one treatment level — a hierarchical design where the effect of patches must be considered within each treatment (Quinn & Keough 2002).
We’ll use a traditional nested ANOVA. You could make this easy by averaging algae per patch and running a one-way ANOVA on the 16 patch means. On a perfectly balanced design that gives the identical F, df and p — but it throws away the within-patch variance, and the moment the design stops being balanced that shortcut starts costing you. We come back to both halves of this at the end of the lecture.
This first attempt is really a regular factorial ANOVA — not appropriate, since it’s pseudoreplicated. Also, the F-value for Treat is using \(MS_{resid}\) when it should use \(MS_{treat:patch}\).


u_fact_model <- aov(algae ~ treat + treat:patch, data = u_df)
cat("Factorial model summary:\n\n")
## Factorial model summary:
summary(u_fact_model)
##             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value       Pr(>F)    
## treat        3  14429    4810  16.108 0.0000000658 ***
## treat:patch 12  21242    1770   5.928 0.0000008323 ***
## Residuals   64  19110     299                         
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: Why the Factorial ANOVA Is Not Correct
text:
Why the Factorial ANOVA Is Not Correct



We can correct this by specifying the error term
The MS needed for the F-value is really MS(patch nested in treatment), because those are the true replicates
We can specify that — the problem is this approach can’t really handle unbalanced designs



# Error(patch) -- not Error(treat:patch). Patch IDs are already unique
# (1-16) and each patch sits in exactly one treatment, so naming the patch
# alone is enough. Writing treat:patch asks for 4 x 16 = 64 combinations
# when only 16 exist, which makes R warn "Error() model is singular".
# Both give identical numbers; this one does it without the warning.
u_nested_model <- aov(algae ~ treat + Error(patch), data = u_df)
cat("Correctly specified nested ANOVA:\n\n")
## Correctly specified nested ANOVA:
summary(u_nested_model)
## 
## Error: patch
##           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)  
## treat      3  14429    4810   2.717 0.0913 .
## Residuals 12  21242    1770                 
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Error: Within
##           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
## Residuals 64  19110   298.6

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Same Numerator, Different Denominator


Both models used the same 80 quadrats and produced the same sums of squares. Only the F-test’s denominator changed:











MS treat
÷ MS error
= F
p




Naive factorial
4810
÷ 299 (quadrats)
16.11
0.00000007


Nested
4810
÷ 1770 (patches)
2.72
0.091









Important



The p-value moved by six orders of magnitude.
The naive model tested the treatment against variation between quadrats within a patch — but quadrats are not what we assigned treatments to. Patches are. 80 quadrats, but only 16 patches: 12 denominator df, not 64.









Note



✅ How to find the right denominator
Ask: what did I randomly assign the treatment to?
That unit — patch here — supplies the error term. Everything measured inside it is a subsample, and subsamples tell you about measurement noise, not about treatment effects.








Tip



🖐 Notice MS(patch) is large
1770 vs 299 — patches genuinely differ from one another. That variability is real biology, and the nested model makes you pay for it. The naive model pretended it was not there.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: Where You Have Seen This Before
text:
Where You Have Seen This Before


This is the pine needle problem again, one level up:




Our pine study
This urchin study




8 needles per side
5 quadrats per patch


within one tree
within one patch


4 trees are the replicates
16 patches are the replicates


64 rows, n = 4
80 rows, n = 16




In Week 1 we solved it by averaging each tree to one number. That works, and it is honest.






Note



✅ Key idea
Averaging throws the subsamples away. Nesting uses them — to estimate how noisy your measurements are — while still refusing to count them as replicates. On a balanced design the treatment test comes out the same either way; the variance components never do, and once the design is unbalanced neither does the test.









Warning



⚠️ The limit of aov(Error(...))
This syntax needs a (near-)balanced design. Ours is perfectly balanced — 4 patches per treatment, 5 quadrats per patch — so it works.
Real data usually is not. That is the problem mixed models solve, and it is where we go next.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: How Do I Know If My Design Is Nested?
text:
How Do I Know If My Design Is Nested?


Three questions, in order. Ask them of your own data before you fit anything.
1. What did I apply the treatment to? → Whole patches. Not quadrats.
2. Does every level of B appear under every level of A? → Patch 7 only ever received the 66% density. It cannot appear under 100%. → No ⇒ nested. (Yes ⇒ crossed/factorial.)
3. How many of those units do I have per treatment? → 4 patches, not 20 quadrats. That is your n.






Important



The answer to Q1 is your error term.
aov(algae ~ treat + Error(patch), data = u_df)
#                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^
#                   the thing treatments were assigned to









Tip



🖐 A quick tell
If two rows of your data share a value for the thing you randomized, they are not independent replicates of it.
Two quadrats in patch 3 share patch 3. Two needles on one tree share that tree.








Warning



⚠️ Nested factors are random
We are not asking “is patch 7 different from patch 12?” — those specific patches are of no interest. They are a sample of possible patches, so patch enters as a random effect.
The factor above it (treat) is fixed: those four densities are exactly the ones we care about.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: Part 9 · Post-Hoc, and What the Test Really Is
text: Part 9 · Post-Hoc, and What the Test Really Is

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Post-Hoc on a Nested Model



u_emm <- emmeans(u_nested_model, ~ treat)
u_emm
##  treat emmean   SE df lower.CL upper.CL
##  0%      39.2 9.41 12    18.70     59.7
##  33%     19.0 9.41 12    -1.50     39.5
##  66%     21.6 9.41 12     1.05     42.0
##  100%     1.3 9.41 12   -19.20     21.8
## 
## Warning: EMMs are biased unless design is perfectly balanced 
## Confidence level used: 0.95

multcomp::cld(u_emm, Letters = letters)
##  treat emmean   SE df lower.CL upper.CL .group
##  100%     1.3 9.41 12   -19.20     21.8  a    
##  33%     19.0 9.41 12    -1.50     39.5  a    
##  66%     21.6 9.41 12     1.05     42.0  a    
##  0%      39.2 9.41 12    18.70     59.7  a    
## 
## Warning: EMMs are biased unless design is perfectly balanced 
## Confidence level used: 0.95 
## P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates 
## significance level used: alpha = 0.05 
## NOTE: If two or more means share the same grouping symbol,
##       then we cannot show them to be different.
##       But we also did not show them to be the same.


Means from 1.3 % to 39.2 % — a thirty-fold spread — and every one of them shares the letter a.
The SE is 9.41 on every mean, and it comes from \(MS_{B(A)}\), the patch stratum. With only 4 patches per treatment there is simply not enough replication to separate them.






Warning



⚠️ emmeans will warn you
“EMMs are biased unless design is perfectly balanced.” Ours is balanced — 4 patches per treatment, 5 quadrats per patch — so read past it. The warning fires on any aovlist object.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: The Nested F Is a One-Way ANOVA on the Patch Means — If Balanced
text:
The Nested F Is a One-Way ANOVA on the Patch Means — If Balanced



# Collapse all 80 quadrats to the 16 patch means ...
patch_df <- u_df %>%
  group_by(treat, patch) %>%
  summarise(mean_algae = mean(algae), .groups = "drop")

# ... and run an ordinary one-way ANOVA on those 16 rows
summary(aov(mean_algae ~ treat, data = patch_df))
##             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)  
## treat        3   2886   961.9   2.717 0.0913 .
## Residuals   12   4248   354.0                 
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


F = 2.717 on 3 and 12 df, p = 0.091 — identical to the nested model, to every digit. The SS are exactly one fifth, and dividing numerator and denominator by the same 5 leaves F untouched.






Note



✅ What the subsamples bought you
Not df for the treatment test — that was 12 either way. They made each patch’s value more precise, and let you estimate the within-patch variance. For power against the treatment you need more patches: twenty quadrats in four patches is still n = 4.








Important



⚠️ All of this depends on BALANCE — 5 quadrats in every patch. Change that and the equality breaks. Next slide.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
section: …And Why Averaging Breaks When You Are Not
text:
…And Why Averaging Breaks When You Are Not



# a storm scours all but one quadrat in four patches
thin_df <- u_df %>%
  filter(!(patch %in% c(2, 6, 10, 14) & quad > 1))

# nested ANOVA on the thinned data
summary(aov(algae ~ treat + Error(patch), thin_df))[[1]]
##           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
## treat      3   8837    2946    2.25  0.135
## Residuals 12  15713    1309

# the patch-mean shortcut, same data
pm <- thin_df %>% group_by(treat, patch) %>%
  summarise(m = mean(algae), .groups = "drop")
anova(aov(m ~ treat, pm))
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Response: m
##           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)  
## treat      3 3174.1  1058.0  2.9628 0.07493 .
## Residuals 12 4285.2   357.1                  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1







nested aov
patch means




balanced
F=2.72, p=0.091
F=2.72, p=0.091


unbalanced
F=2.25, p=0.135
F=2.96, p=0.075




Same data — and the shortcut is now the most optimistic.






Important



⚠️ The patch means are no longer equally precise
\[\operatorname{Var}(\bar y_j) = \sigma^2_{patch} + \frac{\sigma^2_{within}}{n_j}\]
A patch with 1 quadrat is far noisier than one with 5 — but the ANOVA on the means treats them as interchangeable, violating its own equal-variance assumption by construction.
To weight them you need \(\sigma^2_{within}\) — which averaging already threw away. That is the cost of losing sight of the variance inside the nested groups.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Reporting a Nested ANOVA








Note



How to report this result
“Algal cover did not differ significantly among urchin density treatments (nested ANOVA, F₃,₁₂ = 2.72, p = 0.091), with patches treated as a random factor nested within treatment. Variation among patches within treatments was substantial, accounting for approximately 50% of the total variance (σ²_patch = 294, σ²_within = 299; n = 4 patches per treatment, 5 quadrats per patch).”


The three things people get wrong:

The df. It is F(3, 12) — from the patch stratum, not the 64 on the “Within” line. F(3, 64) is the wrong test.
Silence about the nesting. Say “nested” and name the random factor; “F = 2.72” alone tells a reader nothing.
Throwing away the patch variance. It is a result, not a nuisance — here it is half the story.



# Variance components, straight from
# the two mean squares
MS_patch  <- 1770.2   # Error: patch
MS_within <- 298.6    # Error: Within
n_quad    <- 5        # quadrats per patch

var_patch  <- (MS_patch - MS_within) / n_quad
var_within <- MS_within

cat("among patches:", round(var_patch, 1), "
")
## among patches: 294.3
cat("within patch: ", round(var_within, 1), "
")
## within patch:  298.6
cat("% among patches:",
    round(100 * var_patch /
          (var_patch + var_within), 1), "%
")
## % among patches: 49.6 %







Tip



🖐 Half the variance is between patches
Ignore that and you are pretending 80 quadrats are 80 independent observations. They are closer to 16.

title: Lecture: Nested ANOVA
text:
Wrap-up — What You Did Today



Told a nested design from a crossed one, and learned the three questions that decide it
Found the right error term by asking what the treatment was applied to
Watched the same 80 quadrats give F = 16.11 (p < 0.0000001) the wrong way and F = 2.72 (p = 0.091) the right way
Proved the nested F is just a one-way ANOVA on the 16 patch means — and watched that equality fall apart the moment the design went unbalanced
Estimated variance components — half the variation lives between patches
Reported it with the correct degrees of freedom








Important



⚠️ The mistake this lecture exists to prevent
Using the residual mean square as your denominator when the treatment was applied to something coarser than a single measurement.
It inflates F, shrinks p, and it is the most common error in ecological field experiments (Hurlbert 1984).

Take a dataset you actually care about — yours, or one from a paper — and answer the three questions from “How Do I Know If My Design Is Nested?”.
Write down what your true n is. If it is smaller than the number of rows, you have found a nested design.

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Introduction: Why NMDS?
The Problem with Ecological Community Data

Ecological community data presents unique challenges for traditional statistical methods
When sampling species abundances across sites
encounter data that is sparse (most species are absent from most sites) - many zeros
exhibits non-linear relationships between species and environmental gradients
has no clear distributional form
Principal Components Analysis (PCA) works beautifully for continuous environmental variables

assumes linear relationships
can leverage correlations between variables
for species abundance data - assumptions often fail spectacularly

NMDS offers a fundamentally different approach:

instead of trying to preserve exact distances or maximize variance explained
focuses on preserving the rank order of similarities between samples
makes it remarkably robust for ecological data.

Which environmental factors drive community composition?
Are there distinct community types?

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text: Part 2 · The NMDS Algorithm

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS)



What is NMDS?

Overview of NMDS:

Purpose: Visualize dissimilarity between objects in 2D/3D space
Goal: Preserve rank order of distances, not exact distances
Method: Iterative re-positioning to minimize stress
Output: Ordination plot showing relationships between samples

Key Differences from PCA:

Uses dissimilarity matrices (not covariance)
Non-parametric (rank-based)
Better for non-linear ecological relationships
No assumption about data distribution


Before running NMDS - analyzing dissimilarity matrices not raw abundance data

dissimilarity matrix contains values for every pair of samples = “how different”
typically range from 0 (identical) to 1 (completely different).








Note


Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics, Ch. 12 — The Analysis of Multivariate Data, covers ordination methods including NMDS.

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Why Bray-Curtis for Community Data?

Bray-Curtis dissimilarity is standard choice for community data because it handles zeros appropriately (joint absences don’t contribute to similarity)

bounded between 0 and 1
weights by abundance (not just presence/absence) - ignores joint absences entirely
Similarity is based only on what’s actually present and shared between sites
performs well with sparse data


The formula is:
\[BC_{jk} = \frac{\sum_i |y_{ij} - y_{ik}|}{\sum_i (y_{ij} + y_{ik})}\]
Where \(y_{ij}\) is the abundance of species \(i\) at site \(j\)

numerator sums up the absolute differences in abundance for each species between two sites
denominator sums up the total abundance at both sites
Bray-Curtis asks: “Of all the individuals at these two sites, what proportion would need to be moved to make the sites identical?”

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
The NMDS Algorithm

What NMDS Actually Does

NMDS tries to place samples in a low-dimensional space (usually 2D)
so rank order of distances in ordination matches rank order of dissimilarities in original matrix

Not your PCA which preserves exact distances (or variance)
NMDS only cares about relative ordering:

if site A is more similar to site B than to site C in the original data
then A should be closer to B than to C in the ordination

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
section: How NMDS Works step by step
text:
How NMDS Works step by step



The NMDS Algorithm:

Calculate dissimilarity matrix between all pairs of sites
Start with random configuration of points in 2D space
Calculate stress = difference between original distances and ordination distances
Move points to reduce stress
Repeat until stress cannot be reduced further
Try multiple random starts to avoid local minima

Stress Values:

< 0.1: Good representation
0.1-0.2: Acceptable
> 0.2: Poor representation

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text: Part 3 · Stress and Model Diagnostics

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Understanding Stress



What is Stress?

Stress is key diagnostic for NMDS quality
measures disagreement between original dissimilarities and distances in ordination
stress is calculated by first ranking all pairwise dissimilarities
then calculating corresponding distances in the ordination
fitting a monotonic regression line to the relationship between these
finally computing sum of squared deviations from this line.

Lower stress means ordination better represents original relationships
The Shepard Diagram: Visualizing Stress

Shepard diagram (or stress plot) is primary diagnostic tool for NMDS
shows relationship between original dissimilarities (x-axis) and ordination distances (y-axis) with a fitted monotonic line
If NMDS is working well - points should closely follow the line
Scatter indicates loss of information.

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Interpreting the Shepard Diagram



Shepard diagram

each point represents one pair of sites
x-axis shows their original Bray-Curtis dissimilarity
y-axis shows their distance in the 2D ordination
stepped line is a monotonic regression, = can only go up/stay flat not down
because NMDS preserves rank order - “stress” = scatter around line

Insights from our Shepard diagram:

minimal scatter

Stress Guidelines

Clarke (1993) widely-used guidelines for interpreting stress

<0.05 excellent representation w/no misinterpretation
0.05 - 0.10 good ordination - no real risk of false inferences
0.10 - 0.20 usable ordination but details at lower end interpreted cautiously
0.20 and 0.30 used with caution/potentially higher dimensions considered
>0.30 = random placement.

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis

NMDS Assumptions



NMDS Assumptions:
✅ Few assumptions:

Samples are independent
Dissimilarity measure is appropriate
Sufficient data for stable solution

❌ No assumptions about:

Data distribution
Linear relationships
Homoscedasticity
Normality

This makes NMDS very robust for ecological data!

text: Part 5 · PERMANOVA

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
PERMANOVA: Testing Multivariate Differences



What is PERMANOVA?

PERMANOVA (Permutational Multivariate ANOVA):

Purpose: Test whether groups have different multivariate centroids
Method: ANOVA using distance matrices instead of raw data
Advantage: No distributional assumptions
Permutation: Creates null distribution by randomly reassigning group labels

Think of it as:

Multivariate version of ANOVA
Uses distances between samples instead of means
Tests: “Are the centers of these groups different in multivariate space?” .

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
How PERMANOVA Works



PERMANOVA Algorithm:

Calculate distance matrix between all pairs of samples
Calculate F-statistic based on distances:

Between-group sum of squares
Within-group sum of squares

Permute group labels randomly (e.g., 999 times)
Recalculate F-statistic for each permutation
Compare observed F to permutation distribution
P-value = proportion of permuted F ≥ observed F

Why permutation?

No assumptions about data distribution
Creates empirical null distribution
Accounts for complex dependency structures

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
PERMANOVA Hypotheses



Research Question: “Do fish communities differ significantly between river reaches?”
Statistical Hypotheses:

H₀: The centroids of fish communities are the same across all river reaches (Upper = Middle = Lower)
H₁: At least one river reach has a different community centroid

In practical terms: -

H₀: River position doesn’t affect community composition
H₁: River position significantly affects community composition

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
PERMANOVA Assumptions



PERMANOVA Assumptions:
✅ Required:

Independence: Samples are independent
Exchangeability: Under H₀, observations are exchangeable between groups
Homogeneity of dispersion: Groups have similar multivariate spread

❌ Not required:

Normality or other distribution
Linearity

Checking Assumptions:

Use betadisper() to test homogeneity of dispersion
If violated, PERMANOVA is testing dispersion differences and not location differences



## Homogeneity of dispersion test p-value: 0.8037



vegan::betadisper() converts bray-curtis to euclidean distances to calculate distance from sample to center
Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) - ordination for distances between samples in a low-dimensional, Euclidean space

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Running PERMANOVA



PERMANOVA on Fish Communities

Line-by-line interpretation:

reach: The factor being tested (river reach)
Df = 2: Degrees of freedom (3 groups - 1)
SumOfSqs: Between-group sum of squares
R2: Proportion of variance explained by reach
F: F-statistic (ratio of between/within group variation)
Pr(>F): P-value from permutation test

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text: Part 6 · ANOSIM

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
ANOSIM: Analysis of Similarities



ANOSIM (Analysis of Similarities):

Purpose: are samples w/in groups are more similar than samples between groups
Method: Based on rank dissimilarities
Statistic: R-statistic ranging from -1 to +1
Interpretation:

R ≈ 1: Groups are completely separated
R ≈ 0: Groups are indistinguishable
R < 0: More dissimilarity within groups than between


Differences from PERMANOVA:

ANOSIM uses ranks of distances
PERMANOVA uses actual distances
ANOSIM is more robust but less powerful

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
How ANOSIM Works



ANOSIM Algorithm:

Calculate dissimilarity matrix between all samples
Rank all dissimilarities from smallest to largest
Calculate mean rank of within-group dissimilarities (r̄w)
Calculate mean rank of between-group dissimilarities (r̄b)
Compute R-statistic: R = (r̄b - r̄w) / (N(N-1)/4) where N = total number of samples
Permute group labels and recalculate R many times
P-value = proportion of permuted R ≥ observed R

R-statistic interpretation:

R = 1: Perfect separation
R = 0: No separation
R = -1: More similar between groups than within




# Run ANOSIM
anosim_result <- anosim(spe_matrix, doubs_env$reach, 
                       distance = "bray", permutations = 999)

# Display results
anosim_result
## 
## Call:
## anosim(x = spe_matrix, grouping = doubs_env$reach, permutations = 999,      distance = "bray") 
## Dissimilarity: bray 
## 
## ANOSIM statistic R: 0.5082 
##       Significance: 0.001 
## 
## Permutation: free
## Number of permutations: 999

Running ANOSIM



ANOSIM Results Interpretation:

R = 0.5082 : This indicates “good” separation between groups
**p-value = 0.001 - significant result
Biological meaning: Fish communities well-separated between river reaches, with communities within each reach being much more similar to each other than to communities in other reaches

“Within” box is clearly lower than the “Between” box

sites within same river reach tend to be more similar to each other (lower dissimilarity ranks) than sites in different reaches (higher dissimilarity ranks)
R statistic of 0.51 quantifies this separation

there’s clear differentiation, but with some overlap.





Interpreting R:

R = 1 - Complete separation

all within-group dissimilarities smaller than between-group dissimilarities

R > 0.75 Well separated
R > 0.5 Separated, but overlapping
R > 0.25 Barely separated
R ≈ 0 No difference between groups

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
ANOSIM vs PERMANOVA Comparison

When to use which:

PERMANOVA:

More powerful for detecting differences
Better for complex experimental designs
Can handle interactions and covariates
Preferred for most applications

ANOSIM:

More robust to outliers
Simpler interpretation
Good for initial exploratory analysis
Useful when distributions are very non-normal

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
PERMANOVA vs ANOSIM

What’s the Difference? Three Scenarios
Both methods test whether groups differ, but they ask different questions:

PERMANOVA asks: Do the group centroids differ in location?

Uses actual squared distances and partitions variance like ANOVA

ANOSIM asks: Are within-group dissimilarities smaller than between-group?

Uses ranked distances to compares rank distributions

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Scenario 2 is Key!



The Problem:

Groups A and B have the same centroid (same average community)
But Group B is much more variable (spread out)
PERMANOVA will detect this as “significant”!

Why?

PERMANOVA tests distances from points to centroids
More spread = larger distances = detected as “different”

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Dispersion test for PERMANOVA

Solution: Always run betadisper() before interpreting PERMANOVA!

What PERMANOVA “Sees”

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Introduction: Why NMDS?

The Problem with Ecological Community Data

Ecological community data presents unique challenges for traditional statistical methods
When sampling species abundances across sites
encounter data that is sparse (most species are absent from most sites) - many zeros
exhibits non-linear relationships between species and environmental gradients
has no clear distributional form
Principal Components Analysis (PCA) works beautifully for continuous environmental variables

assumes linear relationships
can leverage correlations between variables
for species abundance data - assumptions often fail spectacularly

NMDS offers a fundamentally different approach:

instead of trying to preserve exact distances or maximize variance explained
focuses on preserving the rank order of similarities between samples
makes it remarkably robust for ecological data.

text: Part 2 · The NMDS Algorithm

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS)



What is NMDS?

Overview of NMDS:

Purpose: Visualize dissimilarity between objects in 2D/3D space
Goal: Preserve rank order of distances, not exact distances
Method: Iterative re-positioning to minimize stress
Output: Ordination plot showing relationships between samples

Key Differences from PCA:

Uses dissimilarity matrices (not covariance)
Non-parametric (rank-based)
Better for non-linear ecological relationships
No assumption about data distribution


Before running NMDS - analyzing dissimilarity matrices not raw abundance data

dissimilarity matrix contains values for every pair of samples = “how different”
typically range from 0 (identical) to 1 (completely different).








Note



Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics, Ch. 12 — The Analysis of Multivariate Data, covers ordination methods including NMDS.

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Why Bray-Curtis for Community Data?

Bray-Curtis dissimilarity is standard choice for community data because it handles zeros appropriately (joint absences don’t contribute to similarity)

bounded between 0 and 1
weights by abundance (not just presence/absence) - ignores joint absences entirely
Similarity is based only on what’s actually present and shared between sites
performs well with sparse data


The formula is:
\[BC_{jk} = \frac{\sum_i |y_{ij} - y_{ik}|}{\sum_i (y_{ij} + y_{ik})}\]
Where \(y_{ij}\) is the abundance of species \(i\) at site \(j\)

numerator sums up the absolute differences in abundance for each species between two sites
denominator sums up the total abundance at both sites
Bray-Curtis asks: “Of all the individuals at these two sites, what proportion would need to be moved to make the sites identical?”

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
The NMDS Algorithm

What NMDS Actually Does

NMDS tries to place samples in a low-dimensional space (usually 2D)
so rank order of distances in ordination matches rank order of dissimilarities in original matrix

Not your PCA which preserves exact distances (or variance)
NMDS only cares about relative ordering:

if site A is more similar to site B than to site C in the original data
then A should be closer to B than to C in the ordination

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
section: How NMDS Works step by step
text:
How NMDS Works step by step



The NMDS Algorithm:

Calculate dissimilarity matrix between all pairs of sites
Start with random configuration of points in 2D space
Calculate stress = difference between original distances and ordination distances
Move points to reduce stress
Repeat until stress cannot be reduced further
Try multiple random starts to avoid local minima

Stress Values:

< 0.1: Good representation
0.1-0.2: Acceptable
> 0.2: Poor representation

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text: Part 3 · Stress and Model Diagnostics

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Understanding Stress



What is Stress?

Stress is key diagnostic for NMDS quality
measures disagreement between original dissimilarities and distances in ordination
stress is calculated by first ranking all pairwise dissimilarities
then calculating corresponding distances in the ordination
fitting a monotonic regression line to the relationship between these
finally computing sum of squared deviations from this line.

Lower stress means ordination better represents original relationships
The Shepard Diagram: Visualizing Stress

Shepard diagram (or stress plot) is primary diagnostic tool for NMDS
shows relationship between original dissimilarities (x-axis) and ordination distances (y-axis) with a fitted monotonic line
If NMDS is working well - points should closely follow the line
Scatter indicates loss of information.

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Interpreting the Shepard Diagram



Shepard diagram

each point represents one pair of sites
x-axis shows their original Bray-Curtis dissimilarity
y-axis shows their distance in the 2D ordination
stepped line is a monotonic regression, = can only go up/stay flat not down
because NMDS preserves rank order - “stress” = scatter around line

Insights from our Shepard diagram:

minimal scatter

Stress Guidelines

Clarke (1993) widely-used guidelines for interpreting stress

<0.05 excellent representation w/no misinterpretation
0.05 - 0.10 good ordination - no real risk of false inferences
0.10 - 0.20 usable ordination but details at lower end interpreted cautiously
0.20 and 0.30 used with caution/potentially higher dimensions considered
>0.30 = random placement.

text:
Choosing the Number of Dimensions

How do we know 2 dimensions is enough?

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
NMDS Assumptions



NMDS Assumptions:
✅ Few assumptions:

Samples are independent
Dissimilarity measure is appropriate
Sufficient data for stable solution

❌ No assumptions about:

Data distribution
Linear relationships
Homoscedasticity
Normality

This makes NMDS very robust for ecological data!

text: Part 5 · PERMANOVA

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
PERMANOVA: Testing Multivariate Differences



What is PERMANOVA?

PERMANOVA (Permutational Multivariate ANOVA):

Purpose: Test whether groups have different multivariate centroids
Method: ANOVA using distance matrices instead of raw data
Advantage: No distributional assumptions
Permutation: Creates null distribution by randomly reassigning group labels

Think of it as:

Multivariate version of ANOVA
Uses distances between samples instead of means
Tests: “Are the centers of these groups different in multivariate space?” .

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
How PERMANOVA Works



PERMANOVA Algorithm:

Calculate distance matrix between all pairs of samples
Calculate F-statistic based on distances:

Between-group sum of squares
Within-group sum of squares

Permute group labels randomly (e.g., 999 times)
Recalculate F-statistic for each permutation
Compare observed F to permutation distribution
P-value = proportion of permuted F ≥ observed F

Why permutation?

No assumptions about data distribution
Creates empirical null distribution
Accounts for complex dependency structures

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
PERMANOVA Hypotheses



Research Question: “Do fish communities differ significantly between river reaches?”
Statistical Hypotheses:

H₀: The centroids of fish communities are the same across all river reaches (Upper = Middle = Lower)
H₁: At least one river reach has a different community centroid

In practical terms: -

H₀: River position doesn’t affect community composition
H₁: River position significantly affects community composition

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
PERMANOVA Assumptions



PERMANOVA Assumptions:
✅ Required:

Independence: Samples are independent
Exchangeability: Under H₀, observations are exchangeable between groups
Homogeneity of dispersion: Groups have similar multivariate spread

❌ Not required:

Normality or other distribution
Linearity

Checking Assumptions:

Use betadisper() to test homogeneity of dispersion
If violated, PERMANOVA is testing dispersion differences and not location differences



## Homogeneity of dispersion test p-value: 0.8037



vegan::betadisper() converts bray-curtis to euclidean distances to calculate distance from sample to center
Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) - ordination for distances between samples in a low-dimensional, Euclidean space

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Running PERMANOVA



PERMANOVA on Fish Communities

Line-by-line interpretation:

reach: The factor being tested (river reach)
Df = 2: Degrees of freedom (3 groups - 1)
SumOfSqs: Between-group sum of squares
R2: Proportion of variance explained by reach
F: F-statistic (ratio of between/within group variation)
Pr(>F): P-value from permutation test

text: Part 6 · ANOSIM

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
ANOSIM: Analysis of Similarities



ANOSIM (Analysis of Similarities):

Purpose: are samples w/in groups are more similar than samples between groups
Method: Based on rank dissimilarities
Statistic: R-statistic ranging from -1 to +1
Interpretation:

R ≈ 1: Groups are completely separated
R ≈ 0: Groups are indistinguishable
R < 0: More dissimilarity within groups than between


Differences from PERMANOVA:

ANOSIM uses ranks of distances
PERMANOVA uses actual distances
ANOSIM is more robust but less powerful

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
How ANOSIM Works



ANOSIM Algorithm:

Calculate dissimilarity matrix between all samples
Rank all dissimilarities from smallest to largest
Calculate mean rank of within-group dissimilarities (r̄w)
Calculate mean rank of between-group dissimilarities (r̄b)
Compute R-statistic: R = (r̄b - r̄w) / (N(N-1)/4) where N = total number of samples
Permute group labels and recalculate R many times
P-value = proportion of permuted R ≥ observed R

R-statistic interpretation:

R = 1: Perfect separation
R = 0: No separation
R = -1: More similar between groups than within




# Run ANOSIM
anosim_result <- anosim(spe_matrix, doubs_env$reach, 
                       distance = "bray", permutations = 999)

# Display results
anosim_result
## 
## Call:
## anosim(x = spe_matrix, grouping = doubs_env$reach, permutations = 999,      distance = "bray") 
## Dissimilarity: bray 
## 
## ANOSIM statistic R: 0.5082 
##       Significance: 0.001 
## 
## Permutation: free
## Number of permutations: 999

ANOSIM vs PERMANOVA Comparison

When to use which:

PERMANOVA:

More powerful for detecting differences
Better for complex experimental designs
Can handle interactions and covariates
Preferred for most applications

ANOSIM:

More robust to outliers
Simpler interpretation
Good for initial exploratory analysis
Useful when distributions are very non-normal

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
PERMANOVA vs ANOSIM

What’s the Difference? Three Scenarios
Both methods test whether groups differ, but they ask different questions:

PERMANOVA asks: Do the group centroids differ in location?

Uses actual squared distances and partitions variance like ANOVA

ANOSIM asks: Are within-group dissimilarities smaller than between-group?

Uses ranked distances to compares rank distributions

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Scenario 2 is Key!



The Problem:

Groups A and B have the same centroid (same average community)
But Group B is much more variable (spread out)
PERMANOVA will detect this as “significant”!

Why?

PERMANOVA tests distances from points to centroids
More spread = larger distances = detected as “different”

title: Lecture: NMDS & Cluster Analysis
text:
Dispersion test for PERMANOVA

Solution: Always run betadisper() before interpreting PERMANOVA!

What PERMANOVA “Sees”

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Where We Left Off


A brief review:

Hypotheses
One- and two-sided t-tests
One-sample, two-sample, and paired t-tests — and how much more the paired test got out of the same four trees
Assumptions of parametric tests
What next — when assumptions fail!

we will always cover parametric tests first
then non-parametric approaches
later, other approaches use the appropriate underlying distribution when it isn’t normal, but Poisson or other








Note


✅ Key idea from last lecture
A t-test’s p-value is only trustworthy if its assumptions hold. Today is about how to tell whether they do — and what to do when they don’t.







Photo comparing needle length and bundle count across six pine species (Pinus ponderosa, nigra, resinosa, strobus, sylvestris, banksiana).








Warning


⚠️ The trap we’re walking into first
It is tempting to treat non-parametric tests as the “safe” option you can always fall back on. We are going to start by showing why that instinct is wrong.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Today’s Overview


Today runs in two halves, and the order matters:

Our own pine needles first. We check the assumptions on the data you collected, find that they hold, measure how big the effect actually was with Cohen’s d, and then run the non-parametric tests anyway — to see exactly what they cost.
Then the lake trout. A dataset where the assumptions are genuinely, badly broken — which is where robust tests, rank-based tests, and permutation tests earn their keep.







Note


✅ The question behind today
Not “which test is safest?” but “which test does this data deserve?”

            .groups = "drop")

p_wide_df <- p_df %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = side, values_from = needle_length_mm)

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Do our assumptions actually hold?






Note


🔮 Predict first: Before we run anything — do you expect needle length to be normally distributed with equal variance on the two sides of a tree? Commit to an answer.





Before reaching for anything non-parametric, we have to establish that we need it. Same two checks as last week.

# normality, one side at a time -- all 32 needles per side
shapiro.test(pine_df$needle_length_mm[pine_df$side == "sunny"])


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  pine_df$needle_length_mm[pine_df$side == "sunny"]
W = 0.96105, p-value = 0.2934

shapiro.test(pine_df$needle_length_mm[pine_df$side == "shady"])


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  pine_df$needle_length_mm[pine_df$side == "shady"]
W = 0.98213, p-value = 0.8586



# equal variance
leveneTest(needle_length_mm ~ factor(side), data = pine_df)

Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
      Df F value Pr(>F)
group  1   2e-04 0.9887
      62               









Important


⚠️ Everything passes



Check
p




Shapiro-Wilk, sunny
0.29


Shapiro-Wilk, shady
0.86


Levene’s
0.99



Remember the direction of these tests: H₀ is that the assumption holds. A large p means we have no evidence against it.
There is nothing wrong with this data. The paired t-test we ran last week was entitled to every bit of its p = 0.072.









Tip


🖐 So why are we here?
Because “my data are fine” is a conclusion you have to earn, not assume — and because plenty of students would have reached for a rank test anyway, thinking it was the cautious choice. Let’s find out what that caution would have cost.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
section: Effect Size — How Big, Not Just Whether
text:
Effect Size — How Big, Not Just Whether


Our paired t-test gave p = 0.072. The usual reflex is to call that “not significant” and stop.
But p never told us the one thing a reader actually wants to know: how much shorter are shady needles? A p-value answers “could this be noise?” — not “does this matter?”
Cohen’s d answers the second question. It is the difference between the groups expressed in standard deviations, so it has no units and can be compared across studies:
\[d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s}\]
For a paired design the difference is the paired difference, and s is the standard deviation of those differences:

diffs <- p_wide_df$shady - p_wide_df$sunny

mean(diffs) / sd(diffs)     # Cohen's d, by hand

[1] -1.361371









Note


✅ Read the formula out loud
“The shady side averaged 1.36 standard deviations below the sunny side.”
That sentence stands on its own. It does not depend on how many trees we sampled, and it would mean the same thing to someone measuring a different pine species in a different forest.









Tip


🖐 Cohen’s rough conventions



|d|
Label




0.2
small


0.5
medium


0.8
large



Ours is 1.36. These are rules of thumb, not laws — what counts as “large” is a question about pine trees, not about statistics.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
section: Why We Report It — What d Tells Us That p Could Not
text:
Why We Report It — What d Tells Us That p Could Not


Here is the relationship that explains everything:
\[t = d \times \sqrt{n}\]

2.7227 / sqrt(4)      # our t statistic, over root n

[1] 1.36135


The t-statistic is the effect size multiplied by the square root of your sample size. So a p-value confounds two completely different things: how big the effect is, and how hard you looked.

A huge effect with n = 4 → large p. That is us.
A trivial effect with n = 10,000 → tiny p, and no biological meaning at all.

Effect size separates them. That is why journals, and every reporting guideline written in the last twenty years, ask for it alongside the p-value.


library(effectsize)

cohens_d(p_wide_df$shady,
         p_wide_df$sunny,
         paired = TRUE)

Cohen's d |        95% CI
-------------------------
-1.36     | [-2.74, 0.10]








Important


⚠️ Look at that confidence interval: [-2.74, 0.10]
This is the honest summary of our four trees: the effect is probably large and probably negative, but with n = 4 we cannot rule out zero.
Notice that the CI crossing zero is the same fact as p > 0.05 — but it says it far more usefully. “No significant difference” sounds like we found nothing. “d = -1.36, CI [-2.74, 0.10]” says we found a large effect we could not pin down, which is a completely different message to a reader, and the correct one.









Tip


🖐 Where this goes next
Effect size is the input to a power analysis — given d, how many trees would we have needed? That is next week’s lecture.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Ranks, in one slide


Every non-parametric test today works the same way: throw away the measurements, keep only their order.

p_df %>%
  mutate(rank = rank(needle_length_mm)) %>%
  arrange(rank)

# A tibble: 8 × 4
  team       side  needle_length_mm  rank
  <chr>      <chr>            <dbl> <dbl>
1 waterbugs  shady             11.7     1
2 one        shady             13.2     2
3 waterbugs  sunny             13.8     3
4 one        sunny             14.2     4
5 grace_jace shady             15.4     5
6 grace_jace sunny             15.5     6
7 botany     shady             16.1     7
8 botany     sunny             17.3     8









Note


✅ What just happened
The shortest tree-side average became rank 1, the longest rank 8. A needle that was 4 mm longer than its neighbour and one that was 0.1 mm longer are now exactly one rank apart.
That is the whole trade. You become immune to outliers and to any weird distribution — and in exchange you give up the magnitudes.
A rank-based test then asks: are the ranks of one group systematically higher than the other’s?









Tip


🖐 Watch for the statistic
Rank tests report W (Mann-Whitney) or V (signed-rank), never t. If you see a W, you are reading rank-based output.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Running both rank-based tests



# Unpaired: Mann-Whitney U  (the t-test's two-sample partner)
wilcox.test(needle_length_mm ~ side, data = p_df)


    Wilcoxon rank sum exact test

data:  needle_length_mm by side
W = 5, p-value = 0.4857
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0



# Paired: Wilcoxon signed-rank  (the paired t-test's partner)
wilcox.test(p_wide_df$shady, p_wide_df$sunny, paired = TRUE)


    Wilcoxon signed rank exact test

data:  p_wide_df$shady and p_wide_df$sunny
V = 0, p-value = 0.125
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0









Tip


🖐 Notice V = 0
The signed-rank statistic is zero — meaning every single tree moved in the same direction. There is no arrangement of these four trees that would look more consistent.
Notice too that R says “exact test” for both. With no tied values it enumerates every possible arrangement rather than approximating. Hold on to that word — the next slide explains why it matters.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Same answer, less power










Comparison
Parametric
Non-parametric




Unpaired (2 groups)
t-test p = 0.425
Mann-Whitney p = 0.486


Paired (4 trees)
paired t p = 0.072
signed-rank p = 0.125



Both methods tell the same story:

the unpaired comparison finds nothing
the paired comparison is far more sensitive
the direction is identical — shady needles shorter

But the rank test costs you. In both rows the non-parametric p-value is larger. That is the price of throwing away the actual measurements and keeping only their order — and we paid it on data that never needed it.







Important


⚠️ At n = 4, the signed-rank test hits a wall
With 4 pairs there are only 2⁴ = 16 possible arrangements of plus and minus signs. The most extreme possible result — all four the same way, which is exactly what we got — has a two-sided p of 2/16 = 0.125.
So with four trees, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test can never return a p-value below 0.125, no matter how enormous the effect.

2 / 2^4     # smallest possible two-sided p, 4 pairs

[1] 0.125


The test did not fail to find our effect. It was arithmetically incapable of declaring it significant.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
What that means in practice



Non-parametric tests are the right call when normality is genuinely broken and cannot be fixed
But they are not free, and they are not a safe default
At small n they can be so blunt that no result could ever reach significance — check the floor before you run one







Note


✅ Key idea
Choose the test that matches your data’s distribution, not the one that feels safest. For our four trees, the parametric paired t-test — whose assumptions we just checked and could not reject — is the more honest and more informative choice.










Tip


🖐 Try it yourself
How many pairs would you need before a signed-rank test could reach p < 0.05?
2 / 2^5    # 5 pairs
2 / 2^6    # 6 pairs









Warning


⚠️ Where we go next
We have now seen what these tests cost. What we have not seen is what they buy you — because nothing about the pine data was broken.
For that we need a dataset that is a genuine mess.
