title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text: Part 3 · Assumptions of Parametric Tests

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Tests


T-tests are parametric tests.

Parametric tests:

specify/assume the probability distribution the parameters came from
basic assumptions of parametric t-tests: random sampling, normality, equal variance (or Welch’s t-test), no outliers

Non-parametric tests: no assumption about the probability distribution/normality

Mukasa et al. 2021, DOI: 10.4236/ojbm.2021.93081








Note


📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Analysis of Biological Data, Ch. 13 — Handling Violations of Assumptions, is the core reference for this whole lecture.







Flowchart of hypothesis tests branching into parametric and nonparametric tests, each split into one-sample and two-sample (independent vs. paired) tests, listing specific tests under each branch (e.g., t test and z test under parametric one-sample; Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon under nonparametric two-sample).

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Assumptions of Parametric Tests — Overview



If a parametric test’s assumptions are violated, the test becomes unreliable
This is because the test statistic may no longer follow the distribution it’s supposed to
Most parametric tests are robust to mild/moderate violations of normality





Three probability density curves for a right-skewed distribution family at different sigma values (0.25, 0.5, 1) with mu = 0, showing how larger sigma produces a flatter, more spread-out, and less peaked skewed curve.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Assumptions — Random Sampling


Basic assumptions of parametric t-tests: random sampling, normality, equal variance, no outliers.
Random sampling:

samples are randomly collected from populations; part of experimental design
necessary for sample → population inference





Diagram of a large circle labeled ‘population’ full of dots, with orange arrows showing a subset being drawn down into a small circle labeled ‘sample’, illustrating random sampling from a population.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Assumptions — Normality Testing






Note


🔮 Predict first: We’re about to look at histogram, dotplot, boxplot, and QQ-plot views of the same NE 12 mass data. Which of the four do you expect to be most convincing about normality?





Let’s test normality for one lake — NE 12 — as if we were going to run a one-sample t-test. We need a new data frame with only NE 12 data, called ne12_data.
Normality: samples from a normally distributed population

Graphical tests: histograms, dotplots, boxplots, QQ-plots
“Formal” tests: Shapiro-Wilk test — sometimes not useful

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Shapiro-Wilk Test for Normality


H₀ is that the data ARE normally distributed — so a small p-value rejects normality.

Graphical tests: histograms, dotplots, boxplots, QQ-plots
“Formal” tests: Shapiro-Wilk — sometimes not useful



shapiro.test(ne12_data$mass_g)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  ne12_data$mass_g
W = 0.85148, p-value < 2.2e-16








Warning


⚠️ p prints as < 2.2e-16
That is R telling you the p-value is smaller than it will bother to print. Not a borderline call — NE 12 mass is strongly non-normal, exactly as the histogram and QQ-plot showed. This is the case the rest of the lecture is for.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Testing the Equal Variance Assumption


Equal variance: samples are from populations with a similar degree of variability.
Equal variance is about two groups, so here we bring in the comparison we will use for the rest of the lecture: NE 12 vs. Island Lake.

Graphical test: boxplots
Formal test: Levene’s test — H₀ is “the variances are equal,” so you want p > 0.05



isl_ne12_df <- lt_df %>%
  filter(lake %in% c("NE 12", "Island Lake")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(mass_g))

isl_ne12_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(lake, mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_regular(base_size = 10)









leveneTest(mass_g ~ factor(lake), data = isl_ne12_df)

Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
       Df F value    Pr(>F)    
group   1  25.997 5.775e-07 ***
      330                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


p is far below 0.05 — the variances are not equal.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Testing for Outliers


No outliers: no “extreme” values very different from the rest of the sample.

Graphical tests: boxplots, histograms
“Formal tests”: Grubbs’ test — no one really does this

















Warning


⚠️ Watch out!
Outliers are a problem for non-parametric tests as well — switching to a rank-based test doesn’t make an outlier stop mattering.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text: Part 4 · When Assumptions Fail

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Alternative Tests When Assumptions Fail


What if t-test assumptions fail? Alternative tests, with more relaxed assumptions, are available. In which case would you use each?

Welch’s t-test: distribution normal but variance unequal
Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test: distribution not normal and/or outliers present (but both groups should still have similar distributions and ~equal variance)
Permutation test for two samples: distribution not normal (but both groups should still have similar distributions and ~equal variance)

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Understanding QQ-Plots


QQ-plots: a tool for assessing normality.

On x: theoretical quantiles from a standard normal distribution
On y: ordered sample values
Deviation from normal can be detected as deviation from a straight line

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Data Transformations


In some cases, data can be mathematically “transformed” to meet the assumptions of parametric tests. This usually involves:

log₁₀ transformations
square root transformations
and many others


log_box_plot <- isl_ne12_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(lake, log10(mass_g))) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_regular(base_size = 9)

ne12_island_box_plot + log_box_plot








The log scale pulls the two spreads much closer together — but it does not fix them completely. Levene’s test on log10(mass_g) is still significant.




Reference chart of six common data transformations (square root, logarithm, inverse, and their ‘reflect and’ variants for left-skewed data), each shown as a small curve with its transformation formula, used to pick a transformation that matches a variable’s skew shape.


source

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Data Transformations — Why Log?


Log isn’t a trick you try at random — it fixes a specific shape of problem:

Right-skewed data (a long tail of large values) → log10(x)
Effects that are multiplicative rather than additive (doubling a value, not adding a fixed amount) → log10(x)
Ratio-scale ecological measurements — mass, concentration, population size, area — are almost always multiplicative








Note


✅ The mechanism, in one line
A trout that is twice as heavy as another isn’t “500 g more” — it’s “2×.” Log turns that multiplicative relationship into an additive one, which is what a t-test’s equal-spread assumption expects. It compresses the right tail: 100 g → 1000 g and 1000 g → 10,000 g become the same distance, one log unit.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Data Transformations — Beyond Log


Log is the one you will reach for most in ecology, but match the transform to the shape of the problem:







Transformation
Use when…




log10(x)
right-skewed, multiplicative, ratio-scale data (mass, concentration, abundance)


sqrt(x)
count data, moderate right skew (Poisson-like variance)


asin(sqrt(x))
proportions or percentages bounded 0–1


1/x
rates, or extreme right skew that log doesn’t fix


Box-Cox
no obvious transform works — let the data pick the power



None of these are guaranteed to work. You check afterward, every time — that’s Part 5 of the worksheet, and it’s the whole point of the take-home.


sqrt_box_plot <- isl_ne12_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(lake, sqrt(mass_g))) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_regular(base_size = 9)

log_box_plot + sqrt_box_plot








sqrt() narrows the spread less than log10() did here — this skew behaves more like a multiplicative effect than a count.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
section: A Transformation Can Fix One Problem, Not the Other
text:
A Transformation Can Fix One Problem, Not the Other



leveneTest(log10(mass_g) ~ factor(lake), data = isl_ne12_df)

Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
       Df F value    Pr(>F)    
group   1   11.77 0.0006784 ***
      330                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Compare that to the Levene’s result on raw mass_g a few slides back — both fail. Normality improved with the log transform. Equal variance did not. Checking a transformation is not one pass/fail box — you re-test every assumption, separately, on the transformed variable.







Important


⚠️ This is the take-home’s whole trap
The sagebrush cricket data works the same way: a transformation can help one assumption without rescuing the other. There is no single “correct” test hiding in the data — there’s a best-justified one. Check every assumption on the raw data, then again on any transformed version, before you decide.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
section: Part 5 · Welch’s T-Test — a One-Slide Refresher
text: Part 5 · Welch’s T-Test — a One-Slide Refresher

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
section: Welch’s t-Test — why it exists, in one number
text:
Welch’s t-Test — why it exists, in one number


You met Welch’s last week: same t-statistic idea, separate variance estimates, fractional degrees of freedom. Nothing new to learn. What is new is this dataset, which shows you why it matters.

# Student's -- assumes equal variances
t.test(mass_g ~ lake, data = isl_ne12_df, var.equal = TRUE)


    Two Sample t-test

data:  mass_g by lake
t = 14.181, df = 330, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Island Lake and group NE 12 is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 2266.304 2996.360
sample estimates:
mean in group Island Lake       mean in group NE 12 
                3165.0000                  533.6677 



# Welch's -- does not
t.test(mass_g ~ lake, data = isl_ne12_df, var.equal = FALSE)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  mass_g by lake
t = 5.1368, df = 9.0578, p-value = 0.0006016
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Island Lake and group NE 12 is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 1473.676 3788.989
sample estimates:
mean in group Island Lake       mean in group NE 12 
                3165.0000                  533.6677 









Important


⚠️ Same data. Same means. Sixty orders of magnitude apart.




t
df
p




Student’s
14.18
330
5.7 × 10⁻³⁶


Welch’s
5.14
9.06
0.0006



(R only prints < 2.2e-16 for the first one — that is the smallest number it will show you. The true value is 5.7 × 10⁻³⁶.)
Look at the df. Student’s pooled 322 Island-sized fish with 10 NE 12-sized ones and claimed 330 degrees of freedom. Welch’s looked at the same data and said: you really only have about 9.
Both still reject H₀ — but Student’s was never entitled to that much confidence. With n = 322 vs 10 and Levene’s p ≈ 6 × 10⁻⁷, the pooled variance is meaningless.









Tip


🖐 The rule
Unequal n and unequal variance is exactly the combination Welch’s was built for. When in doubt, var.equal = FALSE is the safer default — it costs you almost nothing when variances really are equal.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text: Part 6 · Rank-Based Tests

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
section: Rank-Based Tests — now on data that needs them
text:
Rank-Based Tests — now on data that needs them


Same two tests you ran on the pine needles in Part 1 — ranks instead of measurements, no assumption about the distribution.

Ranks of data: observations are assigned ranks; sums (and signs, for paired tests) of ranks for groups are compared
Mann-Whitney U test — common alternative to the independent-samples t-test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test — alternative to the paired t-test
Assumptions: similar distributions for groups, equal variance
Less power than parametric tests
Best when normality can’t be met by transformation (weird distribution) or there are large outliers







Note


✅ The difference from Part 1
On the pine needles the rank test was a cost — we gave up power on data that was already well behaved.
Here, NE 12 mass is non-normal at p < 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ and full of outliers. There is nothing to give up. This is the case the test was built for.










Note


📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 13, covers the Mann-Whitney U test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test as the standard rank-based alternatives.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Mann-Whitney U Test Results



wilcox_test_result <- wilcox.test(mass_g ~ lake, data = isl_ne12_df)

wilcox_test_result


    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  mass_g by lake
W = 3205.5, p-value = 9.506e-08
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0









Tip


🖐 W again, and no “exact” this time
The statistic is W, not t — rank-based output, as in Part 1.
But notice what R doesn’t say: with 332 fish and plenty of tied masses it cannot enumerate every arrangement, so this is the normal approximation, not an exact test. At this sample size that is fine — the floor problem that crippled our four trees does not exist here.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text: Part 7 · Permutation Tests

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Permutation Tests — Concept



Permutation tests are based on resampling: reshuffling the original data
Resampling allows parameter estimation when the distribution is unknown, including SEs and CIs of statistics (means, medians)
A common approach is the bootstrap: resample with replacement many times, recalculate sample stats
We use the perm package
H₀: µ_A = µ_B, Hₐ: µ_A ≠ µ_B
Calculates the difference Δ in means between two groups

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Permutation Tests — Method



Randomly reshuffle observations between groups (keeping n₍NE 12₎ = 322 and n₍Island₎ = 10), calculate Δ
Repeat > 1,000 times
Record the proportion of the differences in means as extreme as (or more extreme than) observed
This is equivalent to a p-value, and can be used in the “traditional” hypothesis-testing framework








Tip


🖐 For a graphical explanation
jwilber.me/permutationtest

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Permutation Test Implementation


In R, using the perm package. Assumptions: both groups have a similar distribution; equal variance.

library(perm)

# Balance the design: take 10 NE 12 fish, keep all of Island Lake
set.seed(123)
perm_df <- bind_rows(
  isl_ne12_df %>%
    filter(lake == "NE 12") %>%
    slice_sample(n = 10),
  isl_ne12_df %>%
    filter(lake == "Island Lake")
)

# The difference the test is about
perm_df %>% group_by(lake) %>% reframe(summary_stats(mass_g))

# A tibble: 2 × 7
  lake            n  mean    sd    se ci_lower ci_upper
  <chr>       <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Island Lake    10 3165  1617.  511.    2008.    4322.
2 NE 12          10  645.  538.  170.     260.    1030.




permTS(mass_g ~ lake,
       data = perm_df,
       alternative = "two.sided",
       method = "exact.mc",
       control = permControl(nmc = 10000))


    Exact Permutation Test Estimated by Monte Carlo

data:  mass_g by lake
p-value = 2e-04
alternative hypothesis: true mean lake=Island Lake - mean lake=NE 12 is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
mean lake=Island Lake - mean lake=NE 12 
                                 2519.9 

p-value estimated from 10000 Monte Carlo replications
99 percent confidence interval on p-value:
 0.000000000 0.001059383

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text: Part 8 · Summary

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Summary — Testing Assumptions


Key assumptions:

Random sampling — samples are randomly collected from populations
Normality — data follows a normal distribution
Equal variance — samples come from populations with similar variability
No outliers — no extreme values that can skew results








Note


Assessing assumptions

Key to do every time
Should be acknowledged in the manuscript

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Summary — Effect Size


Always report an effect size next to your p-value.

Cohen’s d = the difference between groups, in standard deviations — unitless, and comparable across studies
t = d × √n, so a p-value confounds how big the effect is with how hard you looked
A confidence interval on d says what a bare “n.s.” never can: whether you found nothing, or found something you could not pin down
Effect size is also the input to a power analysis — next week







Note


✅ On our four trees
Paired d = −1.36, CI [−2.74, 0.10], p = 0.072. A large effect, imprecisely measured. Reporting only “p = 0.072, n.s.” would have thrown that away.










Tip


🖐 In a results sentence

Needles on the shady side were 1.09 mm shorter than on the sunny side (paired t₃ = −2.72, p = 0.072, d = −1.36, 95% CI [−2.74, 0.10]).

Every number there does work the others cannot.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Summary — Data Transformations


When assumptions aren’t met, transformations may help normalize data:

Log transformation: log10(x) — useful for right-skewed data, multiplicative effects
Square root: sqrt(x) — useful for count data, moderately right-skewed distributions
Box-Cox: a more flexible family of power transformations
More specialized transformations exist, especially for percentages or proportions








Tip


🖐 Recall
We saw log10() shrink the gap between the NE 12 and Island Lake boxplots earlier — that’s the transformation working.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Summary — Parametric Test Options


1. Standard t-test
Strengths:

High statistical power when assumptions are met
Well understood and widely accepted

Weaknesses:

Sensitive to violations of normality, equal variance
Heavily influenced by outliers


2. Welch’s t-test
Covered in full in the T-Tests lecture; the one-slide refresher in Part 5 is all we needed today.

Robust to unequal variances and unequal n — which is exactly our NE 12 vs. Island Lake case
Still parametric: it fixes the variance assumption, not the normality one
Costs almost nothing when variances really are equal, so it is a safe default
On these data it moved df from 330 to 9.06 — that is the whole story

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Summary — Non-Parametric Options


3. Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test
Strengths:

Non-parametric: doesn’t assume normal distribution
Robust against outliers
Works with ordinal data

Weaknesses:

Less statistical power than parametric tests
Still assumes similar distributions and approximately equal variance
Tests median differences rather than mean differences
At small n there is a hard floor on the p-value — with 4 pairs a signed-rank test cannot go below 0.125 (see Part 1)


4. Permutation tests
Strengths:

Distribution-free: doesn’t assume a specific distribution
Can be applied to many types of test statistics
Valid at small n — the p-value is exact, not an approximation
Directly estimates p-values through resampling

Weaknesses:

Computationally intensive
Assumes exchangeability under the null hypothesis
Requires similar distributions and equal variance
Hits the same small-n floor as the rank tests — being exact is not the same as being powerful, because there are only so many ways to rearrange 8 numbers

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Key Takeaway


Statistical tests have different strengths and assumptions. The choice should be guided by your data’s characteristics, not just convenience.
Always visualize your data before deciding on the appropriate test.







Note


✅ Key idea
Standard t-test → Welch’s → Mann-Whitney/Permutation isn’t a strict ladder of “better” tests — each answers a slightly different question (means vs. medians) under different assumptions. Pick based on what your data actually looks like.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Looking Ahead — The Take-Home


Part 8 of the worksheet (sagebrush crickets, due before Study Design & Sampling) hands you a new dataset and asks you to run the whole decision process from today:

Check normality and equal variance on the raw data
Try a transformation if the raw data doesn’t pass
Check normality and equal variance again, on the transformed data — don’t assume it worked
Pick a test, justify the pick, and report it properly

There is no lecture slide that tells you the answer this time.







Tip


🖐 Remember from today
log10() fixed normality for the lake trout but not equal variance. Expect the crickets to behave similarly — a transformation earning partial credit is a completely normal outcome, not a sign you did something wrong.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Today’s Overview


Today runs in two halves, and the order matters:

Our own pine needles first. We check the assumptions on the data you collected, find that they hold, measure how big the effect actually was with Cohen’s d, and then run the non-parametric tests anyway — to see exactly what they cost.
Then the lake trout. A dataset where the assumptions are genuinely, badly broken — which is where robust tests, rank-based tests, and permutation tests earn their keep.







Note



✅ The question behind today
Not “which test is safest?” but “which test does this data deserve?”






Photo comparing needle length and bundle count across six pine species (Pinus ponderosa, nigra, resinosa, strobus, sylvestris, banksiana).





Illustration of a lake trout in profile, showing its mottled brown-and-cream coloring and forked tail, the species whose weight and length data are used in the second half of this lecture.

Our pine needles, where we left them



library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(car)          # leveneTest()
library(patchwork)
library(perm)         # permutation tests
library(effectsize)   # cohens_d()

source("themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R")

pine_df <- read_csv("data/pine_data.csv")


# same two-stage summary as last week: one value per tree per side
p_df <- pine_df %>%
  group_by(team, side) %>%
  summarise(needle_length_mm = mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

p_wide_df <- p_df %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = side, values_from = needle_length_mm)

p_wide_df

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  team       shady sunny
  <chr>      <dbl> <dbl>
1 botany      16.1  17.3
2 grace_jace  15.4  15.5
3 one         13.2  14.2
4 waterbugs   11.7  13.8


📥 Pine needle data 📥 Lake trout data 📥 Sagebrush cricket data
📥 Tools script 📥 Script skeleton







Note



✅ Reminder
4 teams, 4 trees, both sides of each tree. The data are paired by design.
Last week these four trees gave us:



Comparison
p




Unpaired two-sample t
0.425


Paired t
0.072











Note



✅ Same two tools as last week
source() gives you theme_regular() and summary_stats() again. Nothing new to learn.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Do our assumptions actually hold?






Note



🔮 Predict first: Before we run anything — do you expect needle length to be normally distributed with equal variance on the two sides of a tree? Commit to an answer.




Before reaching for anything non-parametric, we have to establish that we need it. Same two checks as last week.

# normality, one side at a time -- all 32 needles per side
shapiro.test(pine_df$needle_length_mm[pine_df$side == "sunny"])


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  pine_df$needle_length_mm[pine_df$side == "sunny"]
W = 0.96105, p-value = 0.2934

shapiro.test(pine_df$needle_length_mm[pine_df$side == "shady"])


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  pine_df$needle_length_mm[pine_df$side == "shady"]
W = 0.98213, p-value = 0.8586



# equal variance
leveneTest(needle_length_mm ~ factor(side), data = pine_df)

Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
      Df F value Pr(>F)
group  1   2e-04 0.9887
      62               









Important



⚠️ Everything passes



Check
p




Shapiro-Wilk, sunny
0.29


Shapiro-Wilk, shady
0.86


Levene’s
0.99



Remember the direction of these tests: H₀ is that the assumption holds. A large p means we have no evidence against it.
There is nothing wrong with this data. The paired t-test we ran last week was entitled to every bit of its p = 0.072.








Tip



🖐 So why are we here?
Because “my data are fine” is a conclusion you have to earn, not assume — and because plenty of students would have reached for a rank test anyway, thinking it was the cautious choice. Let’s find out what that caution would have cost.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
section: Effect Size — How Big, Not Just Whether
text:
Effect Size — How Big, Not Just Whether


Our paired t-test gave p = 0.072. The usual reflex is to call that “not significant” and stop.
But p never told us the one thing a reader actually wants to know: how much shorter are shady needles? A p-value answers “could this be noise?” — not “does this matter?”
Cohen’s d answers the second question. It is the difference between the groups expressed in standard deviations, so it has no units and can be compared across studies:
\[d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s}\]
For a paired design the difference is the paired difference, and s is the standard deviation of those differences:

diffs <- p_wide_df$shady - p_wide_df$sunny

mean(diffs) / sd(diffs)     # Cohen's d, by hand

[1] -1.361371









Note



✅ Read the formula out loud
“The shady side averaged 1.36 standard deviations below the sunny side.”
That sentence stands on its own. It does not depend on how many trees we sampled, and it would mean the same thing to someone measuring a different pine species in a different forest.








Tip



🖐 Cohen’s rough conventions



|d|
Label




0.2
small


0.5
medium


0.8
large



Ours is 1.36. These are rules of thumb, not laws — what counts as “large” is a question about pine trees, not about statistics.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
section: Why We Report It — What d Tells Us That p Could Not
text:
Why We Report It — What d Tells Us That p Could Not


Here is the relationship that explains everything:
\[t = d \times \sqrt{n}\]

2.7227 / sqrt(4)      # our t statistic, over root n

[1] 1.36135


The t-statistic is the effect size multiplied by the square root of your sample size. So a p-value confounds two completely different things: how big the effect is, and how hard you looked.

A huge effect with n = 4 → large p. That is us.
A trivial effect with n = 10,000 → tiny p, and no biological meaning at all.

Effect size separates them. That is why journals, and every reporting guideline written in the last twenty years, ask for it alongside the p-value.


library(effectsize)

cohens_d(p_wide_df$shady,
         p_wide_df$sunny,
         paired = TRUE)

Cohen's d |        95% CI
-------------------------
-1.36     | [-2.74, 0.10]








Important



⚠️ Look at that confidence interval: [-2.74, 0.10]
This is the honest summary of our four trees: the effect is probably large and probably negative, but with n = 4 we cannot rule out zero.
Notice that the CI crossing zero is the same fact as p > 0.05 — but it says it far more usefully. “No significant difference” sounds like we found nothing. “d = -1.36, CI [-2.74, 0.10]” says we found a large effect we could not pin down, which is a completely different message to a reader, and the correct one.








Tip



🖐 Where this goes next
Effect size is the input to a power analysis — given d, how many trees would we have needed? That is next week’s lecture.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Ranks, in one slide


Every non-parametric test today works the same way: throw away the measurements, keep only their order.

p_df %>%
  mutate(rank = rank(needle_length_mm)) %>%
  arrange(rank)

# A tibble: 8 × 4
  team       side  needle_length_mm  rank
  <chr>      <chr>            <dbl> <dbl>
1 waterbugs  shady             11.7     1
2 one        shady             13.2     2
3 waterbugs  sunny             13.8     3
4 one        sunny             14.2     4
5 grace_jace shady             15.4     5
6 grace_jace sunny             15.5     6
7 botany     shady             16.1     7
8 botany     sunny             17.3     8









Note



✅ What just happened
The shortest tree-side average became rank 1, the longest rank 8. A needle that was 4 mm longer than its neighbour and one that was 0.1 mm longer are now exactly one rank apart.
That is the whole trade. You become immune to outliers and to any weird distribution — and in exchange you give up the magnitudes.
A rank-based test then asks: are the ranks of one group systematically higher than the other’s?








Tip



🖐 Watch for the statistic
Rank tests report W (Mann-Whitney) or V (signed-rank), never t. If you see a W, you are reading rank-based output.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Running both rank-based tests



# Unpaired: Mann-Whitney U  (the t-test's two-sample partner)
wilcox.test(needle_length_mm ~ side, data = p_df)


    Wilcoxon rank sum exact test

data:  needle_length_mm by side
W = 5, p-value = 0.4857
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0



# Paired: Wilcoxon signed-rank  (the paired t-test's partner)
wilcox.test(p_wide_df$shady, p_wide_df$sunny, paired = TRUE)


    Wilcoxon signed rank exact test

data:  p_wide_df$shady and p_wide_df$sunny
V = 0, p-value = 0.125
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0









Tip



🖐 Notice V = 0
The signed-rank statistic is zero — meaning every single tree moved in the same direction. There is no arrangement of these four trees that would look more consistent.
Notice too that R says “exact test” for both. With no tied values it enumerates every possible arrangement rather than approximating. Hold on to that word — the next slide explains why it matters.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Same answer, less power










Comparison
Parametric
Non-parametric




Unpaired (2 groups)
t-test p = 0.425
Mann-Whitney p = 0.486


Paired (4 trees)
paired t p = 0.072
signed-rank p = 0.125



Both methods tell the same story:

the unpaired comparison finds nothing
the paired comparison is far more sensitive
the direction is identical — shady needles shorter

But the rank test costs you. In both rows the non-parametric p-value is larger. That is the price of throwing away the actual measurements and keeping only their order — and we paid it on data that never needed it.







Important



⚠️ At n = 4, the signed-rank test hits a wall
With 4 pairs there are only 2⁴ = 16 possible arrangements of plus and minus signs. The most extreme possible result — all four the same way, which is exactly what we got — has a two-sided p of 2/16 = 0.125.
So with four trees, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test can never return a p-value below 0.125, no matter how enormous the effect.

2 / 2^4     # smallest possible two-sided p, 4 pairs

[1] 0.125


The test did not fail to find our effect. It was arithmetically incapable of declaring it significant.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
What that means in practice



Non-parametric tests are the right call when normality is genuinely broken and cannot be fixed
But they are not free, and they are not a safe default
At small n they can be so blunt that no result could ever reach significance — check the floor before you run one







Note



✅ Key idea
Choose the test that matches your data’s distribution, not the one that feels safest. For our four trees, the parametric paired t-test — whose assumptions we just checked and could not reject — is the more honest and more informative choice.









Tip



🖐 Try it yourself
How many pairs would you need before a signed-rank test could reach p < 0.05?
2 / 2^5    # 5 pairs
2 / 2^6    # 6 pairs








Warning



⚠️ Where we go next
We have now seen what these tests cost. What we have not seen is what they buy you — because nothing about the pine data was broken.
For that we need a dataset that is a genuine mess.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text: Part 3 · Assumptions of Parametric Tests

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Tests


T-tests are parametric tests.

Parametric tests:

specify/assume the probability distribution the parameters came from
basic assumptions of parametric t-tests: random sampling, normality, equal variance (or Welch’s t-test), no outliers

Non-parametric tests: no assumption about the probability distribution/normality

Mukasa et al. 2021, DOI: 10.4236/ojbm.2021.93081








Note



📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Analysis of Biological Data, Ch. 13 — Handling Violations of Assumptions, is the core reference for this whole lecture.






Flowchart of hypothesis tests branching into parametric and nonparametric tests, each split into one-sample and two-sample (independent vs. paired) tests, listing specific tests under each branch (e.g., t test and z test under parametric one-sample; Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon under nonparametric two-sample).

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Assumptions of Parametric Tests — Overview



If a parametric test’s assumptions are violated, the test becomes unreliable
This is because the test statistic may no longer follow the distribution it’s supposed to
Most parametric tests are robust to mild/moderate violations of normality





Three probability density curves for a right-skewed distribution family at different sigma values (0.25, 0.5, 1) with mu = 0, showing how larger sigma produces a flatter, more spread-out, and less peaked skewed curve.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Assumptions — Random Sampling


Basic assumptions of parametric t-tests: random sampling, normality, equal variance, no outliers.
Random sampling:

samples are randomly collected from populations; part of experimental design
necessary for sample → population inference





Diagram of a large circle labeled ‘population’ full of dots, with orange arrows showing a subset being drawn down into a small circle labeled ‘sample’, illustrating random sampling from a population.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Assumptions — Normality Testing






Note



🔮 Predict first: We’re about to look at histogram, dotplot, boxplot, and QQ-plot views of the same NE 12 mass data. Which of the four do you expect to be most convincing about normality?




Let’s test normality for one lake — NE 12 — as if we were going to run a one-sample t-test. We need a new data frame with only NE 12 data, called ne12_data.
Normality: samples from a normally distributed population

Graphical tests: histograms, dotplots, boxplots, QQ-plots
“Formal” tests: Shapiro-Wilk test — sometimes not useful

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Shapiro-Wilk Test for Normality


H₀ is that the data ARE normally distributed — so a small p-value rejects normality.

Graphical tests: histograms, dotplots, boxplots, QQ-plots
“Formal” tests: Shapiro-Wilk — sometimes not useful



shapiro.test(ne12_data$mass_g)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  ne12_data$mass_g
W = 0.85148, p-value < 2.2e-16








Warning



⚠️ p prints as < 2.2e-16
That is R telling you the p-value is smaller than it will bother to print. Not a borderline call — NE 12 mass is strongly non-normal, exactly as the histogram and QQ-plot showed. This is the case the rest of the lecture is for.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Testing the Equal Variance Assumption


Equal variance: samples are from populations with a similar degree of variability.
Equal variance is about two groups, so here we bring in the comparison we will use for the rest of the lecture: NE 12 vs. Island Lake.

Graphical test: boxplots
Formal test: Levene’s test — H₀ is “the variances are equal,” so you want p > 0.05



isl_ne12_df <- lt_df %>%
  filter(lake %in% c("NE 12", "Island Lake")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(mass_g))

isl_ne12_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(lake, mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_regular(base_size = 10)









leveneTest(mass_g ~ factor(lake), data = isl_ne12_df)

Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
       Df F value    Pr(>F)    
group   1  25.997 5.775e-07 ***
      330                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


p is far below 0.05 — the variances are not equal.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Testing for Outliers


No outliers: no “extreme” values very different from the rest of the sample.

Graphical tests: boxplots, histograms
“Formal tests”: Grubbs’ test — no one really does this

















Warning



⚠️ Watch out!
Outliers are a problem for non-parametric tests as well — switching to a rank-based test doesn’t make an outlier stop mattering.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text: Part 4 · When Assumptions Fail

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Alternative Tests When Assumptions Fail


What if t-test assumptions fail? Alternative tests, with more relaxed assumptions, are available. In which case would you use each?

Welch’s t-test: distribution normal but variance unequal
Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test: distribution not normal and/or outliers present (but both groups should still have similar distributions and ~equal variance)
Permutation test for two samples: distribution not normal (but both groups should still have similar distributions and ~equal variance)

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Understanding QQ-Plots


QQ-plots: a tool for assessing normality.

On x: theoretical quantiles from a standard normal distribution
On y: ordered sample values
Deviation from normal can be detected as deviation from a straight line

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Data Transformations


In some cases, data can be mathematically “transformed” to meet the assumptions of parametric tests. This usually involves:

log₁₀ transformations
square root transformations
and many others


log_box_plot <- isl_ne12_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(lake, log10(mass_g))) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_regular(base_size = 9)

ne12_island_box_plot + log_box_plot








The log scale pulls the two spreads much closer together — but it does not fix them completely. Levene’s test on log10(mass_g) is still significant.




Reference chart of six common data transformations (square root, logarithm, inverse, and their ‘reflect and’ variants for left-skewed data), each shown as a small curve with its transformation formula, used to pick a transformation that matches a variable’s skew shape.


source

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Data Transformations — Why Log?


Log isn’t a trick you try at random — it fixes a specific shape of problem:

Right-skewed data (a long tail of large values) → log10(x)
Effects that are multiplicative rather than additive (doubling a value, not adding a fixed amount) → log10(x)
Ratio-scale ecological measurements — mass, concentration, population size, area — are almost always multiplicative








Note



✅ The mechanism, in one line
A trout that is twice as heavy as another isn’t “500 g more” — it’s “2×.” Log turns that multiplicative relationship into an additive one, which is what a t-test’s equal-spread assumption expects. It compresses the right tail: 100 g → 1000 g and 1000 g → 10,000 g become the same distance, one log unit.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Data Transformations — Beyond Log


Log is the one you will reach for most in ecology, but match the transform to the shape of the problem:







Transformation
Use when…




log10(x)
right-skewed, multiplicative, ratio-scale data (mass, concentration, abundance)


sqrt(x)
count data, moderate right skew (Poisson-like variance)


asin(sqrt(x))
proportions or percentages bounded 0–1


1/x
rates, or extreme right skew that log doesn’t fix


Box-Cox
no obvious transform works — let the data pick the power



None of these are guaranteed to work. You check afterward, every time — that’s Part 5 of the worksheet, and it’s the whole point of the take-home.


sqrt_box_plot <- isl_ne12_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(lake, sqrt(mass_g))) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_regular(base_size = 9)

log_box_plot + sqrt_box_plot








sqrt() narrows the spread less than log10() did here — this skew behaves more like a multiplicative effect than a count.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
section: A Transformation Can Fix One Problem, Not the Other
text:
A Transformation Can Fix One Problem, Not the Other



leveneTest(log10(mass_g) ~ factor(lake), data = isl_ne12_df)

Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
       Df F value    Pr(>F)    
group   1   11.77 0.0006784 ***
      330                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Compare that to the Levene’s result on raw mass_g a few slides back — both fail. Normality improved with the log transform. Equal variance did not. Checking a transformation is not one pass/fail box — you re-test every assumption, separately, on the transformed variable.







Important



⚠️ This is the take-home’s whole trap
The sagebrush cricket data works the same way: a transformation can help one assumption without rescuing the other. There is no single “correct” test hiding in the data — there’s a best-justified one. Check every assumption on the raw data, then again on any transformed version, before you decide.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
section: Part 5 · Welch’s T-Test — a One-Slide Refresher
text: Part 5 · Welch’s T-Test — a One-Slide Refresher

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
section: Welch’s t-Test — why it exists, in one number
text:
Welch’s t-Test — why it exists, in one number


You met Welch’s last week: same t-statistic idea, separate variance estimates, fractional degrees of freedom. Nothing new to learn. What is new is this dataset, which shows you why it matters.

# Student's -- assumes equal variances
t.test(mass_g ~ lake, data = isl_ne12_df, var.equal = TRUE)


    Two Sample t-test

data:  mass_g by lake
t = 14.181, df = 330, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Island Lake and group NE 12 is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 2266.304 2996.360
sample estimates:
mean in group Island Lake       mean in group NE 12 
                3165.0000                  533.6677 



# Welch's -- does not
t.test(mass_g ~ lake, data = isl_ne12_df, var.equal = FALSE)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  mass_g by lake
t = 5.1368, df = 9.0578, p-value = 0.0006016
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Island Lake and group NE 12 is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 1473.676 3788.989
sample estimates:
mean in group Island Lake       mean in group NE 12 
                3165.0000                  533.6677 









Important



⚠️ Same data. Same means. Sixty orders of magnitude apart.




t
df
p




Student’s
14.18
330
5.7 × 10⁻³⁶


Welch’s
5.14
9.06
0.0006



(R only prints < 2.2e-16 for the first one — that is the smallest number it will show you. The true value is 5.7 × 10⁻³⁶.)
Look at the df. Student’s pooled 322 Island-sized fish with 10 NE 12-sized ones and claimed 330 degrees of freedom. Welch’s looked at the same data and said: you really only have about 9.
Both still reject H₀ — but Student’s was never entitled to that much confidence. With n = 322 vs 10 and Levene’s p ≈ 6 × 10⁻⁷, the pooled variance is meaningless.








Tip



🖐 The rule
Unequal n and unequal variance is exactly the combination Welch’s was built for. When in doubt, var.equal = FALSE is the safer default — it costs you almost nothing when variances really are equal.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text: Part 6 · Rank-Based Tests

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
section: Rank-Based Tests — now on data that needs them
text:
Rank-Based Tests — now on data that needs them


Same two tests you ran on the pine needles in Part 1 — ranks instead of measurements, no assumption about the distribution.

Ranks of data: observations are assigned ranks; sums (and signs, for paired tests) of ranks for groups are compared
Mann-Whitney U test — common alternative to the independent-samples t-test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test — alternative to the paired t-test
Assumptions: similar distributions for groups, equal variance
Less power than parametric tests
Best when normality can’t be met by transformation (weird distribution) or there are large outliers







Note



✅ The difference from Part 1
On the pine needles the rank test was a cost — we gave up power on data that was already well behaved.
Here, NE 12 mass is non-normal at p < 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ and full of outliers. There is nothing to give up. This is the case the test was built for.









Note



📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 13, covers the Mann-Whitney U test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test as the standard rank-based alternatives.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Mann-Whitney U Test Results



wilcox_test_result <- wilcox.test(mass_g ~ lake, data = isl_ne12_df)

wilcox_test_result


    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  mass_g by lake
W = 3205.5, p-value = 9.506e-08
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0









Tip



🖐 W again, and no “exact” this time
The statistic is W, not t — rank-based output, as in Part 1.
But notice what R doesn’t say: with 332 fish and plenty of tied masses it cannot enumerate every arrangement, so this is the normal approximation, not an exact test. At this sample size that is fine — the floor problem that crippled our four trees does not exist here.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text: Part 7 · Permutation Tests

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Permutation Tests — Concept



Permutation tests are based on resampling: reshuffling the original data
Resampling allows parameter estimation when the distribution is unknown, including SEs and CIs of statistics (means, medians)
A common approach is the bootstrap: resample with replacement many times, recalculate sample stats
We use the perm package
H₀: µ_A = µ_B, Hₐ: µ_A ≠ µ_B
Calculates the difference Δ in means between two groups

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Permutation Tests — Method



Randomly reshuffle observations between groups (keeping n₍NE 12₎ = 322 and n₍Island₎ = 10), calculate Δ
Repeat > 1,000 times
Record the proportion of the differences in means as extreme as (or more extreme than) observed
This is equivalent to a p-value, and can be used in the “traditional” hypothesis-testing framework








Tip



🖐 For a graphical explanation
jwilber.me/permutationtest

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Permutation Test Implementation


In R, using the perm package. Assumptions: both groups have a similar distribution; equal variance.

library(perm)

# Balance the design: take 10 NE 12 fish, keep all of Island Lake
set.seed(123)
perm_df <- bind_rows(
  isl_ne12_df %>%
    filter(lake == "NE 12") %>%
    slice_sample(n = 10),
  isl_ne12_df %>%
    filter(lake == "Island Lake")
)

# The difference the test is about
perm_df %>% group_by(lake) %>% reframe(summary_stats(mass_g))

# A tibble: 2 × 7
  lake            n  mean    sd    se ci_lower ci_upper
  <chr>       <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Island Lake    10 3165  1617.  511.    2008.    4322.
2 NE 12          10  645.  538.  170.     260.    1030.




permTS(mass_g ~ lake,
       data = perm_df,
       alternative = "two.sided",
       method = "exact.mc",
       control = permControl(nmc = 10000))


    Exact Permutation Test Estimated by Monte Carlo

data:  mass_g by lake
p-value = 2e-04
alternative hypothesis: true mean lake=Island Lake - mean lake=NE 12 is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
mean lake=Island Lake - mean lake=NE 12 
                                 2519.9 

p-value estimated from 10000 Monte Carlo replications
99 percent confidence interval on p-value:
 0.000000000 0.001059383

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text: Part 8 · Summary

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Summary — Testing Assumptions


Key assumptions:

Random sampling — samples are randomly collected from populations
Normality — data follows a normal distribution
Equal variance — samples come from populations with similar variability
No outliers — no extreme values that can skew results








Note



Assessing assumptions

Key to do every time
Should be acknowledged in the manuscript

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Summary — Effect Size


Always report an effect size next to your p-value.

Cohen’s d = the difference between groups, in standard deviations — unitless, and comparable across studies
t = d × √n, so a p-value confounds how big the effect is with how hard you looked
A confidence interval on d says what a bare “n.s.” never can: whether you found nothing, or found something you could not pin down
Effect size is also the input to a power analysis — next week







Note



✅ On our four trees
Paired d = −1.36, CI [−2.74, 0.10], p = 0.072. A large effect, imprecisely measured. Reporting only “p = 0.072, n.s.” would have thrown that away.









Tip



🖐 In a results sentence

Needles on the shady side were 1.09 mm shorter than on the sunny side (paired t₃ = −2.72, p = 0.072, d = −1.36, 95% CI [−2.74, 0.10]).

Every number there does work the others cannot.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Summary — Data Transformations


When assumptions aren’t met, transformations may help normalize data:

Log transformation: log10(x) — useful for right-skewed data, multiplicative effects
Square root: sqrt(x) — useful for count data, moderately right-skewed distributions
Box-Cox: a more flexible family of power transformations
More specialized transformations exist, especially for percentages or proportions








Tip



🖐 Recall
We saw log10() shrink the gap between the NE 12 and Island Lake boxplots earlier — that’s the transformation working.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Summary — Parametric Test Options


1. Standard t-test
Strengths:

High statistical power when assumptions are met
Well understood and widely accepted

Weaknesses:

Sensitive to violations of normality, equal variance
Heavily influenced by outliers


2. Welch’s t-test
Covered in full in the T-Tests lecture; the one-slide refresher in Part 5 is all we needed today.

Robust to unequal variances and unequal n — which is exactly our NE 12 vs. Island Lake case
Still parametric: it fixes the variance assumption, not the normality one
Costs almost nothing when variances really are equal, so it is a safe default
On these data it moved df from 330 to 9.06 — that is the whole story

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Summary — Non-Parametric Options


3. Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test
Strengths:

Non-parametric: doesn’t assume normal distribution
Robust against outliers
Works with ordinal data

Weaknesses:

Less statistical power than parametric tests
Still assumes similar distributions and approximately equal variance
Tests median differences rather than mean differences
At small n there is a hard floor on the p-value — with 4 pairs a signed-rank test cannot go below 0.125 (see Part 1)


4. Permutation tests
Strengths:

Distribution-free: doesn’t assume a specific distribution
Can be applied to many types of test statistics
Valid at small n — the p-value is exact, not an approximation
Directly estimates p-values through resampling

Weaknesses:

Computationally intensive
Assumes exchangeability under the null hypothesis
Requires similar distributions and equal variance
Hits the same small-n floor as the rank tests — being exact is not the same as being powerful, because there are only so many ways to rearrange 8 numbers

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Key Takeaway


Statistical tests have different strengths and assumptions. The choice should be guided by your data’s characteristics, not just convenience.
Always visualize your data before deciding on the appropriate test.







Note



✅ Key idea
Standard t-test → Welch’s → Mann-Whitney/Permutation isn’t a strict ladder of “better” tests — each answers a slightly different question (means vs. medians) under different assumptions. Pick based on what your data actually looks like.

title: Lecture: Non-Parametric T-Tests
text:
Looking Ahead — The Take-Home


Part 8 of the worksheet (sagebrush crickets, due before Study Design & Sampling) hands you a new dataset and asks you to run the whole decision process from today:

Check normality and equal variance on the raw data
Try a transformation if the raw data doesn’t pass
Check normality and equal variance again, on the transformed data — don’t assume it worked
Pick a test, justify the pick, and report it properly

There is no lecture slide that tells you the answer this time.







Tip



🖐 Remember from today
log10() fixed normality for the lake trout but not equal variance. Expect the crickets to behave similarly — a transformation earning partial credit is a completely normal outcome, not a sign you did something wrong.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text: Part 1 · Where We Left Off

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Last Week: The Multivariate Toolkit


Three steps, in order

Standardize — because units are not biology.
Choose a distance — Euclidean for continuous traits, Bray–Curtis for species counts, Jaccard for presence–absence. This is the modelling decision.
Ordinate — draw the resemblances on a readable 2-D map.

Where PCA sits

PCA is the eigen-decomposition branch of that map: it works on a correlation or covariance matrix, implies Euclidean distance, and assumes linear relationships.
In exchange it gives you ordered axes, % variance explained, and loadings — which NMDS cannot.





Example NMDS ordination plot from a published lake-ecology study (‘Summer’), with lake samples plotted as colored points (by lake) and shapes (by geographic location) and environmental-variable vectors (dissolved P and N, mixed-layer depth, temperature) overlaid as arrows with their R² and p-values, illustrating a real multivariate ordination used to summarize many variables at once.


An ordination of the kind we are building toward.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Today’s Question


Open the box

Last week we ran prcomp() and read the answer. Today we ask what it actually solved.
By the end you will be able to say, precisely:

what an eigenvalue is and why it equals a variance
what an eigenvector is and why its entries are the loadings
why there are exactly p components for p variables
why component signs are arbitrary, and what to do about it
how to decide how many components to keep








Note


Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics, Ch. 12 — The Analysis of Multivariate Data — is the core reference.




The core equation
For object i and component k:
\[z_{ik} = c_{k1}y_{i1} + c_{k2}y_{i2} + \cdots + c_{kp}y_{ip}\]

\(y_{i1} \ldots y_{ip}\) — the original values for object i
\(c_{k1} \ldots c_{kp}\) — the loadings: coefficients saying how much each original variable matters to component k
\(z_{ik}\) — the score: object i’s position on component k
PCA’s whole job is to find the \(c\)’s.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Today’s Data: Iris


Four measurements, three species

150 flowers, 4 measurements (cm), 50 from each of three species.
Small enough to follow every number by hand, correlated enough for PCA to have something to do.
The test we will apply: PCA is never told which species a flower belongs to. Does it recover them anyway?


iris_df <- iris %>% clean_names()

iris_data <- iris_df %>%
  dplyr::select(-species)

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
The Problem PCA Solves


Four dimensions is already too many

With 4 variables there are 6 pairwise scatterplots. With 10 there are 45. With 27 there are 351.
No set of 2-D plots shows you how all the variables move together.
PCA’s offer: a small number of new axes, built from the old ones, that carry most of the information.
And it will do it without being told about species.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text: Part 2 · Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors, and Rotation

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
PCA Is a Rotation


The 2-variable picture

Start with two correlated variables — crab burrows and crab biomass. The cloud of points runs diagonally.
The original axes are a bad description: both of them carry some of the same information.
PCA keeps the points exactly where they are and turns the axes until the first one lies along the direction of greatest spread.
Nothing is lost in a rotation. The distances between points are identical before and after.





Scatterplot of number of crab burrows versus total crab biomass, with the original centered axes drawn as a horizontal/vertical cross through the data cloud and two diagonal lines labeled PC1 and PC2 showing the rotated principal-component axes, where PC1 runs along the direction of greatest spread in the data.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
The Same Data, New Axes





The same crab burrow and biomass data redrawn after axis rotation, with PC1 and PC2 now shown as the new horizontal and vertical axes and the original burrow-number and biomass axes appearing as diagonal reference lines, illustrating that PCA is literally a rotation of the coordinate system around the data’s center.



After the rotation

PC1 is now horizontal and carries most of the spread; PC2 is vertical and carries what is left.
The two new axes are orthogonal, which is the geometric way of saying the two components are uncorrelated.
The old variables are still in there — they are now the diagonal reference lines, and the angle each one makes with PC1 is exactly what its loading records.
The rotation is chosen to maximize the variance on PC1. That one sentence is the whole of PCA.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Beyond Two Dimensions


Same idea, more axes

In 3-D the rotation finds a first axis through the long direction of the cloud, a second at right angles to it through the longest remaining direction, and a third fixed by the first two.
With p variables you get exactly p components — the rotation uses up every dimension.
You do not do this by eye. The components are extracted from the p × p covariance or correlation matrix of the original variables, and the extraction is an eigen-decomposition.





3D scatterplot of a point cloud within a cube, with three colored arrows (red ‘1st’, blue ‘2nd’, green ‘3rd’) radiating from the cloud’s center marking the first three principal-component axes, extending the rotation idea from 2D to 3D multivariate space.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors


Eigenvalue (\(\lambda\))

How much variance the component captures, in the units of the input matrix.
Run PCA on a correlation matrix and each original variable contributes exactly 1 unit of variance, so:

the eigenvalues sum to p
an eigenvalue of 1 means “this component is worth one average variable”

% variance for component k: \(\lambda_k / \sum_{j=1}^{p}\lambda_j\)


Eigenvector (c)

The list of coefficients — one per original variable — that builds the component. There are p entries in each eigenvector and p eigenvectors.
Each eigenvector has length 1: the loadings’ squares sum to 1.
Eigenvectors are orthogonal to one another: any two of them have a dot product of 0. That is why the components are uncorrelated.
Each component has one eigenvalue and one eigenvector: how big, and which way.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Correlation Matrix or Covariance Matrix?


The choice is the standardization choice

Covariance matrix → variables keep their original variances, so a variable measured in big numbers dominates.

Use it when all variables are in the same units and the differences in spread are real biology.

Correlation matrix → every variable is rescaled to variance 1 before decomposition, so every variable gets an equal vote.

Use it when the units differ — almost always, in ecology.

prcomp(x, scale. = TRUE) is “use the correlation matrix”.


Why correlation matters so much

PCA earns its keep by collapsing redundancy. If the original variables are uncorrelated, there is no redundancy to collapse:

every eigenvalue comes out near 1
the “components” are just the original variables, reordered
nothing has been reduced

Correlated variables → fewer components carry more variance. Check the correlation matrix before you run anything.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text: Part 3 · Assumptions and Standardization

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
What PCA Assumes


Check these first

Linear relationships between variables — PCA sees only straight lines.
No extreme outliers — one wild object can define a whole component.
Variables are correlated — otherwise there is nothing to collapse.
Adequate sample size — at least 3× as many objects as variables; n > 50 is comfortable. We have 150 flowers and 4 variables.
Complete cases — prcomp() will not handle missing values for you.


Are the iris variables correlated?










Petal length and petal width correlate at 0.96. Plenty of redundancy to collapse.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Checking Linearity and Outliers











Relationships are close to straight lines — the setosa cluster makes some panels look bent, but within species they are linear.










A handful of mild sepal-width outliers, nothing extreme. Note how much wider petal length spreads than sepal width — that is the standardization problem in one picture.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Standardization


Why it is needed here

## sepal_length  sepal_width petal_length  petal_width 
##        0.828        0.436        1.765        0.762


Petal length varies about 4× as much as sepal width does. On a covariance matrix it would dominate PC1 for no better reason than that.
Z-score: \(Z = (Y_i - \bar{Y})/s\), giving mean 0 and SD 1.
A sepal length of 5.1 cm becomes -0.9 — just under one SD below average.



iris_scaled <- scale(iris_data)

# check it worked
round(colMeans(iris_scaled), 3)
## sepal_length  sepal_width petal_length  petal_width 
##            0            0            0            0
round(apply(iris_scaled, 2, sd), 3)
## sepal_length  sepal_width petal_length  petal_width 
##            1            1            1            1







Note


scale() here, then prcomp(..., scale. = FALSE), is exactly equivalent to handing the raw data to prcomp(..., scale. = TRUE). We do it in two steps so the standardized values are visible.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
section: Part 4 · Running PCA and Reading the Output
text: Part 4 · Running PCA and Reading the Output

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Running the Analysis


The call

iris_pca <- prcomp(iris_scaled,
                   center = FALSE,
                   scale. = FALSE)


center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE because scale() already did both. Doing it twice is harmless but confusing.
vegan::rda(iris_scaled) gives the identical decomposition under a different name — PCA is PCA.


What is inside the result




Element
What it holds




sdev
\(\sqrt{\lambda}\) — SD of each component


rotation
the eigenvectors: loadings, variables × components


x
the scores: objects × components


center, scale
what was subtracted and divided





sdev^2 gives the eigenvalues. Everything else in this lecture is read off rotation and x.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
The Summary Table

summary(iris_pca)
## Importance of components:
##                           PC1    PC2     PC3     PC4
## Standard deviation     1.7084 0.9560 0.38309 0.14393
## Proportion of Variance 0.7296 0.2285 0.03669 0.00518
## Cumulative Proportion  0.7296 0.9581 0.99482 1.00000


Standard deviation is \(\sqrt{\lambda}\), not the eigenvalue itself — square it to get the variance.
PC1 explains 73%, PC2 22.9%; together 95.8% of all the variation in four variables.
The four eigenvalues sum to 4 — one unit per standardized variable, as promised.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Eigenvalues in a Table



tibble(
  Component  = paste0("PC", 1:4),
  Eigenvalue = round(eigenvalues, 3),
  Percent    = round(prop_variance * 100, 2),
  Cumulative = round(cumsum_variance * 100, 2))
## # A tibble: 4 × 4
##   Component Eigenvalue Percent Cumulative
##   <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl>      <dbl>
## 1 PC1            2.92    73.0        73.0
## 2 PC2            0.914   22.8        95.8
## 3 PC3            0.147    3.67       99.5
## 4 PC4            0.021    0.52      100


Reading it

PC1’s eigenvalue is 2.92: it is worth about 2.9 of the original variables all by itself.
PC3 and PC4 together carry 4.2% — essentially measurement noise.
We have reduced 4 variables to 2 numbers and kept 95.8% of the information. That is dimension reduction working.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
section: Part 5 · How Many Components Do You Keep?
text: Part 5 · How Many Components Do You Keep?

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
The Scree Plot


What it is

“Scree” is the geological term for the loose rubble at the base of a cliff. The plot usually shows a cliff then rubble.
Y-axis: % variance explained. X-axis: component number.
The elbow method: find where the line stops dropping steeply and flattens out. Keep the components before the flattening.
Here the cliff runs PC1 → PC2 and the rubble starts at PC3. The elbow says keep two.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
section: Three Rules, and What To Do When They Disagree
text:
Three Rules, and What To Do When They Disagree



# Kaiser criterion: eigenvalue > 1
sum(eigenvalues > 1)
## [1] 1

# first PC reaching 80% cumulative
which(cumsum_variance >= 0.80)[1]
## [1] 2


Kaiser (\(\lambda > 1\)) says keep 1.
80% cumulative says keep 2.
The elbow says keep 2.


Resolving it

The rules are guidelines, not tests, and they routinely disagree. Kaiser is known to be strict with few variables — with only 4 variables a second component has to be very strong to clear an eigenvalue of 1, and PC2’s is 0.91.
Two more criteria settle it in practice:

Does the component have an interpretable biological meaning? PC2 does — see Part 6.
Does keeping it change what you can see? It does: PC2 is what separates the species that PC1 alone confuses.

We keep two. Say which rule you used and why.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text: Part 6 · Loadings and Interpretation

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
What Loadings Are


Recipes for the components

A loading is one coefficient \(c_{kj}\) — how much original variable j goes into component k.
Values run from −1 to +1, like correlations.
|loading| > 0.5 → dominates the component. |loading| ≈ 0 → irrelevant to it.
Signs within a component are what carry the meaning:

all the same sign → a size axis, everything moving together
mixed signs → a shape axis, a trade-off




round(iris_pca$rotation, 3)
##                 PC1    PC2    PC3    PC4
## sepal_length  0.521 -0.377  0.720  0.261
## sepal_width  -0.269 -0.923 -0.244 -0.124
## petal_length  0.580 -0.024 -0.142 -0.801
## petal_width   0.565 -0.067 -0.634  0.524


Each column is one eigenvector. Square a column and the entries sum to 1.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Eigenvector Properties, Checked


The three claims from Part 2

# 1. unit length
round(colSums(iris_pca$rotation^2), 3)
## PC1 PC2 PC3 PC4 
##   1   1   1   1

# 2. orthogonal: PC1 . PC2 = 0
round(sum(iris_pca$rotation[, 1] *
          iris_pca$rotation[, 2]), 10)
## [1] 0

# 3. scores are uncorrelated
round(cor(iris_pca$x[, 1],
          iris_pca$x[, 2]), 10)
## [1] 0


Why this matters practically

Unit length is why loadings can be compared across variables within a component — they are competing for a fixed budget of 1.
Orthogonality is why you can drop PC scores straight into an ANOVA or a regression with no multicollinearity. That is one of PCA’s most useful side effects.
It is also why PC2 can only describe what PC1 left behind: it is constrained to be at right angles to it.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
section: ⚠️ The Sign of a Component Is Arbitrary
text:
⚠️ The Sign of a Component Is Arbitrary


Expect this, do not fight it

An eigenvector defines a line, and a line has no preferred end. Multiply a component’s loadings and its scores by −1 and you have an equally valid answer:

same eigenvalue, same % variance
same distances between points
same biology

Different software, different R versions, or dropping one flower can all flip a sign. Nothing is wrong when that happens.
The real error is to flip the loadings and not the scores, or to write “higher PC1” without saying what higher means.



# flip PC2 entirely
flip_load <- -iris_pca$rotation[, 2]
flip_score <- -iris_pca$x[, 2]

round(c(
  var_original = var(iris_pca$x[, 2]),
  var_flipped  = var(flip_score)), 4)
## var_original  var_flipped 
##        0.914        0.914

The rule: before you write a sentence about a component, translate the sign into biology. Say “larger flowers”, not “higher PC1”.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
PC1: Overall Flower Size



## sepal_length  sepal_width petal_length  petal_width 
##        0.521       -0.269        0.580        0.565

The pattern

Three variables load together and strongly: sepal length 0.52, petal length 0.58, petal width 0.56.
Sepal width opposes them at -0.27 — moderate, and in the other direction.


The interpretation

PC1 is an overall size axis, with a twist. On this run a high PC1 score means a flower with long sepals, long petals and wide petals, but relatively narrow sepals.
That is not a bookkeeping quirk — it is real iris biology. The big virginica flowers are big in every dimension except that their sepals are proportionally narrower than setosa’s.
So PC1 is better described as “large, elongated flowers vs. small, broad-sepalled flowers” than as pure size.
It carries 73% of all the variation.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
PC2: Sepal Width



## sepal_length  sepal_width petal_length  petal_width 
##       -0.377       -0.923       -0.024       -0.067

The pattern

Sepal width dominates completely at -0.92.
Sepal length contributes moderately (-0.38).
The two petal measurements are effectively absent (-0.024 and -0.067).


The interpretation

PC2 is not a general shape contrast — it is very nearly “sepal width, by itself”, plus a little sepal length.
Because the loading is negative, on this run:

low PC2 → wide sepals
high PC2 → narrow sepals

This is PC1’s leftovers: sepal width was the one variable PC1 could not account for, so PC2 is built almost entirely out of it.
22.9% of the variation — the sepal-width story is a real and separate axis of iris variation.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
The Loading Plot












Reading the arrows

Direction = which components the variable builds. Length = how well this plane represents it. The circle is the maximum possible.
Petal length, petal width and sepal length point right — they build positive PC1 together, and their small mutual angles say they are strongly correlated.
Sepal width points down and slightly left — nearly at right angles to the petals, which is the plot’s way of saying it carries almost independent information.
That near-90° angle is why sepal width got its own component.

text: Part 7 · Scores, Biplots, and Species

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Scores: Where Each Flower Lands


From loadings to positions

A score is an object’s coordinate on a component — the result of the recipe, applied to that object’s standardized values.
iris_pca$x holds them, 150 rows × 4 components.


## # A tibble: 9 × 5
##   species      PC1   PC2   PC3   PC4
##   <fct>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
## 1 setosa     -2.26 -0.48  0.13  0.02
## 2 setosa     -2.07  0.67  0.23  0.1 
## 3 setosa     -2.36  0.34 -0.04  0.03
## 4 versicolor  1.1  -0.86  0.68  0.03
## 5 versicolor  0.73 -0.59  0.09  0   
## 6 versicolor  1.24 -0.61  0.55  0.01
## 7 virginica   1.84 -0.87 -1    -0.05
## 8 virginica   1.15  0.7  -0.53 -0.04
## 9 virginica   2.2  -0.56  0.2   0.06

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
The Biplot












Points and arrows together

Points = flowers (scores). Arrows = variables (loadings), on the same plane.
A flower lying out along an arrow is high in that variable.
Setosa sits far left — low PC1, so short petals and sepals, but (per PC1’s negative sepal-width loading) broad sepals.
Virginica sits right — long petals and sepals, narrower sepals.
Versicolor sits between, overlapping virginica slightly.
PCA was never told about species. It recovered them from morphology alone.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Did PCA Recover the Species?



as_tibble(iris_pca$x) %>%
  mutate(species = iris_df$species) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(across(PC1:PC2,
                   \(z) round(mean(z), 2)))
## # A tibble: 3 × 3
##   species      PC1   PC2
##   <fct>      <dbl> <dbl>
## 1 setosa     -2.22 -0.29
## 2 versicolor  0.49  0.55
## 3 virginica   1.72 -0.26


Reading it, sign resolved

PC1 orders the species cleanly: setosa → versicolor → virginica, smallest and broadest-sepalled to largest and narrowest-sepalled.
PC2 does something different: versicolor stands apart from both others. Setosa and virginica have similar PC2 scores despite sitting at opposite ends of PC1.
That is exactly the job of a second component — it describes what the first one could not. Dropping PC2 on Kaiser’s advice would have thrown away a real signal.
