title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Reporting a PCA


Methods

“The four floral measurements were standardized to zero mean and unit variance and subjected to principal component analysis on the correlation matrix (prcomp(), R 4.6.1). Two components were retained on the basis of the scree plot and cumulative variance (> 80%).”

Results

“PC1 and PC2 together explained 95.8% of the variation (PC1 73%, PC2 22.9%). PC1 loaded positively on petal length (0.58), petal width (0.57) and sepal length (0.52), and negatively on sepal width (−0.27)…”


Always include

Whether you used the correlation or covariance matrix
% variance for every component you interpret
The loadings for retained components
How you decided how many to keep
The biological reading of each axis, with the sign resolved

Never include

All p components when 2 are meaningful
Loadings below |0.3|
Raw eigenvalues instead of percentages
Every individual score

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
section: When PCA Is and Is Not the Tool
text:
When PCA Is and Is Not the Tool


Use PCA when

Variables are continuous and correlated
Relationships are linear
Few zeros, and Euclidean distance is sensible
The goal is dimension reduction or exploration
You want uncorrelated variables for a downstream model


Use something else when

Species composition with many zeros → NMDS or PCoA on Bray–Curtis (week 15)
Categorical variables → CA or MCA
You already have a dissimilarity matrix → PCoA or NMDS
You want to classify or predict → discriminant analysis
You want to test groups → PERMANOVA (week 15)

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Summary


What PCA did

Rotated 4 correlated axes into 4 uncorrelated ones, ordered by variance.
PC1 (73%) — large elongated flowers vs. small broad-sepalled ones.
PC2 (22.9%) — sepal width, almost by itself.
Together 95.8% of the variation in 2 numbers instead of 4.
And it separated three species it was never told about.


What to carry forward

Eigenvalue = variance; eigenvector = loadings. On a correlation matrix the eigenvalues sum to p.
Standardize unless the units are identical and the spreads are biology.
Component signs are arbitrary — translate to biology before writing.
Retention rules disagree; interpretability breaks the tie.
Next week: when the data are counts and Euclidean distance fails — NMDS, cluster analysis, PERMANOVA and ANOSIM.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Readings

Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics, Ch. 12 — The Analysis of Multivariate Data
Quinn & Keough, Experimental Design and Data Analysis for Biologists, Ch. 17 — Principal components and correspondence analysis
Whitlock & Schluter does not cover ordination.

Data source

Iris: Anderson, E. (1935), The irises of the Gaspé Peninsula; made famous by Fisher, R.A. (1936), Annals of Eugenics 7:179–188. Shipped with base R as iris.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Last Week: The Multivariate Toolkit



Three steps, in order

Standardize — because units are not biology.
Choose a distance — Euclidean for continuous traits, Bray–Curtis for species counts, Jaccard for presence–absence. This is the modelling decision.
Ordinate — draw the resemblances on a readable 2-D map.



Where PCA sits

PCA is the eigen-decomposition branch of that map: it works on a correlation or covariance matrix, implies Euclidean distance, and assumes linear relationships.
In exchange it gives you ordered axes, % variance explained, and loadings — which NMDS cannot.






Example NMDS ordination plot from a published lake-ecology study (‘Summer’), with lake samples plotted as colored points (by lake) and shapes (by geographic location) and environmental-variable vectors (dissolved P and N, mixed-layer depth, temperature) overlaid as arrows with their R² and p-values, illustrating a real multivariate ordination used to summarize many variables at once.


An ordination of the kind we are building toward.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Today’s Question



Open the box

Last week we ran prcomp() and read the answer. Today we ask what it actually solved.
By the end you will be able to say, precisely:

what an eigenvalue is and why it equals a variance
what an eigenvector is and why its entries are the loadings
why there are exactly p components for p variables
why component signs are arbitrary, and what to do about it
how to decide how many components to keep








Note



Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics, Ch. 12 — The Analysis of Multivariate Data — is the core reference.





The core equation
For object i and component k:
\[z_{ik} = c_{k1}y_{i1} + c_{k2}y_{i2} + \cdots + c_{kp}y_{ip}\]

\(y_{i1} \ldots y_{ip}\) — the original values for object i
\(c_{k1} \ldots c_{kp}\) — the loadings: coefficients saying how much each original variable matters to component k
\(z_{ik}\) — the score: object i’s position on component k
PCA’s whole job is to find the \(c\)’s.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Today’s Data: Iris



Four measurements, three species

150 flowers, 4 measurements (cm), 50 from each of three species.
Small enough to follow every number by hand, correlated enough for PCA to have something to do.
The test we will apply: PCA is never told which species a flower belongs to. Does it recover them anyway?


iris_df <- iris %>% clean_names()

iris_data <- iris_df %>%
  dplyr::select(-species)

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
The Problem PCA Solves



Four dimensions is already too many

With 4 variables there are 6 pairwise scatterplots. With 10 there are 45. With 27 there are 351.
No set of 2-D plots shows you how all the variables move together.
PCA’s offer: a small number of new axes, built from the old ones, that carry most of the information.
And it will do it without being told about species.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text: Part 2 · Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors, and Rotation

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
PCA Is a Rotation



The 2-variable picture

Start with two correlated variables — crab burrows and crab biomass. The cloud of points runs diagonally.
The original axes are a bad description: both of them carry some of the same information.
PCA keeps the points exactly where they are and turns the axes until the first one lies along the direction of greatest spread.
Nothing is lost in a rotation. The distances between points are identical before and after.






Scatterplot of number of crab burrows versus total crab biomass, with the original centered axes drawn as a horizontal/vertical cross through the data cloud and two diagonal lines labeled PC1 and PC2 showing the rotated principal-component axes, where PC1 runs along the direction of greatest spread in the data.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
The Same Data, New Axes





The same crab burrow and biomass data redrawn after axis rotation, with PC1 and PC2 now shown as the new horizontal and vertical axes and the original burrow-number and biomass axes appearing as diagonal reference lines, illustrating that PCA is literally a rotation of the coordinate system around the data’s center.




After the rotation

PC1 is now horizontal and carries most of the spread; PC2 is vertical and carries what is left.
The two new axes are orthogonal, which is the geometric way of saying the two components are uncorrelated.
The old variables are still in there — they are now the diagonal reference lines, and the angle each one makes with PC1 is exactly what its loading records.
The rotation is chosen to maximize the variance on PC1. That one sentence is the whole of PCA.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Beyond Two Dimensions



Same idea, more axes

In 3-D the rotation finds a first axis through the long direction of the cloud, a second at right angles to it through the longest remaining direction, and a third fixed by the first two.
With p variables you get exactly p components — the rotation uses up every dimension.
You do not do this by eye. The components are extracted from the p × p covariance or correlation matrix of the original variables, and the extraction is an eigen-decomposition.






3D scatterplot of a point cloud within a cube, with three colored arrows (red ‘1st’, blue ‘2nd’, green ‘3rd’) radiating from the cloud’s center marking the first three principal-component axes, extending the rotation idea from 2D to 3D multivariate space.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors



Eigenvalue (\(\lambda\))

How much variance the component captures, in the units of the input matrix.
Run PCA on a correlation matrix and each original variable contributes exactly 1 unit of variance, so:

the eigenvalues sum to p
an eigenvalue of 1 means “this component is worth one average variable”

% variance for component k: \(\lambda_k / \sum_{j=1}^{p}\lambda_j\)




Eigenvector (c)

The list of coefficients — one per original variable — that builds the component. There are p entries in each eigenvector and p eigenvectors.
Each eigenvector has length 1: the loadings’ squares sum to 1.
Eigenvectors are orthogonal to one another: any two of them have a dot product of 0. That is why the components are uncorrelated.
Each component has one eigenvalue and one eigenvector: how big, and which way.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Correlation Matrix or Covariance Matrix?



The choice is the standardization choice

Covariance matrix → variables keep their original variances, so a variable measured in big numbers dominates.

Use it when all variables are in the same units and the differences in spread are real biology.

Correlation matrix → every variable is rescaled to variance 1 before decomposition, so every variable gets an equal vote.

Use it when the units differ — almost always, in ecology.

prcomp(x, scale. = TRUE) is “use the correlation matrix”.




Why correlation matters so much

PCA earns its keep by collapsing redundancy. If the original variables are uncorrelated, there is no redundancy to collapse:

every eigenvalue comes out near 1
the “components” are just the original variables, reordered
nothing has been reduced

Correlated variables → fewer components carry more variance. Check the correlation matrix before you run anything.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text: Part 3 · Assumptions and Standardization

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
What PCA Assumes



Check these first

Linear relationships between variables — PCA sees only straight lines.
No extreme outliers — one wild object can define a whole component.
Variables are correlated — otherwise there is nothing to collapse.
Adequate sample size — at least 3× as many objects as variables; n > 50 is comfortable. We have 150 flowers and 4 variables.
Complete cases — prcomp() will not handle missing values for you.




Are the iris variables correlated?










Petal length and petal width correlate at 0.96. Plenty of redundancy to collapse.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Checking Linearity and Outliers











Relationships are close to straight lines — the setosa cluster makes some panels look bent, but within species they are linear.










A handful of mild sepal-width outliers, nothing extreme. Note how much wider petal length spreads than sepal width — that is the standardization problem in one picture.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Standardization



Why it is needed here

## sepal_length  sepal_width petal_length  petal_width 
##        0.828        0.436        1.765        0.762


Petal length varies about 4× as much as sepal width does. On a covariance matrix it would dominate PC1 for no better reason than that.
Z-score: \(Z = (Y_i - \bar{Y})/s\), giving mean 0 and SD 1.
A sepal length of 5.1 cm becomes -0.9 — just under one SD below average.




iris_scaled <- scale(iris_data)

# check it worked
round(colMeans(iris_scaled), 3)
## sepal_length  sepal_width petal_length  petal_width 
##            0            0            0            0
round(apply(iris_scaled, 2, sd), 3)
## sepal_length  sepal_width petal_length  petal_width 
##            1            1            1            1







Note



scale() here, then prcomp(..., scale. = FALSE), is exactly equivalent to handing the raw data to prcomp(..., scale. = TRUE). We do it in two steps so the standardized values are visible.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
section: Part 4 · Running PCA and Reading the Output
text: Part 4 · Running PCA and Reading the Output

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Running the Analysis



The call

iris_pca <- prcomp(iris_scaled,
                   center = FALSE,
                   scale. = FALSE)


center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE because scale() already did both. Doing it twice is harmless but confusing.
vegan::rda(iris_scaled) gives the identical decomposition under a different name — PCA is PCA.




What is inside the result




Element
What it holds




sdev
\(\sqrt{\lambda}\) — SD of each component


rotation
the eigenvectors: loadings, variables × components


x
the scores: objects × components


center, scale
what was subtracted and divided





sdev^2 gives the eigenvalues. Everything else in this lecture is read off rotation and x.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
The Summary Table

summary(iris_pca)
## Importance of components:
##                           PC1    PC2     PC3     PC4
## Standard deviation     1.7084 0.9560 0.38309 0.14393
## Proportion of Variance 0.7296 0.2285 0.03669 0.00518
## Cumulative Proportion  0.7296 0.9581 0.99482 1.00000


Standard deviation is \(\sqrt{\lambda}\), not the eigenvalue itself — square it to get the variance.
PC1 explains 73%, PC2 22.9%; together 95.8% of all the variation in four variables.
The four eigenvalues sum to 4 — one unit per standardized variable, as promised.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Eigenvalues in a Table



tibble(
  Component  = paste0("PC", 1:4),
  Eigenvalue = round(eigenvalues, 3),
  Percent    = round(prop_variance * 100, 2),
  Cumulative = round(cumsum_variance * 100, 2))
## # A tibble: 4 × 4
##   Component Eigenvalue Percent Cumulative
##   <chr>          <dbl>   <dbl>      <dbl>
## 1 PC1            2.92    73.0        73.0
## 2 PC2            0.914   22.8        95.8
## 3 PC3            0.147    3.67       99.5
## 4 PC4            0.021    0.52      100



Reading it

PC1’s eigenvalue is 2.92: it is worth about 2.9 of the original variables all by itself.
PC3 and PC4 together carry 4.2% — essentially measurement noise.
We have reduced 4 variables to 2 numbers and kept 95.8% of the information. That is dimension reduction working.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
section: Part 5 · How Many Components Do You Keep?
text: Part 5 · How Many Components Do You Keep?

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
The Scree Plot



What it is

“Scree” is the geological term for the loose rubble at the base of a cliff. The plot usually shows a cliff then rubble.
Y-axis: % variance explained. X-axis: component number.
The elbow method: find where the line stops dropping steeply and flattens out. Keep the components before the flattening.
Here the cliff runs PC1 → PC2 and the rubble starts at PC3. The elbow says keep two.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
section: Three Rules, and What To Do When They Disagree
text:
Three Rules, and What To Do When They Disagree



# Kaiser criterion: eigenvalue > 1
sum(eigenvalues > 1)
## [1] 1

# first PC reaching 80% cumulative
which(cumsum_variance >= 0.80)[1]
## [1] 2


Kaiser (\(\lambda > 1\)) says keep 1.
80% cumulative says keep 2.
The elbow says keep 2.



Resolving it

The rules are guidelines, not tests, and they routinely disagree. Kaiser is known to be strict with few variables — with only 4 variables a second component has to be very strong to clear an eigenvalue of 1, and PC2’s is 0.91.
Two more criteria settle it in practice:

Does the component have an interpretable biological meaning? PC2 does — see Part 6.
Does keeping it change what you can see? It does: PC2 is what separates the species that PC1 alone confuses.

We keep two. Say which rule you used and why.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text: Part 6 · Loadings and Interpretation

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
What Loadings Are



Recipes for the components

A loading is one coefficient \(c_{kj}\) — how much original variable j goes into component k.
Values run from −1 to +1, like correlations.
|loading| > 0.5 → dominates the component. |loading| ≈ 0 → irrelevant to it.
Signs within a component are what carry the meaning:

all the same sign → a size axis, everything moving together
mixed signs → a shape axis, a trade-off





round(iris_pca$rotation, 3)
##                 PC1    PC2    PC3    PC4
## sepal_length  0.521 -0.377  0.720  0.261
## sepal_width  -0.269 -0.923 -0.244 -0.124
## petal_length  0.580 -0.024 -0.142 -0.801
## petal_width   0.565 -0.067 -0.634  0.524


Each column is one eigenvector. Square a column and the entries sum to 1.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Eigenvector Properties, Checked



The three claims from Part 2

# 1. unit length
round(colSums(iris_pca$rotation^2), 3)
## PC1 PC2 PC3 PC4 
##   1   1   1   1

# 2. orthogonal: PC1 . PC2 = 0
round(sum(iris_pca$rotation[, 1] *
          iris_pca$rotation[, 2]), 10)
## [1] 0

# 3. scores are uncorrelated
round(cor(iris_pca$x[, 1],
          iris_pca$x[, 2]), 10)
## [1] 0




Why this matters practically

Unit length is why loadings can be compared across variables within a component — they are competing for a fixed budget of 1.
Orthogonality is why you can drop PC scores straight into an ANOVA or a regression with no multicollinearity. That is one of PCA’s most useful side effects.
It is also why PC2 can only describe what PC1 left behind: it is constrained to be at right angles to it.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
section: ⚠️ The Sign of a Component Is Arbitrary
text:
⚠️ The Sign of a Component Is Arbitrary



Expect this, do not fight it

An eigenvector defines a line, and a line has no preferred end. Multiply a component’s loadings and its scores by −1 and you have an equally valid answer:

same eigenvalue, same % variance
same distances between points
same biology

Different software, different R versions, or dropping one flower can all flip a sign. Nothing is wrong when that happens.
The real error is to flip the loadings and not the scores, or to write “higher PC1” without saying what higher means.




# flip PC2 entirely
flip_load <- -iris_pca$rotation[, 2]
flip_score <- -iris_pca$x[, 2]

round(c(
  var_original = var(iris_pca$x[, 2]),
  var_flipped  = var(flip_score)), 4)
## var_original  var_flipped 
##        0.914        0.914

The rule: before you write a sentence about a component, translate the sign into biology. Say “larger flowers”, not “higher PC1”.

##   species      PC1   PC2
##   <fct>      <dbl> <dbl>
## 1 setosa     -2.22 -0.29
## 2 versicolor  0.49  0.55
## 3 virginica   1.72 -0.26



Reading it, sign resolved

PC1 orders the species cleanly: setosa → versicolor → virginica, smallest and broadest-sepalled to largest and narrowest-sepalled.
PC2 does something different: versicolor stands apart from both others. Setosa and virginica have similar PC2 scores despite sitting at opposite ends of PC1.
That is exactly the job of a second component — it describes what the first one could not. Dropping PC2 on Kaiser’s advice would have thrown away a real signal.

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Reporting a PCA



Methods

“The four floral measurements were standardized to zero mean and unit variance and subjected to principal component analysis on the correlation matrix (prcomp(), R 4.6.1). Two components were retained on the basis of the scree plot and cumulative variance (> 80%).”



Results

“PC1 and PC2 together explained 95.8% of the variation (PC1 73%, PC2 22.9%). PC1 loaded positively on petal length (0.58), petal width (0.57) and sepal length (0.52), and negatively on sepal width (−0.27)…”




Always include

Whether you used the correlation or covariance matrix
% variance for every component you interpret
The loadings for retained components
How you decided how many to keep
The biological reading of each axis, with the sign resolved



Never include

All p components when 2 are meaningful
Loadings below |0.3|
Raw eigenvalues instead of percentages
Every individual score

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
section: When PCA Is and Is Not the Tool
text:
When PCA Is and Is Not the Tool



Use PCA when

Variables are continuous and correlated
Relationships are linear
Few zeros, and Euclidean distance is sensible
The goal is dimension reduction or exploration
You want uncorrelated variables for a downstream model




Use something else when

Species composition with many zeros → NMDS or PCoA on Bray–Curtis (week 15)
Categorical variables → CA or MCA
You already have a dissimilarity matrix → PCoA or NMDS
You want to classify or predict → discriminant analysis
You want to test groups → PERMANOVA (week 15)

title: Lecture: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Summary



What PCA did

Rotated 4 correlated axes into 4 uncorrelated ones, ordered by variance.
PC1 (73%) — large elongated flowers vs. small broad-sepalled ones.
PC2 (22.9%) — sepal width, almost by itself.
Together 95.8% of the variation in 2 numbers instead of 4.
And it separated three species it was never told about.




What to carry forward

Eigenvalue = variance; eigenvector = loadings. On a correlation matrix the eigenvalues sum to p.
Standardize unless the units are identical and the spreads are biology.
Component signs are arbitrary — translate to biology before writing.
Retention rules disagree; interpretability breaks the tie.
Next week: when the data are counts and Euclidean distance fails — NMDS, cluster analysis, PERMANOVA and ANOSIM.

text: Part 1 · Two Ways to Be Wrong

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text:
The Decision Table


Even a well-run study can reach the wrong conclusion. Crossing the statistical decision against the unknown truth gives exactly four outcomes:









H₀ actually true (no real effect)
H₀ actually false (real effect)




Reject H₀
Type I error — rate α
Correct decision


Fail to reject H₀
Correct decision
Type II error — rate β




Type I error (α): you found an effect that isn’t real — a false positive
Type II error (β): you missed an effect that is real — a false negative
Power = 1 − β: the probability of correctly rejecting a false H₀
α is set before data collection — it is a policy about acceptable false-positive risk, not something read off a p-value afterward







Note


📖 Reference
Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics, Ch. 4 — Framing and Testing Hypotheses, covers the decision table and both error types. Whitlock & Schluter, Analysis of Biological Data, Ch. 6 — Hypothesis Testing, is the same material from the other textbook.










Tip


🖐 Which type of error, if any?

A study concludes sunny-side pine needles are longer, when really there is no difference.
A study fails to detect a real horn-length difference between surviving and predated lizards, and concludes there is none.
A study correctly detects that predated lizards have shorter horns.

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text:
Seeing α and β



Black curve — distribution of the test statistic if H₀ is true
Green curve — distribution if Hₐ is true, shifted by an assumed effect size
Red areas (α/2 each) — both tails of the null curve beyond the critical values: Type I error, α total
Blue area (β) — alternative curve between the critical values: Type II error
Power (1 − β) — the rest of the green curve, beyond the critical value

You live on only one curve — you just don’t know which. α comes from the black curve and β from the green one, so α + β need not equal 1.
Moving the critical values trades one error for the other. For a fixed sample size, you cannot shrink both at once.

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text: Part 2 · Statistical Power

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
section: What Is Power, and What Moves It
text:
What Is Power, and What Moves It


Statistical power is the probability of detecting a true effect — of rejecting H₀ when it really is false. 80% power means an 80% chance of finding a real effect of a given size.
Power increases with:

Larger sample size (n)
Larger effect size — a bigger true difference
Lower variability in the data
Higher α — a more lenient significance threshold

A power analysis is typically run for one of three purposes:

Before data collection, to determine the sample size a study needs — by far the most useful
After a study, to evaluate whether its sample size was adequate
To find the minimum effect size a given sample could realistically detect








Note


✅ Key idea
80% power is the usual convention for an adequately powered study. Everything in this lecture asks: for a given effect, n, and α, what is 1 − β?

text:
Cohen’s d, and Cohen’s Own Benchmarks


You met Cohen’s d in the Non-Parametric worksheet: the difference between means, divided by the pooled standard deviation. It is unitless, so it is comparable across studies — and it is exactly what pwr and power.t.test()-style functions want as input.

cohen.ES(test = "t", size = "small")$effect.size

[1] 0.2

cohen.ES(test = "t", size = "medium")$effect.size

[1] 0.5

cohen.ES(test = "t", size = "large")$effect.size

[1] 0.8


Jacob Cohen himself proposed these as rough, field-general benchmarks — not a substitute for a real pilot estimate when you have one.




Size
d

0.5


Large
0.8









Tip


🖐 Where does our data land?
Keep these three numbers in mind — the next section computes real d’s for two datasets, and you can judge for yourself which bucket each falls into.

text:
Low Power and High Power, Side by Side


Two two-sample comparisons, two very different amounts of power:

Pine needles — our own class data, 4 trees per side
Horned lizards — squamosal horn length of lizards that survived shrike predation vs. those that were killed (Young et al., the running example of Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 12 — Comparing Two Means)


pine_df <- read_csv("data/pine_data.csv")

p_df <- pine_df %>%
  group_by(team, side) %>%
  summarise(
    needle_length_mm = mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

lizard_df <- read_csv("data/horned_lizards.csv") %>%
  filter(!is.na(squamosal_horn_length_mm))

p_df %>% group_by(side) %>% reframe(summary_stats(needle_length_mm))

  group_by(survival) %>%

d_unpaired

The Comparison







Note


✅ Key idea
Same statistical machinery, same kind of test, wildly different power — because sample size and effect-size-relative-to-noise differ. Nothing about the pine data is broken; it simply cannot see an effect this size with 4 trees per side.

text: Part 5 · A Priori Power: Planning Before You Collect Data

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
section: The Question to Ask Before the Field Season
text:
The Question to Ask Before the Field Season


The most useful power analysis happens before you collect a single data point: guess or borrow an effect size, then ask what sample size would give you 80% power.

pwr.t.test(
  d = d_unpaired$Cohens_d,
  power = 0.80,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  type = "two.sample"
)


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 43.89921
              d = 0.6047825
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group


44 trees per side (always round n up). We collected 4.
And that d came from just 4 trees — its 95% CI (shady − sunny) runs from -2.01 to 0.84, which includes zero. An a priori n is only as good as the effect size you feed it; published values or a conservative guess are often safer than a tiny pilot.






Note


📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 14 — Designing Experiments, and Gotelli & Ellison, Ch. 4, both cover planning sample size before a study.










Warning


⚠️ This is why “we found no difference” is usually the wrong conclusion
A non-significant result from an underpowered study does not mean there is no effect. It means the study could never have found one.

Practice 5 · A Priori Power for a Smaller Effect

text: Part 6 · The pwr Package, and Unequal Group Sizes

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
section: When Your Two Groups Aren’t the Same Size
text:
When Your Two Groups Aren’t the Same Size


pwr generalizes power analysis beyond the two-sample t-test — pwr.anova.test(), pwr.r.test(), and pwr.chisq.test() cover ANOVA, correlation, and categorical data, all with the same interface, for later units.
Right now, the feature we need is pwr.t2n.test() — it takes the two actual group sizes directly. No averaging, no workaround:

pwr.t2n.test(
  n1 = sum(lizard_df$survival == "living"),
  n2 = sum(lizard_df$survival == "killed"),
  d = d_lizard$Cohens_d,
  sig.level = 0.05
)


     t test power calculation 

             n1 = 154
             n2 = 30
              d = 0.8679866
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.9910174
    alternative = two.sided









Important


⚠️ The old workaround
Before pwr.t2n.test(), an unbalanced design forced you to fake a single n — usually the harmonic mean of n₁ and n₂ — and feed that to a function built for equal groups. It is an approximation. pwr.t2n.test() uses both real sample sizes directly and is the better tool whenever n₁ ≠ n₂.

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text: Part 7 · Retrospective (Post-Hoc) Power

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
section: Computing Power From What You Actually Observed
text:
Computing Power From What You Actually Observed


The other direction: after a study, ask what power your actual n and observed effect size gave you.

pwr.t.test(
  n = 4,
  d = d_unpaired$Cohens_d,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  type = "two.sample"
)


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 4
              d = 0.6047825
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.112253
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group


11% power. Even if the pine difference is completely real, an unpaired study with 4 trees per side would miss it about 9 times out of 10.







Warning


⚠️ A warning about “post-hoc power”
Computing power from the effect size you observed is a known trap. It is fine for what we used it for here: planning the next study.
It is not a valid way to explain away a non-significant result — observed power is just a re-expression of the p-value you already have. “Our result was non-significant, but we had low power” says the same thing twice.

section: Practice 6 · Retrospective Power for the Paired Design
text:
Practice 6 · Retrospective Power for the Paired Design






Tip


🖐 Your turn — run this
You already calculated d_paired in Part 4 (the same four trees, paired instead of unpaired). Compute the retrospective power of the paired design at n = 4, the same way Part 7 just did for the unpaired one.

pwr.t.test(n = 4, d = d_paired$Cohens_d, sig.level = 0.05, type = "paired")


     Paired t test power calculation 

              n = 4
              d = 1.361371
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.4635201
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number of *pairs*


How much higher is it than the unpaired 11%?

text: Part 8 · Pairing Buys You Power

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
section: The Whole Economics of the Study
text:
The Whole Economics of the Study


Pairing does not just give a smaller p-value — it changes what the study needed to begin with.

pwr.t.test(
  d = d_paired$Cohens_d,
  power = 0.80,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  type = "paired"
)


     Paired t test power calculation 

              n = 6.406838
              d = 1.361371
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number of *pairs*


7 trees, total — for 80% power, paired.




Design
Power at n = 4
Trees for 80% power




Unpaired
11%
44 per side (88 trees)


Paired
46%
7 total









Important


Same trees. Same needles. Same measurements.
Pairing takes this study from needing 88 trees (44 per side) to needing 7 trees. That is not a statistical trick — it is what respecting the design of your own experiment is worth.

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text: Part 9 · Error Bars, Revisited

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
section: SD, SE, and CI Answer Different Questions
text:
SD, SE, and CI Answer Different Questions



Standard deviation (SD) — spread of the raw data
Standard error (SE) — precision of the mean, SD / sqrt(n)
95% confidence interval (CI) — plausible range for the true mean, built from SE and the t-distribution

summary_stats() gives you all three from one call. A large sample doesn’t shrink SD — it shrinks SE and the CI, because you’re now estimating the mean more precisely, not describing less variable lizards.

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text: Part 10 · Pseudoreplication

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text:
Sampling and Pseudoreplication


Pseudoreplication occurs when measurements that are not independent are analyzed as if they were.

Measuring the same individual multiple times
Treating multiple fish from the same tank as independent
Using multiple data points from a single site

It results in underestimated standard errors and inflated Type I error rates — it makes a study look more precise, and more significant, than it actually is.







Important


We have been doing this all along
Our pine needle data has 64 rows. Analyzed as 64 independent needles it would look like a large, well-powered study. Analyzed honestly — 4 trees — it has 11% power unpaired, 46% paired.
Pseudoreplication would not have made the study better. It would only have made us believe it was.

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text: Pseudoreplicated vs. True Replication

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text: Aside · The 0.05 Debate

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
section: A Number That Was Always Meant to Be a Guideline
text:
A Number That Was Always Meant to Be a Guideline



“If p is between 0.1 and 0.9 there is certainly no reason to suspect the hypothesis tested. If it is below 0.02 it is strongly indicated that the hypothesis fails to account for the whole of the facts. We shall not often be astray if we draw a conventional line at .05 …”

— R.A. Fisher, on the p-value as an informal measure of discrepancy between data and H₀
Fisher proposed 0.05 as a rough guideline, not a bright line. Modern critiques of “statistical significance” as a binary pass/fail argue power and effect size deserve at least as much attention as whether p cleared 0.05.




Screenshot of a Nature comment article titled ‘Scientists rise up against statistical significance,’ by Valentin Amrhein, Sander Greenland, Blake McShane and 800+ signatories, illustrated with a cartoon of two scientists shelving a book labeled ‘Statistical Significance’ in a dusty cabinet of retired scientific relics like phlogiston and spontaneous generation, symbolizing calls to retire strict significance thresholds.

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text:
Summary and Key Takeaways


Key concepts covered:

Type I (α) and Type II (β) error — the two ways a decision can be wrong; power = 1 − β
Power rises with larger n, larger effect size, lower variability, and higher α
A priori power (before data collection) tells you the n a study needs — the most useful use of this whole toolkit
Retrospective power tells you what your finished study could have detected — useful for planning the next one, not for excusing a null result



The pwr package generalizes power analysis, and pwr.t2n.test() handles unequal group sizes directly
Pairing a design can be worth far more than adding raw sample size
SD, SE, and CI answer three different questions about the same data
Pseudoreplication inflates apparent precision by treating non-independent measurements as independent replicates







Note


📖 References
Gotelli & Ellison, Ch. 4 — Framing and Testing Hypotheses (errors and power); Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 6 — Hypothesis Testing, and Ch. 14 — Designing Experiments (sample size and power planning).

Cohen’s d, and Cohen’s Own Benchmarks


You met Cohen’s d in the Non-Parametric worksheet: the difference between means, divided by the pooled standard deviation. It is unitless, so it is comparable across studies — and it is exactly what pwr and power.t.test()-style functions want as input.

cohen.ES(test = "t", size = "small")$effect.size

[1] 0.2

cohen.ES(test = "t", size = "medium")$effect.size

[1] 0.5

cohen.ES(test = "t", size = "large")$effect.size

[1] 0.8


Jacob Cohen himself proposed these as rough, field-general benchmarks — not a substitute for a real pilot estimate when you have one.




Size
d

0.8









Tip



🖐 Where does our data land?
Keep these three numbers in mind — the next section computes real d’s for two datasets, and you can judge for yourself which bucket each falls into.

Low Power and High Power, Side by Side


Two two-sample comparisons, two very different amounts of power:

Pine needles — our own class data, 4 trees per side
Horned lizards — squamosal horn length of lizards that survived shrike predation vs. those that were killed (Young et al., the running example of Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 12 — Comparing Two Means)


pine_df <- read_csv("data/pine_data.csv")

p_df <- pine_df %>%
  group_by(team, side) %>%
  summarise(
    needle_length_mm = mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

lizard_df <- read_csv("data/horned_lizards.csv") %>%
  filter(!is.na(squamosal_horn_length_mm))

p_df %>% group_by(side) %>% reframe(summary_stats(needle_length_mm))

# A tibble: 2 × 7

  group_by(survival) %>%
  reframe(summary_stats(squamosal_horn_length_mm))

d_unpaired <- cohens_d(needle_length_mm ~ side, data = p_df)
d_unpaired

Cohen's d |        95% CI
-------------------------

text:
The Comparison















Note



✅ Key idea
Same statistical machinery, same kind of test, wildly different power — because sample size and effect-size-relative-to-noise differ. Nothing about the pine data is broken; it simply cannot see an effect this size with 4 trees per side.

text: Part 5 · A Priori Power: Planning Before You Collect Data

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
section: The Question to Ask Before the Field Season
text:
The Question to Ask Before the Field Season


The most useful power analysis happens before you collect a single data point: guess or borrow an effect size, then ask what sample size would give you 80% power.

pwr.t.test(
  d = d_unpaired$Cohens_d,
  power = 0.80,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  type = "two.sample"
)


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 43.89921
              d = 0.6047825
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group


44 trees per side (always round n up). We collected 4.
And that d came from just 4 trees — its 95% CI (shady − sunny) runs from -2.01 to 0.84, which includes zero. An a priori n is only as good as the effect size you feed it; published values or a conservative guess are often safer than a tiny pilot.






Note



📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 14 — Designing Experiments, and Gotelli & Ellison, Ch. 4, both cover planning sample size before a study.









Warning



⚠️ This is why “we found no difference” is usually the wrong conclusion
A non-significant result from an underpowered study does not mean there is no effect. It means the study could never have found one.

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
section: Practice 5 · A Priori Power for a Smaller Effect
text:
Practice 5 · A Priori Power for a Smaller Effect






Tip



🖐 Your turn — run this
The horned lizards gave us a large effect (d ≈ 0.87). Suppose instead you are planning a new study where you only expect a medium effect (d = 0.5, Cohen’s own benchmark). Assuming equal group sizes, how many lizards per group would you need for 80% power?

pwr.t.test(d = 0.5, power = 0.80, sig.level = 0.05, type = "two.sample")


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 63.76561
              d = 0.5
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group


How does that n compare to the 44 trees per side the pine study needed?

section: Part 6 · The pwr Package, and Unequal Group Sizes
text: Part 6 · The pwr Package, and Unequal Group Sizes

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
section: When Your Two Groups Aren’t the Same Size
text:
When Your Two Groups Aren’t the Same Size


pwr generalizes power analysis beyond the two-sample t-test — pwr.anova.test(), pwr.r.test(), and pwr.chisq.test() cover ANOVA, correlation, and categorical data, all with the same interface, for later units.
Right now, the feature we need is pwr.t2n.test() — it takes the two actual group sizes directly. No averaging, no workaround:

pwr.t2n.test(
  n1 = sum(lizard_df$survival == "living"),
  n2 = sum(lizard_df$survival == "killed"),
  d = d_lizard$Cohens_d,
  sig.level = 0.05
)


     t test power calculation 

             n1 = 154
             n2 = 30
              d = 0.8679866
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.9910174
    alternative = two.sided









Important



⚠️ The old workaround
Before pwr.t2n.test(), an unbalanced design forced you to fake a single n — usually the harmonic mean of n₁ and n₂ — and feed that to a function built for equal groups. It is an approximation. pwr.t2n.test() uses both real sample sizes directly and is the better tool whenever n₁ ≠ n₂.

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text: Part 7 · Retrospective (Post-Hoc) Power

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
section: Computing Power From What You Actually Observed
text:
Computing Power From What You Actually Observed


The other direction: after a study, ask what power your actual n and observed effect size gave you.

pwr.t.test(
  n = 4,
  d = d_unpaired$Cohens_d,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  type = "two.sample"
)


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 4
              d = 0.6047825
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.112253
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group


11% power. Even if the pine difference is completely real, an unpaired study with 4 trees per side would miss it about 9 times out of 10.







Warning



⚠️ A warning about “post-hoc power”
Computing power from the effect size you observed is a known trap. It is fine for what we used it for here: planning the next study.
It is not a valid way to explain away a non-significant result — observed power is just a re-expression of the p-value you already have. “Our result was non-significant, but we had low power” says the same thing twice.

pwr.t.test(n = 4, d = d_paired$Cohens_d, sig.level = 0.05, type = "paired")

              n = 4
              d = 1.361371

How much higher is it than the unpaired 11%?

text:
The Whole Economics of the Study


Pairing does not just give a smaller p-value — it changes what the study needed to begin with.

pwr.t.test(
  d = d_paired$Cohens_d,
  power = 0.80,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  type = "paired"
)


     Paired t test power calculation 

              n = 6.406838
              d = 1.361371
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number of *pairs*


7 trees, total — for 80% power, paired.




Design
Power at n = 4
Trees for 80% power




Unpaired
11%
44 per side (88 trees)


Paired
46%
7 total









Important



Same trees. Same needles. Same measurements.
Pairing takes this study from needing 88 trees (44 per side) to needing 7 trees. That is not a statistical trick — it is what respecting the design of your own experiment is worth.

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text: Part 9 · Error Bars, Revisited

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
section: SD, SE, and CI Answer Different Questions
text:
SD, SE, and CI Answer Different Questions



Standard deviation (SD) — spread of the raw data
Standard error (SE) — precision of the mean, SD / sqrt(n)
95% confidence interval (CI) — plausible range for the true mean, built from SE and the t-distribution

summary_stats() gives you all three from one call. A large sample doesn’t shrink SD — it shrinks SE and the CI, because you’re now estimating the mean more precisely, not describing less variable lizards.

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text: Part 10 · Pseudoreplication

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text:
Sampling and Pseudoreplication


Pseudoreplication occurs when measurements that are not independent are analyzed as if they were.

Measuring the same individual multiple times
Treating multiple fish from the same tank as independent
Using multiple data points from a single site

It results in underestimated standard errors and inflated Type I error rates — it makes a study look more precise, and more significant, than it actually is.







Important



We have been doing this all along
Our pine needle data has 64 rows. Analyzed as 64 independent needles it would look like a large, well-powered study. Analyzed honestly — 4 trees — it has 11% power unpaired, 46% paired.
Pseudoreplication would not have made the study better. It would only have made us believe it was.

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text: Aside · The 0.05 Debate

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
section: A Number That Was Always Meant to Be a Guideline
text:
A Number That Was Always Meant to Be a Guideline



“If p is between 0.1 and 0.9 there is certainly no reason to suspect the hypothesis tested. If it is below 0.02 it is strongly indicated that the hypothesis fails to account for the whole of the facts. We shall not often be astray if we draw a conventional line at .05 …”

— R.A. Fisher, on the p-value as an informal measure of discrepancy between data and H₀
Fisher proposed 0.05 as a rough guideline, not a bright line. Modern critiques of “statistical significance” as a binary pass/fail argue power and effect size deserve at least as much attention as whether p cleared 0.05.




Screenshot of a Nature comment article titled ‘Scientists rise up against statistical significance,’ by Valentin Amrhein, Sander Greenland, Blake McShane and 800+ signatories, illustrated with a cartoon of two scientists shelving a book labeled ‘Statistical Significance’ in a dusty cabinet of retired scientific relics like phlogiston and spontaneous generation, symbolizing calls to retire strict significance thresholds.

title: Lecture: Power and Type I & II Error
text:
Summary and Key Takeaways


Key concepts covered:

Type I (α) and Type II (β) error — the two ways a decision can be wrong; power = 1 − β
Power rises with larger n, larger effect size, lower variability, and higher α
A priori power (before data collection) tells you the n a study needs — the most useful use of this whole toolkit
Retrospective power tells you what your finished study could have detected — useful for planning the next one, not for excusing a null result



The pwr package generalizes power analysis, and pwr.t2n.test() handles unequal group sizes directly
Pairing a design can be worth far more than adding raw sample size
SD, SE, and CI answer three different questions about the same data
Pseudoreplication inflates apparent precision by treating non-independent measurements as independent replicates







Note



📖 References
Gotelli & Ellison, Ch. 4 — Framing and Testing Hypotheses (errors and power); Whitlock & Schluter, Ch. 6 — Hypothesis Testing, and Ch. 14 — Designing Experiments (sample size and power planning).

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Probability and Statistical Inference


Today we build one chain of reasoning, start to finish:

Real data have a distribution
Any normal distribution can be standardized to standard normal distribution
Area under that curve is probability
All of it assumes normality — so we check
From one fish to the mean: SD, SE, confidence intervals
When σ is unknown we use the t-distribution the safe alternative
Putting a number on evidence: hypothesis tests

📥 Download the data

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: Part 1 · From data to a distribution
text: Part 1 · From data to a distribution

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
The normal distribution


A probability distribution spreads probability across the possible outcomes — but how depends on the data:

Discrete (a die): each outcome has its own probability, P(4) = 1/6
Continuous (fish length): any exact value has probability zero. Probability lives in ranges, as area under the curve

The curve’s height is a density — probability per mm, not a probability. Density × width ≈ probability.

Density is a rate, so it is not capped at 1: dnorm(0, sd = 0.1) = 3.989. Nothing is 399% likely — proof that height ≠ probability.

The normal is the density we lean on: symmetric, fixed by μ (where it sits) and σ (how wide), total area 1.
Lake I3: μ ≈ 265.6 mm, σ ≈ 28.3 mm — our curve. Every dataset has its own.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Why we standardize


There is a different normal curve for every μ and σ. Nobody can tabulate infinitely many curves.
So we rescale every value into the same units — standard deviations from the mean:
\(z = \frac{x_i - \mu}{\sigma}\)

\(x_i\) = the observation
\(μ\) = mean of the distribution
\(σ\) = standard deviation of the distribution

Subtracting μ slides the curve to centre 0. Dividing by σ squeezes it to width 1.
The result is the standard normal distribution: μ = 0, σ = 1. One curve. One table.

A z-score is not a new measurement. It is the same fish, expressed as “how many SDs from average.”

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Practice 1 · Standardize the I3 fish






Tip


z = (length − mean) / standard deviation

i3_mean <- mean(i3_df$length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
i3_sd   <- sd(i3_df$length_mm,   na.rm = TRUE)

i3_df <- i3_df %>%
  mutate(z_score = (length_mm - i3_mean) / i3_sd)

i3_df %>%
  select(lake, length_mm, z_score) %>%
  head(4)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  lake  length_mm z_score
  <chr>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 I3          266  0.0139
2 I3          290  0.862 
3 I3          262 -0.127 
4 I3          275  0.332 


A fish of 266 mm gets z = 0. A fish one SD above average gets z = 1.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: The same fish, two sets of units
text:
The same fish, two sets of units


Standardizing changes the axis labels, not the shape.

Top: millimetres, centred near 266
Bottom: z, centred at 0
Same fish, same bars, same skew — only the ruler changed

That matters: standardizing does not make non-normal data normal. It only puts it on a common ruler. We come back to this in Part 3.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: Part 2 · Area under the curve is probability
text: Part 2 · Area under the curve is probability

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
The 68–95–99.7 rule


Because the standard normal is one fixed curve, its areas are fixed too:

68% of the curve within ±1σ
95% within ±1.96σ — “±2” is the rule of thumb, 1.96 is the number
99.7% within ±3σ

Our I3 fish, counted directly:

within_1sd <- mean(abs(i3_df$z_score) <= 1, na.rm = TRUE)
round_half_up(100 * within_1sd, 1)   # percent within 1 SD

[1] 81.8


Theory says 68%. We get 81.8%.
Hold that gap. It is the whole point of Part 3.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: pnorm, qnorm, dnorm — which is which
text:
pnorm, qnorm, dnorm — which is which


All three describe the same standard normal curve. They differ in what you hand them and what you get back.



Function
You give it
You get back




pnorm(z)
a z
the area to the left of it


qnorm(p)
an area
the z that cuts it off


dnorm(z)
a z
the height of the curve




p = probability, q = quantile — and they are inverses
dnorm is the curve’s height, used to draw it. A height is not a probability — only area is


pnorm(1.96)     # area left of 1.96

[1] 0.9750021

qnorm(0.975)    # the z that puts 97.5% on its left

[1] 1.959964

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Reading the z-table


The z-table is pnorm() printed on paper: cumulative area to the LEFT of z.

Find the ones and tenths of z down the left column
Find the hundredths across the top
Read the area where they meet

One table works for every dataset — because every dataset gets standardized first. (Contrast the t-table later, which needs a row for each sample size.)

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: Worked example — how rare is a 300 mm grayling?
text:
Worked example — how rare is a 300 mm grayling?


Step 1 — standardize.
\(z = \frac{300 - 265.61}{28.3} = 1.22\)
Step 2 — look it up. Row 1.2, column 0.02 → 0.8888
Step 3 — read it as biology.

88.9% of I3 fish are shorter than 300 mm
100 − 88.9 = 11.1% are longer

Catch 100 fish in I3 and about 11 should beat 300 mm.
Same answer, in R — no table:

z_fish <- (300 - i3_mean) / i3_sd
round_half_up(z_fish, 2)              # 1.22, matches the table

[1] 1.22

round_half_up(100 * (1 - pnorm(z_fish)), 1)   # % longer than 300 mm

[1] 11.2

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Running it backwards — qnorm


The table question can be asked the other way round, and in fisheries it usually is:

We had a length and wanted a probability. Now we have a probability and want a length.

“How big must a grayling be to land in the top 5%?” — the trophy-fish question, and the size-limit question.

qnorm(0.95) = 1.645 — the z with 5% above it
Back to millimetres: \(x = \mu + z\sigma\)


z_top5 <- qnorm(0.95)
length_top5 <- i3_mean + z_top5 * i3_sd
round_half_up(length_top5, 1)   # mm

[1] 312.2


Only 5% of I3 fish should exceed 312.2 mm.
Every number on this slide assumed the fish are normal. Do we know that?

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text: Part 3 · Checking the assumption

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Shapiro-Wilk — and its backwards logic


The Shapiro-Wilk test asks one question, and its hypotheses run opposite to what you expect:

H₀: the data ARE normal
Hₐ: the data are NOT normal

So:

p > 0.05 → no evidence against normal → carry on
p < 0.05 → evidence of non-normality → be careful


A small p-value here is bad news, not a result. That reversal is why this test gets misread every semester.

Two cautions: with large n it flags departures too small to matter; with small n it misses ones that matter. Always read the Q-Q plot too — points on the line = normal.


shapiro.test(i3_df$length_mm)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  i3_df$length_mm
W = 0.91051, p-value = 0.0001623

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
So how wrong were we?


p = 0.0002. The I3 fish are not normal. Every probability in Part 2 assumed they were — so let’s audit them against the fish themselves.









normal theory
actual data




within ±1 SD
68%
81.8%


95th percentile
312.2 mm
310 mm


P(fish > 300 mm)
11.2%
7.6%



The centre is fine. The tail is off by a third.
And the tail is exactly where inference lives — critical values, rejection regions, p-values all sit out in the tails.
This is why we check assumptions before trusting a p-value.


# theory vs. the actual fish, out in the tail
round_half_up(100 * (1 - pnorm(300, i3_mean, i3_sd)), 1)

[1] 11.2

round_half_up(100 * mean(i3_df$length_mm > 300, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

[1] 7.6

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: Part 4 · From one fish to the mean
text: Part 4 · From one fish to the mean

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: SD and SE answer different questions
text:
SD and SE answer different questions


Everything so far described individual fish. Science usually asks about the mean. Those need different spreads.



Question
Spread




How long is a single fish?
SD (s)


Where is the population mean?
SE (s/√n)




Fish spread is however wide the fish are — more fish does not narrow it
Mean spread shrinks as n grows — averages are steadier than individuals
“5% of fish exceed 312.2 mm” uses SD; “the mean is near 265.6” uses SE

Using SE where you meant SD makes your interval √n times too narrow.


i3_n  <- sum(!is.na(i3_df$length_mm))
i3_se <- i3_sd / sqrt(i3_n)

tibble(
  n  = i3_n,
  SD = round_half_up(i3_sd, 1),
  SE = round_half_up(i3_se, 1)
)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
      n    SD    SE
  <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1    66  28.3   3.5

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: What a confidence interval actually is
text:
What a confidence interval actually is


We have one sample and one mean, 265.6 mm. The true μ is some other number we will never see. A confidence interval is our honest statement of how close we probably are.
The recipe: \(\bar{y} \pm (\text{critical value}) \times SE\)
What “95%” means: repeat the whole study many times, build an interval each time, and 95% of those intervals will contain μ. The figure shows 20 such studies — one misses.






Warning


The interpretation everyone gets wrong
❌ “There is a 95% chance μ is in my interval.”
✅ “95% of intervals built this way capture μ.”
μ is a fixed number — it is not moving around. The interval is what is random. Yours either caught μ or it didn’t; you don’t get to know which.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: If we knew σ, we would use z
text:
If we knew σ, we would use z


When the population σ is genuinely known, the critical value comes straight off the standard normal:
\(CI = \bar{y} \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

1.96 because 95% of the standard normal lies within ±1.96
90% CI → 1.645 · 99% CI → 2.576 · all from qnorm()


qnorm(0.975)   # 95%

[1] 1.959964

qnorm(0.95)    # 90%

[1] 1.644854


Wider confidence costs a wider interval. You cannot be more certain and more precise at the same time — only a bigger n buys you both.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: But we never know σ — so z is too confident
text:
But we never know σ — so z is too confident


Look again at that formula. It needs σ, the population standard deviation. We have never once had it.
What we actually have is s, computed from our 66 fish. And s is itself an estimate — a different sample gives a different s.
Two sources of uncertainty, not one:

the mean wobbles from sample to sample
our estimate of the spread also wobbles

Using 1.96 accounts for the first and ignores the second. Intervals come out too narrow and we claim more precision than we earned.
Gosset hit exactly this at Guinness — tiny barley samples, σ never known. His fix: use a curve with fatter tails, so the critical value is bigger and the interval honest.
That curve is Student’s t.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
The t-distribution


Same bell shape as the normal, but heavier in the tails — that extra thickness is the price of estimating σ.

Shape set by degrees of freedom, df = n − 1
Small df → very heavy tails → large critical values
df grows → t creeps toward the normal
Past n ≈ 30 they agree to about two decimals — which is where the “n > 30” rule of thumb came from







Important


The rule that matters: whenever σ is estimated from the sample, use t — at any sample size. “n > 30, use z” is a convenience from the era of paper tables, not a statistical law. R uses t always.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Reading the t-table


\(CI = \bar{y} \pm t \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\)
Only the multiplier changed: t in place of 1.96.

Rows = degrees of freedom (n − 1)
Columns = probability, with two header rows: one-tail and two-tail
A CI is always two-tailed — it has two ends. Use the two-tail column

The bottom row (df = ∞) is 1.96: the t-table contains the z-table.

qt(0.975, df = 8)    # 95% CI, n = 9

[1] 2.306004

qt(0.975, df = 65)   # 95% CI, n = 66

[1] 1.997138

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: Worked CI — by table and by R
text:
Worked CI — by table and by R


A sample of 9 fish: mean = 272.8, s = 37.81

df = 9 − 1 = 8
Two-tail 0.05 column, row 8 → t = 2.306
SE = 37.81 / √9 = 12.60
Margin = 2.306 × 12.60 = 29.06
CI = 272.8 ± 29.06 = 243.7 to 301.9 mm


“The 95% CI for mean length is 243.7–301.9 mm.”

Had we wrongly used 1.96, we’d have reported ±24.7 — an interval 15% too narrow, claiming precision we never had.

Tip

  <chr>       <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>

[1] 234.0564 283.7436
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text: Part 5 · Hypothesis testing

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
The logic


A confidence interval asks where is μ? A hypothesis test asks is μ equal to some specific value? Same machinery, different question.

H₀ — the boring claim: no effect, no difference
Hₐ — what we suspect instead
Assume H₀ is true and ask: how likely is data like ours?
p-value — probability of our result, or more extreme, if H₀ is true
α — how rare is rare enough, set before looking. Usually 0.05
Decide — p < α → reject H₀

\(t = \frac{\bar{y} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}\) — how many SEs is our mean from the claim?

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: One-tailed: all of α at one end
text:
One-tailed: all of α at one end


Use when the question has a direction: are these fish longer than 285 mm? A shorter result would not interest us — it goes with H₀.

H₀: μ ≤ 285 · Hₐ: μ > 285
n = 20, so df = 19
All 5% sits in the upper tail
t-table, one-tail 0.05, row 19 → t = 1.729

Reject H₀ only if our t exceeds +1.729.

qt(0.95, df = 19)     # one-tailed, α = 0.05

[1] 1.729133

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: Two-tailed: α split between both ends
text:
Two-tailed: α split between both ends


Use when either direction would matter: do these fish differ from 285 mm? Longer or shorter, we want to know.

H₀: μ = 285 · Hₐ: μ ≠ 285
Same df = 19, same total α = 0.05
But now 2.5% in each tail
t-table, two-tail 0.05, row 19 → t = 2.093


qt(0.975, df = 19)    # two-tailed, α = 0.05

[1] 2.093024








Important


Same α, same df, bigger critical value (2.093 > 1.729) — splitting α pushes each cutoff further out, so a two-tailed test is harder to pass.
Pick your tails from the question, before seeing the data. When in doubt, two-tailed — it is also R’s default.

Are I8 fish longer than I3 fish? Directional → one-tailed.

data:  length_mm by lake

alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group I3 and group I8 is less than 0

mean in group I3 mean in group I8

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
What a p-value is not


It is: the probability of data like ours if H₀ were true.
It is not:

the probability that H₀ is true
the probability the result is due to chance
a measure of how big the effect is

Small p means detectable, not large. With n = 168, a biologically meaningless 2 mm difference can return p = 10⁻¹⁶.
So, every time:

report p < 0.001, not p = 1.2e-16
report the effect size — the difference in millimetres
report the CI — it shows size and uncertainty in one line
significant ≠ important. That call is biology, not arithmetic

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Summary
The chain, end to end:

Data have a distribution — μ and σ describe a normal one
z = (x − μ)/σ collapses every normal curve onto one standard curve
Area under that curve is probability — pnorm for areas, qnorm for cutoffs
All of it assumes normality. Shapiro-Wilk plus a Q-Q plot; our fish failed, and the tail was off by a third
SD describes fish; SE = s/√n describes means. Never swap them
CI = ȳ ± t · SE — 95% of intervals built this way capture μ
σ is never known, so the multiplier is t, not 1.96 — fatter tails, wider interval, honest
A p-value is tail area under H₀. It measures detectability, never importance







Note


Up next — t-Tests, then Power and Error, where Type I/II errors and statistical power get the full treatment they need.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: Part 1 · From data to a distribution
text: Part 1 · From data to a distribution

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
The normal distribution


A probability distribution spreads probability across the possible outcomes — but how depends on the data:

Discrete (a die): each outcome has its own probability, P(4) = 1/6
Continuous (fish length): any exact value has probability zero. Probability lives in ranges, as area under the curve

The curve’s height is a density — probability per mm, not a probability. Density × width ≈ probability.

Density is a rate, so it is not capped at 1: dnorm(0, sd = 0.1) = 3.989. Nothing is 399% likely — proof that height ≠ probability.

The normal is the density we lean on: symmetric, fixed by μ (where it sits) and σ (how wide), total area 1.
Lake I3: μ ≈ 265.6 mm, σ ≈ 28.3 mm — our curve. Every dataset has its own.






Note



📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 10 — The Normal Distribution.
Gotelli & Ellison Ch. 2 — Random Variables and Probability Distributions.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Why we standardize


There is a different normal curve for every μ and σ. Nobody can tabulate infinitely many curves.
So we rescale every value into the same units — standard deviations from the mean:

\(z = \frac{x_i - \mu}{\sigma}\)

\(x_i\) = the observation
\(μ\) = mean of the distribution
\(σ\) = standard deviation of the distribution

Subtracting μ slides the curve to centre 0. Dividing by σ squeezes it to width 1.
The result is the standard normal distribution: μ = 0, σ = 1. One curve. One table.

A z-score is not a new measurement. It is the same fish, expressed as “how many SDs from average.”

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Practice 1 · Standardize the I3 fish






Tip



z = (length − mean) / standard deviation

i3_mean <- mean(i3_df$length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
i3_sd   <- sd(i3_df$length_mm,   na.rm = TRUE)

i3_df <- i3_df %>%
  mutate(z_score = (length_mm - i3_mean) / i3_sd)

i3_df %>%
  select(lake, length_mm, z_score) %>%
  head(4)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  lake  length_mm z_score
  <chr>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 I3          266  0.0139
2 I3          290  0.862 
3 I3          262 -0.127 
4 I3          275  0.332 


A fish of 266 mm gets z = 0. A fish one SD above average gets z = 1.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: The same fish, two sets of units
text:
The same fish, two sets of units


Standardizing changes the axis labels, not the shape.

Top: millimetres, centred near 266
Bottom: z, centred at 0
Same fish, same bars, same skew — only the ruler changed

That matters: standardizing does not make non-normal data normal. It only puts it on a common ruler. We come back to this in Part 3.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: Part 2 · Area under the curve is probability
text: Part 2 · Area under the curve is probability

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
The 68–95–99.7 rule


Because the standard normal is one fixed curve, its areas are fixed too:

68% of the curve within ±1σ
95% within ±1.96σ — “±2” is the rule of thumb, 1.96 is the number
99.7% within ±3σ

Our I3 fish, counted directly:

within_1sd <- mean(abs(i3_df$z_score) <= 1, na.rm = TRUE)
round_half_up(100 * within_1sd, 1)   # percent within 1 SD

[1] 81.8


Theory says 68%. We get 81.8%.
Hold that gap. It is the whole point of Part 3.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: pnorm, qnorm, dnorm — which is which
text:
pnorm, qnorm, dnorm — which is which


All three describe the same standard normal curve. They differ in what you hand them and what you get back.



Function
You give it
You get back




pnorm(z)
a z
the area to the left of it


qnorm(p)
an area
the z that cuts it off


dnorm(z)
a z
the height of the curve




p = probability, q = quantile — and they are inverses
dnorm is the curve’s height, used to draw it. A height is not a probability — only area is


pnorm(1.96)     # area left of 1.96

[1] 0.9750021

qnorm(0.975)    # the z that puts 97.5% on its left

[1] 1.959964

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Reading the z-table


The z-table is pnorm() printed on paper: cumulative area to the LEFT of z.

Find the ones and tenths of z down the left column
Find the hundredths across the top
Read the area where they meet

One table works for every dataset — because every dataset gets standardized first. (Contrast the t-table later, which needs a row for each sample size.)






Note



📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 10 — standardizing a value and reading the standard normal table.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: Worked example — how rare is a 300 mm grayling?
text:
Worked example — how rare is a 300 mm grayling?


Step 1 — standardize.
\(z = \frac{300 - 265.61}{28.3} = 1.22\)
Step 2 — look it up. Row 1.2, column 0.02 → 0.8888
Step 3 — read it as biology.

88.9% of I3 fish are shorter than 300 mm
100 − 88.9 = 11.1% are longer

Catch 100 fish in I3 and about 11 should beat 300 mm.
Same answer, in R — no table:

z_fish <- (300 - i3_mean) / i3_sd
round_half_up(z_fish, 2)              # 1.22, matches the table

[1] 1.22

round_half_up(100 * (1 - pnorm(z_fish)), 1)   # % longer than 300 mm

[1] 11.2

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Running it backwards — qnorm


The table question can be asked the other way round, and in fisheries it usually is:

We had a length and wanted a probability. Now we have a probability and want a length.

“How big must a grayling be to land in the top 5%?” — the trophy-fish question, and the size-limit question.

qnorm(0.95) = 1.645 — the z with 5% above it
Back to millimetres: \(x = \mu + z\sigma\)


z_top5 <- qnorm(0.95)
length_top5 <- i3_mean + z_top5 * i3_sd
round_half_up(length_top5, 1)   # mm

[1] 312.2


Only 5% of I3 fish should exceed 312.2 mm.
Every number on this slide assumed the fish are normal. Do we know that?

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text: Part 3 · Checking the assumption

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Shapiro-Wilk — and its backwards logic


The Shapiro-Wilk test asks one question, and its hypotheses run opposite to what you expect:

H₀: the data ARE normal
Hₐ: the data are NOT normal

So:

p > 0.05 → no evidence against normal → carry on
p < 0.05 → evidence of non-normality → be careful


A small p-value here is bad news, not a result. That reversal is why this test gets misread every semester.

Two cautions: with large n it flags departures too small to matter; with small n it misses ones that matter. Always read the Q-Q plot too — points on the line = normal.


shapiro.test(i3_df$length_mm)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  i3_df$length_mm
W = 0.91051, p-value = 0.0001623

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
So how wrong were we?


p = 0.0002. The I3 fish are not normal. Every probability in Part 2 assumed they were — so let’s audit them against the fish themselves.









normal theory
actual data




within ±1 SD
68%
81.8%


95th percentile
312.2 mm
310 mm


P(fish > 300 mm)
11.2%
7.6%



The centre is fine. The tail is off by a third.
And the tail is exactly where inference lives — critical values, rejection regions, p-values all sit out in the tails.
This is why we check assumptions before trusting a p-value.






Note



📖 Reference
Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 13 — Handling Violations of Assumptions.




# theory vs. the actual fish, out in the tail
round_half_up(100 * (1 - pnorm(300, i3_mean, i3_sd)), 1)

[1] 11.2

round_half_up(100 * mean(i3_df$length_mm > 300, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

[1] 7.6

section: Part 4 · From one fish to the mean
text: Part 4 · From one fish to the mean

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: SD and SE answer different questions
text:
SD and SE answer different questions


Everything so far described individual fish. Science usually asks about the mean. Those need different spreads.



Question
Spread




How long is a single fish?
SD (s)


Where is the population mean?
SE (s/√n)




Fish spread is however wide the fish are — more fish does not narrow it
Mean spread shrinks as n grows — averages are steadier than individuals
“5% of fish exceed 312.2 mm” uses SD; “the mean is near 265.6” uses SE

Using SE where you meant SD makes your interval √n times too narrow.


i3_n  <- sum(!is.na(i3_df$length_mm))
i3_se <- i3_sd / sqrt(i3_n)

tibble(
  n  = i3_n,
  SD = round_half_up(i3_sd, 1),
  SE = round_half_up(i3_se, 1)
)

# A tibble: 1 × 3
      n    SD    SE
  <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1    66  28.3   3.5

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: What a confidence interval actually is
text:
What a confidence interval actually is


We have one sample and one mean, 265.6 mm. The true μ is some other number we will never see. A confidence interval is our honest statement of how close we probably are.
The recipe: \(\bar{y} \pm (\text{critical value}) \times SE\)
What “95%” means: repeat the whole study many times, build an interval each time, and 95% of those intervals will contain μ. The figure shows 20 such studies — one misses.






Warning



The interpretation everyone gets wrong
❌ “There is a 95% chance μ is in my interval.”
✅ “95% of intervals built this way capture μ.”
μ is a fixed number — it is not moving around. The interval is what is random. Yours either caught μ or it didn’t; you don’t get to know which.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: If we knew σ, we would use z
text:
If we knew σ, we would use z


When the population σ is genuinely known, the critical value comes straight off the standard normal:

\(CI = \bar{y} \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

1.96 because 95% of the standard normal lies within ±1.96
90% CI → 1.645 · 99% CI → 2.576 · all from qnorm()


qnorm(0.975)   # 95%

[1] 1.959964

qnorm(0.95)    # 90%

[1] 1.644854


Wider confidence costs a wider interval. You cannot be more certain and more precise at the same time — only a bigger n buys you both.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
section: But we never know σ — so z is too confident
text:
But we never know σ — so z is too confident


Look again at that formula. It needs σ, the population standard deviation. We have never once had it.
What we actually have is s, computed from our 66 fish. And s is itself an estimate — a different sample gives a different s.
Two sources of uncertainty, not one:

the mean wobbles from sample to sample
our estimate of the spread also wobbles

Using 1.96 accounts for the first and ignores the second. Intervals come out too narrow and we claim more precision than we earned.
Gosset hit exactly this at Guinness — tiny barley samples, σ never known. His fix: use a curve with fatter tails, so the critical value is bigger and the interval honest.
That curve is Student’s t.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
The t-distribution


Same bell shape as the normal, but heavier in the tails — that extra thickness is the price of estimating σ.

Shape set by degrees of freedom, df = n − 1
Small df → very heavy tails → large critical values
df grows → t creeps toward the normal
Past n ≈ 30 they agree to about two decimals — which is where the “n > 30” rule of thumb came from







Important



The rule that matters: whenever σ is estimated from the sample, use t — at any sample size. “n > 30, use z” is a convenience from the era of paper tables, not a statistical law. R uses t always.

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Reading the t-table



\(CI = \bar{y} \pm t \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\)
Only the multiplier changed: t in place of 1.96.

Rows = degrees of freedom (n − 1)
Columns = probability, with two header rows: one-tail and two-tail
A CI is always two-tailed — it has two ends. Use the two-tail column

The bottom row (df = ∞) is 1.96: the t-table contains the z-table.

qt(0.975, df = 8)    # 95% CI, n = 9

[1] 2.306004

qt(0.975, df = 65)   # 95% CI, n = 66

[1] 1.997138

text:
What a p-value is not


It is: the probability of data like ours if H₀ were true.
It is not:

the probability that H₀ is true
the probability the result is due to chance
a measure of how big the effect is

Small p means detectable, not large. With n = 168, a biologically meaningless 2 mm difference can return p = 10⁻¹⁶.
So, every time:

report p < 0.001, not p = 1.2e-16
report the effect size — the difference in millimetres
report the CI — it shows size and uncertainty in one line
significant ≠ important. That call is biology, not arithmetic







Note



📖 Reference
Gotelli & Ellison Ch. 4 — “Statistical Significance and P-Values.”

title: Lecture: Probability & Inference
text:
Summary
The chain, end to end:

Data have a distribution — μ and σ describe a normal one
z = (x − μ)/σ collapses every normal curve onto one standard curve
Area under that curve is probability — pnorm for areas, qnorm for cutoffs
All of it assumes normality. Shapiro-Wilk plus a Q-Q plot; our fish failed, and the tail was off by a third
SD describes fish; SE = s/√n describes means. Never swap them
CI = ȳ ± t · SE — 95% of intervals built this way capture μ
σ is never known, so the multiplier is t, not 1.96 — fatter tails, wider interval, honest
A p-value is tail area under H₀. It measures detectability, never importance







Note



Up next — t-Tests, then Power and Error, where Type I/II errors and statistical power get the full treatment they need.
