title: Activity: Study Design & Sampling
text:
Worksheet: Reading a Design
📥 Knees data 📥 Tools script (.R) 📥 Script skeleton (.R)
The study. Wright & Czeisler (2002) asked whether bright light shone on the back of the knee could reset a person’s circadian clock, the way light in the eyes does. Each volunteer was randomly assigned to one of three treatments and their circadian rhythm shift was measured in hours (negative = the clock shifted later).

control — no light at all
knee — light on the back of the knee
eyes — light in the eyes

Why this study is here. knee is not really a third treatment. It is a placebo — it puts a person through the entire procedure (the apparatus, the room, the night, the measurement) while delivering light somewhere it should not work. Today you decide whether that arm earned its place.
This is Whitlock & Schluter, Example 15.1.



Part 1 · Setup and the data
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 1.1 · Setup and the data ───────────────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)
library(effectsize)

source("themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R")

knees_df <- read_csv("data/knees.csv")

knees_df



Part 2 · Read the design off the data
Before any test: how many replicates, at what level, and is it balanced?
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 2.1 · Read the design off the data ─────────────────────────────
count(knees_df, treatment)
✏️ Your turn: What is the experimental unit here, and is the design balanced?
unit = ____________________    balanced? ____________________
▶ Run this — the numbers for each group:
# ── Part 2.2 · Read the design off the data ─────────────────────────────
knees_df %>%
  group_by(treatment) %>%
  reframe(summary_stats(shift_h))
▶ Run this — look at the data before you test it:
# ── Part 2.3 · Read the design off the data ─────────────────────────────
ggplot(knees_df, aes(treatment, shift_h)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15)
✏️ Your turn: From the plot alone, which treatment looks different from the other two?
________________________



Part 3 · Did the placebo do anything?
This is the bias question: does going through the procedure, without useful light, shift the clock on its own?
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 3.1 · Did the placebo do anything? ─────────────────────────────
knees_df %>%
  filter(treatment %in% c("control", "knee")) %>%
  t.test(shift_h ~ treatment, data = .)
✏️ Your turn: p = __________ . Is there a procedural artifact in this experiment?
________________________



Part 4 · Did the real treatment do anything?
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 4.1 · Did the real treatment do anything? ──────────────────────
knees_df %>%
  filter(treatment %in% c("control", "eyes")) %>%
  t.test(shift_h ~ treatment, data = .)
▶ Run this — how big is it?
# ── Part 4.2 · Did the real treatment do anything? ──────────────────────
knees_df %>%
  filter(treatment %in% c("control", "eyes")) %>%
  cohens_d(shift_h ~ treatment, data = .)
✏️ Your turn: p = __________ , d = __________ .






Note



Two comparisons, both decided in advance
We ran two tests against the same control rather than one test across all three groups. That is legitimate here because we chose both comparisons before looking — each one answers a specific design question. Three groups at once is a one-way ANOVA, which is Week 8.





Part 5 · What the design bought
✏️ Your turn: In the sponge experiment from lecture, the sham control (foam) did differ from the bare control, and the real treatment added nothing. Here the result came out the other way around. One sentence: what would you have concluded in this study if the knee arm had never been run?
________________________________________________________






Tip



🚀 If you finish early: This design is unbalanced (8, 7, 7). Work out how much precision that costs: compare the standard error of the control mean with what it would be if all 22 subjects had been split evenly into three groups of about 7.3.
# ── Part 5.1 · What the design bought (bonus) ───────────────────────────
# Write your code in the R script:





Part 6 · The figure you hand in
This is the only plot that gets labels, a theme and a title — because this is the one being graded on presentation.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 6.1 · The figure you hand in ───────────────────────────────────
knees_summary <- knees_df %>%
  group_by(treatment) %>%
  reframe(summary_stats(shift_h))

final_plot <- ggplot(knees_summary, aes(treatment, mean)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey70", width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.15) +
  labs(
    title = "Circadian shift by light treatment",
    subtitle = "Mean ± 1 SE; light on the knee behaves like no light at all",
    x = "Light treatment",
    y = "Circadian shift (hours)"
  ) +
  theme_regular(base_size = 12)

final_plot

ggsave(
  "figures/knees_figure.pdf",
  plot   = final_plot,
  width  = 6,
  height = 4,
  units  = "in"
)
✏️ Your turn: Open the PDF and check the axis labels are readable before you submit it.



Review and checkpoint
At this point you can:

State the experimental unit and say whether a design is balanced
Explain what a placebo or sham control is for
Test whether a procedural artifact exists, and interpret the answer either way
Say why the same test can support opposite conclusions in two different designs
Export a labelled, themed figure to PDF







Note



📤 What to turn in

09_study_design_sampling.R
figures/knees_figure.pdf
This worksheet, with your written answers






Homework
Homework 5 — Study Design & Sampling: Finding the Real Replicate
1022 mangrove periwinkles from 18 sites, nine on each side of the tropical Atlantic, analysed twice: once with the snail as the replicate and once with the site as the replicate. The comparison is the same both times; the answer is not. The homework is about deciding which of those two analyses you are entitled to report.
Data: littoraria.csv — Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics, Chapter 12 archive; originally Merkt & Ellison (1998), Malacologia 40(1–2): 279–295.

text:
1.1 · Setup
Download the tools script from the button at the top. In your project folder, make a new folder called themes_functions and save the file into it, so the path is themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R.
That is a different folder from scripts/ — scripts/ holds the code you write, themes_functions/ holds tools you source() and do not edit.
One source() line then gives you two things you will use for the rest of the semester:

theme_regular() — the publication theme from the Graphing lecture

title: Activity: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
1.4 · Average out the pseudoreplication
The 8 needles from one side of one tree are pseudoreplicates — they are not 8 independent measurements, they are 8 looks at the same tree side. Average them so each tree side is one data point.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 1.4 · Average out pseudoreplication ────────────────────────────
p_df <- pine_df %>%
  group_by(team, side) %>%
  summarise(needle_length_mm = mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

p_df

⚠️ Watch out! 64 rows became 8. That is not data loss — it is the correct sample size. We measured 8 needles per side, but only 4 trees.

✏️ Your turn: What is our true sample unit here — needles? branches? trees? tree sides? Why does that matter for the rest of this worksheet?

⚠️ Watch out! Choosing the tail after looking at your means is not a one-tailed test. It is a two-tailed test with the p-value secretly halved, and it is one of the most common ways people accidentally cheat. Pick the direction from the biology, before you collect data, or use two-tailed.







Tip



🚀 If you finish early: A one-tailed test is defensible when a result in the opposite direction would lead to the same action as no result at all — a drug that harms patients and a drug that does nothing are both “do not approve.” For our pine needles, is “sunny is longer” and “shady is longer” both interesting biology? So which should we use?

"A two-tailed, two-sample t-test at alpha = 0.05 showed __________

____________________________________________________________________

t(______) = ________, p = ________."






Tip



🚀 If you finish early — compute the t-statistic by hand and confirm it matches t.test():
\[t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}}\]
# ── Part 3.6 · Two-sample t by hand ─────────────────────────────────────
sunny_df <- p_df %>% filter(side == "sunny")   # shady_df is from Part 2.1

n1 <- length(shady_df$needle_length_mm)
n2 <- length(sunny_df$needle_length_mm)
s1 <- sd(shady_df$needle_length_mm)
s2 <- sd(sunny_df$needle_length_mm)

sp <- sqrt(((n1 - 1) * s1^2 + (n2 - 1) * s2^2) / (n1 + n2 - 2))

(mean(shady_df$needle_length_mm) - mean(sunny_df$needle_length_mm)) /
  (sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2))
Look at the denominator of sp: n1 + n2 - 2. That is the degrees of freedom. df is not a rule to memorise — it is whatever you divided by.

title: Activity: T-Tests: One, Two, Paired
text:
4.2 · Reshape and run the test
t.test() needs the two sides side by side, one row per tree.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 4.2 · Paired t-test ────────────────────────────────────────────
p_wide_df <- p_df %>%

title: Homework 10 — ANCOVA
text:
2.1 ANCOVA Model Statement






ImportantModel Specification



Type of Analysis: Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA)
Model Equation: pulse_rate = β₀ + β₁(temperature) + β₂(species) + β₃(temperature × species) + ε
Where: - pulse_rate = chirp rate (response variable) - β₀ = intercept for reference species - β₁ = slope for temperature effect in reference species - β₂ = difference in intercept between species - β₃ = difference in slope between species (interaction term) - ε = random error term
Hypotheses Being Tested:

Main effect of temperature: H₀: β₁ = 0 vs H₁: β₁ ≠ 0
Main effect of species: H₀: β₂ = 0 vs H₁: β₂ ≠ 0

Interaction effect: H₀: β₃ = 0 vs H₁: β₃ ≠ 0

ANCOVA Assumptions: 1. Independence of observations 2. Normality of residuals 3. Homogeneity of variance (homoscedasticity) 4. Linear relationship between covariate and response 5. Homogeneity of regression slopes (if no interaction)

title: Homework 9 — Linear Mixed Models
text:
Data Description
The dataset contains growth measurements from a common garden experiment where young-of-year (YOY) rusty crayfish from native (Ohio) and invasive (Wisconsin) populations were grown in enclosures in three northern Wisconsin lakes during summer 2011. The hierarchical structure includes individual crayfish nested within lakes.
Key variables:

- range: Population origin (Native vs Invasive)
- fixed effect - lake: Lake location (Big, High, Papoose)
- random effect - growth_per_day: Daily growth rate (mm/day)
- response variable - initial_length: Starting length (mm)
- final_length: Ending length (mm)
- days: Duration of experiment

title: Homework 9 — Linear Mixed Models
text:
2.1 Analysis Type and Model
Type of Analysis: Linear Mixed Effects Model (Hierarchical/Nested Design)
Model Equation: Growth Rate_ij = β₀ + β₁(Range_i) + u_j + ε_ij
Where:

- Growth Rate_ij = daily growth rate for individual i in lake j
- β₀ = fixed intercept (overall mean)
- β₁ = fixed effect of range (Native vs Invasive)
- u_j ~ N(0, σ²_lake) = random effect of lake j
- ε_ij ~ N(0, σ²_error) = residual error for individual i in lake j

Hypotheses:

Fixed Effect

- Range:

- H₀: β₁ = 0 (no difference in growth between ranges)
- H₁: β₁ ≠ 0 (difference exists between ranges)


Random Effect

- Lake: - Accounts for correlation within lakes and lake-to-lake variability


Variables:

- Response: growth_per_day (continuous, mm/day)
- Fixed Effect: range (categorical, 2 levels: Native, Invasive)
- Random Effect: lake (categorical, 3 levels: Big, High, Papoose)
- Level 1: Individual crayfish (n = 84)
- Level 2: Lakes (n = 3)

Biological Rationale: Individual crayfish within the same lake are likely to be more similar to each other than to crayfish in different lakes due to shared environmental conditions. The mixed effects model accounts for this hierarchical structure while testing for range differences.

title: Homework 5 — Study Design & Sampling
text:
Worksheet: Finding the Real Replicate
📥 Littoraria data 📥 Tools script (.R) 📥 Script skeleton (.R)






Note📚 Where these data come from



Book source: Gotelli & Ellison, A Primer of Ecological Statistics (2nd ed.) — the Chapter 12 data archive, file FullLittorariaData.txt.
Original study: Merkt, R.E. & Ellison, A.M. (1998). Geographic and habitat-specific morphological variation of Littoraria (Littorinopsis) angulifera (Lamarck, 1822). Malacologia 40(1–2): 279–295.
What we changed: whitespace-delimited text converted to CSV, columns renamed (shell_breadth_mm, shell_height_mm, aperture_length_mm), and coast coded as East Atlantic / West Atlantic. All 1022 snails and 18 sites are the originals.


The study. Littoraria angulifera is a mangrove periwinkle found on both sides of the tropical Atlantic. Gotelli & Ellison’s dataset holds shell measurements from 1022 snails collected at 18 sites — nine on the East Atlantic coast of Africa, nine on the West Atlantic coast of the Americas.
The question. Are West Atlantic snails bigger than East Atlantic snails?
In class you took a small, tidy, balanced experiment and asked whether one of its treatment arms earned its place. This is the same workflow on a dataset that is none of those things — 1022 rows, wildly uneven sampling, and nobody assigned anything to anything. One decision in Part 2 determines whether you get the right answer, and the data will not warn you if you get it wrong.
Columns: site, coast, latitude, longitude, shell_breadth_mm, shell_height_mm, aperture_length_mm.



Part 1 · Setup and the data
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 1.1 · Setup and the data ───────────────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)

source("themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R")

snail_df <- read_csv("data/littoraria.csv")

snail_df



Part 2 · Read the design off the data
In class this was one count() call and the answer was obvious. Here it is not.
▶ Run this — how many snails per coast?
# ── Part 2.1 · Read the design off the data ─────────────────────────────
count(snail_df, coast)
▶ Run this — how many snails per site?
# ── Part 2.2 · Read the design off the data ─────────────────────────────
count(snail_df, coast, site)
✏️ Your turn: Look at the two tables. There are two candidate experimental units in this dataset. Name both, and say how many replicates each one gives you.
Candidate 1: ____________________   n = ______
Candidate 2: ____________________   n = ______
✏️ Your turn: Which one is the right replicate for the question “are West Atlantic snails bigger than East Atlantic snails?” Why? (One sentence. Think about what varies between coasts and what varies within a site.)
________________________________________________________
✏️ Your turn: One of the two levels is badly unbalanced and the other is perfectly balanced. Which is which?
________________________



Part 3 · The analysis almost everyone runs first
▶ Run this — every snail treated as an independent replicate:
# ── Part 3.1 · The analysis almost everyone runs first ──────────────────
t.test(shell_breadth_mm ~ coast, data = snail_df)
✏️ Your turn: p = __________ . Write down the two group means.
________________________



Part 4 · The analysis the design actually calls for
▶ Run this — collapse to one number per site first, then test:
# ── Part 4.1 · The analysis the design actually calls for ───────────────
site_df <- snail_df %>%
  group_by(coast, site) %>%
  summarise(mean_breadth = mean(shell_breadth_mm), n_snails = n(), .groups = "drop")

site_df
✏️ Your turn: Write the code for the t-test on site_df, comparing mean_breadth between coasts.
# ── Part 4.2 · The analysis the design actually calls for ───────────────
# Write your code in the R script:
✏️ Your turn: p = __________ . Do the two analyses agree?
________________________



Part 5 · Why they disagree
▶ Run this — the standard error at each level:
# ── Part 5.1 · Why they disagree ────────────────────────────────────────
snail_df %>%
  group_by(coast) %>%
  reframe(summary_stats(shell_breadth_mm))

site_df %>%
  group_by(coast) %>%
  reframe(summary_stats(mean_breadth))
✏️ Your turn: Compare the two se columns. Roughly how many times larger is the site-level standard error?
________________________
✏️ Your turn: The snail-level test says the coasts differ. The site-level test does not. Neither test is broken — they are answering different questions. What question does each one actually answer?
Snail-level test answers: _______________________________
Site-level test answers:  _______________________________
✏️ Your turn: Florida contributes 301 snails; Liberia contributes 3. In the snail-level analysis, how much does Florida count relative to Liberia? In the site-level analysis?
________________________________________________________



Part 6 · The twist
In class, the placebo arm existed and you got to check whether it mattered. Here, something is missing that you cannot add.
✏️ Your turn: This is a natural experiment — nobody assigned snails to coasts. Name one confounding variable that differs between the East and West Atlantic and could plausibly drive shell size, and say which column in this dataset you could use to partly adjust for it.
Confounder: ____________________  Column: ____________________
✏️ Your turn: From lecture: would controlling for that variable be treating it as a confounder or as a mediator? Does it change what you should do?
________________________________________________________






Tip



🚀 If you finish early: site_df has an n_snails column. A site mean built from 301 snails is a far more precise estimate than one built from 3, yet the site-level t-test treats them as equally reliable. Look up weights = in ?lm and run a weighted version. Does weighting by n_snails move the p-value toward the snail-level answer or the site-level one, and does that seem right to you?
# ── Part 6.1 · The twist (bonus) ────────────────────────────────────────
# Write your code in the R script:





Part 7 · The figure you hand in
The only plot with labels, a theme and a title. Show both levels at once so the reader can see where the uncertainty actually lives.
▶ Run this:
# ── Part 7.1 · The figure you hand in ───────────────────────────────────
final_plot <- ggplot(site_df, aes(coast, mean_breadth)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(size = n_snails), width = 0.12, alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.4, linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Shell breadth of Littoraria angulifera by coast",
    subtitle = "One point per site (n = 9 per coast); point size is snails sampled",
    x = "Coast",
    y = "Mean shell breadth (mm)",
    size = "Snails"
  ) +
  theme_regular(base_size = 12)

final_plot

ggsave(
  "figures/littoraria_figure.pdf",
  plot   = final_plot,
  width  = 6,
  height = 4,
  units  = "in"
)

text:
Semester - Fall 2025
Instructor: Bill Perry




When: Monday and Wednesday 14:00 - 15:50

Where: We will see
Assistant: someone please


How: Mostly working through the ideas in the PowerPoint slides using code some of which is prewritten
Assistant email: someone@d.umn.edu


Required materials: The textbook and a laptop and tenacity
Office hours: TBD and by appointment or walk in





Welcome to Ecological Statistics! This is a practical course that will introduce you to the topics of experimental design, hypothesis testing, data analysis and visualization in the ecological sciences context. The goal of the course is to enable you to interpret statistical methods and results in the published literature, carry out your own data analyses and conduct a productive conversation with a statistician. We will learn about common statistical approaches in ecology and use the R statistical computing environment to get practice implementing these approaches. Additionally, this course will provide opportunities for students to practice scientific writing skills.



Learn some useful data skills nd organizaiton and statistical methods and R skills.



The course will be taught in a combined lecture and computer lab format with mostly hands on activities assuming you have read the materials. Some of our meetings will take a primarily lecture and discussion format, others a primarily computer lab format, but most will have elements of both. Lecture portions will be dedicated to taking up homework questions, going over course concepts and discussing examples. Computer laboratory elements will be dedicated to using the R statistical computing package for data analysis and visualization.
Materials such as lecture slides, computer labs, homework, and assignments will be distributed through the course Canvas site or on the website. The course will mostly be based on the textbook The Analysis of Biological Data (3rd Edition) Experimental Design and Data Analysis for Biologists (1st edition) by Michael C. Whitlock and Dolph Schluter. The text is required and we can talk about how to get it. Other textbooks and resources that you may find of use are:

The R Book (1st or 2nd edition) by MJ Crawley. Highly recommended as an all-around reference book.
A Primer of Ecological Statistics (1st or 2nd edition) by NJ Gotelli and AM Ellison.
Biostatistical Analysis (4th or 5th edition) by JH Zar.
Handbook of Biological Statistics by JH McDonald (online at http://www.biostathandbook.com/).

title: Syllabus
text: Welcome to Ecological Statistics! This is a practical course that will introduce you to the topics of experimental design, hypothesis testing, data analysis and visualization in the ecological sciences context. The goal of the course is to enable you to interpret statistical methods and results in the published literature, carry out your own data analyses and conduct a productive conversation with a statistician. We will learn about common statistical approaches in ecology and use the R statistical computing environment to get practice implementing these approaches. Additionally, this course will provide opportunities for students to practice scientific writing skills.

title: Syllabus
text: Learn some useful data skills nd organizaiton and statistical methods and R skills.

title: Syllabus
text:
The course will be taught in a combined lecture and computer lab format with mostly hands on activities assuming you have read the materials. Some of our meetings will take a primarily lecture and discussion format, others a primarily computer lab format, but most will have elements of both. Lecture portions will be dedicated to taking up homework questions, going over course concepts and discussing examples. Computer laboratory elements will be dedicated to using the R statistical computing package for data analysis and visualization.
Materials such as lecture slides, computer labs, homework, and assignments will be distributed through the course Canvas site or on the website. The course will mostly be based on the textbook The Analysis of Biological Data (3rd Edition) Experimental Design and Data Analysis for Biologists (1st edition) by Michael C. Whitlock and Dolph Schluter. The text is required and we can talk about how to get it. Other textbooks and resources that you may find of use are:

The R Book (1st or 2nd edition) by MJ Crawley. Highly recommended as an all-around reference book.
A Primer of Ecological Statistics (1st or 2nd edition) by NJ Gotelli and AM Ellison.
